docs.title: Friday, August 14, 2026
docs.text: Friday, August 14, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Friday, August 14th. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Wall Street's two straight record closes give way to a quiet Friday tape, and China's own July data just confirmed both its export and consumption legs are cooling at once. But the real thread today is physical, not financial — the AI buildout keeps running into land, copper and steel. A 550-foot easement dispute is stranding a full gigawatt of finished Colorado wind, and Texas's own demand forecaster says most of the large loads chasing power there won't actually have it by 2030. That's the same day Bloomberg flags Texas's own governor cooling on the data-center deals he was championing less than a year ago. And in the Philippines, a fresh graft number just landed — twenty-four billion pesos, straight out of the public-works budget. Plenty to get through. Let's start with the world. Headlines Iran's joint military command declared yesterday that no vessel can transit the Strait of Hormuz without Tehran's permission — flatly rejecting Trump's claim of "total control" over the strait. Senior political-military official Rasoul Sanaei-Rad went further, saying Iran won't actually reopen the strait until the US meets its commitments under last month's interim deal. Shipping traffic through Hormuz is reportedly sitting at three-month lows. That's a genuinely different posture from where we left this story — Tehran isn't just stalling on reparations anymore, it's publicly contesting the basic premise that the US has any control there at all. Which matters beyond the optics — it's the same oil-price uncertainty that's now showing up directly in the Philippines peso, which we'll get to. Second story — US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, a longtime settlement-movement ally, called an Israeli settler siege in the West Bank town of Qusra an "act of terror" yesterday. Settlers besieged three Palestinian homes — including one belonging to a US citizen — trapping around fifteen people, two of them children, without power or water for days. Israel's military dismantled two outposts and detained one Israeli in response. The word choice is the story here. American officials essentially never apply "terrorist" to settlers — that language is reserved for the other side. Coming from Huckabee specifically, of all people, it's a real signal. Worth watching whether that language holds or gets walked back in the next news cycle. Either way, it's a notable crack in a normally very disciplined US line. And it lands at an awkward moment for Washington generally — an administration trying to hold together both a fragile Gaza framework and a stalled Hormuz track can't really afford its own ambassador freelancing on language this loaded, even in service of a legitimate rebuke. Two stories, same underlying pattern really — actors testing exactly how far rhetoric can move before it forces an actual policy response. Market Overview On the tape — Thursday was record number two in a row. S&P 500 closed at 7,798.99, up 0.65%, its first close above 7,800. Nasdaq 26,803.03, up 0.81%, led by Meta, Micron and Netflix. Dow barely moved, up 0.13% to 53,839.99. Russell 2000 up 0.24% to 3,052.85. Ten-year sitting at 4.68% — that print's actually two days stale, nothing fresher available this morning, so take it as a marker, not gospel. Oil's flat — Brent 87.18, up just 0.13%. WTI around 81.30, essentially unchanged. Gold down slightly, 4,407.50, off 0.29% — no safe-haven bid despite the Hormuz rhetoric. Today's tape looks genuinely quiet after that — Europe's mixed, FTSE down 0.3%, CAC flat, DAX actually up half a percent bucking the trend. Asia's mixed too, and US futures are little-changed heading in. No fresh catalyst overnight — Thursday's CPI-driven record run is still the story propping up sentiment. Today's just digestion. Worth flagging the stale ten-year print again, because it matters for how you read today — if yields actually moved meaningfully since Wednesday, this calm surface could be hiding more than it's showing. We'll know for certain by Monday. Until then, treat today as a hold-your-breath session — nothing's forcing a move either way, and that's exactly the kind of tape where a single surprise headline does outsized damage. U.S. Business Two AI-infrastructure earnings landed Thursday and went in completely opposite directions. Super Micro rallied more than 6% on a blowout guide — adjusted EPS of 1.01 to 1.10 dollars against a 76-cent consensus, revenue guide of 14.5 to 15.5 billion. Cerebras went the other way, down 14% after Q2 revenue of 180 million missed the 194 million estimate. Same AI-datacenter trade, same week, completely different verdict — the pattern we've tracked all summer on hyperscaler earnings, just one tier down the supply chain now. Second story — Thoma Bravo is taking insurance platform Accelerant Holdings private, 20.25 dollars a share cash, a 49% premium to Wednesday's close. Deal's worth more than 4 billion. Largest holder Altamont Capital, which controls about 82% of the vote, has already agreed to support it, so this isn't speculative — expected to close in the first half of 2027. Another name on a take-private list that's gotten genuinely long this year. Once a board and a controlling shareholder are aligned like this, the stock just trades to the deal price and stops reacting to anything else. Two very different sectors, same underlying signal — capital's getting more selective and more decisive at the same time. Reward conviction fast, punish a miss fast, and take a whole company off the public market the moment control and price line up. International Business & Politics In Japan — the Bank of Japan's July meeting summary flagged rising inflation risk, with at least one board member floating a faster hike pace than markets had priced. Yen firmed on it, about 0.2% to 159.15 against the dollar — pulling back from the 160 level that's become the market's informal intervention trigger. July producer prices came in at 7.2% year-on-year, just under the 7.4% forecast and down slightly from June. So the signal's consistent — inflation's still hot enough in Japan that a "faster than expected" framing from the BOJ carries real weight, even without an actual move yet. Meanwhile the UK posted its seventh straight quarter of GDP growth — up 0.4% in the second quarter, services doing the work at plus 0.5%, construction up 0.3%. But retail and wholesale trade were flat for the quarter — zero growth — even with the Bank of England holding at 3.75% since July 30th and June CPI down to 2.6%. Consumer confidence is still deeply negative, negative 17, even though that's up six points. Same story in two different economies, really — headline growth or headline inflation moving the way policymakers want, while the consumer-facing part of the economy lags behind and doesn't feel it yet. Worth remembering that gap the next time a GDP print gets read as unambiguously good news — the retail number sitting right next to it is telling a much flatter story. China And in China — today's July activity data from the National Bureau of Statistics missed on both legs at once. Industrial production up 5.7% year-on-year, below the 6% forecast and down sharply from June's 6.8%. Retail sales missed too. The read-through on industrial production specifically is that front-loaded export demand — factories rushing shipments out ahead of US tariff deadlines — is fading now that the rush is over. Which means you can't blame this one purely on external demand. Retail missing in the same release means the domestic consumer leg is cooling right alongside the export leg, at the same time, not offsetting it. That's the more worrying combination for Beijing than either number alone — a slowdown showing up on both the making-things side and the buying-things side simultaneously usually takes more than one policy lever to fix. We'll come back to China's growth question through a very different lens later. For now, let's go deep on today's Deep Dive. Deep Dive Today's Deep Dive comes from a feature in The Generalist newsletter — Part Two of a series called "Saplings," this installment titled "Unstable Ground." It's not a markets story at all, and it's a genuinely good one. The series studies the early lives of legendary founders, looking for patterns in what shaped them before they built anything. Part Two is specifically about the home — the kind of instability that recurs again and again in these childhoods. The opening story is Amadeo Giannini, who founded what became Bank of America. In 1876, when he was six years old, he watched a farmhand shoot his father dead in a dispute over a dollar of unpaid wages. That night, his mother told him: "This is the last time I take you on my knees. From today, you are the man of the house." That pattern — early loss, followed by an abrupt inheritance of adult responsibility — shows up across an enormous list of names. Stan Shih of Acer, George Eastman of Kodak, Fred Smith of FedEx, Jerry Yang of Yahoo, Carlos Slim, Aristotle Onassis, Harland Sanders of KFC, James Dyson, Jim Casey of UPS — all lost a parent in childhood or adolescence. Li Ka-Shing's version is almost identical to Giannini's. His father was dying of tuberculosis when Li was fifteen, and told him "a man must have ambitions." Li promised him, in tears, "I will learn to do business and make lots of money" — and within three years had gone from sweeping factory floors to the company's star salesman. Jorge Paulo Lemann's father was struck and killed by a streetcar when Lemann was fourteen — the same immediate shift into being "the man of the house." The piece's argument is that parental death doesn't just create grief, it compresses childhood into a kind of forced adulthood, and pushes the bereaved child to rely entirely on themselves earlier than anyone should have to. Not every case in the piece is death, either. Larry Ellison found out he was adopted at around twelve, over dinner, with zero elaboration — his words later were something like, "It was like, 'Tonight we're having meatloaf, and by the way, you're adopted.'" No trauma of loss, but the same effect — the story he'd been standing on turned out not to be true. And then there's Ted Turner, whose father agreed to sell part of the family business and then killed himself the very next day, when Turner was twenty-four. Turner spent the rest of his life visibly obsessed with mortality — friends describe him talking about his own potential suicide constantly, almost flippantly, for years afterward. The author's framing, and it's a fair one, is that this isn't a checklist for producing a founder — it's not statistical, it doesn't claim causation. It's an accounting of a pattern he finds genuinely meaningful: early loss, a disappointing father paired with a more dominant mother, love that had to be earned rather than given freely, status that moved rather than stayed fixed, and family expectations placed on a child's shoulders before they were old enough to choose them. What I find most useful about it isn't the individual anecdotes, dramatic as they are — it's the throughline that instability absorbed very young seems to produce a particular relationship to risk later. If you've already learned as a child that your circumstances can change completely overnight, taking a big swing as an adult doesn't feel as reckless as it would to someone who never had that lesson forced on them. There's a less romantic reading too, worth holding alongside the inspiring one — survivorship bias is doing real work in a piece like this. Nobody's writing a "Saplings" essay about the thousand kids who lost a parent young and didn't found anything. We only hear about the instability when it's attached to an eventual bank or an airline. Fair, and the author actually flags that himself — this isn't a formula, it's a study of the people who happened to become extraordinary, read backward. Still worth the read for what it says about risk tolerance and self-reliance, even if you're skeptical of drawing a straight line from childhood loss to entrepreneurial success. It's a good palate-cleanser before we head back into markets — a reminder that behind every one of these company names is an actual person shaped by something that happened decades before the first product ever launched. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities Staying with something structural — this time the AI buildout itself. In Colorado, Xcel's regulated utility PSCo is asking the state Supreme Court to unlock eminent domain powers over a single gen-tie line, and the numbers behind it are wild. Two wind farms — Singing Grass at 603 megawatts and Cheyenne Ridge Two at 450 — are sitting essentially finished, about 1.05 gigawatts and something like 1.8 billion dollars of capital, stranded over a dispute involving roughly 550 feet of easement. A district court ruled back in June that Colorado law doesn't let a regulated utility condemn land for a generation-tie line the way it can for public transmission — the reasoning being a gen-tie serves one private project, not the grid broadly. So PSCo can't force the last landowner to sell. And PSCo didn't help its own case — it reportedly offered under 20,000 dollars for that 550-foot segment, when it paid 585,000 dollars for 90 acres in the same general area back in 2022, and NextEra settled with that very same landowner at market rate for its nearby Dusty Rose project. That's the real story underneath the legal one — a utility trying to lowball the one landowner it actually needs, and now two nearly-finished wind farms are stuck because of it. Colorado's legislature already moved back in March to curb Xcel's eminent domain power generally, so the political wind is against them too. The practitioner read here is that this becomes real precedent — if the Supreme Court agrees a gen-tie doesn't count as public use, every last-mile landowner in Colorado, and in states with similar statutes, just gained enormous leverage over interconnection routing. That's a chokepoint that has nothing to do with queue reform or turbine supply. Speaking of turbine supply — Mitsubishi Power's gas turbine backlog just hit 35 gigawatts, up 52% year-on-year, and orders booked this quarter are already slotting into 2028 through 2030 delivery. Put that next to what we already know — Siemens Energy sitting around 70 gigawatts, GE Vernova at 116. All three major OEMs are now effectively fully booked into the next decade. This isn't one company being cautious, it's the entire global turbine supply chain maxed out at once. There's a second bottleneck getting far less attention than turbines, though, and it might matter more. A startup called Heron Power, founded by an ex-Tesla battery executive, is building a 100-million-dollar factory outside San Jose to mass-produce a chip-based, software-controlled alternative to the standard steel-and-oil grid transformer. Standard transformers are running lead times of up to four years right now — arguably the single biggest hardware chokepoint behind interconnection delays, longer even than the turbine wait. Heron's targeting mass production of its solid-state unit by late 2027, more than 600 jobs, up to 10,000 units a year at full run rate. Whether silicon actually beats copper and steel at this scale remains to be proven — but it's a genuinely different kind of bet than anything else we've covered in this space, substituting semiconductors for heavy industrial manufacturing rather than just trying to build more of the same thing faster. And Texas just handed us the clearest evidence yet that all of this matters. ERCOT hit a new all-time peak demand of 91.1 gigawatts on July 22nd, six percent above the old record — but Ascend Analytics is now warning that more than 80% of the new large loads chasing power in Texas won't actually have matching generation online by 2030. The interconnection queue has grown by over 200 gigawatts since 2024, and Ascend puts the realistic completion rate at only about 55%. So even setting aside the politics of the queue-cull fight we've covered before, there's a hard physical cap here — roughly half the projects that get through the process still won't have power to run on. Three different bottlenecks, three different fixes being tried — a legal fight over 550 feet of land, a chip company betting against a four-year transformer wait, and a state grid operator's own forecaster admitting the math doesn't work at current build rates. None of them are about capital anymore. Capital's the one input in this cycle that's never actually been the constraint. Philippines In the Philippines — a genuinely fresh corruption story broke this week, and it's a big number. Former DPWH Secretary Manuel Bonoan testified before the Sandiganbayan on Tuesday that every single senator received a share of what he called a 24-billion-peso "leadership fund" tucked into the 2025 Department of Public Works budget. At least 500 million pesos per senator, up to a billion for committee chairs, according to the testimony. Senate President Migz Zubiri is disputing that 24-billion figure outright, and Senator Panfilo Lacson renewed his call to abolish the fund entirely yesterday, calling it — his words — "not pork barrel, worse." The Palace weighed in today too — spokesperson Claire Castro said Marcos has "no personal knowledge" of the fund, and that nothing like it exists in the 2027 budget currently before Congress. "No personal knowledge" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. It answers a much narrower question than the one everyone's actually asking, and it leaves the door open either way depending on what investigators turn up next. On the economic side, the peso closed at 61.343 to the dollar Thursday, down about 16 centavos, its weakest level in two weeks. The driver ties directly back to our first headline today — the stalled US-Iran talks are pushing oil and the dollar higher together, and the Philippines imports essentially all of its oil. BSP Governor Eli Remolona put a fresh, notably more sanguine spin on that same growth number today, calling it "disappointing, but not that bad" — a softer read than the central bank's tone when the 2.3% print first landed. He says weak growth gives room to ease up on tightening, but wants clearer disinflation evidence before actually doing that. Here's the tension worth flagging, though — Citi's own economists are still penciling in two more 25-basis-point hikes this year, in August and October, landing the policy rate at 5.25% by year-end. So Remolona's public tone right now is running noticeably softer than what the market's own forecasters still expect the BSP to actually do. Quick status check on the impeachment trial, since we've been following it closely — day fifteen wrapped Tuesday with the Senate adjourning after a sharp clash between the defense and prosecution over COA testimony. Next session isn't until Monday the 17th, so nothing new to report there today. Skipping the PSEi today too — it fell about 1.2% on profit-taking and the weaker peso, a routine move, not the kind of swing worth spending time on. And no active weather signal from PAGASA right now, so we'll leave that alone as well. The throughline across both Philippine stories today is really about how much external pressure keeps landing on a country managing its own accountability problems at the same time — Hormuz uncertainty hitting the currency from outside, a fresh graft number complicating the politics from inside. And the two aren't actually separate problems, either — a weaker peso raises the landed cost of everything the government imports for its own infrastructure programs, which is the exact same budget the leadership-fund allegations are about. External pressure doesn't just sit next to the domestic story, it makes the domestic story more expensive to fix. Vocab Of The Day 好，来看看今天的两个中文词。第一个跟今天的能源新闻有关——"不容忽视"。 "不容忽视"的意思是"cannot be tolerated to be ignored"，也就是不能被忽视。今天Ascend Analytics的报告说，到2030年，得州超过八成的大型用电项目可能拿不到匹配的发电量——这个风险不容忽视。 翻译过来就是：this risk cannot be ignored — by 2030, more than 80% of Texas's large power projects may not have matching generation available。 "不容忽视"是比较正式的书面语，常用在政策报告、分析师笔记里，后面常搭配"问题"、"风险"、"趋势"。跟"值得关注"比，"不容忽视"语气强得多——"值得关注"只是提醒你注意，"不容忽视"是警告你，不管它后果会很严重。 第二个词跟中国今天的经济数据有关——"由此可见"。 "由此可见"的意思是"from this it can be seen that"，专门用来从已经摆出的事实里推出结论。今天中国七月的工业增加值和零售数据同时不及预期，可以说：由此可见，出口和消费两方面同时放缓，问题不只是外部需求。 翻译：from this it can be seen that both exports and consumption are slowing at the same time — this isn't just an external-demand problem。 "由此可见"是很正式的过渡词，一般放在句子开头，专门总结前面的证据。比简单的"可见"更强调推理过程；平时聊天更常直接说"看来"或者"看样子"，没有这么严谨的论证语气。 好，从中文换到菲律宾语。Ngayon, tara na sa Tagalog. Una, "katiwalian." "Katiwalian" ay nangangahulugang corruption o malfeasance — hindi lang basta pangungurakot, kundi ang pang-aabuso ng tiwalang ibinigay sa isang opisyal. Halimbawa: Idinetalye ni dating DPWH Sekretaryo Bonoan ang umano'y katiwalian sa 24-bilyong-pisong "leadership fund." Ibig sabihin: former DPWH Secretary Bonoan detailed the alleged corruption in the 24-billion-peso "leadership fund." Iyan mismo ang balitang sumabog ngayong linggo. "Katiwalian" ay mas malakas at mas pormal kaysa sa kolokyal na "korap" — ang "korap" parang tsismis o kaswal na akusasyon, habang ang "katiwalian" ang salitang ginagamit sa balita, sa investigative reports, at sa mismong kaso sa Sandiganbayan. Pangalawa, "pag-aalinlangan." "Pag-aalinlangan" ay nangangahulugang hesitation o uncertainty — ang pagdududa kung dapat kumilos o hindi. Halimbawa: Dahil sa mahinang GDP, nasa pag-aalinlangan ang BSP kung ipagpapatuloy pa nila ang mahigpit na patakaran sa interes. Ibig sabihin: because of the weak GDP print, the BSP is in a state of hesitation over whether to continue its tight interest-rate policy. Ang pagkakaiba ng "pag-aalinlangan" sa mas kaswal na "medyo nag-aalangan" — ang una ay isang mas matimbang, mas institusyonal na pag-aatubili, habang ang huli ay parang personal at pang-araw-araw na pagdududa lang. Magandang pares din ito — isang salita tungkol sa katiwalian sa pulitika, isa tungkol sa pag-aalinlangan sa patakarang pang-ekonomiya. Pareho namang tungkol sa mga desisyong ginagawa — o hindi ginagawa — sa likod ng saradong pinto. Arts & Culture Arts and culture — starting with the auction world's biggest single-collection news this year. Sotheby's has landed the Blaquier collection, the Impressionist and post-Impressionist holdings of the late Argentine industrialists Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and Carlos Pedro Blaquier, beating out Christie's with a guarantee. It's heading to a dedicated November sale in New York, and the headline lot is a Van Gogh — "Châtaignier en fleurs roses et blanches" from 1890, estimated at 150 to 200 million dollars. There's also a Cézanne from his Harlequin series estimated above 120 million, plus Degas, Pissarro and Renoir works each expected above 25 million. This is exactly the kind of generational-wealth-transfer consignment the market's been waiting for to power an autumn recovery — one collection, assembled over decades by a single family, hitting the block all at once. In museums — the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art finally opens September 22nd in Los Angeles's Exposition Park, after roughly a decade of construction and years before that spent finding a city willing to host it. George Lucas has framed it explicitly as "a museum for the people" — but the twenty-five-dollar adult admission is drawing real pushback given that framing, especially sitting next to LA's mostly-free major institutions. The museum's partial answer is offering free access to residents of the neighboring 90037 zip code specifically. It's a genuinely unusual collection, too — narrative and figurative art spanning illustration, animation, comic art and film alongside more traditional painting, built almost entirely from Lucas's own decades of private collecting. Worth watching whether that zip-code carve-out becomes a template other billionaire-funded museums start copying, or stays a one-off gesture tied to this specific neighborhood. And in opera — Decca just released the world-premiere recording of an opera that's been lost for almost a hundred and forty years. Umberto Giordano wrote "Marina" at twenty-one, for the same 1888 competition that Mascagni ended up winning with "Cavalleria Rusticana." Giordano shelved it after losing, folded some of the music into a later opera, and it just sat there. The actual world-premiere staging happened this past February at Teatro Dal Verme in Milan, and the recording pairs Eleonora Buratto in the title role with tenor Freddie De Tommaso. Gramophone called it "a triumph" in this month's issue. There's something genuinely rare about a work getting its actual premiere a hundred and thirty-eight years after it was written, rather than just being revived from an existing performance history — this is Giordano's music meeting an audience for the very first time. Op-Eds & Commentary Op-eds today — Ben Casselman, the New York Times's chief economics correspondent, published a piece called "AI Is Reshaping the Economy, but the Data Can't Keep Up." His steelman is basically intellectual honesty about uncertainty — official government statistics were built for a slower, pre-AI economy, response rates to surveys keep falling, and the agencies collecting this data are themselves underfunded. He points to the Yale Budget Lab's occupational-churn tracker, which so far finds no clear link between AI adoption and job losses — and notably, the firms investing the most in AI are actually hiring faster, not shedding workers. The counter is that waiting for clean, aggregate data to settle the question is itself a choice, and it favors inaction. AI-attributed layoffs at Amazon, Salesforce, Meta, Accenture and IBM topped roughly fifty thousand in a single bad month last October, and companies are increasingly naming AI explicitly in their layoff filings even if economists can't yet prove causation in the topline numbers. "Too soon to tell" can be a genuinely honest position, but it can also quietly become a permanent alibi — the data will always lag the disruption it's trying to measure, and by the time it's clean enough to be certain, the disruption's already happened to the people it happened to. Second piece — Liam Denning at Bloomberg Opinion, "When Texas Cools on AI Data Centers, Big Tech Has a Problem," published yesterday. His steelman ties directly into our energy segment today. Governor Abbott stood on a stage with Alphabet's Sundar Pichai less than a year ago, calling Texas the epicenter of AI development — and now he's visibly cooler on the buildout, as grid strain, local opposition and ratepayer anger have all sharpened. Denning's point is that if even the most AI-friendly state in the country is hedging, that's a leading indicator for how hyperscalers should be pricing political risk everywhere else. The counter is that local friction in one or two counties isn't the same thing as statewide policy risk. ERCOT's market structure and a genuinely pro-growth legislature both have strong incentives to keep courting hyperscaler tax revenue, and the actual grid buildout — the turbines, the transformers, the interconnection fights we just covered — keeps proceeding regardless of one governor's rhetorical mood. Read those two together with everything else in today's show, and there's a real pattern — the AI story keeps getting harder to cleanly measure or cleanly predict, on the labor-market side and the political-support side both, exactly while the physical buildout underneath it keeps moving forward on its own momentum regardless. Which might be the most honest one-line summary of where this cycle actually is right now — nobody can prove the disruption yet, nobody can stop the buildout yet, and both of those things are true for the same underlying reason: reality's simply moving faster than anyone's ability to measure or govern it. One Good Thing One good thing today — a postcard that took twenty-six years to arrive. Bob Sheppard, in Long Beach, California, opened his mailbox this week and found a postcard his parents had mailed him from Copenhagen back in July of 2000. Signed simply "M and D" — Mom and Dad. Both of his parents have since passed — his mother four years ago, his father six years ago. The postal service has no real explanation for where it sat for a quarter of a century, or why it finally moved now. There's something genuinely lovely about a small, ordinary piece of mail outlasting the two people who sent it, and then landing in exactly the right hands anyway, decades later than planned. Sheppard said it felt like hearing from them again, out of nowhere, on an otherwise completely normal day. Sometimes the good thing really is just that simple. That's the show for today. That's The Morning Commute. We'll see you tomorrow. Take care, everyone. 不容忽视 cannot be ignored / cannot be tolerated to be overlooked (a risk or problem serious enough that ignoring it has real consequences) Energy segment — Ascend Analytics's warning that most large Texas loads chasing power won't have matching generation by 2030 由此可见 from this it can be seen that / this shows that (draws a conclusion from evidence just stated) China segment — July industrial production and retail sales both missing forecasts at once katiwalian corruption, malfeasance (abuse of entrusted authority, not just petty wrongdoing) Philippines — the ₱24 billion DPWH "leadership fund" testimony before the Sandiganbayan pag-aalinlangan hesitation, uncertainty (doubt over whether to act, especially in a deliberative or institutional sense) Philippines — BSP Governor Remolona's cautious tone on further rate hikes after a weak Q2 GDP print

docs.title: Thursday, August 13, 2026
docs.text: Thursday, August 13, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Thursday, August 13th. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Markets hit fresh records again overnight on a cooling CPI print, and underneath that calm tape the AI-power buildout's capital discipline just spread somewhere new — from gas turbines into long-duration batteries, and from voluntary best practice into a hard federal reliability rule. At the same time the geopolitical picture got sharper on almost every front — Ukraine hit the Russian navy directly for the first time, North Korea fired its second missile in a week, and Congress is fast-tracking real teeth on Russian oil sanctions. And closer to home for our Philippines segment, Beijing's embassy in Manila just tried a genuinely unusual pressure tactic, right as a Senate impeachment trial produced its first hard liability number. Lots to get through. Let's start with the world. Headlines Ukraine struck four Russian Black Sea Fleet warships at Novorossiysk yesterday — a joint drone and Neptune-missile attack that's a real escalation, because it's the fleet itself, not another cargo ship in the grain corridor. Three killed, more than ten injured, and it knocked out two grain terminals plus the Sheskharis oil-terminal pier. Satellite imagery doesn't show anything sunk, so call it a mission-kill on port operations rather than a naval kill. But the target selection is the story. Kyiv has spent two years hitting logistics and refineries. Going after the fleet in port, at its main Black Sea base, is a different kind of message — that Russian naval assets aren't safe anywhere in that theater anymore. Meanwhile North Korea fired its second ballistic missile in under a week yesterday — roughly 700 kilometers into the East Sea from Wonsan, the eleventh suspected test this year. Timing matters here too — this lands five days before the US and South Korea start joint drills on the 17th. Pyongyang also used the moment to denounce Seoul's nuclear-submarine program separately, so read the missile and the statement together as one signal. Two very different theaters, same underlying pattern — actors testing exactly how much daylight exists between deterrence rhetoric and consequences right now. Worth flagging too — Ukraine's strike lands right as the Hormuz de-escalation trade we've tracked all month stays stalled between the US and Iran over reparations. Two separate fronts, both testing whether last month's diplomatic momentum actually holds or was just a pause. And on North Korea, the pattern of an almost-weekly cadence is itself the signal — eleven tests this year isn't a single provocation to react to, it's a baseline the region's now had to price in as normal. Market Overview On the tape — records again. S&P 500 closed at 7,748.50, up 0.26%. Nasdaq 26,588.49, up 0.54%. Russell 2000 hit 3,045.48, up 0.61% and sitting right at its own 52-week high. Dow essentially flat, down 21 points to 53,770.27. All of it traces back to one number — July CPI, out Tuesday. Headline up just 0.1% month-on-month, annual rate down to 3.4% from 3.5%. Core came in at 0.2% month-on-month, 2.5% year-on-year, down from 2.6%. Shelter did almost all the damage on the upside, up 0.1%. Energy actually fell 1.5% on the month, though it's still up 14.7% year-on-year — so the disinflation story is real but uneven under the hood. The read-through is straightforward — this keeps a September or October Fed cut squarely in play. Ten-year's sitting around 4.69%. Gold's actually down slightly, 4,449.90, off 0.39% — no real safe-haven bid today. July PPI lands this morning at 8:30 Eastern, and it hasn't printed yet as of this recording, so that's the next data point that could either confirm or complicate this story. Oil's soft too — WTI 82.11, Brent 87.92, both down over 1% — nothing dramatic, just drifting with a slightly firmer dollar. The setup into PPI is worth stating plainly — a soft print today keeps the September-cut narrative intact and probably extends the record run. A hot one reopens the "sticky services inflation" argument that's been dormant since spring, and small caps, which just hit that Russell high, are exactly the part of the market most exposed if that argument comes back. U.S. Business Wendy's jumped as much as 15% yesterday and got briefly halted for volatility on a take-private report — Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management, which already owns 7.85% of the company with Peltz personally holding 16.24%, is reportedly assembling a consortium with BlueFive Capital and Flynn Group, Wendy's largest franchisee, to take the whole thing private. The Flynn Group detail is what makes this credible rather than speculative — you don't typically get your biggest operating partner into a buyout conversation unless there's real substance behind it. A formal bid could land within weeks. And the "neocloud" earnings trade just had its best week yet — Nebius up 34% yesterday, CoreWeave up 19%. Nebius's numbers justify it — Q2 revenue of 582 million dollars, up 454% year-on-year, beating consensus of 575 million. Adjusted EBITDA swung from a 21 million dollar loss to positive 236 million. ARR hit 3 billion dollars, and they signed four new AI-cloud deals averaging over a billion each in total contract value. CoreWeave's Q2 revenue came in at 2.6 billion, up 112% year-on-year, with a 104 billion dollar backlog. We flagged CoreWeave's debt structure on the show Tuesday — this is the revenue side of that same balance sheet, and it's running hot enough that the market's not asking hard questions about it today. Which is exactly the pattern to watch — strong prints get read as vindication, and the leverage underneath gets a pass as long as the growth number keeps beating. Notice the two stories together, actually — a 150-year-old fast-food chain drawing private-equity-style leverage interest, and a two-year-old neocloud drawing public-market enthusiasm on the same day. Completely different assets, same underlying appetite for leverage while credit stays cheap and a cut's on the table. International Business & Politics In Washington, the House introduced a companion bill Monday to the Senate's Russia and Iran sanctions act, which passed 86 to 11 back on the 7th. The mechanism is blunt — it would let the President levy tariffs up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, and China and India are named specifically. The fact that the House is fast-tracking this during recess, rather than letting it sit, signals real momentum toward a floor vote in September. If that actually lands, it's a much bigger lever than the sanctions regime we've been tracking — this is secondary-sanctions territory, hitting China and India's energy relationship with Moscow rather than Russia directly. Separately, Trump restarted his effort to fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook — a letter dated the 5th, with a response deadline of the 26th, citing mortgage-fraud allegations. This is the first move since the Supreme Court's 5-to-4 ruling in June, which blocked his earlier attempt specifically for lack of due process. Cook's lawyer is calling this one a pretext too, but the administration's clearly trying to build a cleaner procedural record this time around. Worth watching against the Warsh transition at the Fed generally — there's already tension over how the new chair communicates policy. A parallel fight over Cook's seat adds a second front to Fed-independence questions right as markets are pricing in cuts. Put the two stories together and you get a genuinely aggressive week out of Washington on the international-economic-policy front — a tariff bill aimed at Russia's oil customers, and a renewed push against a sitting Fed governor. Different targets, same appetite for using executive and legislative leverage more forcefully than markets had priced in even a month ago. China In China — Bloomberg flagged something structurally interesting this week. More than a trillion yuan, roughly 148 billion dollars, of non-residential Chinese property sits on leases with 20 years or less remaining. Standard terms are 40 years for retail, 50 for office and industrial — so a big pool of commercial real estate is aging into a refinancing problem. Banks are balking at extending credit against assets with under ten years left on the lease, which chokes off collateral value exactly when developers need it most. Shanghai's response is to let non-residential leases extend on demand, city-wide — a direct administrative fix for a deflationary-era problem that the market alone won't solve, because nobody wants to be the lender holding a depreciating leasehold. It's a small mechanical story, but it's a good window into how China is handling debt-deflation generally — not with a big stimulus headline, but with quiet regulatory patches that buy time on the collateral side of the balance sheet, one asset class at a time. And it's a reminder of how differently a leasehold system handles a downturn compared to freehold markets in the West — you can't just write down the asset's value and move on when the underlying right to use the property itself has a countdown clock attached to it. Extending the lease is Beijing's way of resetting that clock without ever having to call it a bailout. Deep Dive Today's Deep Dive comes from a feature in CTVC's Currence newsletter — issue 308, "Long duration energy storage finds its buyer" — and it's a genuinely sharp read on where LDES financing is actually headed. The core argument is that the buyer for long-duration storage just changed, and that changes who wins. For years, LDES sold into government procurement — tenders that reward system value, resilience, decarbonization — value that utilities in a cost-of-service world are structurally reluctant to pay for. That kept the sector stuck without a real commercial anchor. Now hyperscalers are becoming the primary new demand source, and they buy for completely different reasons than a government tender does — speed to power, supply-chain certainty, cycle life under heavy AI-training load. Not lowest levelized cost. And that's re-ranking the technology stack. Non-lithium chemistries — iron-air, compressed-air, flow batteries — are climbing past lithium-ion for the first time, specifically because they fit what a hyperscaler actually needs better than a price-only bid ever rewarded. The evidence in the piece is concrete. No final investment decisions have closed since January, but the second half is bringing real construction starts — Energy Dome's 18-megawatt Columbia Energy Storage project in Ohio, and Hydrostor's 500-megawatt Willow Rock compressed-air project. The headline deal, though, is Form Energy's 300-megawatt iron-air contract with Xcel Energy and Google at Pine Island — the first commercial-scale iron-air agreement priced competitively rather than as a demonstration project. Crusoe separately reserved 120 megawatts of Form Energy capacity on its own. And here's the part that should sound familiar — Google reportedly holds right-of-first-refusal-style positions with both Form Energy and Energy Dome. That's the exact same logic as the turbine lockups we've covered on the generation side, PPL and Blackstone reserving gas years ahead of signed contracts. Lock up the category leader before your competitors can. In Mandarin later this hour we'll actually use the phrase for that — seizing the advantage of being first. It's precisely what's happening here. Data centers are now the second-largest offtake source for non-lithium LDES overall, and the piece flags a twelve-to-twenty-four month window before the next tier of names — Hydrostor, Sage Geosystems, Invinity, CMBlu, XL Batteries, Inlyte — becomes financeable at scale. One more number from the same issue that puts real stakes behind all this — the average US household electricity bill hit a record 217 dollars a month in July. Which is the honest tension underneath the whole storage-financing story — hyperscaler money accelerates the buildout of technology that could eventually stabilize grid costs for everyone, but in the near term, it's competing for the same interconnection capacity and capital that residential ratepayers are also depending on. So watch the next twelve months less for the exciting new chemistry, and more for who actually signs the second wave of contracts — that tells you whether this genuinely broadens out or stays a hyperscaler-only phenomenon. There's a second-order read worth pulling out too — non-lithium storage's whole pitch used to be cost, and it kept losing on cost to lithium-ion at scale. What actually broke the logjam wasn't a chemistry breakthrough, it was a buyer showing up who cares more about deliverable cycle life under sustained AI-training load than about levelized cost per megawatt-hour. Which means the technology didn't win the argument — the customer's priorities changed the argument. That's a pattern worth watching elsewhere in the capex cycle too, anywhere a technology's been stuck for years on a cost basis alone. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities Staying with power — PJM is drafting ride-through reliability requirements for data-center and crypto load, and this is a bigger deal than it sounds. Ride-through rules already exist for generators — you don't get to just trip offline the instant there's a grid disturbance, you're required to stay connected through minor faults. PJM's now writing the demand-side mirror of that for large computational loads. The trigger was a July event — a 230-kilovolt transmission fault in Northern Virginia caused roughly 3.8 gigawatts of data-center load to switch to onsite backup generation essentially all at once. That's not a rounding error, that's a meaningful chunk of grid demand disappearing and reappearing in the same afternoon. FERC directed NERC on July 16th to file new or modified computational-load reliability standards by December 31st this year, with registry criteria and a Phase Two work plan due March 1st, 2027. The number to watch is NERC's draft registration threshold — aggregate connected load of 20 megawatts or more at a single point of interconnection, 60 kilovolts or higher, hosting at least 1 megawatt of computational load. That's the first hard technical line drawn between a facility that must comply with federal reliability standards and smaller colocation that doesn't. Important to separate this from the PJM 70-gigawatt backstop-auction filing we covered last week — that was about who pays for new capacity. This is a completely different track — grid stability engineering, not cost allocation. Two separate regulatory fights running in parallel on the same load growth. And the equipment side confirms the same buildout is running hot at every scale. Caterpillar posted its first-ever 20.5 billion dollar quarter, up 24% year-on-year, with 3.1 billion of that increase tied directly to data-center power-generation equipment. Power and Energy segment revenue up 17% to 8.2 billion, power-gen retail sales up 72% year-on-year. Order backlog hit a record 72 billion dollars, customers are now placing orders through 2030, and 59% of that backlog is scheduled to ship within twelve months. That's the behind-the-meter generator supply chain — the diesel and gas gensets that back up a facility during exactly the kind of event PJM is now writing rules around — running just as hot as the big gas-turbine OEM backlogs at Siemens and GE Vernova that we've already flagged. It's a second, distinct bottleneck at the smaller-unit end of the market, and it's not getting nearly as much attention as the marquee turbine numbers. So the picture across both segments today — reliability rules catching up to what's already happened operationally, and equipment lead times stretching out at every layer of the stack, from gigawatt gas turbines down to onsite backup gensets. There's a real tension buried in the PJM ride-through story too, worth naming directly. The 3.8-gigawatt trip happened precisely because facility operators did what they're supposed to do — switch to backup power the instant grid quality degrades, to protect equipment and uptime. The new rule is effectively asking them to accept more risk to their own operations for the sake of grid stability everyone else depends on. Which is a genuinely hard ask, and it's exactly why FERC gave NERC a year and a half to work through registry criteria rather than just mandating it overnight — you can't write a ride-through standard without also solving who bears the liability if a facility stays connected through a fault and it damages their own hardware. That liability question is probably the real fight buried inside this rulemaking, more than the megawatt threshold itself. Philippines In the Philippines — a genuinely unusual diplomatic pressure tactic. PAOCC's executive director, Benjamin Acorda Jr., told a Senate joint hearing today that the Chinese Embassy warned it would move to arrest Filipino workers in China if Manila didn't release 69 Chinese nationals PAOCC arrested back in May at the Sanjia-Steel plant in Tagoloan, Misamis Oriental. Senator Risa Hontiveros called it inappropriate retaliation, and said it isn't the first time that embassy has made a threat like this. Reciprocal detention threats over a labor-enforcement action are an escalation in tone, even if nothing further happens — it signals Beijing is willing to use OFWs as leverage in a dispute that started as a domestic labor case. Meanwhile the impeachment trial hit Day 16, and it produced the first hard number in this entire proceeding. COA state auditor Xylene del Campo testified that Vice President Sara Duterte and two OVP officials are personally liable for 73 million pesos of the 125 million in confidential funds that auditors disallowed. The specific violation was routing cash-advance disbursements through then-VPSPG chief Colonel Raymund Dante Lachica — which the joint circular on confidential-fund use doesn't permit. Testimony may not wrap until Monday, but going from a procedural dispute to an actual peso figure of personal liability changes what this trial is now measuring. And on the economic side, the peso had its worst single day since late April — sliding 55.5 centavos to close at 61.26 to the dollar on Tuesday, from 60.705 the Monday before. The proximate cause is external — a stalled US-Iran track plus a firmer dollar broadly, which reversed the gains the peso had made the prior week. PSEi actually still edged up about 0.6% into the 6,300s on bargain-hunting, so this reads as a currency story specifically, not a broader risk-off move in Philippine assets. No active PAGASA storm signal right now, so we'll leave weather there — worth noting Metro Manila and eleven provinces did suspend classes today under a Heavy Rainfall Warning, but that's routine habagat continuation, not a new weather event. Two very different kinds of pressure landing the same week — an external actor testing how far it can push on a labor dispute, and an internal accountability process finally attaching a real number to it. Worth noting the PAOCC case sits on top of an already tense run of Philippines-China labor stories — DOLE canceled Chuangxing Steel's Chinese workers' permits just this week over labor-law violations. Sanjia-Steel and Chuangxing aren't the same company, but the pattern of Chinese industrial operations in Mindanao running into Philippine labor enforcement, and Beijing pushing back hard, is now the second time this month, not a one-off. And the peso move ties back to the throughline in a quieter way — a weaker currency raises the cost of everything the Philippines imports, oil included, right as WTI and Brent both eased today. Small mercies, but real ones, for an economy managing external pressure on two fronts simultaneously. Vocab Of The Day 好，我们来看看今天的两个中文词。第一个和今天的观点节目有关——"不可否认"。 "不可否认"的意思是"it cannot be denied that"，用来先承认对方论点里合理的部分，然后再提出反驳。今天《纽约时报》有一篇关于AI泡沫的评论，可以这样说：不可否认，今年七月Anthropic和OpenAI的收入都超过了预期，但支撑这一切的杠杆非常脆弱。 翻译过来就是：it cannot be denied that Anthropic and OpenAI both beat their revenue targets in July, but the leverage underneath it all is extremely fragile。 "不可否认"是比较正式的书面语，常见于社论、研究报告，念稿子的主播也会用；口语里更常说"确实"或者"说实话"，随便聊天的时候用那两个就够了。 对，而且"不可否认"专门用在"先让步、后反驳"的结构里——你先承认对方说得有道理，紧接着话锋一转。这跟单纯说"显然"不一样，"显然"没有让步的意味，只是在陈述一个事实。 第二个词跟今天的Deep Dive有关——"抢占先机"。 "抢占先机"的意思是"to seize the first-mover advantage"，字面是"抢先占据有利的时机"。今天的storage新闻里，Google跟Form Energy和Energy Dome都签了优先购买权，可以说：Google在长时储能这个赛道上抢占先机，提前锁定了最好的供应商。 翻译：Google is seizing the first-mover advantage in the long-duration-storage race, locking up the best suppliers ahead of time。 "抢占先机"是商业报道里很常见的搭配，"抢占"后面还可以接"市场"、"份额"，意思都是趁别人还没反应过来的时候先下手；跟单纯的"提前准备"不一样，"抢占先机"强调的是竞争性、排他性，别人抢到了你就没有了。 好，从中文换到菲律宾语。Ngayon, tara sa Tagalog. Una, "pananagutan." "Pananagutan" ay nangangahulugang accountability o liability — hindi lang basta responsibilidad sa salita, kundi isang bagay na maaaring pananagutin ka sa harap ng batas o awtoridad. Halimbawa: idineklara ng COA na may pananagutan si Bise Presidente Duterte sa 73 milyong pisong hindi wastong paggastos. Ibig sabihin: the COA declared that Vice President Duterte has liability for 73 million pesos in improperly spent funds. Iyan mismo ang balita ngayon mula sa Araw 16 ng paglilitis. Mahalagang tandaan, "pananagutan" ay mas malakas kaysa sa "responsibilidad" — hindi lang ito tungkol sa tungkulin mo, kundi sa posibleng kahihinatnan kung hindi mo iyon tinupad nang maayos, tulad ng isang legal na paglilitis. Pangalawa, "panggigipit." "Panggigipit" ay ang paggamit ng presyon o puwersa para pilitin ang isang tao o bansa na gawin ang gusto mo — hindi ito basta banta, kundi patuloy na pagpapataw ng presyon. Halimbawa: nag-panggigipit umano ang embahada ng Tsina sa pamamagitan ng banta ng pag-aresto sa mga OFW. Ibig sabihin: the Chinese embassy allegedly engaged in coercive pressure through the threat of arresting OFWs. Iyan mismo ang sinabi ni Senator Hontiveros kanina. Ang pagkakaiba sa "banta," na natutunan na natin dati — ang "banta" ay ang mismong sinasabi, habang ang "panggigipit" ay ang buong estratehiya ng patuloy na presyon, kadalasang gamit ang isang banta bilang kasangkapan lang. Magandang pares ngayon — isa sa impeachment trial, isa sa diplomatic pressure — pareho namang tungkol sa accountability at consequences. Arts & Culture Arts and culture — starting with a genuinely useful data point on the London gallery market. Two respected mid-size galleries, Sid Motion and Beers, both announced closure this week. Sid Motion's been going ten years, built a name backing emerging and mid-career artists out of South Bermondsey. They're closing in October after a final show called "That Which Appears," running September 18th through October 31st. Beers, fourteen years old, near the Barbican, made its name on young painters — that one closes at the end of this month. What's notable is the framing. Sid Motion's founder said she's choosing to close "while the gallery remains in a position to properly support its artists" — closing from strength, on her own terms, rather than letting the finances force a messier ending later. It's a clean, unglamorous data point on the mid-market gallery squeeze — rising overheads, costly fair participation, collectors staying cautious even as the top of the market, the big auction houses, keeps recovering. The middle is where the pressure actually shows up first. In literature — Deborah Levy has a new essay collection out from FSG, "The Position of Spoons: And Other Intimacies." Thirty-six essays spanning twenty-five years, on art, aging, psychoanalysis, celebrity, and a lovely piece specifically on Gertrude Stein's years in Paris. The Art Newspaper and the TLS both reviewed it this week, and the interesting critical point is that most of these pieces were originally commissioned introductions or journal essays, written for other purposes entirely — but read together, they cohere into what one critic called an "untethered, free-form autobiography." Levy's better known as a novelist — Booker-shortlisted twice, for "Hot Milk" and "Swimming Home." It's a nice reminder that a writer's nonfiction, even when it's scattered and occasional by design, can end up saying something more personal than the novels ever did directly. Two very different stories, but both about what happens when you look at a body of work — or a body of galleries — assembled over decades, all at once. Op-Eds & Commentary Op-eds — David Wallace-Wells, writing with Yale economist Natasha Sarin in New York Times Opinion, published a piece Tuesday called "Why the U.S. Economy Needs A.I. — Bubble or Not." Their steelman is that AI is simultaneously a real technology story and a real financial bubble at the same time — both true, not contradictory. Anthropic and OpenAI both beat their revenue targets in July, so the demand is genuine. But the buildout's financed with leverage precarious enough that a hedge fund betting on imminent AGI, run by a 24-year-old, nearly collapsed on four-times leverage when markets wobbled. Sarin's line is the one worth remembering — "the markets can remain irrational longer than you can stay solvent." Her point is you can be directionally right about the technology and still get wiped out by the financing structure sitting on top of it. Here's the counter, though — an economy whose growth now depends on a debt-financed speculative boom staying inflated isn't being saved by AI, it's being made hostage to it. That's the exact "too big to fail, too big to correct" logic that turned a genuinely real technology — subprime-enabled homeownership — into 2008. And if the underlying revenue really is as strong as Anthropic and OpenAI's July numbers suggest, it should be able to stand without the leveraged wrapper around it. If it can't stand without that leverage, calling the leverage "necessary" just launders the risk instead of pricing it honestly. Second piece — Noah Smith, on Noahpinion, published "Banning Data Centers Would Blow Up the U.S. Economy" last Saturday. His steelman — a genuinely bipartisan backlash is building, a Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate running on a data-center ban, moratoriums already in place in blue New York and red Texas alike. He concedes the long-run resource-competition concern is legitimate, but argues an abrupt ban now, with nowhere else for growth to come from, risks a self-inflicted collapse. He also argues the water-usage panic specifically is overblown, since cooling water gets recirculated rather than consumed. The counter — calling data centers "the engine keeping the economy afloat" is itself an admission that growth has gotten dangerously narrow and concentrated. And it skips over who's actually paying for that engine's fuel right now — households already absorbing rate surcharges as utilities like FirstEnergy and Dominion push gigawatt-scale interconnection costs onto ratepayers. The real choice on the table was never "ban versus nothing" — it was targeted permitting and cost-allocation reform versus a status quo that quietly externalizes the bill onto residential customers. Treating the maximalist ban as the only alternative to unconditional buildout stacks the deck before the argument even starts. Read together, both pieces are basically making the same move from opposite directions — conceding a real risk, then arguing the fix on offer is worse than the disease. Worth being skeptical of that structure on both sides, not just the side you already disagree with. And there's a direct line from both pieces back to today's other stories — Wallace-Wells and Sarin's fragile-leverage argument is exactly what's sitting underneath yesterday's Nebius and CoreWeave rally, and Smith's ratepayer-backlash argument is exactly what PJM's cost-allocation fight and Caterpillar's genset boom are both downstream of. Which is really the honest state of this whole debate right now — nobody serious is arguing the technology is fake. The argument is entirely about who's exposed if the financing or the political tolerance breaks first, and on the evidence today, both remain genuinely untested. One Good Thing One good thing today — Voyager 2. Forty-nine years into flight, and it's still transmitting from interstellar space. On August 4th, JPL engineers executed a power-saving maneuver they nicknamed the "Big Bang" — shutting off an old onboard tape recorder and two heaters, switching to lower-power alternatives instead. That single maneuver cuts the spacecraft's annual power draw by nearly 10 watts, which sounds tiny, but for a plutonium power source that's been decaying for half a century, it buys at least one more year of operation, possibly two, for its three remaining working science instruments. NASA's planning the same maneuver on Voyager 1 in the coming months. Two spacecraft, still doing real science, kept alive a little longer by engineers finding a few more watts to squeeze out of a design from the 1970s. There's something genuinely moving about that kind of patient, unglamorous engineering — nobody's writing headlines about ten watts, but it's the difference between a working instrument and a dead one, a few hundred million miles from home. That's the show for today. That's The Morning Commute. We'll see you tomorrow. Take care, everyone. 不可否认 it cannot be denied that / admittedly (concede a valid point before pivoting to a rebuttal) Op-Eds & Commentary — Wallace-Wells/Sarin's NYT piece on AI as both real technology and real financial bubble 抢占先机 to seize the first-mover advantage (grab a favorable position before competitors can react) Deep Dive — Google's right-of-first-refusal lockups with Form Energy and Energy Dome in the LDES race pananagutan accountability, liability (answerable for consequences before the law or an authority, not just a duty in name) Philippines — Day 16 of the Duterte impeachment trial, the first hard peso liability figure panggigipit coercion, applying sustained pressure to force compliance (a strategy, not just a single statement) Philippines — the Chinese Embassy's threat to arrest Filipino workers over the Sanjia-Steel dispute
