docs.text: Tuesday, August 11, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Tuesday, August 11th. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Today's thread is speed versus certainty, and it runs through almost everything we're covering. Vistra wants Texas's data-center queue culled down to what's real. PPL and Blackstone are reserving gas turbines years before they've signed a single hyperscaler contract. And Constellation's making a third case entirely — that existing nuclear beats greenfield gas because it's already there. Three incumbents, three different bets on the same shortage. The same argument shows up in software today too — a SemiAnalysis piece on how a code layer, not new chips, is closing the gap between commodity GPUs and purpose-built inference hardware. Markets are taking a breather after Friday's jobs-miss rally, Iran and Washington have hardened into a reparations standoff instead of reopening Hormuz, and the Philippines is dealing with its worst flood toll of the year the same week a very awkward political secret came out about how the Marcos-Duterte alliance actually fell apart. Let's get into it. Headlines Starting with Iran, because the tone shifted overnight. Trump has rejected Tehran's demand for war reparations. Reparations — for what, exactly? For the Strait of Hormuz standoff and everything around it. But here's the twist — Trump didn't just say no, he counter-demanded that Iran pay for, quote, 50 years of damage. Over 600 US troops killed in Iraq between 2003 and 2011, plus Iranian protesters killed by their own regime over the decades. So instead of both sides inching toward a Hormuz reopening, they've both just hardened their opening positions. Exactly. This was supposed to be the de-escalation track. Now it's a standoff measured in weeks, not days. Worth remembering this is the same dispute that already produced a toll-fee fight between Iran and Oman — this is a new sticking point layered on top, not a rerun. The other story worth your attention is Ukraine. Kyiv hit a Russian petrochemical plant more than 2,000 kilometers from the border. Zelensky is calling it the deepest Ukrainian strike of the entire war. Moscow's not exactly de-escalating either — Russia logged 170 combat engagements yesterday, and their deputy foreign minister, Galuzin, is on record saying Russia won't, quote, freeze the war without addressing what he calls root causes. Meanwhile Washington's reportedly weighing reviving talks that would include some kind of air-attack halt. So you've got maximalist rhetoric and a diplomatic track running in parallel again. It's worth noting how quickly this flipped. A week ago the story was Iran and Oman fighting over who keeps the toll revenue on a deal both sides had basically agreed to. Now Washington's rejecting the whole reparations premise outright. Which tells you the underlying trust never really got rebuilt — the toll dispute was a symptom, not the disease. Every time these talks get close to something concrete, one side finds a new sticking point to reopen the whole negotiation. Worth watching what this does to shipping traffic through the Strait too — every prior de-escalation signal has produced a partial recovery, and every new sticking point has stalled it right back out. Right, and that back-and-forth is exactly why the oil market's been range-bound rather than spiking or collapsing — it's pricing genuine uncertainty about which way this goes, not a clear direction either way. Let's do markets — and I promise we'll be quick, because there isn't much here. Market Overview Monday's close: S&P 500 at 7,753.11, down just 4.53 points, 0.06%. Nasdaq 26,605.36, off 0.32%. Dow 53,975.98, down 0.11%. Russell 2000 the laggard at 3,017.40, down 0.56%. So essentially flat across the board. A breather, not a reversal. This is the first small give-back after Friday's jobs-miss rally pushed everything to records. No catalyst behind it — just digestion. Gold ticked up to $4,440 an ounce, about half a percent, and that one does have a driver — the Iran reparations escalation we just covered. Brent's holding near $87.43, still close to a four-day high after last week's 5% spike. Week ahead — Cisco reports Thursday, sorry, Wednesday after the close, consensus $1.17 EPS on $16.7 to $16.9 billion revenue, and Applied Materials follows Thursday. Those are your next AI-capex data points. Onto US business, and two beat-but-fell stories, which tells you something about where investor patience sits right now. U.S. Business Datadog first. Q2 EPS 65 cents, beat the 58-cent estimate. Revenue $1.12 billion, up 36% year-on-year, also a beat. Customers spending over $100,000 a year grew 23% to roughly 4,720, and they raised the full-year guide to $4.45 to $4.47 billion. And the stock fell 15 to 17% premarket anyway. On a clean beat and raise. This isn't a demand problem — it's a valuation reset. The market's gotten fussier about what "good" needs to look like for high-multiple software names. Same story, different sport — On Holding. Revenue up 21.6% constant-currency to 850.3 million Swiss francs, missed the 881.4 million estimate. EPS beat at 31 centimes versus 29 expected, net income swung to 105 million from a 40.9 million loss a year ago. DTC channel up 34.3% constant-currency — the direct-to-consumer strength is real. But the stock's down 13 to 15% on the top-line miss. Growth quality is being priced with a much finer comb than it was a month ago. Internationally — Japan just cut its own growth forecast, and the reason is the story we've been tracking all week. International Business & Politics Japan trimmed its fiscal 2026 real GDP growth forecast to 0.9%, down from 1.3%, and cited higher energy costs from the Middle East war directly. That's the Hormuz oil premium showing up in a G7 government's own numbers — not analyst commentary, an official forecast revision. And on the industrial side of the AI buildout — ArcelorMittal's Q2. Revenue $16.5 billion, underlying operating profit $2.1 billion, and the stock is up 65.3% year to date. Steel doesn't usually run like a growth stock. This is the AI-capex-into-hard-infrastructure trade landing another rung down the supply chain — data centers and grid buildout need steel long before they need chips. It's the same logic we keep coming back to on this show — every gigawatt of planned compute drags a whole chain of unglamorous industrial demand behind it. Turbines, transformers, steel, cable. The AI story isn't just chips anymore. And it's the part of the trade that's easiest to miss if you're only watching Nvidia's stock price. China China — one number, and it's a quiet one. July CPI up just 0.5% year-on-year, core CPI up 0.9%, but month-on-month actually negative 0.1%. PPI up 3.5%, missed the 3.8% estimate, and decelerated from June. So even with the AI-stock rally and the record trade surplus dominating headlines, domestic demand is still soft and producer prices are still deflationary. That's the counter-read sitting underneath the export story we've covered before — don't let the trade number distract from the demand number. Deep Dive Alright, Deep Dive. This one's dense, but it's genuinely one of the sharper technical arguments we've read in a while — a SemiAnalysis feature that landed in the inbox yesterday. The piece is about a piece of software called TileRT, and the claim is that it closes most of the interactivity gap between ordinary Nvidia GPUs and the purpose-built low-latency chips — Cerebras, Groq's LPU, SambaNova. Walk me through why that gap exists in the first place. So the roofline math — the theoretical ceiling based purely on memory bandwidth — says an 8-GPU B200 node, with 64 terabytes a second of HBM bandwidth, should be capable of about 3,047 tokens per second per user running a model like GLM-5 at batch size one. And real-world engines don't get anywhere close. Nowhere close. And the reason isn't bandwidth — bandwidth has actually grown 2 to 3 times per hardware generation. The bottleneck is kernel-launch latency. Every step of generating a token involves thousands of sequential kernel launches, and that overhead hasn't moved even as the hardware got faster. So TileRT's fix is? A single, statically-compiled "persistent engine kernel" that stays resident on the GPU for the entire decode lifecycle, instead of launching thousands of separate kernels per token. Software, not silicon. Give me the actual numbers, because "closes most of the gap" is a big claim. On a single B200 8-GPU node: 340 tokens per second per user at an 8,000-token input, 1,000-token output setup — that's 1.9 times the prior best result, which was a GB300 NVL72 system at 181.4. At a shorter 1,000-in, 1,000-out FP8 setup, TileRT hits 494.2 tokens per second per user — 3.6 times the previous best conventional FP8 engine. And end-to-end latency? Beats the prior-best GLM-5.1 setup by 4.5 times at that same 1,000-in, 1,000-out configuration. And on an iso-cost basis — same dollar spend — TileRT runs roughly twice as interactive as a traditional engine. There's got to be a catch. There is — it only works at batch size one. Throughput comes in at 160.4 tokens per GPU, versus a GB300's 240 tokens per GPU when you're running 12 concurrent requests. SemiAnalysis calls it "a single-passenger rocketship" — blazing fast for one user, but you sacrifice the multi-tenant efficiency that makes serving cheap at scale. Is anyone actually running this in production, or is it a benchmark exercise? Two real deployments already — Xiaomi's MiMo V2.5 Pro UltraSpeed tier, and Z.ai's GLM-5.1 HighSpeed tier. Both use a split architecture — vLLM handles the prefill stage, TileRT handles decode — and critically, neither provider bought any new hardware to do it. Which is the whole argument, isn't it — that fungibility beats purity. That's the author's actual thesis. A GPU-fleet operator can carve out a premium "speed tier" from capacity they already own, and reallocate the prefill-to-decode ratio just by changing a config file. An ASIC fleet locks in a fixed speed-to-capacity ratio the day you buy it, and re-racking it to change that ratio takes months. So this directly squeezes Cerebras, Groq, and SambaNova's addressable market. From below, yes — though the piece is careful to say the SRAM-based roofline those chips run on still wins outright on raw ceiling, and on small dense models specifically. This isn't "ASICs are dead." It's "the GPU fleet you already have can now compete with them on the metric that used to be their whole reason to exist." A software layer eating a hardware moat. That's the throughline of the day in miniature, honestly — speed and flexibility beating a fixed, purpose-built bet. There's a real business question buried in here too — this is already live in production at Xiaomi and Z.ai, which means the "speed tier" pricing model is going to spread fast. If you can sell a premium interactivity tier off hardware you already own, with zero incremental capex, that's close to pure margin. Which raises the question of whether Cerebras and Groq need to cut prices just to defend their reason for existing, given a chunk of their pitch was "GPUs simply can't do this." That's exactly the pressure the piece flags. It doesn't kill the ASIC case outright — small dense models and the raw ceiling still favor purpose-built silicon — but it meaningfully narrows the range of workloads where "we need dedicated hardware" is actually true. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities And speaking of fixed bets versus flexible ones — let's go straight into energy, because today's digest from the inbox has three incumbents making three genuinely different calls on the same power shortage. Start with the cull-it-down camp. Vistra. CEO Jim Burke, on the Q2 call: "I'd like to see the queues culled, at the end of the day." He's calling ERCOT's headline interconnection queue — cited as high as 474 gigawatts — overstated by more than 20 times against what he thinks is a realistic 2030 number, which he puts at just 12 to 15 gigawatts. That's a stunning gap between the official queue and what one of the biggest generators actually believes will get built. It is, and it matters because Vistra's Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $1.77 billion, up 30% year-on-year, full-year guide reaffirmed at $6.8 to $7.6 billion. They're not hurting — they're the first major incumbent to publicly back Governor Abbott's interconnection pause rather than fight it, because a smaller, more credible queue protects the value of the generation they already have. They also announced something called Helix. A $1 billion data-center partnership with KKR and Nvidia — so even the culling advocate is still building. It's not anti-growth, it's anti-speculation. Now the opposite bet. PPL and Blackstone, through a joint venture called Invitium, in Pennsylvania. They've secured reservation agreements for over 5 gigawatts of combined-cycle gas turbines, and PJM has already accepted north of 5 gigawatts of Invitium's interconnection requests. They've got land secured for 8 to 14 gigawatts total, and up to $15 billion of potential JV investment through 2032. How many actual customers have signed on? Zero. Zero hyperscaler offtake agreements to date. PPL's own advanced-stage data-center pipeline is 31.8 gigawatts, with 11 signed — but Invitium itself is a pure build-ahead-of-offtake bet. CEO Vincent Sorgi expects bilateral contracting, not PJM's centralized backstop auction, to be the real path to new generation. So Vistra says "prove the demand is real before we build," and PPL-Blackstone says "reserve the turbines now, because the multi-year lead times mean waiting for a signature is the actual risk." Exactly the tension. And then there's a third position entirely — Constellation. CEO Joe Dominguez put it bluntly: "the bedrock of building out this early phase of the data economy is going to rely heavily on existing generation... we're never going to build this economy if we have to wait for new power plants." The incumbency argument. Constellation's sitting on about 55 gigawatts of owned generation, 22 of it nuclear, with 1.1 gigawatts of uprates already in the pipeline. Dominguez expects Texas's paused Batch Zero to resume, quote, "without meaningful delay." So where Vistra wants certainty before new build and PPL-Blackstone is betting on speed of new build, Constellation's betting that what's already running and licensed beats both. What's actually constraining all three of them at once? Equipment. Siemens Energy's gas-turbine backlog hit 69 gigawatts as of the quarter ended June 30th — 15 gigawatts booked in that quarter alone — and they're guiding to 90 to 100 gigawatts of total commitments by the end of their fiscal year. Lead times are now 3-plus years. It doesn't matter which of these three strategies you like — you're all waiting on the same turbine factories. And there's a real dollar cost to picking the wrong side of the Texas pause specifically. Reuters, via the same Utility Dive digest — developers who posted the required $50,000-per-megawatt security deposits for ERCOT's Batch Zero are looking at losing hundreds of millions of dollars, with no clear timeline for when the audit-driven freeze lifts. That's the first hard number on what's actually stranded, not just delayed. So today's energy story in one line — the shortage is real, the turbines are the bottleneck, and everyone's placing a different bet on how to get to the front of a line that Siemens, not Texas, actually controls. And it's worth watching which strategy actually gets validated first. If PPL-Blackstone lands a signed hyperscaler offtake in the next couple of quarters, the build-ahead bet looks prescient. If it takes years, Vistra's skepticism about the queue looks like the disciplined read. Either way, Constellation's the one that doesn't have to wait on that answer at all — they're monetizing capacity that's already turning. Which might be the quiet lesson underneath all three of today's positions — in a supply-constrained market, whoever already owns generation gets to watch everyone else's bet play out from a position of strength. It's a genuinely useful lens for reading every future gigawatt announcement this year — ask whether it's contracted demand, speculative queue-squatting, or existing capacity being repriced, because those are three completely different investment cases wearing the same headline. Philippines Philippines, and there's a genuine human toll to lead with today, not a market line. The combined death toll from Tropical Storm Luis, Tropical Storm Maymay, and the enhanced habagat monsoon rains has risen to 19 — up from 12 on Sunday, 15 on Monday. NDRRMC puts the affected population at 2.27 million people, 646,676 families, across ten regions. Roughly 95,000 people are currently in evacuation centers. Where's it hitting hardest? Landslides — nine deaths in Baguio City alone, three more in Benguet. There's no active cyclone in the Philippine Area of Responsibility right now — the former tropical storm Peilou exited Tuesday morning without making landfall — but the habagat rains are continuing, and PAGASA's got an orange rainfall warning up for Zambales, Bataan, and Occidental Mindoro, 100 to 200 millimeters. This is a live, escalating disaster, not a forecast recap. There's also a political story that's landed with real force — an actual account of how the Marcos-Duterte alliance fell apart. This is a notable one. Congressman Sandro Marcos revealed that the Duterte camp demanded control of the Executive Secretary post, the Senate presidency, and the Speakership as their 2022 price for backing Bongbong Marcos's presidential run. That's a remarkably specific and remarkably damaging thing to reveal publicly. Malacañang has confirmed the account — the President himself said his son "will not lie." It's the first detailed public telling of how UniTeam actually collapsed, and the timing isn't subtle — it lands the same week the Duterte impeachment trial resumed. Speaking of which — where does the trial stand? Back underway Tuesday morning at 10am after Monday's session was postponed for weather. COA auditor Xylene Mae del Campo is back on the stand, covering the confidential-fund audit portions the trial didn't get through on Monday. There's also a cabinet change worth a line. Edwin Mercado, the former PhilHealth CEO, has been named the new Health Secretary, replacing Jose Pujalte Junior, who resigned less than a month into the job. And the economic story — BSP looks like it's shifting its posture. Governor Remolona is signaling a softer tilt ahead of the August 27th Monetary Board meeting — "everything on the table," including a pause, after Q2 GDP growth slumped to just 2.3%, the worst print since the 2021 pandemic contraction, well below the 5.4% year-on-year print prior. The policy rate currently sits at 4.75% after hikes in April and June, and markets had actually been pricing a third straight hike. That's a real reversal in expectations. It is — weak growth is now outweighing the inflation case for tightening. The peso closed Monday at 60.70 to the dollar, strengthening from Friday's 60.90 close. We're skipping the PSEi today — it was flat, 6,289.21, essentially a non-move. It's a genuinely difficult needle for Remolona to thread — the same disaster driving up that flood death toll is also going to weigh on Q3 growth, right as the central bank is deciding whether 2.3% growth already justifies easing. And it lands on top of a government that just submitted a 7.2-trillion-peso budget built on stronger growth assumptions than 2.3%. If the slowdown persists, the gap between what Congress is being asked to fund and what the economy can actually generate gets harder to paper over. Vocab Of The Day 到了语言时间了。 没错,我们先说普通话。今天第一个词是"与其…不如",发音是 yǔqí bùrú。 与其等,不如先动手 — 与其等待确定性,不如先行动。这跟今天的能源故事完全对应,对吧? 完全对应。Vistra 说"与其现在建,不如先把队列清理干净";而 PPL 和黑石说"与其等合同,不如先把涡轮机订下来"。这是一个很正式的书面语结构,常见于财经评论,比口语的"比起…更"更有力度。 那第二个词呢? 第二个是"说到底",shuōdàodǐ — 意思是"归根到底""追根究底地说"。 说到底,TileRT 的论点是软件的灵活性胜过硬件的专用性。这个词也是分析性很强的表达,比口语的"说白了"更沉稳、更有分寸,常用在深度分析的结尾,总结整个论证的核心。 对,而且它是一个很好的HSK四级抽象搭配 — 不是具体名词,而是一种逻辑总结方式,这正是听众需要加强的地方。 Good, now let's switch — Tagalog. Sige, tara na. Unang salita ngayon: "nabuwag." Nabuwag ang alyansang UniTeam nang malantad ang tunay na kasunduan noong 2022 — ibig sabihin, "naghiwalay" o "nasira," pero mas espesipiko ito para sa isang alyansa o relasyon, hindi para sa isang gusali. Tama — iba ito sa "bumagsak," na parang isang gusali o presyo na biglang gumuho. Kapag alyansa o relasyon ang usapan, "nabuwag" ang tamang salita. Pangalawang salita: "lumala." Lumala ang bagyo, lumala ang baha, lumala ang bilang ng mga namatay — mula 12, hanggang 15, hanggang 19 ngayon. "Lumala" ay ginagamit kapag ang isang masamang sitwasyon ay nagiging mas malala pa — hindi lang tumataas ang bilang, kundi tumitindi ang buong sitwasyon. Malungkot na balita, pero mahalagang bokabularyo. Apat na salita ngayon — dalawa sa Mandarin, dalawa sa Tagalog — lahat konektado sa mga balita natin ngayon. Arts & Culture Arts and culture, and I know you've had your eye on this first one specifically. Tokyo Gendai — the fourth edition of the fair runs September 11th through 13th at PACIFICO Yokohama, VIP preview on the 10th, and VIP registration opened today. You've actually got a pass for this one. I do. Fair director Eri Takane has named 63 exhibitors this year, split across five tiers. The main Galleries section has 17, including Pace, Sadie Coles HQ, Ceysson and Bénétière, Taka Ishii, and Mizuma Art Gallery. There's a "Hana" section for emerging and mid-career galleries, an "Eda" section for historically significant figures, and — new this year — a section called "Miki," dedicated entirely to works on paper, photography, and printmaking. What's the thinking behind adding that? It's a deliberate nod to Japan's own ukiyo-e and print lineage — and honestly, it reads as Tokyo Gendai courting a more connoisseurial, market-cautious buyer rather than chasing the blue-chip Basel-and-Frieze circuit head-on. There's also a city-wide festival tied into the VIP programming. The inaugural Maebashi Biennale — September 19th through December 20th, theme "Mebuku." It's an 80-day festival spread across Arts Maebashi, the Maebashi Literature Museum, and public spaces touched by architect Sou Fujimoto. It's a real bet that Gunma's a declining regional capital can pull off what Naoshima and Echigo-Tsumari managed before it — using contemporary art to actually revive a place, not just decorate it. Second item — White Cube's made a real signing. They now represent the Ethiopian painter Tesfaye Urgessa, born 1983 — he was the first artist to represent Ethiopia at its inaugural national pavilion, Venice Biennale 2024. His debut show with the gallery, "The Lingering Departure," opens in Hong Kong September 9th, new paintings on migration and family. And there's a coordinated push beyond just the one show. A companion piece, "Fiber of grace," goes to Frieze Seoul the same week. That kind of 2-city rollout is how a mega-gallery signals a new signing is meant to be taken seriously immediately, not built up slowly. Last one, and it's a sharp piece of criticism, not an exhibition. Daniel Mendelsohn, the classicist, has a piece in the NYRB's August 20th issue on Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey." His read is that the film is, quote, "densely braided," but its hero "sounds like the heroes of Christopher Nolan movies." Ouch. It's a genuinely sharp critique of what happens when an epic gets run through a very specific directorial voice — worth reading if you've seen the film and felt something was slightly off about Odysseus's register. It's the classic adaptation problem — the source material survives 3,000 years of retelling precisely because it isn't any one voice, and the moment a famously singular director gets his hands on it, the hero starts sounding like every other protagonist that director's ever made. Mendelsohn's point, more or less — technically dazzling, but Homer's polytropos, the "man of many turns," becomes just another Nolan puzzle-box lead. It's the kind of review that's more useful than a straightforward pan, honestly — it tells you exactly what you're getting and exactly what you're trading away for it, which is more than most opening-weekend coverage manages. That's the value of having an actual classicist review it instead of a film critic alone — he's grading it against 3,000 years of prior adaptations, not just this year's box office. Op-Eds & Commentary Op-eds — two pieces genuinely shaping conversation right now, and they're in tension with each other in an interesting way. First, John Authers and Richard Abbey in Bloomberg Opinion, a piece called "AIndicators Hint at Doubts in Credit Markets," published yesterday. Steelman it for me. They're launching a new framework — "AIndicators" — that tracks AI-buildout risk through credit markets instead of equities, on the theory that lenders' willingness to keep financing data centers, chips, and power is the real signal, not stock prices. They draw the nineteenth-century railroad-bond parallel — Jay Cooke, Northern Pacific — transformative technology still needs financing to outrun the crisis it creates, and their early readings already show credit-market doubt creeping in even as equities keep hitting records. And the counter? The 1873 railroad panic came from over-leveraged speculative lines, not from the railroads being a bad idea — and railroads did eventually pay off. Today's hyperscaler capex, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, Google, is funded mostly off fortress balance sheets and free cash flow, not junk debt, which weakens the historical parallel considerably. Credit-spread "doubt" might just as easily be pricing Fed-policy uncertainty as anything specific to AI. The second piece is about the Fed directly. Anil Kashyap, guest column in the Washington Post, "The Fed should explain its decisions," from last week. His steelman — Chair Warsh rattled markets with vague "determined to hit target" language and no operational roadmap, after five years of inflation misses, and with reports surfacing of direct Trump-Warsh phone calls, the Fed needs to over-communicate right now to actively defend its independence. Where does that argument break down? More talk doesn't fix a structural conflict. Warsh was installed explicitly as a Trump-aligned pick — no amount of explaining resolves that independence problem at its root. And over-communicating in real time actually risks a reactive, whipsawing Fed that ends up telegraphing into political pressure instead of shielding against it. Sometimes the honest position is less certainty, not more words. Two very different theories of what transparency is actually for, in two very different institutions. One Good Thing One good thing to close on — tomorrow, August 12th, there's a total solar eclipse. Where's it visible? It's the first total eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999, and Spain's first in over a century — the last one there was in 1905. The path of totality is about 290 kilometers wide, up to 2 minutes 18 seconds of totality, sweeping from Siberia across eastern Greenland and west Iceland, ending over northern Spain and Portugal right at sunset. A sunset total eclipse sounds genuinely spectacular. If the skies cooperate, it should be one of the more photographed astronomical events of the year. That's The Morning Commute for Tuesday, August 11th. Speed versus certainty, from power grids to GPUs to political alliances — and tomorrow, literally, the sky puts on its own show. We'll see you tomorrow. 与其…不如 rather than X, better to Y (weighing two options and favoring the second) Energy segment — Vistra's queue-cull-first posture versus PPL-Blackstone's build-ahead-of-contract bet on gas turbines 说到底 when you get down to it, in the final analysis (cutting through to the core claim) Deep Dive — SemiAnalysis's TileRT piece, where GPU fungibility beats purpose-built ASIC hardware nabuwag broken up, dissolved (an alliance, relationship, or organization coming apart) Philippines — Rep. Sandro Marcos's account of how the 2022 Marcos-Duterte alliance actually fell apart lumala worsened, intensified (a bad situation growing more severe, not just more frequent) Philippines — the habagat/tropical-storm flood death toll rising through the week

docs.text: Monday, August 10, 2026 Cold Open Good morning — this is The Morning Commute for Monday, August 10th. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex, and the headline number today is a strange one — the US economy actually lost jobs in July, and markets rallied anyway. Payrolls fell by 23,000 when everyone expected a gain of 80,000. That is objectively bad data, and the S&P still closed the week up. Bad-news-is-good-news, because a weak labor market makes rate cuts more likely. We'll get into whether that's a healthy read or a dangerous one — Paul Krugman and the Washington Post editorial board are already fighting about exactly that. The same split shows up inside earnings too — Atlassian posting its fifth straight beat on AI adoption, while The Trade Desk got hammered 22% on collapsing ad demand. Same economy, two completely different stories. And it shows up again in the power market, where SpaceX is muscling in as a new gigawatt-scale electricity buyer at the exact moment RWE is cashing out of US offshore wind entirely. Plus the Philippines turning its SONA promises into an actual budget number, a new nuclear-armed defense pact reshaping the Middle East, and Sudan's civil war reopening urban warfare near Khartoum. Let's get into it. Headlines Starting in Gaza, and there's a real gap opening up between what Israeli officials are saying publicly and what they're actually doing on the ground. Walk me through it. Publicly, Netanyahu and Defense Minister Katz have been adamant — no reconstruction in Gaza until Hamas fully disarms. That's been the line for weeks. But we've learned that on Saturday, the two of them privately approved rehabilitation and housing infrastructure work in an IDF-controlled pocket of eastern Rafah, right near the so-called Yellow Line. So the private posture and the public posture don't match. Not even close. And there's a backdrop that makes it more plausible — there have now been five straight days with zero Israeli strikes inside Gaza, and the IDF has pulled back behind that Yellow Line. Israeli officials are framing that quiet as the signal for Hamas to actually start disarming under the July 30th Board of Peace deal. Does Hamas see it that way? No. Their negotiator, Ghazi Hamad, told Al Jazeera they won't disarm until Israel meets its own obligations first — halting attacks, withdrawing troops. So you've still got a sequencing deadlock. But this Rafah move is the first concrete, on-the-ground action either side has taken since that dispute became public last week, and it's a real test of whether the framework survives actual implementation, not just statements. Second world story, and this one's had almost zero coverage anywhere despite being enormous — Sudan's civil war just escalated into open urban warfare again. The Sudanese Armed Forces have launched their biggest ground offensive since retaking Khartoum, recapturing five towns in North Kordofan in the last two weeks. What's the strategic value of those towns? They dismantle a key Rapid Support Forces logistics corridor and reopen the Saderat Road, the main supply line into the state capital, El-Obeid. But the RSF commander, Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo — everyone calls him Hemedti — put out a video on July 30th ordering his forces to retake Khartoum outright. Heavy clashes are now happening at Um Samima, about 50 kilometers west of El-Obeid. That's a real escalation, not posturing. It gets worse — on August 2nd, an SAF drone strike killed 37 people at a civil court in an RSF-held village in Darfur. And the UN said on the 7th that more than a thousand days into this war, millions of Sudanese children are now either displaced or out of school entirely. This is the world's largest displacement crisis, and it's sliding back toward the exact kind of urban combat that flattened Khartoum the first time. And it's getting a fraction of the attention Gaza or Ukraine get. Market Overview Onto markets, and Friday's close, since today's session just opened. S&P 500 finished at 7,757.64, up 47.68 points, 0.62%. Nasdaq led the pack — up 342 points, 1.30%, to 26,690.62. Dow up a more modest 0.28% to 54,036.93. Russell 2000 up 1.10% to 3,034.49. A genuinely strong session across the board, but the reason WHY is the interesting part, because it traces straight back to that jobs number I mentioned at the top. Nonfarm payrolls for July came in at negative 23,000 — an outright loss — against a consensus estimate of positive 80,000. That's not a miss, that's a completely different sign. And it's not a one-off. May and June got revised down by a combined 103,000 jobs. Unemployment did tick down to 4.1%, from an expected 4.2%, but that's largely a function of people leaving the labor force, not people finding work. Put together, that's about as clean a rate-cut signal as the Fed could ask for, and markets read it exactly that way — yields fell, stocks rallied. Ten-year Treasury eased to 4.65% from 4.69% the day before. Elsewhere — Brent crude 84.75, up 1.44%. Gold basically flat at 4,394.60. In FX, the yen stayed soft, dollar-yen at 158.83, up 0.69%. No records, no war-premium spike — this was entirely a rates story. Bad labor data, read as good news, because it makes the Fed's next move easier to call. Which sets up a real argument later in the show about whether that read is actually healthy. U.S. Business Two earnings prints that couldn't look more different, and together they tell you exactly where corporate spending is and isn't holding up. Start with Atlassian — fiscal Q4, and it's a clean, big beat. EPS $1.87 against an estimate of $1.50, a 24.5% beat. Revenue $1.77 billion versus $1.66 billion expected. What's driving it? Cloud revenue accelerated to 31% growth. Non-GAAP operating margin hit 36%, up from 24% a year ago — that's real operating leverage, not just top-line growth. And their AI product, Rovo, is now deployed at more than 80% of the Fortune 500. Stock jumped 35% on the print. That's their fifth straight beat-and-raise quarter. So enterprise software spend on AI tooling is still very much alive. Very much. Now flip to The Trade Desk, and it's the mirror image. Q2 revenue $715.1 million, only up 3% year over year — a real miss. Non-GAAP EPS $0.34, down 15.1% versus consensus. And the guide for Q3 is the part that actually spooked the market — $650 million, more than 19% below what analysts expected, which implies revenue actually SHRINKS about 12% year over year. That's a rough one. Stock fell nearly 22% on the day, and kept sliding as Evercore ISI, Guggenheim, BMO, and DA Davidson all cut their ratings. Management pointed to weak demand from consumer packaged goods and auto advertisers specifically. So put those two next to each other — enterprise software spending on AI tools, booming. Discretionary ad spend from consumer-facing brands, contracting hard. That's not one economy, that's two economies running at different speeds inside the same earnings season. Which is exactly the tension underneath that jobs number too. International Business & Politics Big geopolitical story first — Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a mutual-defense pact in Mecca on Friday. This is genuinely significant — it's structured like NATO's Article 5, an attack on one treated as an attack on all three. Who signed it? MBS, Erdogan, and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, building on a bilateral Saudi-Pakistan deal from last September. And the composition matters enormously — Turkey brings NATO's second-largest military. Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim-majority state in the world. So this is explicitly a deterrent. That's how analysts are reading it — a shield against further strikes on Saudi Arabia tied to the broader Iran conflict. Iran itself dismissed the pact within a day, saying it won't actually guarantee Saudi security. But the more interesting reaction came from Israel — Netanyahu and his allies are now casting Turkey as, quote, "the new Iran," warning of an emerging radical Sunni axis. Which is a notable thing to say with Israeli elections looming. Very notable. This is a brand-new nuclear-armed bloc reshaping the entire regional chessboard the Hormuz story has been running on, and it happened without a single additional shot fired. Second story is closer to our usual beat — India's own AI-infrastructure buildout just went supersized. Adani Group has proposed a 1-trillion-rupee data center in Odisha — that's roughly 12 billion dollars — for a single 1-gigawatt AI facility. It would be India's second-largest, behind only Google's project in Andhra Pradesh. How does Adani's financing model compare to what we've seen from Microsoft or Meta? Completely different shape. This is conglomerate financing, not hyperscaler balance-sheet financing. Adani Green's operational renewable capacity already hit 20.1 gigawatts as of June 30th, up 27% year over year, and power revenue is up 29%. But today, Adani's CFO, Jugeshinder Singh, told analysts that rising group-wide capex now requires treating contractors as, quote, "strategic partners" rather than vendors — and Adani group stocks traded red on those remarks. Meaning the market's nervous about how much of that capex risk gets pushed downstream onto contractors. Exactly. It's the AI-capex arms race, but running through an entirely different corporate structure than the one we've been tracking in the US. China China's July inflation data landed Sunday, and it points the same direction as everything else we've covered on China lately — cooling domestic demand underneath a still-strong export engine. CPI came in at just 0.5% year over year, down sharply from June's 1.0%, and well below the 0.8% forecast. What about core inflation? Core CPI, stripping out food and energy, held up better at 0.9%. But headline CPI actually fell month over month, down 0.1%. Producer prices told the same story — PPI up 3.5% year over year, down from 4.1% in June, missing estimates, and down 0.7% on the month. So consumer and factory-gate prices both losing momentum at once. Right, and remember, this lands right on top of the July trade data we covered last week — a $112.5 billion surplus, exports still growing at nearly 24%. That external strength is intact. It's the internal, consumer-facing side of the economy that keeps softening every time a new data point comes in. Same two-speed China story, just with a new data set attached to it. Deep Dive Alright, Deep Dive, and this one's straight from the inbox — SemiAnalysis, a piece published last week titled "SpaceX 10GW in 2027," and it's a genuinely wild read on how fast SpaceX is about to become a power-buying whale. Set the scene — what did Musk actually say? On SpaceX's first-ever public earnings call, Musk guided to 6 to 8 gigawatts of INCREMENTAL compute capacity in 2027 alone, with what he called "potential well above 10 gigawatts." SemiAnalysis prices that out at roughly 50 billion dollars per gigawatt, which puts total 2027 capex somewhere between 300 and 500 billion dollars. That's Amazon-or-Google-scale annual capex, from a company that doesn't remotely have Amazon or Google's cash generation. Which is exactly the puzzle the piece is trying to solve. The economics that justify it are genuinely staggering — running a frontier model on a GB300 cluster can generate more than 100 billion dollars per gigawatt per year in API inference revenue, against roughly 12 billion dollars per gigawatt per year in cost. Anthropic's Opus model is reportedly running gross margins above 85%. So inference itself is wildly profitable, and the constraint isn't demand, it's raw electricity and compute supply. Exactly — and that's why SemiAnalysis names Microsoft as the largest likely buyer of SpaceX's capacity. Microsoft reworked its OpenAI deal back in April, dropping the old 20% revenue-share arrangement, which means Microsoft now keeps the full upside on OpenAI-model inference instead of splitting it. They've already signed more than 10 gigawatts of binding capacity so far this year — something like 300 billion dollars in new commitments — a total reversal of the leasing pause they had in place as recently as last year. What's the actual math pushing Microsoft that hard? Serving OpenAI under the old IaaS-style arrangement nets Azure only about 14 million dollars per megawatt per year. But if Microsoft instead sells that same GPU footprint itself, through products like Foundry or Copilot, the model says the opportunity is worth more than 100 million dollars per megawatt per year. That gap is why SemiAnalysis thinks Azure's revenue growth could jump from around 42% to over 100% next year, just by shifting the mix. Now, SpaceX doesn't have a hyperscaler balance sheet to fund any of this. How are they actually paying for it? Two mechanisms. First, Nvidia vendor financing — which the piece says explains why Musk declared himself "Nvidia exclusive" on that same earnings call, abandoning prior signals that SpaceX was evaluating TPUs and AMD chips. Second, premium pricing — SpaceX is charging 30 to 50 million dollars per megawatt per year, well above cost-plus norms, justified by build speeds nobody else can match. How fast are we talking? Their first site, Colossus 1 — 300 megawatts — went up in 122 days. There's a gas plant built one kilometer across the Mexico border specifically to dodge US permitting timelines. And their Southaven, Mississippi site scaled from about 495 megawatts in February to over 1.2 gigawatts by July. Current total SpaceX capacity is only around 2 gigawatts by the end of this year — so hitting 10 gigawatts in 2027 means roughly a five-times acceleration in a single year, almost entirely on onsite gas generation. Here's the question I keep coming back to — is this genuinely different from the Nvidia-OpenAI circular financing story we've already covered, where Nvidia is effectively bankrolling the customer that buys its own chips? Or is it the same trick with a different name on the door? I'd argue it's a real distinction, actually — with OpenAI, the revenue backing the financing is still mostly promised, forward-looking. Here, the inference economics SemiAnalysis is modeling — that 100-billion-per-gigawatt figure — already exist today, in Anthropic's actual margins. The demand side of this bet is validated, not hypothetical. That doesn't make it risk-free, but it's a materially different kind of bet than pure circular financing. Attributed clearly — that's SemiAnalysis, from the inbox, published last week. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities And that SpaceX story is actually the perfect bridge into today's Energy segment, because it turns SpaceX into a fourth gigawatt-scale power buyer, competing for exactly the same gas turbines and interconnection capacity as the hyperscalers — but the two biggest energy stories today are actually about someone walking AWAY from power infrastructure, not toward it. Start with the RWE number, because it's a real one — 1.22 billion dollars. RWE Americas just relinquished all three of its remaining US offshore-wind leases — New York Bight, offshore California, offshore Louisiana — to the Department of the Interior for that amount. How does that compare to other developers walking away? This is the fifth DOI lease buyout under the current administration, but it's the first one at this scale, which matters because it gives the market an actual clearing price for exiting a permitted-but-stalled US offshore position. Up to now, everyone's been guessing at DOI's settlement appetite. Now Ørsted, Avangrid, anyone else stuck in the same position has a real number to benchmark against. Is the offshore-wind retreat total, or is there pushback? There's real pushback — a federal judge ordered the Pentagon just last week to lift its freeze on a separate wind project, so this isn't a uniform policy being applied evenly. It's being litigated project by project, with genuinely split outcomes depending on the specific legal posture. Meanwhile, capital is still pouring into energy infrastructure more broadly, just rotating away from stalled-permit risk. Energy Capital Partners closed its sixth flagship fund at 8.1 billion dollars — more than 50% above its original 5 billion dollar target. That's a big oversubscription. And it's not isolated — Avantus just doubled its corporate credit facility to 1.05 billion dollars. Both of those are the same signal — money moving from merchant, permit-exposed offshore wind into asset-backed, build-own-operate infrastructure plays. Developer-to-IPP, basically, is where the capital wants to sit right now. Which loops straight back to the SpaceX story from the Deep Dive — SpaceX is now a fourth entrant fighting for the same gas-turbine supply and interconnection capacity that AEP's 13-gigawatt turbine lockup and Texas's ERCOT freeze are already straining. The difference is SpaceX isn't waiting in a queue at all — with that three-to-five-month build speed, they may simply bypass ERCOT and PJM entirely and go fully behind-the-meter. So you've got wind developers exiting stalled permits with a fresh clearing price, private capital rotating into asset-backed generation, and a brand-new, faster-moving buyer skipping the interconnection queue altogether. Three different responses to the exact same bottleneck. That's the state of the grid right now — everyone's solving for the same constraint, just choosing completely different paths around it. Philippines Big Philippines story today, and it's the number we've been waiting on since the SONA speech — the actual 2027 budget. The Department of Budget and Management formally submitted a 7.2 trillion peso National Expenditure Program to Marcos this morning, ahead of transmittal to Congress tomorrow. How does that compare to this year? It's up 407 billion pesos, about 6%, from this year's 6.793 trillion budget, and it works out to 21.7% of GDP. The theme is "People-Centered Growth" — education, health, food security, infrastructure, disaster resilience all prioritized. This is the first hard number attached to everything Marcos promised at SONA, and it sets up what's going to be a real fight in Congress over the next few months. Any concrete legislative movement to go with it? Yes, actually — the House ways and means committee approved a bill today raising the personal income-tax exemption ceiling. That's the first committee-level vote on a SONA tax priority, so it's moved from a promise into actual legislation, just two weeks after Marcos flagged it. Separate story, and a genuinely notable one — the Palace signaled today that a decision on the US extradition request for Apollo Quiboloy is coming "in a couple of weeks." Remind people who that is. Quiboloy is the founder of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ church, facing US sex-trafficking and child-trafficking charges from a 2021 indictment. Palace Press Officer Claire Castro confirmed the Department of Justice received the formal extradition request last Friday. There are two legal pathways available — temporary surrender, where he'd be extradited now and returned later for any Philippine trial, or deferred surrender, where Philippine cases get resolved first. That's a genuinely consequential decision either way. One quick procedural note — the Duterte impeachment trial got postponed today because of weather disruptions from the Habagat monsoon; it resumes tomorrow. And speaking of the weather — no active tropical cyclone in the Philippine Area of Responsibility right now, the storm system that was being tracked has moved outside PAR with no landfall threat. But PAGASA did raise an orange rainfall warning today for Bataan, Zambales, Metro Manila, and parts of Bulacan, Pampanga, Rizal, and Cavite, from the enhanced Southwest Monsoon. That's real, active weather, not a routine forecast — worth flagging. A busy day on every front — budget, tax policy, and a major legal decision all landing at once. Vocab Of The Day 现在是"每日词汇"时间。今天的两个中文词都跟今天的新闻直接相关。 好,那我们开始吧。第一个词是什么? 第一个词是"在…的推动下" — zài… de tuīdòng xià,意思接近"driven by"或者"propelled by"。今天的市场就是个好例子——在疲软就业数据的推动下,股市反而全线上涨了。 这个说法听起来挺正式的,跟口语里的"因为…所以"有什么不一样? 问得好。"因为…所以"只是说明一个简单的因果关系,谁都能这么说。但"在…的推动下"是财经报道里非常固定的搭配,强调某个具体的力量在背后持续推着事情往前走,而不只是一个一次性的诱因。所以记者写市场分析、行业趋势的时候特别喜欢用它。 明白了 — 所以如果我要形容SpaceX明年的建设速度,应该说"在英伟达供应商融资的推动下"。 完全正确,这就是标准的财经用法。第二个词是"供需失衡" — gōngxū shīhéng,意思是"supply-demand imbalance"。数据中心用电的供需失衡,逼着SpaceX这样的公司自己建电厂。 这个词跟口语里说的"不够用"有什么区别? "不够用"只是简单说数量不够,谁都能这么说。但"供需失衡"是一个更专业、更结构性的说法——不只是"不够",而是供应和需求这两条曲线本身就对不上,不是暂时缺一点就能解决的。分析师专门用这个词描述电力、芯片这些行业的深层问题,而不是一时的缺货。 原来"供需失衡"更强调背后的结构性问题,不只是表面上"不够用"这么简单。 完全正确。学到了吧? 学到了,谢谢!Alright, that's Mandarin — now Tagalog. Sam, ako naman. Sige, simulan mo. Ang unang salita ay "pagbaba" — ibig sabihin, decline o drop. Malaking pagbaba ang naitala sa trabaho sa Estados Unidos noong Hulyo, at pagbaba rin ang tema ng datos ng presyo sa Tsina. Paano ito naiiba sa "bumagsak," na natutunan na natin noong isang linggo? Magandang tanong. Ang "bumagsak" ay biglaan at malakas — parang isang sektor na sumadsad nang husto sa loob ng isang quarter. Pero ang "pagbaba" ay mas pangkalahatan, mas neutral — pwede itong gamitin sa unti-unting pagbagal, tulad ng inflation na dumarahan nang paunti-unti, hindi biglaang bagsak. Kaya sasabihin nating "pagbaba ng trabaho sa Estados Unidos," pero hindi natin sasabihing "bumagsak," dahil hindi naman bigla — nangyari ito sa loob ng ilang buwan. Tama iyan. Ngayon, ang pangalawang salita — "ipinasa," ibig sabihin, passed o forwarded, gaya ng isang batas o badyet. Ipinasa na ng Kagawaran ng Badyet ang 7.2 trilyong pisong badyet kay Pangulong Marcos ngayong araw. Ginagamit din ba ito para sa isang panukalang batas sa Kongreso? Oo, madalas — kagaya ng ipinasa ng House committee ngayong araw ang panukalang batas tungkol sa income tax exemption. Ang "ipinasa" ay laging may pormal na proseso sa likod nito — hindi lang basta ibinigay, kundi dumaan muna sa boto o pagsang-ayon ng isang grupo. Kaya magkaiba ito sa "ibinigay," na mas simple lang, walang kinakailangang proseso. Eksakto. Iyon na ang apat nating salita ngayong araw. Arts & Culture Into Arts and Culture, and we're leading with a real critical fight — MoMA's Marcel Duchamp retrospective, which closes this week after running since April. How big a show is it? Nearly 300 works spanning his entire six-decade career, and it's the first major US retrospective of Duchamp in more than 50 years. It travels to the Philadelphia Museum of Art in October, so this is genuinely the last week to see it in New York. And the reviews are split, from what I understand. Sharply. ARTnews calls it "brilliant," and says it forces a full reconsideration of Duchamp's work — high praise for a show covering an artist this well-documented. But Frieze went the other way entirely, writing that the exhibition is, quote, "built like a mausoleum when it should be a monument to the artist's ungovernable wit and wonder." That's a pointed line — accusing a Duchamp show specifically of killing the humor. Which is the whole critique — Duchamp's entire career was built on wit, provocation, refusing to be pinned down. Frieze's argument is that a big, reverent museum retrospective is almost structurally the wrong format for an artist whose whole project was undermining exactly that kind of institutional reverence. ARTnews would say the scale is what finally lets you see the full arc of his thinking. Genuinely contested, and worth catching before it closes. Second item, opera — Romeo Castellucci's new staging of Messiaen's only opera, "Saint François d'Assise," premiered at the Salzburg Festival on the 4th, marking the 800th anniversary of Francis of Assisi's death. How's it landing critically? German critics — Die Deutsche Bühne, ORF, Bachtrack — are calling it one of the strongest productions of the festival's current era. Castellucci's staging is archaic and austere — live animals, body art — and one review said it found, quote, "rare, immediately gripping clarity" in taking the saint's life literally, as a defense of what it called "the dignity of creaturely wretchedness." How does that compare to Salzburg's other big new premiere this summer? That's the interesting contrast — the festival's other marquee opening is Currentzis and Grigorian's new "Carmen," and reviews on that one are genuinely split, some calling it a triumph, others calling it curiously disembodied. Same festival, same summer, two productions landing in opposite directions critically. Last one, literature and music criticism together — Matthew Aucoin has a profile in the new issue of The New York Review of Books on composer Dylan Mattingly, who spent his entire twenties writing a six-hour opera called "Stranger Love," then followed it with ANOTHER six-hour piece, "History of Life." That's an enormous commitment to a single artistic idea. And Aucoin's praise for it is specific — he says Mattingly has "summoned into being a region of musical experience that's all his own," built on retuned pianos and extended, sun-drenched grooves. It's the kind of profile that's really an argument about scale and patience in composition, not just a write-up of one composer's career. Op-Eds & Commentary Op-Eds today, and it's a genuine head-to-head — two pieces published the same day, both reacting to Friday's jobs report, arguing completely opposite things. Start with Krugman. Paul Krugman, on his Substack, in a piece called "News of the Weak Labor Market." His steelman case is straightforward — the jobs report, that negative 23,000 print against an expected positive 80,000, plus heavy downward revisions to the prior two months, exposes real rot underneath all the boom talk. He points out that underlying job growth has averaged only about 26,000 a month over the past year, alongside falling wage growth. What's the counter? Here's the thing — Krugman's own framework actually undercuts his alarm, if you read it closely. He separately acknowledges that immigration crackdowns have shrunk the available labor pool by roughly the same amount as the employment drop. Which means at least part of this weak payroll number reflects fewer available workers, not collapsing demand for workers. Building a "the boom is fake" verdict on one noisy, heavily-revised report, while ignoring record stock highs sitting right alongside it, is thinner evidence than the piece's confidence suggests. It's a K-shaped economy — some parts weak, some parts strong — not a uniformly weak one. And the second piece is arguing almost the opposite question entirely. Right — the Washington Post editorial board, same day, arguing the Fed itself is the problem, not the economy. Their case is that Fed Chair Warsh was, quote, "unnecessarily opaque" at his press conference after last week's hold, which drew the first dissents of his tenure. He reiterated the Fed's determined to hit its inflation target after five straight years of missing it, but gave no real roadmap for how. What's your counter to that one? Honestly, it's a little rich coming from an editorial page that spent the Powell years complaining the Fed talked TOO much, and moved markets on stray words in a press conference. You could just as easily read Warsh's minimalism as intellectual honesty — an admission that the Fed doesn't actually have a high-confidence forecast to hand markets right now. Demanding more Fed talk risks re-anchoring investors to WORDS instead of data, which is the exact dependency the whole pullback on forward guidance was designed to break in the first place. So one piece says the data's worse than it looks, the other says the Fed's communication is the actual failure — and they're both reacting to the same Friday morning. Which tells you something on its own — when smart people can't agree on whether a weak jobs report is a crisis or a communications problem, that's usually a sign the underlying picture is genuinely murky, not that one side is simply wrong. One Good Thing One Good Thing today, and it's a real full-circle story out of South Africa. Back in 2017, poachers killed the mothers of six white rhino calves in KwaZulu-Natal, and the orphaned calves were taken in by Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife's rehabilitation program. What happened to them? They spent five years being raised and prepared for release back into the wild. And now, all six of them have given birth to their own calves, out in the wild, on their own. It's the first clean proof that orphaned rhinos raised this way can genuinely rebuild a population themselves, not just survive as individuals. That's a real conservation milestone, not just a nice photo. And there's a second piece of good news in the same story — Ezemvelo says the same dehorning and guardianship strategy that raised these calves has also driven an 80% drop in poaching across Hluhluwe-iMfolozi Park. So the whole program is compounding — fewer poached mothers, more orphans successfully rewilded, and now those orphans are having babies of their own. A genuinely full circle, five years in the making. That's it for us today — thank you for spending this half hour with us. We'll be back tomorrow with more. Take care of yourselves. See you then. 在…的推动下 driven by / propelled by (a specific force pushing an outcome forward) Market Overview / Deep Dive — markets rallying on the weak jobs print, and SpaceX's build pace accelerating on Nvidia's vendor financing 供需失衡 supply-demand imbalance (a structural mismatch between supply and demand) Energy segment — the data-center power/interconnection crunch driving SpaceX, Microsoft, and RWE's exit from US offshore wind pagbaba decline, drop (a gradual or general decrease) Market Overview / China — the July US jobs decline and China's cooling CPI/PPI data ipinasa passed, forwarded (a bill, budget, or formal proposal through official process) Philippines — the ₱7.2 trillion 2027 budget submission and the House panel's income-tax exemption bill

docs.title: Friday, August 7, 2026
docs.text: Friday, August 7, 2026 Cold Open Good morning — this is The Morning Commute for Friday, August 7th. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex, and today's got a real hinge in it. Wall Street's record streak finally cracked overnight — the Dow gave back 464 points, the first full-tape pullback we've had in days. Which, on its own, is just noise. But look at what's underneath it. Google effectively conceded the frontier AI race this week — gutted DeepMind's leadership — to bet everything on selling compute instead of building the smartest model. And that capital-allocation logic is rippling everywhere — into Texas's paused data-center queue, into Duke Energy raising 10 billion dollars in fresh equity just to keep the gas turbines coming. Meanwhile the geopolitical fault lines that never really closed are flaring again — a fight over how Gaza's disarmament actually gets sequenced, and the deadliest Houthi strike on Yemen's government in years — both sitting right on top of that Hormuz oil trade that's been running for two weeks now. And the growth cost of all of that friction shows up hardest today in the Philippines, where GDP just posted its weakest quarter since 2009. So — a lot of threads, one rope. Let's start with the world. Headlines First up, Gaza — and this is a genuine reversal from what we told you a week and a half ago. Right, we reported the Board of Peace's disarmament roadmap as done — signed July 31st. Netanyahu just blew that framing up. In a video message yesterday he said, flatly, Israel "did not agree" to it. The dispute is sequencing. The Board's plan is gradual — Hamas disarms in phases, the IDF pulls back in matching phases. Netanyahu wants full Hamas disarmament finished first, before any Israeli withdrawal past the so-called Yellow Line. Hamas, for its part, is saying it's still committed to the roadmap as written. So you've got the two sides that supposedly signed the same deal describing two different deals. Which is the oldest trick in a ceasefire negotiation — agree to the headline, fight over the fine print for as long as it buys you. And the Yellow Line detail matters more than it sounds — that's the internal buffer zone Israeli forces have held since the original ceasefire lines were drawn. Netanyahu holding onto it until AFTER full disarmament means Israel keeps its strongest point of leverage right up to the very end, instead of trading it away in stages the way the Board's roadmap assumed. So from Hamas's side, that reads as Israel asking them to give up their only card first, and trust the rest follows. Exactly the kind of asymmetric ask that's killed plenty of ceasefires before this one. Second world story, and it's grim — Houthi forces launched a large-scale drone and missile attack on Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in Hadramout yesterday, hitting them mid-training-exercise. Somewhere between 45 and 58 government troops killed. That's the deadliest single strike on Yemen's internationally recognized government since 2022. And it didn't stop there — follow-on Houthi strikes this morning wounded 11 civilians across the border in Najran, inside Saudi Arabia itself. So while everyone's watching the Strait of Hormuz for the next tanker headline, the Houthis just reminded the region there's a second front that never actually went quiet. Right, and that's the frame for today — the Hormuz trade gets all the ink, but Yemen's civil war is still live, still capable of pulling Saudi Arabia back in. Market Overview Onto markets, and Thursday finally broke the streak. S&P 500 closed at 7,709.96, down 0.18%. Nasdaq basically flat at 26,348.35. But the Dow dropped 464 points — 0.85% — down to 53,885.10. Russell 2000 off 0.58% to 3,001.55. What's notable isn't the size of the move, it's that it's the FULL tape. Wednesday was a split session — Dow hit a record while the Nasdaq and Russell pulled back. Thursday, even the Dow gives it back. The record-every-day pattern is done, at least for now. Ten-year Treasury barely moved, 4.61, 4.62%. Oil kept sliding — Brent 81.82, down 0.81%, WTI down around 77 to 78 — that Hormuz de-escalation trade is still compounding, still pulling crude toward 75. But the number everyone's actually watching this morning is gold, which popped 1.86% in premarket trade, up almost 80 dollars to 4,379.40. That's not a random move — that's a market positioning ahead of the July jobs report, due at 8:30 Eastern. Consensus is 83,000 nonfarm payrolls. For context, June was a weak 57,000, and that was itself revised down from May's 129,000. Unemployment rate's expected to hold at 4.2%. So this whole show, in a sense, is airing into a number we don't have yet. If payrolls miss again, that gold spike looks prescient and the Fed-cut case gets a lot louder. If it beats, you could see some of this morning's positioning unwind fast. We'll leave it there — quiet-to-negative tape, gold doing the talking, jobs number is the real catalyst today. U.S. Business Two earnings prints worth your time. First, Airbnb, out after the bell — and it's a clean beat despite a real headwind. Revenue 3.61 billion dollars, up 17% year over year, ahead of the 3.58 billion estimate. Adjusted EPS 1.37 versus 1.26 expected. Gross booking value 27.2 billion, up 16%. And nights-and-experiences booked up 10% — actually ACCELERATING from the pace in Q1, which is the number that matters more than the headline beat. Net income 816 million, adjusted EBITDA 1.3 billion, up 21%, a 35% margin. They raised full-year guidance — mid-teens revenue growth, EBITDA margin at least 35.5%. And they did all of that while flagging a Middle East demand headwind — which, given everything we just covered on Gaza and Yemen, is not exactly a surprise. Travel demand is a pretty honest barometer of how nervous people actually are about a region, headlines aside. Second story is the opposite shape — Warner Bros Discovery missed. Revenue 8.717 billion against a 9.21 billion estimate, net income just 100 million dollars. But look inside the miss. Streaming was genuinely strong — up 9% to 3.1 billion in revenue, EBITDA up 75% to 512 million, riding HBO Max international growth plus Euphoria, House of the Dragon, The Pitt. What dragged it down was legacy media — theatrical revenue down 46%, because Supergirl and The Bride both bombed. Ad revenue down 22%, because they lost NBA rights on Turner. And all of this is happening against the backdrop of the 110 billion dollar Paramount merger, which is stuck — a 12-state attorney general coalition has a trial date now, March 2nd, 2027. And starting October 1st this year, Paramount Skydance owes WBD shareholders a 7 million dollar PER DAY "ticking fee" until the deal either closes or gets abandoned. 7 million a day is real money to just sit there accruing while lawyers argue. It's basically WBD getting paid to wait. Not a bad trade if you're the one collecting. International Business & Politics Trade policy story first — the US 50% tariff on Brazilian goods took full effect yesterday. That's now the highest US tariff rate on any country in Latin America. Break down the math — it's a 10% baseline tariff plus a 40% Section 301 penalty, which the administration ties to how Brazil treats US tech firms and broader trade practices. And that stacks on TOP of the separate 50% copper tariff that's already been in force since August 1st. There are narrow carve-outs — beef and orange juice are exempted. Everything else Brazilian pays the full freight. That's a serious escalation with a G20 economy, and it's the kind of story that tends to get buried under the AI-capex headlines, but the trade-policy fallout here is real for anyone with Latin America exposure. Second international item, and we're going to come back to this in much more depth later in the show — the Philippines posted its actual Q2 GDP number this morning. 2.3% year over year, against a consensus estimate of 2.8%. That's the weakest print since 2009. We'll dig into why in the Philippines segment — there's a real domestic story underneath that headline number, not just a global-growth story. But flagging it here because it's genuinely a big miss on the international economic calendar today. China China's July trade data landed this morning, and it's the same two-speed economy we've been tracking, just showing up in a new data set. Trade surplus 112.5 billion dollars — beat the 107 billion estimate, up from 97.7 billion a year ago. Exports up 23.9% year over year, also ahead of the 22.2% estimate — but that's decelerating from June's 27%, which itself was the fastest pace since October of 2021. This is the second straight month exports have slowed. Imports up 27.5%, just under the 27.9% estimate, also cooling from June. But here's the detail that actually matters — shipments to the US accelerated, to 17% year over year, up from around 14% in June. That's not a demand story, that's a front-running story. Exporters are racing shipments out the door ahead of whatever tariff uncertainty is still on the table, not responding to some genuine pickup in US appetite for Chinese goods. Exports to the EU, by contrast, up 16%, while EU imports FROM China actually fell 1%. So Europe's not absorbing the same surge. Put it together and you get the same tension we saw in last week's contracting manufacturing PMI and the industrial-profit slowdown — strong external numbers propped up by front-loading and AI-hardware demand, soft internal numbers underneath. The trade print isn't contradicting that story, it's just the latest place it shows up. Deep Dive Alright, Deep Dive — and today's the good stuff, straight out of the inbox. SemiAnalysis published a piece overnight called "Gemini is Cooked but GCP is Cooking," and it is a genuinely big story about how Google is choosing to fight the AI war. Start with the personnel, because it's dramatic. Google has effectively gutted DeepMind's leadership. Demis Hassabis has been pushed out of day-to-day operations. And Jeff Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, Quoc Le, Oriol Vinyals — some of the most senior technical names in the company's history — are all departing to found their own lab, something called Discovery Loop. That's not a resignation letter, that's an exodus. And SemiAnalysis's read is blunt — this is Google conceding, at the leadership level, that Gemini isn't going to be the frontier-model winner. Their evidence: Gemini's token growth has decelerated from 60% quarter over quarter down to 38%. But here's the twist, and it's the part I actually find more interesting than the personnel drama. While DeepMind loses, Google Cloud wins internally. Thomas Kurian's strategy is what SemiAnalysis calls a "platform company" play — instead of reserving Google's TPU capacity for Gemini, GCP is selling more than 20% of TPU output on long-term contracts to OTHER labs. Anthropic. Meta. Wait — Google is selling its custom chips to Anthropic, one of Gemini's direct competitors? Correct. Because the math works better that way. SemiAnalysis models GCP's 2027 growth guide landing in the mid-100s percent, against a Street consensus of just 64%. They're expecting roughly 250 billion dollars of ADDITIONAL TPU bookings to land in Google Cloud's backlog over the coming quarters. And the unit economics behind it — TPU systems are selling at roughly 35 billion dollars per gigawatt of capacity. So walk me through why that's the smarter bet than just trying to out-model OpenAI. Because frontier-model competition is a zero-sum, capital-incinerating race where even the winner burns enormous cash for years before it pays off — and Google's just watched Gemini's growth decelerate in real time. Selling infrastructure, on the other hand, is a picks-and-shovels business. Every lab racing to build a bigger model needs compute regardless of who wins that race. Google just decided it would rather be the arms dealer than one of the armies. That's a genuinely different bet than Microsoft or Meta are making — they're both still funding frontier-model ambitions AND infrastructure at the same time. Right, and that's exactly why this matters for the capex throughline we've been tracking all week. This isn't just "AI spending continues." It's the first hyperscaler to visibly choose ONE side of that spending — infrastructure monetization over frontier-model prestige — and the market hasn't fully priced what that choice does to the competitive landscape. If Google's TPU backlog really does hit 250 billion in new bookings, that reshapes who's actually capturing the economics of this entire buildout, and it's not necessarily the labs with the flashiest model benchmarks. Attributed clearly — that's SemiAnalysis, this morning's edition, for anyone who wants the full piece. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities And that TPU economics number is actually the perfect bridge into Energy, because the same inbox — Utility Dive this time — has four stories that all connect to exactly this compute-allocation fight playing out on the ground. Start in Texas, since we've been tracking the ERCOT interconnection pause since Wednesday. NRG's CEO, Robert Gaudette, says the company is closing in on a 1.2 gigawatt hyperscaler colocation deal — and doing it WHILE the statewide pause is still active. Which sounds contradictory until you hear his framing. NRG's model is built on creditworthy, contracted load — real offtake commitments, not speculative capacity reservations. Gaudette's argument is that the pause actually helps incumbents like NRG, because it screens out exactly the kind of queue-squatting that's been clogging Texas's interconnection pipeline. The restriction becomes a moat. And there's a hard number attached to how much that pipeline is actually clogged — BloombergNEF now estimates 20% of the ENTIRE US data-center pipeline is at risk of delay because of the Texas moratorium alone. That's the first real quantification we've had of how far this ripples beyond Texas. One state's regulatory pause, one-fifth of the national buildout at risk. That's the kind of number that should be showing up in every hyperscaler's risk disclosures. Second story, and it's a financing one — Duke Energy's CEO Harry Sideris announced the company will issue 10 billion dollars in new equity to fund gas-generation buildout. That's on top of what they're already spending — over a billion dollars a MONTH — to meet what they're calling record demand. Ten billion in fresh equity is a massive dilution ask, and North Carolina's ratepayer advocates are already pushing back, arguing Duke's load-growth projections are inflated specifically to justify that capex number. So the underwriting-discipline fight we've seen play out at Southern and at Exelon — is the load real, or is it padded — is now showing up as a straight equity-dilution fight, and at a utility that ISN'T even in the PJM footprint. This isn't a PJM-specific problem anymore. Third — Dominion's offshore wind project, Coastal Virginia, just got more expensive again. We told you a couple weeks back the cost stack was 11.7 billion, with 228 million in tariff exposure and a 502 million dollar swing from a PJM cost reallocation. Add another roughly 300 million now. What's driving the new number? Three things, per Dominion's own executives — a revised PJM network-upgrade cost re-assignment, the April tariff impact working its way fully through the supply chain, and a slip in the turbine-installation schedule. The practitioner read here is that PJM's interconnection cost-allocation methodology isn't a one-time line item anymore, it's an active variable moving CVOW's cost stack basically every quarter. And for context — RWE, a pure-renewables developer, just took the opposite path entirely. 1.22 billion dollar deal to CANCEL its US offshore wind leases outright and redirect that capital into gas. Same cost-deterioration signal Dominion's dealing with, except RWE just walked away rather than absorb it. There's actually a research framework floating around right now that explains WHY these cost overruns keep landing on the "novel technology" side specifically — a study of over 900 infrastructure projects found that first-time technology providers carry roughly a 32% median cost overrun, against just 10% for established, standardized technology. And that premium concentrates hardest in complex, non-standardized builds — nuclear, gasification, carbon capture. Which tracks with what we've actually seen — Vogtle came in 114% over budget, Olkiluoto 3 in Finland landed at 244% over, and those overruns didn't just hurt ratepayers, they bankrupted the contractors who signed fixed-price deals on them. Right, and it's exactly why financiers now price novel nuclear — small modular reactors, anything first-of-a-kind — with much riskier, variable-cost contract structures instead of the lump-sum deals utilities would prefer. Nobody wants to be the next Vogtle contractor. And there's a labor angle compounding it too — all the skilled-trades capacity that would normally build that kind of first-of-a-kind plant is currently being pulled into data-center construction instead, which has pushed skilled-trades wages 25 to 30% above historical norms. So even if you wanted to build novel nuclear cheaply right now, the workforce to do it is busy pouring concrete for hyperscalers. Which brings us back to the TPU number from the Deep Dive — 35 billion dollars per gigawatt for Google's TPU systems. Put that next to what these utilities are spending per gigawatt of GENERATION just to keep the lights on for that compute, and you start to see the real shape of this buildout — the chip economics and the grid economics are now two completely separate capital markets, moving at different speeds, and increasingly in tension with each other. The compute side is printing the growth guides. The generation side is issuing equity just to keep pace. Philippines Now the story we flagged earlier — Philippine GDP, and it's worse than the headline number suggests once you look inside it. The topline: 2.3% year over year for Q2, against a consensus estimate of 2.8%, and down from Q1's own 2.8%. Quarter over quarter, seasonally adjusted, just 0.6%, down from 0.9% the prior quarter. That's the weakest print since 2009. Break down the sectors, because this isn't a broad-based slowdown — it's concentrated. Services grew 4.5%, agriculture 2.7% — both fine. But industry actually CONTRACTED, down 2.4%. What's behind the industry contraction specifically? Public construction spending has essentially frozen — and that traces directly back to the flood-control infrastructure graft scandal we've been following. When state auditors started digging into how those contracts were awarded, agencies pulled back on new disbursements almost across the board. Add the Mideast oil shock hitting household consumption on top of that, and you get a real, not just statistical, industrial slowdown. NEDA's Balisacan put a number on how bad the hole is — the economy now needs to average 3.7% growth for the rest of the year, Q2 through Q4, just to hit the ALREADY-CUT full-year target of 3.5 to 4.5%. That target itself was slashed down from an original 6 to 7%. And Q2 itself missed even that lowered bar. Marcos is calling it "transitory" and pledging cash aid, fuel subsidies, and tax relief for workers and small businesses. The peso weakened for a second straight day on the miss, down 8.5 centavos to 60.90 to the dollar. The PSEi actually ticked UP 0.2% on some bargain-hunting, but that's not a large enough move to be a story on its own. There's a political angle threading through this too — at Wednesday's 4th LEDAC meeting, on top of the 24-priority-bill legislative package we already told you about, Marcos asked Congress for something new: to temporarily SUSPEND implementation of his OWN 2024 property-valuation law, the Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act. His own law? His own law. The argument is that the new market-value-based tax assessment system is adding costs on businesses and households at exactly the wrong moment, with growth this weak. It's a pretty striking admission — asking to pause your own signature reform because the timing turned out to be terrible. Meanwhile the Duterte impeachment trial ground through more procedure yesterday — Day 13. Presiding officer Escudero ruled that defense lawyer Michael Poa doesn't have a conflict of interest, despite a 2023 meeting with the Commission on Audit over confidential-fund use, after Senator-Judge Tulfo raised the question. The court also formally recognized that House impeachment-hearing records exist, but ruled the contents aren't automatic proof on their own — that's a real evidentiary fight, not just process for its own sake. And one quick real-time note before we move on — no active tropical cyclone in the Philippine Area of Responsibility right now, the storm we mentioned earlier this week has weakened to a low-pressure area well east of Isabela. But Habagat-enhanced rain triggered in-person class suspensions across Metro Manila today — Quezon City, Manila, Las Piñas, Muntinlupa, Parañaque, Malabon, Valenzuela. Not a storm story, just today's operational reality on the ground.
