The 2.6 gigawatt Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project's budget rose about 300 million dollars to 11.7 billion, up from 11.4 billion in April — and they broke it down line by line. Plus 228 million from Trump-administration tariffs. Minus 502 million from PJM reallocating network-upgrade cost assignment away from the project. Plus 234 million in misc costs — cable protection, jacking mitigation, final onshore construction. Their financing partner absorbs about a third of the net increase. Why does that level of line-item detail matter beyond just this one project? Because it's the first time this cycle tariffs, PJM's own cost-allocation reshuffling, and turbine-install schedule risk have all been priced out separately on one live project rather than buried in a single number — a template for reading every other offshore and onshore cost revision this earnings season. And the interconnection-queue fight just went formal at the federal level. PJM's backstop capacity-auction proposal is now an actual FERC filing as of Monday, justified by PJM's own forecast that data-center demand could grow by 70 gigawatts by 2038 — success explicitly conditioned on states protecting retail customers from cost shifts. Same week, the DC Circuit upheld FERC's Order 2023 interconnection-speedup rule against a legal challenge. Separately, New Jersey proposed a statewide virtual power plant framework — notable because Google and Voltus have already partnered there on demand response and accredited capacity. So PJM's putting a number on the table that's roughly ten times its earlier near-term shortfall estimate. And using it to justify shifting backstop costs onto ratepayers — the same who-pays fight we've tracked through the DC transmission rider case, just migrated into the capacity market. Meanwhile Google's starting to sell flexibility back into the same grid its own data centers are straining — a genuinely different posture than just consuming load. Not every utility's telling the same shrinking-pipeline story though, right? Correct — DTE Energy's Q2 call reaffirmed its 30 billion dollar electric capital plan completely unchanged from Q1, execs saying their large-load pipeline, quote, remains steady. That's the mirror opposite of Exelon's 40% pipeline collapse. Treat the TSA-driven queue-shrinkage story as mechanism-and-utility-specific, not an industry-wide trend yet. And there was a real wave of capital into non-gas power this past week too. About 2 billion dollars in a single week — Commonwealth Fusion Systems raised a 1 billion dollar Series B for its Massachusetts tokamak. Antares raised 370 million in Series C plus 100 million in debt for compact nuclear microreactors out of Torrance, California. Antora Energy raised 550 million Series C for thermal storage. And AirTrunk raised 2.3 billion in project-finance debt from BNP Paribas, Crédit Agricole, DBS, and HSBC. Separately, the US banned Chinese-made power inverters on national-security grounds — inverters sit in both data-center power electronics and grid-scale renewables interconnection. So that's a fourth hardware chokepoint now, on top of transformers, high-voltage breakers, and turbines. Exactly, and that capital flood into fusion, microreactors, and thermal storage is essentially the market's own direct hedge against turbine-queue and PPA-price inflation — real money betting the gas-turbine bottleneck doesn't clear anytime soon. Philippines Philippines — and the storm that had a signal up yesterday is already gone. Tropical Depression Luis made landfall at Maconacon, Isabela at 5:30pm Monday, weakened to a low-pressure area by 8pm the same night, and fully dissipated by 2pm Tuesday. Its Signal Number 1, which had covered Cagayan, Isabela, Quirino, Apayao, Kalinga, Mountain Province, Ifugao, and northern Aurora, was lifted by 11pm Monday — so as of this morning there are no PAGASA signals up anywhere in the country. That was fast. Anything behind it? There is — a second low-pressure area formed off Balaon, La Union. PAGASA's five a.m. assessment Tuesday initially called it unlikely to develop, but by Tuesday afternoon they'd upgraded it to a high chance of becoming a tropical depression within 24 hours. If it does, that would be the Philippines' thirteenth named cyclone of the year, and its second in August alone. And the habagat's still doing its own thing underneath all that. The southwest monsoon is active over Metro Manila, CALABARZON, both Mindoro provinces, Marinduque, Antique, Iloilo, and Guimaras. There's an orange rainfall warning, 100 to 200 millimeters, over Zambales and Bataan from the two low-pressure systems, and a yellow warning over Metro Manila, Bulacan, Cavite, and Occidental Mindoro from the habagat. Class suspensions today span Bataan, Nueva Ecija, Baguio City, Pangasinan, and towns across Bulacan, Tarlac, Isabela, and La Union. Typhoon Dolphin remains outside the PAR entirely, no landfall threat. Now the peso, which had its best day in over a month right before this new instability set in. Monday's close was striking — 60.93 to the dollar, up 31 centavos from Friday's 61.24, the strongest close in over a month, since June 19th's 60.775. A sharp reversal off the record low of 61.847 set July 24th, driven by the same Middle East de-escalation optimism we opened the show with, plus broad dollar weakness tied to that coordinated BOJ/US yen intervention. And today? Tuesday the peso gave back some ground — trading around 61.18, weakening roughly 0.4% — sourced through aggregator data since the primary Philippine desks are paywalled today, so treat it as directionally solid, not to-the-centavo exact. PSEi told the same story — Monday closed 6,334.72, up 1.58%, but Tuesday fell back to around 6,301, down about 0.53%. Straightforward profit-taking, markets cautious ahead of Wednesday's inflation print and Friday's Q2 GDP — neither's out yet. So the peso and the PSEi are running exactly the same pattern we're seeing in New York and Shanghai this morning. Precisely the throughline — Monday's rally in Manila was priced on the same Iran de-escalation framework that's already fraying by Tuesday. If Tehran's denial holds and this doesn't actually resolve, Wednesday's inflation print becomes a much harder test for the peso than it would have looked twenty-four hours ago. One more item — the Duterte impeachment trial had a specific new witness today. Commission on Audit auditor Roderick Wamil testified for the prosecution that an accomplishment report Vice President Sara Duterte signed listed expenses — medical aid, food aid, incentives, travel — that aren't permitted under confidential-fund rules. That's a concrete documentary detail beyond the general "trial continues" framing we've had the last few days. Vocab Of The Day Vocab time — two Mandarin, two Tagalog, and today's pair up almost too neatly with the theme of the whole show. 没错，今天想聊两个词，都跟"事情看起来解决了，其实还没有"这个主题有关。第一个是一个句型 — "一方面……另一方面"。 一方面……另一方面 — on one hand, on the other hand. 今天的市场就是最好的例子。一方面，标普和纳斯达克都创下新高，帕兰泰尔的财报也让投资人重新买入AI股；另一方面，德黑兰否认了霍尔木兹海峡的框架协议，油价随时可能重新反弹。(Today's market is the perfect example. On one hand, the S&P and Nasdaq both hit new highs, and Palantir's earnings brought investors back into AI stocks; on the other hand, Tehran denies the Hormuz framework exists, and oil could snap back at any time.) 这个句型好像挺常用的，是不是比较正式？ 算是中性偏正式，财经报道和新闻分析里特别常见，因为它天生就适合摆出两个对立的事实，而不做评判。跟它意思相近的还有"虽然……但是"，不过那个更强调转折、有一点让步的意味；一方面……另一方面更平衡，只是单纯陈述两个同时存在的现实，没有谁压过谁的感觉。今天这期节目里，中国的股市和中国的制造业数据就是最典型的一方面另一方面 — 股市在涨,可是制造业还在收缩。(It's neutral-to-formal register, especially common in financial reporting and news analysis, because it's naturally suited to laying out two opposing facts without passing judgment. A close cousin is "虽然……但是" — although...but — but that one leans more toward a turn or concession. 一方面……另一方面 is more balanced, simply stating two realities that exist at the same time, with neither one overriding the other. This episode's China segment is the clearest example — the stock market's rallying, but manufacturing data is still contracting.) 很实用。那第二个词呢？ 第二个词是"逆转" — 动词，意思是彻底扭转局面。 逆转 — to reverse, to turn completely around. 帕兰泰尔这次的财报就是一次典型的逆转。过去两周股价跌了将近百分之四十，市场都在惩罚资本支出跑得比现金流快的公司；结果一份财报公布，股价直接逆转了整整两周的跌势。(Palantir's earnings this time is a textbook reversal. The stock had fallen almost 40% over the past two weeks, with the market punishing companies whose capex was outrunning their cash flow; then one earnings report came out, and the stock completely reversed two weeks of decline.) 逆转跟扭转听起来意思很像，有什么区别吗？ 问得好。两个词都有"转变方向"的意思，但逆转更强调彻底、干净地把原来的方向倒过来，常用在比分、市场走势这种有明确方向的东西上，比如逆转比赛、逆转跌势。扭转则更常用在抽象的局面或者印象上，力度也可以比较温和，比如扭转局势、扭转形象，不一定是百分之百倒过来，而是往好的方向调整。今天帕兰泰尔的情况是逆转 — 干净利落，一次财报就把趋势整个翻过来了。(Two words, both meaning "to change direction," but 逆转 emphasizes a complete, clean flip of the original direction — it's often used for scores or market trends, things with a clear direction, like reversing a game or reversing a downtrend. 扭转, by contrast, is more often used for abstract situations or perceptions, and can be gentler in force — turning around a situation, turning around an image — not necessarily a full hundred-percent flip, just an adjustment toward something better. What happened to Palantir today is 逆转 — clean and complete, one earnings report flipped the whole trend.) Perfect — one connective for the whole show's tension, one verb for the sharpest single reversal in it. Tagalog naman. Sige. Unang salita natin ngayon: umatras. Umatras — to retreat, to back off, to give back ground. Umatras ang piso ngayong araw, mula sa pinakamalakas nitong pagsara sa loob ng mahigit isang buwan noong Lunes. (The peso retreated today, from its strongest close in over a month on Monday.) Bakit umatras, gayong ang datos noong Lunes ay maganda naman? Kasi ang pag-angat ng piso noong Lunes ay nakasalalay sa balitang pag-atras umano ng Iran mula sa tensyon sa Hormuz — at ngayong araw, mismong si Tehran ang tumanggi sa balitang iyon. Kaya kung babagsak ang batayan, umaatras din ang lahat ng umasa rito. (Because Monday's rise in the peso was riding on the news that Iran was supposedly backing off from the Hormuz tension — and today, Tehran itself denied that news. So when the foundation gives way, everything that leaned on it retreats too.) Ano ang pagkakaiba nito sa bumawi na natutunan na natin dati? Magkasalungat sila sa direksyon — bumawi ay pag-angat pabalik pagkatapos ng pagbagsak, tulad ng ginawa ng piso noong Lunes matapos ang record-low noong Hulyo. Umatras naman ay ang kabaligtaran — pagbibigay-daan, pag-urong pabalik pagkatapos ng isang pag-angat. Kaya ang kwento ng piso sa loob lang ng dalawang araw ay parehong salita — bumawi noong Lunes, umatras naman ngayong Martes. (They're opposite directions — bumawi is rising back up after a fall, like what the peso did on Monday after July's record low. Umatras is the reverse — giving way, pulling back after a rise. So the peso's story across just two days uses both words — it recovered Monday, then retreated Tuesday.) Magandang paraan para ilarawan ang buong linggo sa iisang parirala. Pangalawang salita? Lumaho. Lumaho — to vanish, to fade away, to dissipate completely. Lumaho na ang bagyong Luis ilang oras lamang matapos tumama sa lupa — mula sa isang malakas na depresyon, naging mababang presyon, at bandang alas-dos ng hapon, lumaho na nang tuluyan. (Storm Luis vanished just hours after making landfall — from a strong depression, to a low-pressure area, and by around two in the afternoon, it had fully dissipated.) May kaugnayan din ito sa isang bagay na napag-usapan natin sa Arts segment mamaya, tama? Tama — sa eksibit ni Ellen Pau sa New York, ang tema mismo ay ang paglaho ng Hong Kong na dating kilala niya, unti-unting nawawala habang nagbabago ang lungsod. Kaya lumaho ay hindi lamang para sa bagyo — pwede rin itong ilarawan ang isang bagay na dahan-dahang nawawala, hindi biglaan. (That's right — in Ellen Pau's exhibition in New York, the theme itself is the vanishing of the Hong Kong she used to know, gradually disappearing as the city changes. So lumaho isn't just for storms — it can also describe something slowly fading away, not suddenly.) Ano naman ang kaibahan nito sa simpleng mawala? Mas payak at pangkaraniwan ang mawala — basta wala na, kahit anong dahilan. Lumaho naman ay may bahid ng anggulo o kabagalan sa pagkawala — parang usok o hamog na unti-unting kumukupas hanggang sa wala nang bakas. Kaya mas maganda itong gamitin kapag inilalarawan mo ang isang proseso ng pagkawala, hindi lang ang katotohanang wala na. (Mawala is plainer and more everyday — it's simply gone, for whatever reason. Lumaho carries a sense of gradualness in the disappearing — like smoke or mist slowly fading until no trace is left. So it works better when you're describing a process of vanishing, not just the fact that something's gone.) Beautiful — a word for the storm that's already gone, and the exhibition we're about to get to, tied together by the same idea of fading rather than disappearing all at once. Arts & Culture Arts desk, and we open with a first US survey that's been generating real critical attention. Ellen Pau, the Hong Kong video-art pioneer, has her first American survey now open at SculptureCenter in New York — fifteen works spanning the late 1980s through today, anchored by her 1988 installation "She Moves," water trickling down a wall. Water recurs throughout as metaphor — a crying wall, swimmers in Victoria Harbour, even the scent of tear gas invoked in one piece. What's the critical read on why it matters now specifically? Hyperallergic calls it an elegy to a vanishing Hong Kong — the medium itself, analog and video decay, mirrors the city's own accelerating disappearance under political transformation. Artforum's Pauline Yao frames Pau as central to a post-handover "edge conditions" reading of Hong Kong art history — a serious, overdue survey for an artist rarely given full-scale treatment outside Asia. There's also a gallery-market story sitting right alongside that, isn't there. There is, and it echoes David Zwirner's consolidation last week — Gagosian is exiting Basel entirely, closing a space open since 2019 with 17 shows, and permanently shutting London's Burlington Arcade location too, open since 2023 with 16 shows. A mega-gallery real-estate retreat, one week after Zwirner's own consolidation — the K-shaped art market squeezing even the biggest dealers now. And a loss to note as well. Simone Forti, the Judson Dance Theater-adjacent choreographer who spent seven decades fusing movement, holography, drawing, and poetry, died at 91 in Los Angeles, from complications of Parkinson's. She won the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at Biennale Danza back in 2023. Now to something that's actually splitting opinion right down the middle — Bayreuth. The Bayreuth Festival's 150th-anniversary production, titled "Ring 10010110" — the title's binary code for "150" — has swapped out traditional stage direction for AI-generated live projections, curated by Marcus Lobbes, conducted by Christian Thielemann. And the reception has split sharply along exactly the human-machine line you'd expect. How sharply? The Götterdämmerung curtain call drew boos and whistles specifically for Lobbes' production team, while the singers and Thielemann got warm applause. Seen and Heard International's review of the Rheingold night describes a stampede for the doors, unlike anything the critic had seen, and calls the shifting AI imagery — Helmut Kohl, the World Trade Center towers, a reunification stamp — endlessly, pointlessly transforming shapes, disconnected from what's actually being heard. That's not a hype piece about AI in opera, that's a real fight over whether it belongs there. Precisely — a hundred and fifty years of interpretive tradition at the most self-consciously important Wagner house in the world, and a real contingent of that audience is telling you generative AI doesn't belong in the room with it. And in literature — a genuinely serious piece of criticism worth flagging on its own. T.J. Clark, one of the most important living art critics, has a new essay in the London Review of Books called "Night Visitors," reading the Chauvet cave paintings — bison stampedes, lions, the so-called Venus and Bison-Man pendant, around 37,000 years old — as proof that depiction and language are rival, coexisting cognitive modes, not depiction as some precursor to writing. What's his actual argument for that? Language, he argues, is hierarchical, recursive, and conformist by nature. Paleolithic image-making works differently — by reciprocity, overlap, and what he calls excursion, reaching outward rather than folding back on itself the way language does. A serious argument about what pictures are fundamentally for. One Good Thing One good thing today comes from about as far from a trading floor as you can get — the Southern Ocean. Researchers near Antarctica's South Orkney Islands are documenting what they're calling super-aggregations of humpback whales — over a hundred animals feeding together at once, with blows described as stretching from one horizon to the other. A hundred whales in one place sounds almost unbelievable. That's exactly the point being made — scientists are calling it something not witnessed in over a century, meaning not since before industrial whaling devastated the population in that region. Humpbacks have rebounded faster than any other great whale species since the commercial whaling ban, and in this particular stretch of ocean, researchers now believe they're approaching pre-whaling numbers. After a morning spent on turbine shortages and grid strain, it's a nice reminder that recovery on that kind of timescale is actually possible. It really is — a population pushed to the edge, given enough protected time, quietly rebuilding itself back to what it used to be. That's The Morning Commute for Tuesday, August 4. We'll see you tomorrow. Have a good one, and we'll catch you then. 一方面……另一方面 on one hand ... on the other hand market pricing resolution on three fronts while the underlying facts stay unresolved 逆转 to reverse, to turn completely around Palantir's Q2 beat reversing the AI-capex-punishment pullback umatras to retreat, to back off, to give back ground the peso giving back Monday's de-escalation-driven rally lumaho to vanish, to fade away, to dissipate completely Tropical Depression Luis dissipating hours after landfall, and Ellen Pau's elegy to a vanishing Hong Kong

docs.title: Friday, July 31, 2026
docs.text: Friday, July 31, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Friday, July 31. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Today's throughline is the hyperscaler earnings jury handing down its final verdict of the cycle — Amazon rewarded overnight for AWS's fastest growth in 18 quarters and a $220 billion capex raise, while Apple gets punished for a supply-side memory crunch that is, at the very same hour, handing Samsung a record quarter. One company's shortage is another company's best quarter in company history — that's the tell for where the real bottleneck in this whole AI build has moved to. And it's landing the same morning a hawkish Fed-and-BOJ double hold, plus what looks like the largest single-day currency intervention in history out of Tokyo, sent the 30-year Treasury to a 19-year high. Let's get into it. Headlines World desk first, and the Strait of Hormuz is still very much a live story even with the war premium off its highs. IRGC naval forces disabled two tankers this morning that were running an undeclared transit route under US military air escort. Four other vessels reversed course rather than risk the same treatment. And yet Brent barely moved on it — 89.34 dollars, up just 0.35% this morning. Because the market's now pricing this as containment, not new escalation, and the real number underneath it is the recovery rate — strait traffic is back up to only 30 to 35% of pre-war levels, from roughly 10 ships a day at the low point on July 23rd against a normal pace of about 88. So "recovering" here means going from essentially zero to a third of normal. That's not resolution, that's a chokepoint still being run at reduced capacity by a hostile navy. Second story — Ukraine, and both sides escalated overnight. Russia launched 255 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight, on the heels of Thursday's missile-and-drone barrage that killed more than 10 civilians and put a Russian missile into Polish airspace. Ukraine hit back directly at Russian energy infrastructure — a strike on Lukoil's Volgogradneftepererabotka refinery in Volgograd, plus a Pole-21 electronic-warfare complex near Holubivka in Luhansk. So Ukraine's now targeting Russian refining capacity specifically. Which pulls the ground war back into the same oil-supply narrative as Hormuz — two fronts now putting pressure on the same commodity. And diplomatically, Kazakhstan's Tokayev publicly urged Putin to freeze the war and revive what people are calling Istanbul 2.0, standing right next to him in Omsk on the 25th. Peskov rejected it flat two days later — quote, a freeze as such is impossible. Market Overview Let's do Thursday's close, because it was a genuinely huge one. S&P 500 up 1.7% to 7,437.64. Nasdaq up 2.78%, that's plus 679 points, to 25,122.18. Dow up 1.2%, plus 613.92, to 52,208.06. Russell 2000 up 1.37% to 2,946.10. And that Nasdaq move was almost entirely one stock's fault, wasn't it. Microsoft added roughly 450 billion dollars in market cap in a single session — the largest one-day dollar gain by any stock, ever — up 16% after Azure printed 43% year-on-year growth, its fastest in four years. That dragged the whole semiconductor complex with it: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index up 8.19%, Lam Research up 18%, its best day since 1999, Micron up 18%, SanDisk up 26%. Now the rates side is the more interesting story this morning, because it's not just following stocks. Ten-year at 4.68% Thursday, up from 4.61% Wednesday. Thirty-year at 5.21% Thursday, and it's been pushing past 5.23% this morning — a 19-year high. Two-year at 4.23%. What's actually driving the long end? Two things stacked on top of each other. First, a hawkish Fed hold — three dissents, the first FOMC meeting under new Chair Kevin Warsh, and dissents that wanted a hike, not a cut. Second, and this is the one people are missing — suspected Japanese intervention overnight. If Tokyo's selling Treasuries to fund yen support, that's direct upward pressure on our long end from someone else's currency defense. And by one estimate, around 80% of the recent move in the 10-year is coming from breakevens — inflation expectations — not real yields, which tells you this is more a repricing of the inflation path than a growth story. Gold and oil. Gold around 4,080 to 4,130 dollars, extending Wednesday's 2% rally on dollar weakness, the Fed hold, and Mideast tension all pulling the same direction. Oil, Brent closed Thursday at 90.04, down 0.78%, WTI at 83.87, down 0.7% — both easing slightly even with Hormuz still live, which fits the "contained, not escalating" read. And overseas? Nikkei up 0.71% Thursday to 61,867.43, then up another 2,494 points this morning to 64,362.02 — a chip-sector rebound plus relief that the BOJ held. Shanghai Composite down 0.62% Thursday to 3,804.69. Now, about that BOJ hold and the intervention — it's worth its own beat. Go on. BOJ held at 1% this morning as expected, though hawk Takata dissented for a hike to 1.25%, and they raised the FY26 growth forecast to about 0.8% from 0.5%. But the real story is what happened Thursday night — suspected intervention of around 8.45 trillion yen, call it 53 billion dollars, likely the single largest one-day FX intervention on record, moved dollar-yen from 162.80 to 157 in about an hour. South Korea intervened too. The US Treasury did what's being called rate checks, and Bessent called the yen quote seriously undervalued — which, taken together, reads a lot like coordinated action, not Japan acting alone. And that's the carry-trade risk everyone's been waiting to see re-emerge. Exactly — a sharp, coordinated yen move is precisely the kind of shock that unwinds carry trades fast, and it now has a live transmission channel straight into the Treasury curve, which we're already seeing in that 30-year print. Before we move on, it's worth stepping back and totaling up what this earnings season actually cost. Add up the four biggest capex guides now on the table — Microsoft's roughly 255 to 260 billion for its fiscal year, Meta's floor of about 130 billion, Alphabet's 195 to 205 billion, and now Amazon's fresh 220 billion. You're comfortably north of 800 billion dollars in combined annual hyperscaler capex, and that's before you count what Apple's now quietly committing through its multi-year Broadcom silicon agreement. And the market's verdict on all four of those raises has been almost entirely about growth, not the size of the number itself. Right — Microsoft and Amazon got rewarded because Azure and AWS are both reaccelerating, Meta got punished because its growth wasn't judged fast enough to justify the same spend. Same math, opposite verdicts, purely on whether the growth line backs it up. U.S. Business Apple and Amazon both reported last night, closing out the hyperscaler cycle, and they went in completely opposite directions. Start with Apple, Tim Cook's final call as CEO. EPS 2.02 dollars against estimates of 1.88, up 29% year-on-year. Revenue 109.4 billion, beating 108.75 billion, up 16%. iPhone revenue up 22%. Tariff refunds added 11 cents of EPS and about 2 points of gross margin. That's a clean beat across the board. So why did the stock fall about 7% after hours, wiping out something like 360 billion dollars of market cap? Because Cook flagged, in his own words, significant supply constraints — a memory price surge and chip shortages already hitting Macs, and starting to spread into iPhone and iPad. The Q4 guide came in soft, just 9 to 11% revenue growth, and Services and China revenue both missed. So the market didn't punish the quarter, it punished the guide, and specifically the reason behind the guide. Now Amazon, same night, completely different reception. Revenue 201 billion against estimates of 197 billion. EPS 5.75 dollars versus 1.82 expected, though a big chunk of that beat is a 53 billion dollar unrealized gain on the Anthropic stake marked to market. But the number that actually moved the stock is AWS — 42.2 billion in revenue, up 37% year-on-year, the fastest AWS growth since the fourth quarter of 2021, against estimates of 40.6 billion. AI and custom chips, Trainium specifically, are each individually running north of a 25 billion dollar annualized rate now. Jassy raised the full-year capex guide to about 220 billion, up from roughly 200 billion last quarter. Stock up 10 to 12% premarket. So Amazon raises capex guidance and gets rewarded, the exact opposite of what happened to Meta last week for doing the same thing. Which is the cleanest version yet of the rule this whole earnings cycle has been teaching us — a capex raise gets rewarded when the growth backing it up is real and accelerating, and punished when it isn't. AWS at 37% growth, reaccelerating, buys Amazon the right to spend more. And Amazon's Anthropic stake showing up as a 53 billion dollar mark-to-market gain is the first time we're seeing AI investment gains flow through GAAP earnings directly, not just described as strategic spend. And Apple's the mirror image — the punishment mechanism just moved from "too much demand-side capex" to "not enough supply-side chips." International Business & Politics And that supply-side story has a name, and it's Samsung. Samsung's Q2 was a genuine record — revenue of 171.5 trillion won, up 28% quarter-on-quarter, operating profit of 89.5 trillion won, up 1,814% year-on-year. That's not a typo. And it's almost entirely the Device Solutions division — memory — which alone did 127.5 trillion won in revenue and 89.2 trillion won in operating profit, up roughly 250 times year-on-year, because AI datacenters are chasing HBM supply Samsung physically cannot produce fast enough. While mobile and consumer electronics did the opposite. Mobile, networks, and consumer electronics all swung to operating losses, squeezed by the same rising component costs that are eating Samsung's own margins on the other side of the business. And they're flagging that this tightness runs into 2027, not just through year-end — which is exactly the shortage Cook was describing on Apple's call, from the other side of the supply chain. One company's chip shortage is genuinely another company's record quarter, in the same earnings season, possibly even sourced from the same fabs. And the BOJ-intervention story from the market segment belongs here too — a second major Japanese FX intervention this year, after roughly 732 billion dollars was deployed back in April and May, with the US and Korea now signaling they may be coordinating with Tokyo rather than watching from the side. China China, and the data just turned uglier than expected. July manufacturing PMI came in at 49.2, down from 50.3 — the first contraction in five months and worse than forecast. The composite PMI fell to 49.3 from 50.6. Construction PMI hit a record low of 47.0. And the new-orders sub-index dropped to 48.5, the lowest in 38 months. What changed? The tariff-frontloading export rush that had been propping up the headline numbers is now unwinding. That confirms the second-quarter GDP print of 4.3% wasn't a one-off blip — it was the trend, and the export tailwind that had been partially masking weak domestic demand just went into reverse. Puts fresh pressure on Beijing to actually deliver on its incremental-policies pledge rather than keep gesturing at it. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities Energy desk — and the biggest story is a genuinely new category of site. NextEra and Brookfield are building a data center campus north of 100 billion dollars in total investment on the DOE's shuttered Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant in western Kentucky — a Cold War uranium-enrichment site, 3,556 acres. Brookfield develops and operates 1.8 gigawatts of data center load, paired with a dedicated 2 gigawatt gas plant and up to 2.6 gigawatts of battery storage. And the utility side of that deal is not who you'd expect. Not a big investor-owned utility at all — the local counterparties are Big Rivers Electric Corp, Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative, and Paducah Power System. Tiny co-ops and a muni, suddenly underwriting gigawatt-scale interconnection. 8,000 construction jobs, 600 permanent, completion around 2031. This is the first major case of a federal brownfield being repurposed as a data center site rather than a multi-year greenfield siting fight, and it's a real test of whether small co-ops can actually carry that kind of load themselves, or whether NextEra and Brookfield's capital is just quietly substituting for the co-op balance sheet. How does that compare to the other federal-land deals we've tracked — DOE's coal-council loan guarantees, for instance? Those were about propping up existing coal capacity with federal financing. This is different in kind — it's the federal government's own retired nuclear-enrichment real estate becoming a live data center site, which means the environmental and transmission groundwork is already largely done. Expect DOE to shop more of its Cold War-era land portfolio the same way now that there's a template that closed. Second one — the Entergy gas plant deal that's been wobbling. Entergy's 1.8 billion dollar purchase of the 1.26 gigawatt Cottonwood, Texas gas plant from private equity seller Atlas Holdings is now being called, by at least one analyst, increasingly in doubt. CEO Drew Marsh actually defended it on Thursday's call in almost apologetic terms — quote, we know Cottonwood isn't the shiniest new plant out there. That's a remarkable thing for a CEO to say about an acquisition he's trying to close. It is, and the Louisiana Public Service Commission staff's own analysis says the deal could add 7 to 8 dollars a month to a typical residential bill. The plant's had recent unplanned outages, and Atlas is charging roughly a 1 billion dollar premium over replacement value for what is, by Marsh's own description, a second-hand, outage-prone asset. The whole thing is tied to serving Meta's 10 billion dollar, more than 4 million square foot data center in Richland Parish — and Governor Landry has publicly said Entergy promised him Meta, not ratepayers, would bear the cost, then punted the actual fight to the LPSC. Target close is January 2027, but this is the first genuinely concrete "who eats the cost of speed" case study we've seen, not just a policy argument. Third — FirstEnergy's numbers are just startling on their own. FirstEnergy's contracted-and-signed data center book hit 6.4 gigawatts this earnings season, up about 50% quarter-on-quarter, with another 1.5 gigawatts expected to sign within two weeks. And their West Virginia subsidiary, Mon Power, is seeking a customer surcharge to finance 2.7 billion dollars of new generation — a 2.5 billion dollar gas plant targeted online by the end of 2031, plus 182 million dollars of solar — built, in their own words, mainly for a data center. West Virginia's PSC decision is expected in the second half of this year. So that's now two separate states — Louisiana and West Virginia — financing dedicated new generation for one hyperscaler's load through a general ratepayer surcharge rather than a load-specific tariff. Which tells you the cost-allocation fight isn't a one-off anymore, it's recurring simultaneously across multiple utilities and multiple states at once. One more worth flagging quickly — Texas's PUC approved an order letting an AI data center co-locate directly behind the meter with a wind farm, conditioned on rapid curtailment during grid emergencies and limits on how much it can lean on demand response at the same time. Why does the curtailment condition matter so much to regulators specifically? Because behind-the-meter load has, up to now, largely sat outside the interconnection queue entirely — it doesn't wait in line, and it doesn't automatically owe the grid anything in return. Tying it to mandatory curtailment during emergencies is the first real attempt to make that load a good citizen of the grid rather than a free rider on it, and that's an early template other states will be watching closely for their own behind-the-meter dockets. Philippines Philippines — weather first, and it's actually a quiet picture for once. PAGASA says the Philippines stays free of an active tropical cyclone through early August. There's one low-pressure area sitting about 1,195 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon, outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility, with only a low chance of developing — no signals raised. It'll still bring scattered rain August 1st and 2nd to Eastern Visayas, Central Visayas, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, and Davao Region, and the enhanced habagat is active over Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon, Palawan, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal, Quezon, and the Visayas, with flash-flood and landslide risk flagged in vulnerable spots. And there's a monster storm out there, but it's not aimed at the Philippines. Super Typhoon Dolphin, tracking toward Japan's Ogasawara Islands, well outside the PAR, with JTWC forecasting peak gusts near 305 kilometers an hour — one of this year's Category 5 systems. PAGASA notes its outer bands could still add rain over Bicol, Eastern Visayas, Caraga, and Northern Mindanao around August 3rd and 4th, but there's no landfall threat to the Philippines itself. Now the macro side, and inflation's back in the frame. BSP released its July inflation forecast today — a range of 5.6 to 6.6%, against June's actual print of 6.4%. If that holds, it's a fifth straight month above the BSP's 3% target. The official PSA number lands August 5th. Drivers are elevated pump prices, higher electricity rates, rising fish prices, and peso depreciation — partly offset by softer rice prices, regular milled down 0.74% to 49.30 pesos a kilo. And the pump-price piece connects straight back to Hormuz and Brent from the top of the show. Exactly the throughline — BSP is explicitly naming oil pass-through as an inflation driver, the same Brent volatility we've been tracking all week. On the peso, BSP's reference rate is 61.7450 to the dollar today, market spot around 61.53 — a modest give-back from the record-low close near 61.85 set July 24th and 25th, not a new record. PSEi didn't like the setup though. Fell 69.31 points, 1.1%, to close at 6,236.44, on volume of 1.26 billion shares worth 10.81 billion pesos, decliners edging advancers 93 to 88, services leading the drop. That's profit-taking ahead of next week's index rebalancing, plus caution ahead of a real data wall — July inflation on August 5th, second-quarter GDP on August 7th, and the June labor force survey — on top of record national debt, the ongoing US-Iran risk, and a Pasig court temporary restraining order suspending the 85-peso Metro Manila minimum wage hike, which analysts are citing as a fresh source of consumer-spending uncertainty. That wage TRO seems like a small legal detail to be moving a whole index. It's less about the peso amount and more about what it signals — a wage hike that was supposed to be settled policy got pulled back into the courts just as inflation is running hot on pump prices and electricity. That's exactly the kind of consumer-spending uncertainty investors hate pricing into services-sector names right before three separate data releases in one week. Vocab Of The Day Vocab time. Two Mandarin, two Tagalog, and today's picks actually mirror each other across the two supply stories we just covered. 好，我们开始吧。今天想聊聊供应链的词。第一个词是"供不应求"。 供不应求 — supply cannot meet demand. 三星这个季度的存储芯片就是典型的供不应求 — 需求远远超过了产能，所以利润才会暴涨这么多。(Samsung's memory chips this quarter are a textbook case of supply falling short of demand — demand has so far outstripped capacity that profit exploded the way it did.) 那苹果的情况呢，是不是也一样？ 差不多，只是角度相反。苹果是这场供不应求的受害者，而不是受益者 — 库克自己都承认，内存芯片短缺已经开始影响产品供应了。(Roughly the same, just from the opposite angle. Apple is the victim of this same supply shortfall, not the beneficiary — Cook himself admitted memory-chip scarcity is already affecting product supply.) 这个说法听起来挺正式的。 是的，供不应求是书面语，常用在财经报道里，四个字连着说，很紧凑。它和口语里说的"不够"不一样 — "不够"只是笼统地说数量不足，供不应求专指市场里需求超过了供给，是一个经济学概念，而不是简单的短缺。它的反义词是供过于求，也就是供给超过了需求，产能过剩。(This phrasing is fairly formal. 供不应求 is written/formal register, common in financial reporting — four characters run together, very compact. It's different from the colloquial "不够" — "不够" just vaguely means an insufficient quantity, while 供不应求 specifically means demand in a market exceeds supply, an economic concept rather than a simple shortage. Its opposite is 供过于求 — supply exceeding demand, overcapacity.) 明白了。那第二个词呢？ 第二个词是"毕竟"，一个很常用的连接词。 毕竟 — after all, when all is said and done. 亚马逊上调了两百二十亿美元的资本支出预期，股价却不跌反涨，毕竟云业务的增长速度摆在那儿，投资人没什么好担心的。(Amazon raised its capex guidance and the stock still rose rather than fell — after all, the cloud business's growth rate speaks for itself, so investors had nothing to worry about.) 那毕竟跟到底有什么区别？ 很好的问题。到底常用在疑问句里，追问事情的真相，比如"到底发生了什么"；而毕竟不是提问，是给出一个让人信服的理由，承认前面说的情况，但强调背后那个更根本的事实。它是中性偏书面的词，口语和财经评论里都很常见。(Good question. 到底 is typically used in questions, pressing for the real truth of a matter — like "到底发生了什么", what actually happened. 毕竟 isn't a question at all — it offers a convincing reason, acknowledging what was just said while emphasizing the more fundamental fact underneath it. It's neutral-to-formal register, common in both spoken usage and financial commentary.) Good pairing — one supply-side idiom, one connective, both financial-desk vocabulary. Now Tagalog. Sige, tayo naman sa Tagalog. Unang salita: kakulangan. Kakulangan — shortage, scarcity. Ang kakulangan sa memory chips ang dahilan kung bakit umangat nang husto ang kita ng Samsung ngayong quarter. (The shortage in memory chips is the reason Samsung's earnings jumped so sharply this quarter.) Kaya rin siguro naapektuhan ang Apple sa parehong dahilan? Oo, pareho lang ang ugat — kakulangan din sa memory chips ang nagpahina sa forecast ng Apple, kahit maganda ang naunang quarter nila. (Yes, same root cause — the same memory-chip shortage is what weakened Apple's forecast, even though their most recent quarter itself was strong.) Malapit ba ito sa salitang kakapusan na natutunan na natin dati? Magkatulad ang ibig sabihin pero may kaunting pagkakaiba sa gamit — kakapusan ay mas pangkalahatan, madalas ginagamit pagdating sa pera o mapagkukunan sa buhay araw-araw, tulad ng kakapusan sa badyet. Kakulangan naman ay mas angkop kapag pinag-uusapan ang isang partikular na bagay o produkto na hindi sapat ang suplay — kagaya ng kakulangan sa chips, o kakulangan sa manggagawa. (They mean similar things but differ slightly in usage — kakapusan is more general, often used for money or day-to-day resources, like a budget shortfall. Kakulangan fits better when talking about a specific item or product whose supply isn't sufficient — like a chip shortage, or a labor shortage.) Malinaw. Pangalawang salita naman? Pabago-bago. Pabago-bago — fickle, ever-changing, volatile. Pabago-bago talaga ang piso ngayong linggo — bumagsak, bumawi nang kaunti, tapos umuusad-usad na lang habang naghihintay ng datos ng implasyon sa Agosto 5. (The peso has really been volatile this week — it dropped, clawed back a little, and now it's just drifting while the market waits on the August 5 inflation data.) Ginagamit ba ito sa presyo ng langis din? Oo naman — pabago-bago rin ang presyo ng langis dahil sa sitwasyon sa Hormuz, kaya't hindi dapat ipagpalagay ng sinuman na ligtas na ang lahat. (Absolutely — oil prices are just as volatile because of the Hormuz situation, so no one should assume everything's settled.) Anong pagkakaiba nito sa umangat na natutunan natin dati? Umangat ay tumutukoy lamang sa pagtaas — isang direksyon. Pabago-bago naman ay tungkol sa kawalan ng katatagan sa pangkalahatan — minsan pataas, minsan pababa, walang tiyak na direksyon. Kaya mas madalas gamitin ang pabago-bago kapag inilalarawan ang isang merkado o sitwasyon sa kabuuan, hindi lang isang partikular na galaw. (Umangat only refers to a rise — one direction. Pabago-bago is about a general lack of stability — sometimes up, sometimes down, no fixed direction. So pabago-bago gets used more often to describe a whole market or situation, not just one particular movement.) Perfect close to that pairing — one Mandarin idiom and one connective, one Tagalog shortage word and one volatility word, both sets tied to the same two stories. Arts & Culture Arts desk, and we start with a loss — Betye Saar has died at 99. She passed in her sleep in Los Angeles on the 26th, just days before what would have been her hundredth birthday. Saar is the assemblage artist behind "The Liberation of Aunt Jemima" from 1972 — the piece that took a racist, sexist found-object caricature and turned it, quite literally, into an instrument of Black liberation, rifle in hand. The critical consensus across every obituary this week is the same: she didn't just critique that kind of imagery, she armed it and set it against itself. She'd only just formed what's being called a Legacy Group to steward her archive going forward. Second story is less about art and more about the business underneath it — the Philadelphia Museum of Art is in real financial trouble. They posted a 10 million dollar deficit for the fiscal year that ended June 30th — nearly double last year's 5.4 million dollar gap, on a budget of 76.5 million. Director Daniel Weiss and CFO Mitchell Wein are projecting it could widen to 15.9 million this year, blaming flat admissions, membership, and giving. Staff there has already fallen from 500 in 2019 down to 375 now. Is that a Philadelphia-specific problem, or the industry more broadly? It reads like the industry. The pandemic-era attendance bump is fully gone, membership renewal rates haven't recovered to pre-2020 levels almost anywhere, and big encyclopedic museums built their operating budgets on a growth assumption that just isn't there anymore. Philadelphia's simply the one being explicit about the numbers this week — it's a reminder that the museum-funding model that held through the last decade is genuinely cracking at some of America's biggest institutions, not just the small regional ones. On a brighter note — Edinburgh. The Edinburgh International Festival opens August 7th, running through the 30th, Nicola Benedetti's fourth year as director. This year's theme is "All Rise," built around the 250th anniversary of American independence — five world premieres, with the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra, the Berlin Philharmonic, and the LA Phil all in residence. Opening night on the 8th is a newly commissioned jazz symphony at Usher Hall. And in literature — a quieter, more reflective piece worth flagging. The Paris Review has David Schurman Wallace writing on Fanny Howe's posthumous prose collection, "This Poor Book" — an essay less about the book's plot than about what to do with the creative impulse right at the end of a life. Not a headline splash, but exactly the kind of criticism that's worth a specific mention rather than a listings roundup. One Good Thing One good thing today is a genuine energy-transition milestone, and it fits neatly with everything else we've talked about this morning. China's coal-fired power fell below 50% of total electricity output for the first time ever in the first half of this year — 49.7%, to be precise. Wind and solar together made up 41.2% of generation, with installed renewable capacity up 16.8% year-on-year. That's the country burning the most coal on the planet crossing a symbolic line first. Exactly — and it's genuinely surprising given how much of this show is spent on China's own AI-chip buildout, which you'd assume is adding load, not subtracting coal. The renewable build-out is apparently outrunning even that new demand. So it's not that China's using less power, it's that the marginal gigawatt is finally coming from somewhere cleaner. Right — and given everything we've covered this morning about gigawatt-scale gas plants and data center power fights back home, it's worth remembering the other side of the story is moving too, and faster than a lot of people assumed it could. That's The Morning Commute for Friday, July 31. We'll see you Monday. Have a great weekend, and we'll catch you then. 供不应求 supply cannot meet demand (a four-character economic idiom for a market shortfall) Samsung's record Q2 chip profit (memory/HBM demand outstripping supply) set against Apple's supply-constrained guidance from the same shortage 毕竟 after all; when all is said and done (a connective giving the underlying reason that qualifies what preceded) Amazon's stock rising despite a $220B capex raise, because AWS's 37% growth justified it kakulangan shortage; scarcity; deficiency in a specific item or supply The Samsung/Apple memory-chip shortage story pabago-bago fickle; ever-changing; volatile (general instability, no fixed direction) The peso's choppy trading this week and oil-price volatility from the Hormuz standoff

docs.title: Thursday, July 30, 2026
docs.text: Thursday, July 30, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Thursday, July 30. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Today's throughline is the AI-capex jury handing down its first split verdict — Microsoft rewarded, Meta punished, on the same night, after the same quarter, for the same sin of raising capex guidance. Meanwhile the Fed just held with three dissents wanting a hike, Iran rejected the one diplomatic off-ramp on the table for Hormuz, and gold and the 10-year went up together, which is never just one story. And by the time you're listening to this, Apple and Amazon will have reported too, closing out the four biggest capex prints of the year in a single week. Let's get into it. Headlines World desk first. Iran and Hormuz — Oman's proposal is dead. Oman floated what people were calling the Malacca model on Monday — joint management, a user fee on transit through the strait, internationalizing it without handing Iran unilateral control. Tehran rejected it. US, Iranian and European officials are now saying the standoff could run for months, not weeks. No signed ceasefire, no accepted framework — so where does that leave the war premium? Alive, and now open-ended rather than pending resolution, which is a meaningfully worse setup for the curve than "deal imminent." That's the backdrop for gold at $4,137 and change this morning, up 2.5% intraday — a fresh push through last week's $4,122 print. Second story, and it's grim — Russia hit Kyiv and six other Ukrainian regions overnight, a coordinated missile and drone barrage. At least eight dead, six of them in Dnipropetrovsk, one in Poltava, strikes reaching as far west as Lviv — far enough that Poland scrambled fighter jets to secure its own airspace. Russia's defense ministry also claims it hit three cargo ships near Odesa it alleges were carrying weapons. This is one day after Zelensky warned publicly that a massive strike was coming. Which means it landed exactly where he said it would, and the scale — seven regions in one night — is an escalation even against the pattern we've been tracking all month. Market Overview Onto the tape. Wednesday's close, post-FOMC, was ugly across the board. S&P 500 down 1.52% to 7,316.15. Nasdaq down 1.74% to 24,442.94. Dow down 2.19% to 51,594.14 — the worst percentage day of this whole stretch. Russell 2000 off 1.61% to 2,906.31. Two things stacked on top of each other — the Fed held, but hawkishly, and then Iran re-escalated overnight on top of that. Three dissents at the FOMC, all wanting a hike — the first dissents of Chair Warsh's tenure, which tells you the committee is not unified on how much further this hold has room to run. Then overnight, an IRGC missile attempt on US Gulf forces put a fresh bid under oil just as markets were digesting the hawkish hold. Rates did something specific — bear-steepened even as the Fed stood pat. Ten-year up six basis points to 4.67%, two-year down four to 4.22%, thirty-year around 5.20%. That's not a growth scare, that's the market pricing a longer runway of policy uncertainty and a bit more term premium — the long end doing the worrying the Fed didn't do out loud. And gold and yields rising together is the tell — that's both the war premium and the term-premium story at once, not one or the other. Brent's at $87.36 this morning, down about 1%, WTI in the low-$84s — still elevated but not blowing out, because Iranian exports are continuing even with the missile attempt. The market's pricing risk, not disruption, yet. Now the movers that actually set up tonight — Meta and Microsoft, both after Wednesday's close. Meta down 10% after-hours. EPS $6.18 against a $7.22 estimate — a miss — even though revenue beat, $60.8 billion versus $60.17 billion expected. The Q3 revenue guide came in light, $62.5 billion against $63.15 billion consensus, and then they raised the capex floor on top of all that. Microsoft went the other way, up about 2%, on a straightforward Azure beat — 43% constant-currency growth against roughly 40% expected, with backlog described as strong. Same week, same theme, opposite stock reaction — we'll come back to that in Energy, because the mechanics matter. And tonight's the last of it — Apple reports around 2pm Pacific, consensus EPS $1.89, iPhone revenue estimated at $54.8 billion, up 23% year-on-year — and this is Tim Cook's final earnings call as CEO, with John Ternus taking over. Amazon reports after the close, consensus revenue around $196 billion, EPS $1.82. So by tonight, all four of the biggest capex names will have told the market whether the growth justifies the spend. And it's worth noting the Dow underperformed the Nasdaq on a day when tech actually held up relatively better intraday — Boeing and a handful of industrials dragged, so don't read Wednesday as purely an AI-stock story. It was a broad, hawkish-Fed-plus-oil-shock day that just happened to set up tonight's tech-specific verdicts. Right, the Dow's minus 2.19% versus Nasdaq's minus 1.74% is the tell — if this were purely a capex scare, you'd expect the reverse. U.S. Business Staying with that divergence — Meta and Microsoft is really the story of the morning in US business too. It's the cleanest test yet of whether "capex outrunning cash gets punished" is a universal rule or a conditional one. Microsoft's capex is also ripping — Q4 capex was $41 billion, up 70% year-on-year, and they guided fiscal '27 capex to $255 to $260 billion, up from a restated roughly $175 billion. That's an enormous number. But Azure growth is accelerating alongside it, guided to about 45% constant-currency next quarter, so the market read the spend as backlog conversion, not burn. Whereas Meta's operating cash flow was $31.9 billion against capex of $31.1 billion — free cash flow of just $784 million, down from $8.55 billion a year ago. That's the number that actually moved the stock. It's not that Meta spent too much in absolute terms — it's that the cash cushion evaporated to almost nothing while growth stayed flat. Revenue growth cover is the variable separating who gets rewarded and who gets punished for the same behavior. Second story — Mastercard reports before the bell today, consensus EPS $4.77, up almost 15% year-on-year, revenue $9.06 billion, up 11.4%. It's a same-day cross-border and consumer-spend read right after Visa's clean beat got punished earlier this week — so watch whether Mastercard's reaction confirms that the market's gotten skittish on payments names generally, or whether that was Visa-specific. The setup's almost identical to Visa's — a solid consensus beat expected, but the bar for "solid" has clearly moved this earnings season. It has. We've now seen a clean beat get punished twice in one week if you count Visa, and a strong quarter with heavier spending get punished a third time with Meta — so the market's not rewarding growth on its own right now, it's rewarding growth that comes with visible operating leverage. Mastercard's networks-and-fees model, with less capex intensity than the payments-plus-hardware players, is actually a decent test of whether that leverage argument holds outside the AI-capex names entirely. International Business & Politics Shell reported today, and it's basically the mirror image of the Meta story. Adjusted earnings $9.8 billion, cash flow from operations $21.4 billion, free cash flow $17.5 billion, net debt down to $41.8 billion — gearing at 19%. Dividend raised to $0.3906 a share from around $0.30 a year ago, and they launched a new $3 billion buyback on top of resuming $1.2 billion that had been paused during the ARC Resources acquisition. That's nineteen straight quarters of buybacks at $3 billion or more. Capex converting cleanly to cash and shareholder returns — same contrast we've flagged before with names actually generating cash versus names still promising it will show up later. Record Brazil upstream output too, and record refinery utilization despite the Middle East outages we've been tracking — operationally, about as clean a quarter as this sector produces right now. Second item — eurozone growth actually beat this morning. Flash Q2 GDP up 0.4% quarter-on-quarter, 1.0% year-on-year for the eurozone, 0.5% and 1.2% for the wider EU — well above the 0.2% consensus. Germany's flash print beat too, 0.2% against a 0.1% estimate. This is a fresh number on top of the manufacturing-led PMI story we already had — Europe growing without an AI engine, and now the hard GDP data is backing up what the survey data implied. Keeps the ECB's data-dependent tightening bias intact rather than pushing them toward cuts. It's a nice contrast with Shell in the same block — one's an energy major converting capex to cash cleanly, the other's a whole continent growing on manufacturing and services fundamentals rather than a single AI multiple. Two different versions of the same argument — durable growth that doesn't need a narrative to keep working. Neither needs the hyperscaler capex story to be true for the thesis to hold, which is exactly why they're useful counterweights to everything else in today's headlines. China China — a stabilization, not a new shock, one session after the DUV-driven derating hit Seoul and Shanghai together. Shanghai Composite closed up 0.4% Wednesday to 3,828 — so the index-level bleeding stopped. But underneath it there's real selectivity now. Cambricon up 1.7%, Zhongji Innolight up 4.7% rebounding, while SMIC fell another 4.2%, Hygon down 4.8%, Victory Giant down 4.1%. So the market's separating names it thinks can actually execute on the domestic-lithography shift from names it thinks are just exposed to the export-control overhang. Exactly — bifurcation, not blanket relief. That's a more mature market reaction than a straight bounce would have been, and it's worth watching whether that selectivity holds through the rest of the week or the whole sector just re-couples to the next headline. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities Let's go deep on the numbers behind that Meta-Microsoft divergence, because the actuals landed after months of guidance. Microsoft's fiscal Q4: revenue $90.0 billion, beating $87.6 billion; adjusted EPS $4.74 against $4.24 expected. Azure at 43% constant-currency growth. The capex guide for fiscal '27 is $255 to $260 billion — and to be precise about the comparison, fiscal '26 was restated to roughly $175 billion from an original $190 billion guide, which is a useful-life and finance-lease accounting reclassification, not an actual pullback. Implied capex growth into fiscal '27 is somewhere around 45 to 50%. And Meta's raised its capex floor for the third time this year — $125 billion up to $130 billion, ceiling held at $145 billion. Third raise. And that's exactly why the free-cash-flow collapse to $784 million landed so hard — the market's now pricing in that the ceiling could move again, and there's no cushion left to absorb another raise without borrowing or leasing more aggressively. Which is the pivot into the story that actually explains where some of that money is going — Meta and BlackRock, El Paso. Announced Monday. It's an 80-20 joint venture — BlackRock-managed funds own 80%, Meta owns 20%. Meta puts in land and construction-in-progress worth about $2.3 billion, and separately collects a $1 billion payout up front. BlackRock puts in $4.9 billion of cash plus $12.5 billion in debt financing. It's a 1-gigawatt campus targeted online in 2028, and Meta leases the finished facility back rather than owning it outright. So a chunk of the actual build isn't on Meta's balance sheet at all. Right, and that's the second-order read — hyperscaler capex guides keep climbing on the income statement, but a growing share of the physical build is routed through off-balance-sheet leaseback vehicles like this one. It means neither the $255 to $260 billion Microsoft number nor Meta's $130 to $145 billion range fully captures what's actually getting built. The real number is bigger than the guide. Now, SemiAnalysis put out a piece sizing something nobody's really quantified before — the labor bottleneck, not the equipment one. They've built a new modular-construction tracker — 61 gigawatts across more than a thousand sites already, and they project modular penetration hits 30% of live capacity by the end of 2028. The reason is labor: electricians are 30 to 40% of total construction man-hours on a data center build, and they're now modeling a state-level electrician shortage emerging in 2027, worst in Texas and Ohio — which happen to be the two states carrying the heaviest buildout concentration right now. What does going modular actually buy you against that shortage? On a 50-megawatt liquid-cooled baseline, full modular compresses the build window by about 36% — seven to nine months instead of stick-build timelines — and runs roughly 8% cheaper per megawatt, $13.5 million versus $14.6 million. Moving the mechanical, electrical and plumbing scope into a factory cuts on-site labor hours by about 63%, and licensed-electrician hours specifically by around 85%. And there's real money in being early, not just cheaper. SemiAnalysis puts the value of an earlier month at roughly $500,000 per megawatt for an owner-operator running the GPU depreciation math, versus about $190,000 per megawatt for a wholesale colocation lessor working off lease rates. An eight-month modular lead is worth around $4 million a megawatt — call it $200 million undiscounted on a 50-megawatt hall — as long as the building itself, not power or GPU delivery, is actually the binding constraint. They cite a live example. Hut 8's Beacon Point campus in Corpus Christi — Vertiv's full-stack OneCore modular system powering a 704-megawatt IT lease, built to Nvidia's DSX reference architecture, with American Electric Power as the utility counterparty and Jacobs Solutions running EPCM. Vendors are capturing more of the stack too — full-stack modular players are expanding their content per megawatt from around $3.5 million up to roughly $7 million by selling the whole assembly instead of components. Two regulatory wrinkles worth flagging before we move on. First — the EPA. Assistant Administrator Aaron Szabo sent guidance in mid-July saying power plants that serve only a data center, with no grid interconnection at all, may fall outside the Clean Air Act's Acid Rain Program entirely — the SO2 and NOx framework. Roughly 60 such plants are already under construction or operating. So behind-the-meter isn't just bypassing the interconnection queue anymore, it may be bypassing emissions permitting too. And the second — a fight that's actually inverted from the usual script. DOE is weighing repeal of its own 2024 distribution-transformer efficiency standard, framing it as a national-security, supply-chain issue. But EEI — the utility trade group — is opposing the repeal. They want longer compliance timelines, not a rollback, and they're arguing the standard isn't actually what's driving the transformer shortage. So you've got utilities defending a Biden-era rule against a Republican DOE, which is not the fight you'd have predicted a year ago. And tonight closes the loop — Apple and Amazon report after the bell. Amazon's the one to watch on this specific thread — Andy Jassy has already framed roughly $200 billion of 2026 capex as, in his words, "not a hunch," so the question is whether that number moves again following Microsoft and Meta's raises this week, and how AWS growth stacks up against Azure's 43%. Philippines Philippines. Weather first — there's a new low-pressure area, but it's not much of one. PAGASA's 3am bulletin has it sitting over the coastal waters of Nasugbu, Batangas — forecaster Leanne Loreto says there's a low chance it strengthens into a tropical depression in the next 24 hours, and it's actually expected to dissipate within that window. So no signal warnings anywhere in the country. None. What it is doing is enhancing the habagat, the southwest monsoon, so you've got scattered rain and thunderstorms across Metro Manila, Ilocos, the Cordillera, Central Luzon and Calabarzon — enough that some Luzon schools suspended in-person classes yesterday. Once this LPA clears, the easterlies take back over as the dominant pattern. Now the macro side actually moved on the back of something BSP said yesterday. The peso closed at 61.410 Wednesday, up 20.4 centavos from Tuesday's 61.614 — a one-month high. PSEi closed at 6,353.04, up 0.77%, having touched an intraday high of 6,436 before profit-taking trimmed it back. The broader All Shares Index was up 0.59% to 3,447.34. And that rally is being read specifically as a reaction to Governor Remolona's rate-hike comments. He said, quote, "There's a chance, yes, but it's a small chance," on the odds of a 50-basis-point hike at the August 27th meeting. Markets took that as dovish reassurance rather than a live threat, and both the peso and the index rallied on it. Last item — BSP actually launched something concrete yesterday, not just talk. Along with the Philippine Payments Management Inc, they rolled out three new digital rails — Direct Debit PH, InstaPay for Business, and InstaPay Cash-In, plus separate QR PH codes. The headline number is InstaPay for Business raising the maximum transfer limit tenfold, from 50,000 pesos to 500,000 pesos for registered businesses. Direct Debit PH is free for consumers — billers absorb the transaction cost. Remolona's framing was explicit about why this matters beyond convenience. He said interoperability and lower fees do more than lift transaction volume — they bring in more people, and that's what financial inclusion actually looks like. It's a small policy story next to the peso and the rate talk, but it's the kind of infrastructure that compounds quietly for years. Vocab Of The Day 今天的词汇时间到了。(Time for today's vocabulary.) 我们先说普通话，然后说塔加洛语。(We'll do Mandarin first, then Tagalog.) 好，我们从伊朗和霍尔木兹海峡的僵局说起。(Good, let's start from the Iran-Hormuz deadlock.) 第一个词是"除非"。(The first word is "chúfēi.") 除非双方达成新的协议，否则霍尔木兹海峡的僵局恐怕会持续数月。(Unless both sides reach a new agreement, the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz will likely continue for months.) "除非"常常跟"否则"搭配——"除非……，否则……"，先说唯一的条件，再说不满足条件会怎样。(Chúfēi is often paired with fǒuzé — "chúfēi..., fǒuzé...," you state the one condition first, then what happens if it isn't met.) 语气比较中性，口语书面语都常用，但会让人感觉这是一个相当明确、几乎没有别的出路的条件。(The tone is fairly neutral, common in both spoken and written registers, but it signals a fairly definite condition — almost as if there's no other way out.) 对，而且这个词暗示谈判双方目前几乎没有其他选择。(Right, and the word implies the two sides currently have almost no other option.) 官员说，除非出现突破，否则原油的战争溢价很难真正消退。(Officials say unless there's a breakthrough, the war premium in crude oil will be very hard to actually fade.) 好，第二个词跟Meta和微软的分化有关。(Good, the second word connects to the Meta-Microsoft divergence.) 这个词是"相反"。(The word is "xiāngfǎn.") 大家原以为资本支出增加对两家公司都是坏消息，相反，微软股价却因此上涨。(Everyone originally thought rising capex would be bad news for both companies; on the contrary, Microsoft's stock actually rose because of it.) "相反"跟我们以前学过的"反而"不太一样。("Xiāngfǎn" is a bit different from "fǎn'ér," which we taught before.) "反而"藏在同一句话里，强调某个具体结果跟预期相反；"相反"通常单独起头，引出一整个对立的事实，语气更书面、更适合做转折的开场。("Fǎn'ér" sits inside one sentence, emphasizing that a specific result is the opposite of expectation; "xiāngfǎn" usually starts its own clause and introduces a whole contrasting fact — more formal, and better suited to opening a turn in the argument.) 所以两家公司做了同样的事，市场的反应却截然相反——这就是今天的重点。(So the two companies did the same thing, and the market's reaction was completely opposite — that's today's main point.) 好，现在换塔加洛语。(Okay, now let's switch to Tagalog.) Oo, at magsisimula tayo sa piso. (Yes, and we'll start with the peso.) Ang unang salita ay "umangat." (The first word is "umangat.") Umangat ang piso at ang PSEi kahapon, matapos sabihin ni Gobernador Remolona na maliit lang ang tsansa ng malaking pagtaas ng interest rate. (The peso and the PSEi climbed yesterday, after Governor Remolona said there's only a small chance of a big rate hike.) "Umangat" ay iba sa "bumawi" na natutunan natin dati. (Umangat is different from "bumawi," which we learned before.) Ang "bumawi" ay tungkol sa aktibong pagbangon pagkatapos ng malinaw na pagbagsak, pero ang "umangat" ay mas pangkalahatan — basta tumaas o umunlad, hindi kailangang may nauna pang pagbagsak. (Bumawi is about actively recovering after a clear drop, but umangat is more general — anything rising or improving, without necessarily implying a prior fall.) Tama, at karaniwang ginagamit ito sa merkado — "umangat ang presyo," "umangat ang ranggo." (Right, and it's commonly used in markets — "the price climbed," "the ranking improved.") Pang-araw-araw na salita ito, pero madalas ginagamit sa balitang pananalapi. (It's an everyday word, but it's often used in financial news.) Ang ikalawang salita ay "abot-kaya," at ito'y konektado sa bagong serbisyo ng BSP. (The second word is "abot-kaya," and it's connected to BSP's new service.) Mas abot-kaya na ngayon ang paglilipat ng pera dahil sa Direct Debit PH at InstaPay for Business. (Sending money is now more affordable and accessible because of Direct Debit PH and InstaPay for Business.) "Abot-kaya" ay pinagsamang salita — "abot," na nangangahulugang maabot o marating, at "kaya," na nangangahulugang kaya o afford. (Abot-kaya is a compound word — "abot," meaning to reach, and "kaya," meaning to be able to afford.) Kaya literal itong ibig sabihin ay "kayang abutin," at ginagamit ito hindi lang sa presyo, kundi pati sa serbisyo — parang "accessible" sa Ingles, hindi lang "mura." (So literally it means "able to be reached," and it's used not just for prices but for services too — closer to "accessible" in English, not just "cheap.") Perpekto talaga para sa layunin ni Remolona — "financial inclusion" ay tungkol sa pagiging abot-kaya ng serbisyo, hindi lang pagiging mura. (Perfect for Remolona's goal, actually — financial inclusion is about services being accessible, not just cheap.) Eksakto. (Exactly.) Arts & Culture Arts today leads with a rediscovery — Aspen Art Museum's first-ever survey of Arch Connelly. Connelly was a Chicago-born fixture of the East Village scene in the 1980s, dead by 1993 from AIDS-related complications — the poet Rene Ricard called his style "space-age surrealism." He worked with shells, beads and faux pearls, camp, craft-based reworkings of Minimalism and Pop that were basically written out of that era's canon. The show runs through October 11, and it includes pieces unseen publicly in over 35 years. What's notable is who's underwriting it — Maison Valentino, under Alessandro Michele, is behind the survey and actually extending it into the brand's Aspen boutique. That's a fashion house doing real historical rehabilitation of a queer, AIDS-era artist, not just borrowing aesthetics. Auction houses reported their first-half numbers this week too, and the recovery is real but narrow. Christie's did $4.5 billion total revenue in the first half, public auction sales up 71% year-on-year to $3.5 billion, 91% sell-through by lot. Sotheby's public auction sales were $3.4 billion, up 59%, 90% sell-through. But ArtTactic's read is that this is trophy lots and luxury goods — watches, jewels — carrying the recovery, not the broad middle market. Sotheby's ran its "America 250" sale this week in New York, timed to the anniversary. Onto opera — Salzburg's in full swing under this year's theme, "Panorama of Love." 208 performances through August 30. Tuesday night was the "Bonne fête" gala honoring Cecilia Bartoli, and the festival just gave its Salzburg premiere of Rossini's "Il viaggio a Reims" — Barrie Kosky directing, Gianluca Capuano conducting, Bartoli starring. Kosky doing bel canto comedy is exactly the kind of pairing that makes a season interesting rather than just prestigious. BBC Proms had a sharper-edged program this week too — the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra paired Poulenc's Sinfonietta with John Adams's "Harmonium." That's a real curatorial choice — French neoclassical wit next to an American minimalist epic, at the Royal Albert Hall. And for recordings, Gramophone's August pick of the month is Dvořák's "New World" Symphony paired with Carlos Simon's "Four Black American Dances," Manfred Honeck conducting the Pittsburgh Symphony — reviewers are praising both the conductor-orchestra rapport on the Dvořák and calling the contemporary coupling superbly spirited. And the Booker longlist, which dropped Monday, has a real narrative once you look past the headline names. Thirteen books. Two former winners are back — Douglas Stuart, who won for "Shuggie Bain" in 2020, and Marlon James, who won in 2015 for "A Brief History of Seven Killings." Elizabeth Strout picks up her third Booker nomination. And there are three debut novelists on the list, including Rebecca Perry and Djamel White. Chief executive Gaby Wood called it a list that "rewards risk" and has "human fingerprints all over it." Chair Mary Beard put it more simply — the judges wanted books that take the reader somewhere new. Coming off a longlist that already had Whitehead and O'Farrell in the mix, adding two former winners back into contention makes the shortlist call in September genuinely hard to predict. What's the actual case for a repeat winner, though — Booker juries don't usually love giving the prize to someone twice. They don't, which is exactly why it's interesting rather than safe. A former winner only survives the longlist stage if the new book earns it on its own terms with a fresh set of judges, not on reputation — Beard's panel had no obligation to include either of them. So their presence here is a stronger signal about James' "The Disappearers" and Stuart's new novel specifically than it looks at first glance. One Good Thing One good thing today is about frogs, and it's genuinely useful science, not just a nice story. Researchers at UCL, the Zoological Society of London and Imperial College studied common midwife toads in lakes across the Pyrenees, in populations that have been hammered for years by chytrid fungus — one of the worst wildlife disease crises anywhere, it's wiped out entire amphibian populations globally. And they found something specific about why some populations survive and others don't. It's not just whether a population has immune defenses — it's the timing. Surviving populations show earlier immune maturation and a greater diversity of antimicrobial peptides on their skin, and critically, they develop that defense earlier in the tadpole stage, before the fungus gets a foothold. Populations that mature those defenses later just don't make it. Which means there's now a concrete lever for conservation, not just monitoring the decline. Exactly — it opens the door to probiotic or immune-priming interventions timed specifically to that tadpole window, rather than just trying to treat infected adults after the fact. Small win, but the kind of small win that changes how a whole field approaches a crisis it's mostly just been documenting. That's The Morning Commute for Thursday, July 30. We'll be back tomorrow with whatever Apple and Amazon actually said tonight. Have a great day, and we'll see you then. 除非 unless (a formal connective marking the one exclusive condition that would change the outcome) Iran's rejection of Oman's Hormuz proposal, with officials warning the standoff could run for months absent a breakthrough 相反 on the contrary; conversely (a freestanding transition introducing a whole contrasting fact) Microsoft's stock rising and Meta's falling on the same night, for the same behavior — raised AI capex guidance umangat to rise; to climb; to improve (general upward movement, not necessarily a recovery) The peso's and PSEi's climb to a one-month high after BSP's dovish rate-hike framing abot-kaya affordable; accessible (reachable in both price and ease of use) BSP and PPMI's launch of Direct Debit PH and InstaPay for Business, aimed at financial inclusion

docs.title: Wednesday, July 29, 2026
docs.text: Wednesday, July 29, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. It's Wednesday, July 29th. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Here's the thread this morning: three separate forces are all landing on the same Wednesday. Overnight, the Hormuz story re-escalated — an Iranian attempt to strike US forces in the Gulf, Brent up more than 5% in a single session — and that lands just hours before the Fed announces, priced at roughly two-thirds odds of a hold. At the same time, yesterday gave us a preview of how brutal this earnings season can be even on clean numbers — Boeing's loss was rewarded, Visa's beat was punished — right before Microsoft and Meta report tonight. And China's chip de-rating just jumped from Seoul to Shanghai. Oil, the Fed, and AI capex, all on one clock. All on one clock. Let's start with the world. Headlines Two world stories, and the first is out of Paris. Prime Minister Lecornu invoked special constitutional power overnight to force France's 2026 budget through the National Assembly without a floor vote — the French equivalent of daring the opposition to bring the government down rather than let them amend the bill line by line. No-confidence motions are already filed. How real is the collapse risk? Real enough to price. France has burned through governments on exactly this maneuver before — force the budget, dare a no-confidence vote, and either survive by a handful of seats or trigger new elections mid-cycle. The fiscal math is the same as it's been all year: a deficit well north of what Brussels wants, and a government trying to close it without a majority that actually agrees on how. Watch the no-confidence vote count over the next 48 hours — that's the number that tells you whether this is theater or a real crisis. Second story, and it's a genuine break from decades of German policy. Chancellor Merz confirmed Germany will buy and host US Tomahawk cruise missiles on German soil, using Typhon ground launchers. That's a historic reversal — Germany has spent eighty years deliberately not hosting US long-range strike systems on its territory, precisely because of what that represents. Why now? NATO's long-range strike posture has been quietly rebuilding since the Ukraine war exposed how thin Europe's own deep-strike capability actually was. Germany hosting Tomahawks closes a real gap in NATO's ability to hold Russian targets at risk without relying entirely on US assets stationed further west. It's also a political signal to Washington — burden-sharing, not just spending targets. The number to watch is how many launchers, and how fast — that tells you whether this is symbolic or operational. There's also a third thread worth a line, since it's the backdrop to both of those — Ukraine and Russia traded serious blows again overnight. Ukraine fired more than 100 drones at Russian bomber bases, and Russia responded with Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missiles — 14 dead, more than 80 wounded, across five Ukrainian cities. That's the running war escalating in parallel with the diplomacy around it, not instead of it, and it's part of why Berlin hosting Tomahawks lands as urgent rather than symbolic right now. A French government daring its own collapse, a German government ending an eighty-year taboo, and the war underneath both of them still getting sharper. Let's get to the tape. Market Overview Tuesday's close, the most recent print we have: S&P 500 at 7,428.78, up 0.21%. Nasdaq Composite at 24,876.91, down 0.22%. Dow at 52,747.32, up a strong 1.03%. Russell 2000 at 2,953.80, up 0.20%. Dow leading again, Nasdaq lagging again. Same rotation we've been tracking — value over tech for another session. But the number that actually matters this morning happened after that close: an Iranian attempt to strike US forces in the Gulf overnight, with three vessels reportedly hit in the strait according to the IMO. Brent is up 5.3% to 88.55. WTI's up close to 4.7%, near 82.93. That's a real reversal of the de-escalation trade. It is, and the timing is brutal — this lands hours before the Fed announces at 2 PM Eastern, with the statement and press conference back to back.
