Going into this morning, the market had rate-hike odds priced around 35%, hold around 65%, with a widely expected pair of hawkish dissents from Dallas Fed's Logan and Cleveland Fed's Hammack — which would be the first dissents of Chair Warsh's tenure. Now the question is whether an overnight supply shock nudges that hike tail back up right as they're voting. What's gold doing? Because that usually tells you whether this is a fear trade or a supply trade. This is the tell — gold's basically flat, down 0.32% to 4,025.90, while Brent's up more than 5%. If this were a broad risk-off, flight-to-safety event, you'd expect gold moving with oil. It isn't. That's the market reading this as a Hormuz-specific supply shock, not a systemic scare — which argues for the Fed treating it as a data point, not a regime change, though we'll know within hours. And rates going into the decision? Ten-year at 4.61% as of Tuesday's close, down from 4.65% the day before. Two-year at 4.26%, down from 4.31%. Bond market eased into decision day even as oil re-priced overnight — a live divergence hours before the Fed speaks. And underneath all of it, Microsoft and Meta report tonight after the close, with Apple and Amazon tomorrow — so today is genuinely one of the highest-density news days of the cycle. Oil spike, Fed verdict, and two hyperscaler prints, all inside about twelve hours. Let's go to business. U.S. Business First story — Boeing's actual numbers landed, and the market's read on them tells you something important. Boeing's Q2 loss was 67 cents a share, wider than the 34-cent consensus loss, entirely because of a 280 million dollar charge tied to Air Force One. But revenue came in at 24.6 billion, beating consensus, and free cash flow was positive 600 million against a consensus expectation of negative 177 million. Backlog hit a record 715 billion dollars across more than 6,200 jets, and deliveries were up 14% to 171. The stock closed up 4.76% to 221.56. So the market completely ignored the GAAP miss. Correctly, in my view — the GAAP loss was a one-time charge, not an operating problem, and the number that actually predicts the next two years is free cash flow turning positive. That's the capex-to-cash conversion story finally showing up in the print, not just the guidance. Second story is the opposite pattern — Visa beat clean and got sold anyway. Visa's fiscal Q3: EPS of 3.32 against 3.23 consensus, revenue of 11.6 billion beating estimates, up 14% year over year. Cross-border volume up 13%, processed transactions up 10% to 71.7 billion. Every headline number beat. The stock closed up 1.12% Tuesday but then slipped 2.12% in premarket trading, down to 358.80. A clean beat on every metric and the stock still fell. What's that about? It's a valuation and expectations story, not a fundamentals story — when a stock's priced for perfection, a beat that isn't big enough, or that doesn't come with an equally strong forward signal, gets read as deceleration risk rather than strength. And it's worth flagging as a preview: if Visa — a genuinely clean beat — gets punished like that, it's a live warning for tonight. Microsoft reports after the close, consensus EPS 4.24, revenue guided 87.6 to 87.7 billion, Azure guided at 39 to 40% constant-currency growth, capex running above 40 billion this quarter, annualizing past 190 billion. Meta reports the same evening — consensus EPS around 7.13 to 7.18, revenue consensus 60.2 billion, up 27% year over year but decelerating from Q1's 33%, with a capex guide of 125 to 145 billion. So the bar for "good enough" tonight might be higher than the consensus numbers alone suggest. Exactly the lesson from Visa. It's not whether they beat — it's whether the beat and the forward capex commentary together convince the market that the spending is still buying growth, not just burning cash. We'll know by tomorrow morning. A cash-conversion story rewarded, a clean beat punished, and the real test still to come tonight. Let's go abroad. International Business & Politics International, and the first story is a strong one out of London. Barclays' first-half pretax profit rose 17% to 6.1 billion pounds, beating consensus, with the second quarter alone up more than 30% to 3.3 billion. Group income rose 11% to 16.5 billion, and the investment bank was the standout, up 20%. They raised their full-year income target to around 31.5 billion pounds and announced a 1 billion pound buyback on top of an 800 million pound interim dividend. What's driving the investment-banking strength specifically? Trading and advisory volumes have stayed elevated through a year that's been genuinely volatile — oil shocks, a live Fed cycle, geopolitical risk repricing constantly. That volatility is a tailwind for a trading desk even when it's a headwind for corporate clients. Barclays is essentially monetizing the same uncertainty that's been hammering equity markets. Second story is smaller but instructive — Philips, out of the Netherlands. Philips delivered 132 million euros in cost savings this quarter, keeping them on track for 1.5 billion euros total under their 2026-to-2028 restructuring program. It's not a headline-grabbing number, but it's a clean execution story — a European industrial name hitting its own cost targets on schedule, which matters more than usual right now given how much scrutiny capital discipline is getting across every sector. A UK bank monetizing volatility, and a Dutch industrial proving it can cut costs on schedule. Onto China. China China's story today is the AI de-rating jumping borders — it started in Korea yesterday, and today it's hit the mainland directly. How bad? Shanghai Composite down 1.16% to 3,813. Shenzhen Component down a sharper 4.52% to 13,509.7 — its lowest level since early April. And the chip names specifically got hit hard on AI-return-on-investment concerns: Cambricon down 9.1%, Zhongji Innolight down 15.7%, Eoptolink down 17.1%, GigaDevice down 10%. And SMIC — the name that was supposed to be the beneficiary of yesterday's lithography story? Down 4.9% too, which is the detail that tells you this isn't really about the DUV breakthrough anymore. Even the company that stood to gain from China's own equipment mass-production milestone got dragged down with everything else — that's a sign this selloff is about AI-capex valuation broadly, the same worry that's been hitting Nvidia's ecosystem in the US and Samsung and SK Hynix in Korea, not about any single company's competitive position. What's the forward catalyst? The Politburo meets later this week, expected to set H2 growth and policy guidance. If Beijing leans into fiscal support or explicitly addresses the AI-investment pullback, that's the next lever. Until then, the mainland chip complex is trading exactly like its US and Korean counterparts — as a valuation story, not a fundamentals one. The de-rating goes global, one border at a time. Let's get into power. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities Today's lead is out of Texas, and it's the clearest evidence yet of just how much load is trying to jump the interconnection queue. Give me the number. CenterPoint has submitted 17 gigawatts of large-load projects into Texas's new "Batch Zero" interconnection process, with roughly 14 gigawatts expected to be eligible — 10 gigawatts of base-load already fully studied, 4 gigawatts of studied-load with one of two required studies complete. There's about 900 million dollars in customer cash commitments and deposits backing the signed facility-extension agreements. CEO Jason Wells said on this week's earnings call that nearly all of it gets energized by the end of 2030 — which implies roughly 50% growth in Houston-area peak load by the end of 2029, off a current peak of 21 gigawatts. That's the load side. What's the demand model saying now? BNEF just shifted methodology on this — instead of tracking noisy announced-megawatt figures, which get revised constantly, they're now forecasting bottoms-up off actual chip shipments. New base case: 118 gigawatts of US data center capacity by 2030, 207 gigawatts by 2033. That's a meaningfully more credible number because it's anchored to something you can actually count — chips shipping — rather than press releases. And on the supply side, there's real friction in PJM this week. PJM's board proposed a one-time backstop capacity auction starting in September, capped at 555 dollars per megawatt-day, specifically to fill the 6.8 gigawatt shortfall left over from the 2028-29 base auction — which, remember, already cleared at its own cap of 325. Paired with that: new large loads that don't bring their own generation would get curtailed near emergency grid conditions. That filing goes to FERC before the end of July. Walk me through why that backstop cap number actually matters, beyond just being a bigger number. This is the sharpest data point in the whole segment. 555 is 71% above the 325 the base auction just cleared at — and crucially, the backstop only buys curtailable, last-resort capacity, not firm power. So you now have a market-priced number for what unfirm reliability actually costs at the margin. And it lines up almost perfectly with something LBNL just published — their analysis says nationally, inflation-adjusted retail power prices are only 3% above 2019, which pushes back hard on the popular "data centers are spiking your bill" narrative. But in constrained regions — and they name PJM specifically — growth forces urgent, high-cost buildouts that clear expensive auctions before cost-allocation even catches up. The 555 number is the proof: that's what the market is charging for reliability it can't otherwise firm up in time. So the national story and the PJM story are actually two different stories wearing the same headline. Exactly right. Nationally, in real terms, power prices are roughly flat since 2019. But LBNL's regional breakdown shows California up 6 cents a kilowatt-hour and the Northeast up 2 to 4 cents since 2019, while much of the middle of the country is flat to down. The old rule was that load growth lowers unit prices, because you spread fixed costs over more megawatt-hours. In constrained zones, that inverts — growth forces the expensive buildout first, and the bill lands before the benefit does. A few more before we move — New York and Maryland both have relevant developments. New York's data-center moratorium is currently masking stalled legislation that would force large data centers to source at least a third of their power from renewables by 2030 — and that provision could reach existing facilities, not just new ones, especially water-intensive cooling sites, the moment the moratorium lifts. And in Maryland, Pepco's rate case just got sharper — the state's consumer advocate is now arguing for an outright cut to Pepco's allowed return on equity, not just a smaller increase than requested. That's a live test of whether affordability backlash can actually compress utility returns, not just slow their growth. On the cost side, storage got more expensive too. Lazard's latest storage cost benchmark has standalone four-hour battery systems back up to 210 to 292 dollars per megawatt-hour, reversing two years of steady declines — driven by tariffs on Chinese LFP battery cells cutting off the cheap-cell supply chain that had been driving costs down. And DOE's draft national transmission needs study put a number on grid congestion itself: 12 billion dollars in wholesale power costs in 2024, up from 11 billion in 2023, concentrated in roughly 5% of hours — the cold snaps and high-net-load moments. The biggest relief potential sits in NYISO, NorthernGrid South, and MISO, with inter-regional transmission ties flagged as the single highest-value fix. Texas submitting 17 gigawatts at once, a backstop auction pricing what unfirm power actually costs, and battery costs reversing course. A dense one today. One more thing worth flagging before we move — tonight's Microsoft and Meta prints aren't just an AI-capex story, they're a power story too. Every dollar of that capex guide has a megawatt figure attached to it somewhere in a filing, and after today's PJM and CenterPoint numbers, the market's going to be reading those capex lines with a much sharper eye on where the power is actually coming from, not just how much is being spent. So the energy segment and tonight's earnings are really the same story from two different angles. Exactly — capex without a firm power source behind it is just a spending number. The physical build keeps accelerating faster than the market structure meant to price it. On to the Philippines. Philippines To the Philippines, and there's real movement on both the currency and the weather today. Start with the peso — it closed today at 61.410 to the dollar, a third consecutive session of gains: 61.675 Monday, 61.614 Tuesday, 61.410 today, pulling further away from the record low of 61.847 set last week. The driver had been softening oil ahead of this morning's overnight spike, plus broad dollar weakness. Does the overnight Hormuz escalation put that recovery at risk? It's the obvious tension to watch — the Philippines imports something like 98% of its oil, so three days of peso strength built partly on cheaper crude runs straight into a fresh oil spike. If Brent's move holds, expect at least some of this week's peso gains to give back tomorrow. What about equities? PSEi closed today at 6,304.03, down 10.87 points, 0.17%, with the broader All Shares index off 0.24% to 3,427.04 — late profit-taking, with investors still cautious on lingering Mideast uncertainty even as the index holds the 6,300 handle it reclaimed earlier this week. And the weather side? No active tropical cyclone, but there's a live low-pressure area — it was off Rapu-Rapu, Albay at 3 AM, and by 3 PM had crossed to Macalelon, Quezon. It's moving west-northwest and expected to emerge into the West Philippine Sea early tomorrow morning; PAGASA doesn't expect it to develop into a cyclone while it's still inside the area of responsibility. But it's bringing cloudy skies, scattered rain, and thunderstorms across Metro Manila, Central Luzon, CALABARZON, Bicol, Mindoro, Romblon, Marinduque, and parts of northern Luzon and the western Visayas, with flash-flood and landslide risk flagged. There's also a second low-pressure area that's formed outside the area of responsibility, roughly 1,755 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon, not expected to enter. No signal warnings up on either. And BSP Governor Remolona had new comments today, beyond the usual peso framing. This is the sharper line. He said there's a "small chance" of aggressive tightening this year, but explicitly left the door open to a bigger 50 basis-point hike at the next meeting on August 27th if inflation risks worsen. He specifically flagged Metro Manila's bigger-than-expected minimum-wage hike, renewed global market volatility, oil and currency swings, and US tariff uncertainty — though he said the biggest inflation hit from those factors likely lands in 2027, not this year. That's a harder edge than his usual "misleading number" framing. It is — he repeated that framing too, that peso weakness reflects broad dollar strength rather than anything peso-specific, and confirmed BSP did a small intervention last week to smooth the record-low print, arguing that fighting the dollar head-on would just burn reserves for a fight you can't win. But pairing that calm framing with an explicit openness to 50 basis points if conditions worsen tells you he's not ruling anything out — he's just not pre-committing either way, three and a half weeks out from the next decision. A peso clawing back gains that tonight's oil spike might erase, a flood watch with no named storm attached, and a central bank governor keeping a bigger hike explicitly on the table. Time for the vocab. Vocab Of The Day 到了学中文的时间了。 没错。今天两个词都跟今天的新闻直接相关，我们用中文聊。 好，你先来。 第一个词是"分歧"，名词，书面语，今天美联储的新闻里正好能用上。 怎么用？ 今天联储内部很可能出现分歧——达拉斯联储的Logan和克利夫兰联储的Hammack预计都会投反对票，这是沃什主席上任以来第一次出现这种分歧。 "分歧"跟"分裂"有什么不一样？ 区别很关键。"分裂"是真正的破裂，意味着这个机构可能因此分开、无法正常运作。"分歧"程度轻得多，只是内部意见不一致，但整个机构照常运转，决定照样能做出来。今天联储的情况就是分歧，不是分裂——两位委员投反对票，但利率决定还是会正常公布。 明白了，分歧是"意见不合"，分裂是"真的散了"。 对，搭配上也要注意，我们常说"出现分歧"，"内部分歧"，都是固定搭配。 我来说第二个词："未必"，这个可以用在今天Visa的新闻上。 说说看。 Visa这次业绩全面超预期，但是股价盘前还是跌了——这就说明，达标未必意味着上涨。 "未必"跟口语里常说的"不一定"有什么区别？ 意思差不多，但是"未必"更正式，更书面，常常出现在财经评论或者严肃的分析文章里；"不一定"更口语化，日常聊天用得多。而且"未必"这个词本身带一点委婉的反驳语气——不是直接否定，而是说"这不一定成立"，留有余地。 所以今天晚上微软和Meta公布财报的时候，我们也可以说，业绩超预期未必能让股价上涨。 完全可以，这就是"未必"最典型的用法——数字好，未必等于结果好。 一个正式名词，一个正式连接词，都是今天新闻里现成的例子。谢谢，Sam，中文部分就到这里。 Ngayon naman, Alex, dalawang salita mula sa balitang Pilipinas ngayon. Sige, simulan natin sa "gumaan." Paano ito ginamit? Gumaan ang presyon sa piso sa nakaraang tatlong araw, dahil bumaba ang presyo ng langis bago pa ang biglaang pagtaas ngayong gabi. Ano ang pagkakaiba nito sa "bumaba" o "humina"? Malaking pagkakaiba. Ang "bumaba" o "humina" ay tumutukoy lang sa numero mismo — bumaba ang halaga, humina ang piso. Ngunit ang "gumaan" ay tungkol sa pakiramdam ng presyon o bigat — parang may binuhat kang mabigat na bagay, at unti-unti itong naging magaan. Kaya kahit hindi pa lubos na nawala ang presyon sa piso, pwede mo pa ring sabihing gumaan ito, dahil bumawas ang bigat nito sa tatlong araw na iyon. Kaya't ito ay tungkol sa relief, hindi resolution. Eksakto. At ito ang pangalawang salita, mula naman sa balita tungkol sa panahon: "pag-iingat." Gamitin natin sa pangungusap. Nananawagan ang PAGASA ng pag-iingat sa mga lugar na maaaring apektuhan ng baha at pagguho ng lupa, habang tumatawid ang mababang presyon patungo sa West Philippine Sea. Bakit hindi na lang "ingat" nang mag-isa? Magkaiba ang bigat. Ang "ingat" ay isang simpleng salita — pwede mong sabihin nang mabilis, kaswal, halos parang pabalita lamang. Ang "pag-iingat" naman ay mas pormal, mas may bigat — tumutukoy ito sa isang patuloy, sinasadyang gawain, hindi lang isang sandaling babala. Iyon din ang tono ng parehong PAGASA at ni Gobernador Remolona ngayon — hindi sila nagbibigay ng maikling babala lamang, kundi humihiling ng patuloy, sadyang pag-iingat sa parehong panahon at ekonomiya. A word about relief without resolution, and a word about sustained caution rather than a passing warning — both straight from today's Philippines news. Four sharp ones today, two languages, all tied straight to the news. Arts & Culture Arts and culture, and today's lead has real news-day timing — the Aspen Art Fair opens this morning. Third edition, running through Saturday at the Hotel Jerome, and the first under new director Kelly Cornell, who also runs the Dallas Art Fair — that's a cross-fair collector pipeline she's clearly building deliberately. More than 35 exhibitors, with a genuinely notable new feature this year: a debut outdoor sculpture garden extending into the hotel grounds, which reads as a direct pitch to Aspen's collector base's taste for large-scale outdoor work. Who's showing? Newcomers include Albertz Benda, Friedman Benda, Library Street Collective, Monique Meloche, and R & Company. Returning names are Marianne Boesky, Perrotin, Sean Kelly, and Gmurzynska — a tighter, more design-forward roster than you'd see at one of the majors, which is exactly the specificity play a third-year regional fair needs to justify itself against Basel and Frieze fatigue. Second story is a major London opening. Anish Kapoor's first major UK retrospective in 28 years just opened at the Hayward Gallery — the last time the Hayward gave him a survey was 1998. It's a building-wide immersive show, curated by Ralph Rugoff, installations pressing into the walls, floor, and ceiling of the space itself, and it's the centerpiece of Southbank Centre's 75th anniversary programming. Runs through October 18th. And there's a Tate Modern show generating real debate. "Frida: The Making of an Icon" at Tate Modern — deliberately not a conventional retrospective. It traces Kahlo's cultural afterlife rather than just her body of work, more than 130 pieces alongside work from over 80 artists she's influenced, from the surrealists through to pop culture. It's already one of Tate's fastest-selling shows ever, more than 140,000 tickets pre-sold before opening. But the critical reception has split hard — Frieze's review headline was blunt: "Tate Mistakes the Icon for the Artist." What's the actual critique? That by curating around Kahlo's cultural influence rather than her own artistic development, the show risks flattening her into the version of herself that sells tote bags, rather than engaging with the paintings as paintings. It's a real tension in how museums program blockbuster shows around cultural icons versus serious artistic reappraisal — and 140,000 pre-sold tickets suggests the commercial bet is paying off regardless of what the critics think. On to opera. Glyndebourne Festival's new production of Strauss's "Die Fledermaus" opens tonight, directed by Liam Steel, with Thomas Atkins in the cast, running through August 8th — a lighter, comic counterpoint to the heavier programming we've covered from Glyndebourne and Bayreuth this summer. And one from the page. The New York Review of Books' latest issue carries Gabriel Winslow-Yost's review of George Saunders's new book "Vigil" — a Christmas Carol-style structure, but the ghost story is reframed: instead of an afterlife reckoning for a man who wronged other people, it's an oil-company CEO confronting grief for a planet rather than a person. Winslow-Yost reads it as a genuine indictment of corporate greenwashing wrapped in a familiar fable structure, not just a gimmick borrowing Dickens's shape. A fair opening with real cross-disciplinary ambition, a Kapoor survey three decades in the making, a Kahlo show splitting critics even as it sells out, and Saunders turning a Christmas ghost story into a climate reckoning. Let's close warm. One Good Thing One good thing today, and the timing is perfect — it's International Tiger Day. What's the actual number? The global wild tiger population is up roughly 40% between 2015 and 2022 — estimated around 4,500 tigers now, up from a low of about 3,200 in 2010. Numbers are climbing in five countries specifically: Bhutan, China, India, Nepal, and Russia. Any standout among those five? Nepal is the one worth naming. Their tiger count climbed from just 121 in 2009 to 429 this year — more than a threefold increase in under two decades, in a country that's nowhere near the largest or wealthiest of the five, which tells you this isn't just a story about money. It's community-level anti-poaching work, habitat corridors, and sustained political commitment across multiple governments, all compounding over seventeen years. A species that was genuinely trending toward crisis a generation ago, quietly turning a corner in five different countries at once. Genuinely one of the better conservation trend lines out there right now, and worth marking on the one day of the year built for it. That's The Morning Commute for Wednesday, July 29th. Oil re-escalated overnight right before the Fed speaks, Boeing and Visa gave us a preview of how unforgiving this earnings season can be, and wild tiger numbers are up 40% and climbing. Big day ahead — the Fed decision this afternoon, Microsoft and Meta tonight. Wherever you're listening from today, take care of yourselves — we'll see you next time. 分歧 a difference of opinion; divergence (within a group that still functions together) Fed's expected hawkish dissents (Logan, Hammack) at today's FOMC decision 未必 not necessarily (adverb, softly hedges or pushes back on a claim) Visa's clean earnings beat that the market punished anyway, previewing tonight's Microsoft/Meta bar gumaan became lighter/eased — relief from pressure or weight, without the pressure being fully gone The peso's three-session recovery, built on softer oil, now at risk from tonight's overnight spike pag-iingat carefulness; sustained caution (a deliberate, ongoing practice, not a passing warning) PAGASA's flood/landslide advisory and BSP Governor Remolona's watchful policy stance, both today

docs.title: Tuesday, July 28, 2026
docs.text: Tuesday, July 28, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. It's Tuesday, July 28th. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Here's the thread this morning: the AI-capex story just took two fresh hits from two completely different directions, on the same day. Different directions how? One is financial. Nvidia is now reportedly in talks to guarantee up to 250 billion dollars in lease payments so OpenAI can occupy a massive new campus, plus up to 350 billion in financing so OpenAI can buy Nvidia's own chips. Call it 600 billion of combined exposure, on top of a project that could cost half a trillion dollars outright — the largest data center ever proposed. That's not a demand story anymore. That's Nvidia underwriting its own customer's balance sheet. And the other hit is structural, out of Korea. Right — the Kospi fell nearly 11% overnight, Samsung down more than 13%, SK Hynix down close to 15%. And the trigger this time isn't AI-capex valuation nerves — it's a report that a Chinese state-backed firm has started mass-producing its own lithography tools. That's a threat to the machines that make the chips, not just to who's buying them. Financing risk and technology risk, both landing on the same trade in the same 24 hours. Exactly — while, underneath all of it, oil is still easing, the Fed decides tomorrow, and Zelensky is walking into the White House this morning as the Senate weighs a brand-new Russia sanctions bill. A lot to get through. Let's start with the world. Headlines Two world stories, and the first one is the next chapter in the Hormuz story we've been tracking. There's real structure on the table now, which is new. Oman has formally presented Iran with a proposal for a joint transit mechanism through the Strait of Hormuz, modeled explicitly on how the Strait of Malacca is run — voluntary user fees that fund navigation, environmental monitoring, and search and rescue. Crucially, Iran does not get unilateral control of the strait under this model. It's internationalized, funded by the users, not gate-kept by one country. So this is a step beyond the strike pause we covered last week. It is. Iran held follow-up calls with both Saudi Arabia and Oman over the weekend, the US-Iran strike pause is holding into a second and third quiet night, and Trump is calling the talks "good." Iran, for its part, is still denying that formal negotiations with Washington are underway — it insists this is all through Oman. But the fact that there's now an actual mechanism being discussed, not just a pause in the shooting, is what would let Brent's crash become durable instead of dormant. That's the distinction that matters for pricing risk this week. Second world story, and it's happening at the White House as we tape this. Trump is hosting Zelensky today. Zelensky is in Washington partly for Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral, and he's set to meet all 100 senators this evening as the chamber weighs the bill that carries Graham's name — the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act. It's been revised down from an original blanket 500% tariff to a 100% tariff, but specifically targeted at the world's top five buyers of Russian oil and gas. Who's on that list? China and India, at the top. So this isn't abstract Russia sanctions anymore — it's a secondary-tariff weapon aimed at two of the biggest economies on earth, timed to land right next to a Fed decision and a week of hyperscaler earnings. The bill has stalled twice already since Graham's death on July 11th, even with more than sixty cosponsors, so don't assume passage — but the fact that it's back on the floor the same week as everything else makes it a genuine tail risk to price. Structure on oil, sanctions leverage on Russia. Let's get to the tape. Market Overview The board this morning: S&P 500 at 7,413.18, up just 0.02%. Nasdaq Composite at 24,932.08, down 0.18%. Dow at 52,210.08, up a healthy 0.51%. Russell 2000 at 2,948.04, up 0.62%. Same rotation as Monday — value and small-caps over tech. For a second straight session, yes. Nasdaq-100 futures were down as much as 0.8% before the open on chip weakness — Nvidia, Micron — before paring some of that loss. Dow futures were the outperformer overnight, up around 0.3%. It's a narrower, more selective de-rating than a broad risk-off; the mega-caps under AI-capex scrutiny are the ones getting sold, everything else is fine or better. And crude is still falling. Brent's at 84.11, down 4.8% just today, off a prior close of 88.36. That's a second leg lower on top of Friday's roughly 8% crash — the Hormuz mechanism story is compounding the relief, not just holding it. And bonds are following: the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.65% as of yesterday's close, down from 4.69% Friday and 4.71% the day before that. Three straight sessions of yields grinding lower. Which sets up tomorrow perfectly. It really does. The Fed decides Wednesday having lost almost the entire hike case it built last week on the oil spike. And in the same 48 hours, Microsoft and Meta report Wednesday night, Apple and Amazon Thursday night — the same collision week we flagged Monday, except now the oil side of the equation has eased even further and the AI-capex side has gotten two fresh wounds instead of zero. Macro tailwind, micro headwinds. Let's go to business. U.S. Business First story is the one everyone's talking about — the Nvidia-OpenAI numbers. Let's be precise about the shape of it, because "Nvidia invests in OpenAI" undersells what's being reported. Nvidia is in talks to guarantee up to 250 billion dollars in lease payments so OpenAI can take space on SoftBank's 10-gigawatt Ohio campus in Pike County — that's the backstop that lets the landlord get financing, because Nvidia's credit is better than OpenAI's. Separately, Nvidia is reportedly discussing up to 350 billion dollars in financing so OpenAI can buy — Nvidia's own chips. So it's underwriting the building and financing the equipment inside it. Both ends of the transaction. Combined exposure near 600 billion dollars, on a project whose total cost could top half a trillion — the single largest data center commitment ever floated. Michael Burry's line is making the rounds again: "around and around we go." It's early-stage, it could collapse, but the market reacted immediately — Nvidia fell about 5% Monday and was still soft into this morning, Micron down close to 5% premarket, while AMD actually gained, up more than 3%, on the read that a shakeout in Nvidia's financing model could open share for a rival. Why does the market care so much about the structure, not just the size? Because "circular financing" isn't a slur, it's a description of concentrated risk. If Nvidia guarantees the lease AND finances the chip purchase, then a slowdown in OpenAI's revenue doesn't just hit OpenAI — it flows straight back onto Nvidia's balance sheet from two directions at once. That's precisely the kind of interlocking exposure that turns a single counterparty's stumble into a systemic one. Watch whether these terms firm up before Wednesday's hyperscaler prints — if Microsoft or Meta lean into a similar vendor-financing structure in their own guidance, that tells you this is becoming the industry's playbook, not a one-off. And it's worth noting these talks are still explicitly described as early-stage — nothing's signed. Right, and that matters for how you trade it. The stock move Monday wasn't pricing a done deal, it was pricing the mere existence of the conversation — the market deciding that even a proposal this size tells you something true about how strained the financing math has gotten across the industry. If the talks do collapse, you'd expect at least part of Monday's move to reverse. If they firm up into real terms, expect the "circular financing" framing to attach itself to every subsequent hyperscaler capex guide this earnings season, fairly or not. Second story is closer to a straight earnings check — Boeing and Visa, both due today. Boeing reports before the bell — 10:30 Eastern call — with consensus at a loss of somewhere between 28 and 34 cents a share on revenue around 24 to 24.3 billion, up 6 to 7% year over year. Deliveries are expected up 14% to 171 jets, 129 of them 737s, and the FAA restored Boeing's self-certification authority on July 20th, which should show up directly in delivery cadence. Visa reports after the close — consensus 3.22 to 3.23 a share, revenue near 11.4 billion, payments volume around 3.9 trillion. Neither has actually printed as we tape this, so take the numbers as the setup, not the result — Boeing in particular may already be out by the time you're listening, so the read-through is: watch the delivery number and free-cash-flow conversion on Boeing, and cross-border volume on Visa, as your two tells on whether the real economy is as shaky as the AI multiple. A financing structure that could reshape the whole AI trade, and two earnings prints that'll tell us if consumers and industrials are fine regardless. Let's go abroad. International Business & Politics International, and the first story is the scale of that Korea move — worth dwelling on. It's a proper crash, not a dip. The Kospi closed down 10.8% at 6,023.66, its weakest close since April, with trading halted multiple times along the way. Samsung fell 13.4%, SK Hynix 14.7% — and SK Hynix's US-listed ADR closed at 143 dollars, which is actually below its own IPO price of 149. That's a stock erasing its entire post-listing gain in one session. And this is a different trigger than the chip-stock selloff we covered a week ago. Completely different. Last time it was AI-capex valuation fear rippling through memory names. This time the trigger is a report that a Shanghai state-backed firm has begun mass-producing China's first homegrown immersion DUV lithography tools — I'll get into the detail in the China segment — but the read for Korea is that this isn't "the AI trade got expensive," it's "the moat just got a crack in it." Competitive fear prices very differently than valuation fear — it doesn't mean-revert the same way. Second story is a genuine split-screen out of European earnings today. The STOXX 600 is up a modest 0.3% to 646.75, but underneath that calm index there's real dispersion. Unilever is up 6% — its biggest one-day gain in two years — on a strong Q2 sales-growth beat. Mercedes-Benz is up 3% on operating profit climbing 22%. LVMH sales up 3%. That's the "Europe earns the value multiple" thread playing out live — consumer, auto, and luxury names all beating. But not everyone's participating. Saipem, the Italian energy-services name, is down 7.6% after cutting its 2026 core-earnings guidance — and it explicitly cited costs tied to the Middle East crisis. So even as Brent craters and the broader European tape celebrates, there's still a name eating war-premium costs on the ground, because contracts and project costs don't unwind as fast as a futures price does. Two speeds inside the same relief rally. Consumer Europe cheering, energy-services Europe still paying the bill. On to China. China China's story today is the direct cause of that Korea crash, and it's worth being precise about what actually happened, because it's easy to overstate. Go. A Shanghai state-backed company has begun mass production of China's first homegrown immersion DUV lithography machines — roughly five units delivered so far this year to SMIC, Hua Hong, and CXMT, with about twenty more slated for 2027. DUV lithography is the equipment tier that's critical for chips down to about 7 nanometers — the workhorse node for a huge share of the world's actual chip volume, well below the absolute cutting edge but enormously consequential in scale. And the honest caveat? The platform is still viewed as roughly a generation behind ASML on throughput, overlay precision, and reliability — this is not "China has caught up." But it is China's first real domestic mass-production milestone in a category it has never before produced at scale, and ASML shares slid on the report. The read that matters: this is the equipment side, not just the chip side, of what we've been calling China Shock 3.0. Beijing isn't just subsidizing memory output anymore — it's now shipping the tools that make chips, which is the harder, longer-horizon part of import substitution. That's why Korea, which sells both the memory and increasingly competes on the equipment side, took the sharper hit than anyone in the US chip complex did overnight. The tools, not just the chips. Onto power. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities This is where sovereign capital and grid physics collide, and the lead story today is a harder-edged sibling to the NextEra-Dominion merger we've mentioned before. Harder-edged how? NextEra is still negotiating final agreements with both the US and Japanese governments — part of the broader 550 billion dollar Japan trade package — for 9.5 gigawatts of gas-fired data center "hubs." One is 5.2 gigawatts and 16 billion dollars in Anderson County, Texas. The other is 4.3 gigawatts and 17 billion dollars in Pennsylvania. These talks were supposed to close by this spring. They're still open. So sovereign capital is now a bottleneck on gigawatts, the same way turbine supply and interconnection queues are. Precisely — this is one step past Chevron's Project Kilby, where an oil major became a power developer. Here it's a foreign government's trade commitment gating whether a specific gas hub gets built at all. And the merger itself has news too: Virginia's State Corporation Commission has scheduled its first public hearing for November, and NextEra executives are now guiding to closing the Dominion deal "by late 2027" — pushed back from the original second-half-2027 target. Filed with FERC, the NRC, and three state regulators, and still not close to done. There's also a governance fight brewing inside PJM that sounds bigger than the usual cost-allocation squabbles. It is bigger. FERC Chair Laura Swett ran a technical conference on July 23rd and effectively gave PJM until the end of September to reform itself — board independence, a real formal role for states in filing rights — or FERC imposes the reforms unilaterally. And here's the tell that this is serious: some transmission owners inside PJM are now openly discussing leaving the RTO altogether. That's not a rate case, that's a legitimacy crisis for the market structure that clears more data-center interconnection requests than anywhere else in the country. Give me the number that actually quantifies how tight this is getting. SemiAnalysis has the sharpest one. Behind-the-meter data center deployment — generation built on-site, skipping the interconnection queue entirely — is on pace to cross 50% of new US data center capacity by 2028, with the behind-the-meter total addressable market topping 50 gigawatts a year by 2029. But gas turbine additions stay under 10 gigawatts a year through 2026 and 2027. And here's the number that should worry anyone underwriting PJM load: the 2027-2028 capacity auction cleared 134,478 megawatts of unforced capacity against a 20% target reserve margin — the actual reserve margin is 14.4%. That's a physical deficit of roughly 6,517 megawatts, before the next wave of data center load even shows up. Any names attached to that behind-the-meter wave? Three concrete ones worth knowing. Crusoe's Goodnight site in ERCOT — 525.5 megawatts, building toward a roughly 1-gigawatt IT campus. AWS at Comanche Peak — a 1,200-megawatt deal, a 20-year power purchase agreement ramping through 2032. And CyrusOne with Constellation at Freestone — up to 760 megawatts potential. Behind-the-meter isn't a side case anymore, it's becoming the primary path for the biggest loads, precisely because the interconnection queue and that shrinking reserve margin make the grid-connected path slower and riskier. There's also a legal ruling this week that matters for anyone underwriting federal co-investment in this build-out. Right — a federal judge, Amit Mehta, ruled that the Department of Energy's cancellation of 7.6 billion dollars in clean-energy grants across sixteen states — battery plants, hydrogen, grid upgrades, carbon capture — was based, quote, "solely on political identity," a violation of equal protection. DOE actually admitted the political motive in court filings after months of denying it publicly. That's a real regulatory-risk data point: if you're underwriting a project counting on a federal grant, the political durability of that grant just got tested in court, and lost. One more before we move on — a rate case that's a clean illustration of the affordability-versus-return fight utilities are having everywhere right now. Pepco, the DC-area utility owned by Exelon, is asking Maryland regulators to raise its allowed return on equity to 10.5% from 9.5%. Maryland's People's Counsel — the state's consumer advocate — is alleging the ask is inflated through what's called "double leveraging," essentially borrowing at the parent-company level and then asking ratepayers to fund a higher equity return than the underlying economics justify. The Public Service Commission's decision is due in early August. A hundred basis points doesn't sound like much. On a rate base the size of Pepco's, it's real money flowing straight into monthly bills, at the exact moment every one of these utilities is also asking customers to fund gigawatts of new data center interconnection. That's the tension underneath every one of tonight's stories — the capital is there for the build-out, but who actually pays the return on it is being litigated state by state, case by case. Sovereign capital, grid governance, a reserve-margin deficit, a court ruling on federal grant risk, and now a return-on-equity fight in Maryland — a full week of energy news packed into one segment. Let's head east. Philippines To the Philippines, and today's actually a quiet weather day — worth saying plainly rather than manufacturing drama. It is. No active tropical cyclone and no low-pressure area being monitored inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility this morning. What's driving the forecast is just the ordinary southwest monsoon — habagat — bringing partly cloudy to cloudy skies with scattered rain and thunderstorms nationwide. Ilocos, Zambales, and Bataan are getting it from the habagat directly; Eastern Visayas, Caraga, and Davao are getting scattered rain from easterlies on the other side of the country. No signal warnings anywhere. Temperatures running 25.8 to 32.2 degrees. A routine monsoon day, nothing more. Which means the real story is back on the macro side — and there's a genuinely fresh angle today. There is. The peso closed at 61.675 to the dollar today, strengthening by 17.2 centavos from Friday's record-low close of 61.847. The PSEi rose 0.54%, up 33.89 points, to 6,314.90 — back above the 6,300 level. The driver is the same one moving every market this morning: Brent's continued easing, extending Friday's Iran de-escalation crash, and the Philippines imports something like 98% of its oil, so cheaper crude is close to a direct income transfer for this economy. And BSP Governor Remolona actually spoke to reporters today — what did he say? This is the part I'd lead with if I were producing the segment. He confirmed BSP did intervene "in a small way" last week to defend the peso, but kept it deliberately limited — his framing was that heavy defense against a strong dollar is largely futile, it just depletes reserves for a battle you can't really win, so the goal is orderly markets, not a fixed level. But the sharper line was about Friday's record print itself — he called the 61.85 number "misleading," arguing it reflects broad dollar strength against basically every currency, not a peso-specific weakness. Other currencies weakened by similar magnitudes the same day. Is that just a governor managing the narrative, or is there a real distinction there? There's a real distinction, and it matters for what BSP does next. If the move is peso-specific — capital flight, a current-account problem — that argues for a rate response. If it's dollar-broad — every currency moving together on US rate expectations or safe-haven flows — the correct response is closer to what he described: light intervention, patience, no hike. And that's exactly what he signaled — he sees only a "small chance" of aggressive or off-cycle tightening. The one thing he did concede, and it's the honest part: continued peso weakness still stokes inflation through import pass-through, since most of what the Philippines imports is dollar-invoiced. So he's threading a needle — don't overreact to a print he thinks is noise, but don't ignore that weakness itself is an inflation input regardless of its cause. A quiet sky and a governor doing careful signal-processing on his own currency. Time for the vocab. Vocab Of The Day 到了学中文的时间了。 没错。今天有两个词，都跟今天的新闻有关系，我们直接开始，用中文聊。 好，你先来第一个。 第一个是一个连接词，书面语，很正式：不仅，而且。今天英伟达的新闻正好可以用这个词。 那你造个句子。 英伟达这次不仅要为OpenAI的巨额资本支出提供担保，而且还要资助他们购买自己的芯片。 意思是说，英伟达不但是担保人，而且还是资金方，两个角色都占了。这跟口语里常用的"不但，而且"有什么区别？ 意思基本一样，但是"不仅，而且"更正式，更书面，常出现在分析报告或者新闻评论里。而且它常常表示后面这件事比前面更让人意外，或者程度更深。你看我这句话，前半句已经很惊人了——担保两百五十亿美元的租金；后半句更狠——还要资助三千五百亿美元让对方买自己的芯片。 明白了，"不仅，而且"是往上加码，不是简单地并列。 对，这就是它的用法。 好，我来说第二个词，也是今天新闻里的：施压。 这个词很常见，尤其在政治和外交新闻里。 我用今天参议院的新闻造句：参议院正准备立法，向购买俄罗斯石油的国家施压。 说得好。"施压"字面意思是"施加压力"，但是要注意，它跟"逼迫"不一样。 有什么区别？ "逼迫"是直接强迫，对方没有选择的余地。"施压"是从外部施加压力，但是被施压的一方还是可以选择抵抗，或者不理会。参议院对中国和印度施压，但这两个国家完全可以不理，只是要承担后果。搭配也要记住："向"加上对象，再加"施压"——向某人施压，向某国施压。 从担保到施压，两个很有分量的词。谢谢，Alex，中文部分就到这里。 Now let's switch — Sam, take us into Tagalog. Sige, dalawang salita ngayon, pareho galing sa balitang Pilipinas kanina. Simulan natin sa "katatagan." Sabihin mo sa akin kung paano ito ginamit. Pinapanatili ng BSP ang katatagan ng piso sa pamamagitan ng maliit na interbensyon, hindi agresibong pagtaas ng interes. Ibig sabihin, hindi sila nag-aabang ng lakas, kundi ng katatagan — dalawang magkaibang bagay. Tama. "Katatagan" ay hindi pareho ng "lakas." Ang lakas ay tungkol sa kung gaano kalakas, kung gaano ka-mataas ang halaga. Ang katatagan ay tungkol sa kung gaano ito kacontrolado, kung gaano ito kastable — kahit humihina nang dahan-dahan, pwede pa ring may katatagan, basta't kontrolado ang paghina. Galing ito sa salitang-ugat na "tatag," ibig sabihin matatag, hindi natitinag. Kaya naiintindihan natin bakit ganoon ang sinabi ni Gobernador Remolona — hindi niya sinasabing malakas ang piso, sinasabi niyang kontrolado ang sitwasyon. Eksakto. At ito naman ang pangalawang salita, direktang mula sa sinabi niya: "nakaliligaw." Gamitin natin sa pangungusap. Sabi ni Gobernador Remolona, nakaliligaw ang numerong iyon dahil sa pangkalahatang lakas ng dolyar, hindi partikular na kahinaan ng piso. Ano ang pinagkaiba nito sa "peke"? Malaking pagkakaiba. Ang "peke" ay nangangahulugang huwad — parang may sadyang pandaraya, hindi totoo. Pero ang "nakaliligaw" ay galing sa salitang "ligaw," ibig sabihin maligaw ng landas. Totoo ang numero — 61.85 talaga ang naitala — pero ang punto ni Remolona ay hindi ito dapat basahin bilang isang kuwento tungkol sa piso lamang, dahil ililigaw ka nito sa maling konklusyon kung ganoon ang unawain mo. So it's real, but it points you the wrong way. Exactly — "nakaliligaw" is about interpretation, not fraud. Katatagan and nakaliligaw, both straight from Remolona's own briefing today. A formal connective and a hard verb from the Mandarin side, a policy word and a framing word from the Tagalog side — four ways to sound sharper in either language today. Arts & Culture Arts and culture, and today's lead is a genuine fashion-meets-fine-art crossover with a very specific news hook. The Aspen Art Fair opens tomorrow, Wednesday, running through Saturday at the Hotel Jerome — its third edition, and the first under new director Kelly Cornell. More than 35 exhibitors this year, including Anat Ebgi, Perrotin, Friedman Benda, Albertz Benda, Southern Guild, Ryan Lee, and Secci — a genuinely serious roster for a fair still building its identity relative to the bigger summer circuit. And the fashion angle? Balmain is a lead sponsor, and they're using the fair to unveil Antonin Tron's debut collection as the house's new creative director — Fall/Winter 2026 — through something called "La Suite Balmain." They've converted the Hotel Jerome's Executive Suite into a private salon, staging the collection in dialogue with Anat Ebgi's art presentation rather than as a separate, bolted-on activation. Why does that curatorial choice matter, versus just throwing a fashion party next to an art fair? Because it's a bet on continuity of eye — the idea that a serious creative director's first collection and a serious gallery's art selection can be read together, each sharpening the other, rather than the fashion side just borrowing the art world's credibility for a photo backdrop. Balmain putting a debut collection reveal — arguably the single highest-stakes moment of a new creative director's tenure — inside a private art-fair salon rather than a runway show is a statement about where they think the discerning eye actually lives right now. Worth watching whether Tron's first pieces read as in conversation with the art on the walls, or just adjacent to it. How does Aspen fit into the broader art-fair landscape right now? There's been a lot of talk about fair fatigue. That's exactly the pressure a third edition under new leadership has to answer. The bigger fairs — Basel, Frieze, the Armory — have spent the last few years consolidating attention and budget, and a lot of the mid-tier regional fairs have either folded or shrunk. Aspen's answer, at least on paper, is specificity rather than scale: a smaller, tighter roster of thirty-five-odd galleries, a resort setting that guarantees a captive, moneyed audience for four straight days, and now a fashion-house anchor tenant willing to stage its biggest moment of the year there instead of Paris or New York. Kelly Cornell's bet is that you don't beat the majors by imitating them — you beat them by being the one fair a serious collector plans a summer trip around, rather than one stop on a circuit they're already fatigued by. A fair finding its identity, and a fashion house betting its biggest reveal on an art crowd's judgment. Let's close warm. One Good Thing One good thing today, and it's a proper piece of conservation news from the English coast. Tell it. For the first time in more than thirty years, a puffin chick has hatched on mainland England's south coast — at the Dancing Ledge colony in Dorset, managed by the National Trust. This colony had dwindled to just six birds. Volunteers installed trail cameras back in March, tracked adult puffins bringing in fish for weeks between the end of May and early July, and the puffling is now about 38 to 40 days old and getting ready to fledge out to sea. What made the difference after thirty-plus years of nothing? Patient, unglamorous monitoring, mostly — knowing enough about a colony that's down to six birds to protect the one nest that actually worked, rather than managing for a headline number. It's a small population, one chick, one summer. But it's the first proof in three decades that this particular stretch of coastline can still produce a puffin, and that's the kind of quiet, verifiable win that's easy to miss next to a trillion-dollar data center story. One puffling, thirty years in the making. That's The Morning Commute for Tuesday, July 28th. Financing risk and technology risk both hit the AI trade today, oil kept easing into a Fed decision, and a puffin made it back to Dorset. We'll be back tomorrow with the Fed and the first wave of hyperscaler earnings. Take care of yourselves — we'll see you next time. 不仅 not only (formal connective, typically paired later in the sentence with 而且 'but also' to stack a second, stronger fact onto the first) Nvidia's $600B circular financing with OpenAI — lease guarantee AND chip financing 施压 to exert pressure (on someone/something); to pressure The Senate's Russia sanctions bill pressuring China and India as top buyers of Russian oil katatagan stability; steadfastness — the quality of holding firm under pressure BSP's light, deliberate intervention to hold the peso steady rather than defend it aggressively nakaliligaw misleading; causing one to be led astray Remolona calling the peso's record-low print a 'misleading number'
