docs.text: Monday, July 27, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. It's Monday, July 27th. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Here's the thread this morning: the war premium is unwinding, and it's pulling the two forces that terrorized last week apart from each other. Unpack that. For two weeks, everything moved together — a Middle East war bidding crude toward 100, and an AI-capex de-rating bleeding the tech tape. Oil and equities, one risk-off machine. This weekend, one of those two engines cut out. The US paused its airstrike campaign on Iran, diplomacy reopened over the Strait of Hormuz, and Brent has crashed roughly 8% back toward 89 dollars. And the instant relief is everywhere. Asia and Europe are up across the board this morning, gold's firm, the whole oil-and-rates vise just loosened a notch going into the Fed. Right — but here's the tension, and it's the whole show. The oil engine cut out. The AI-capex engine did not. On Friday the Nasdaq still fell while the Dow rose — tech got sold even as the oil scare eased. So the two stories that were compounding have now split apart: crude relief takes pressure off the Fed and off every oil importer, while the market's reckoning with AI spending rolls on, indifferent to the price of a barrel. Which sets up a genuinely brutal collision. The Fed decides Wednesday, having just lost the oil excuse to hike. And the same 72 hours, the four biggest spenders in tech report — Microsoft and Meta Wednesday night, Apple and Amazon Thursday. Macro relief and micro reckoning, in one window. War premium out, capex verdict in. Let's get into it, starting with the reason crude cracked. Headlines Two world stories to open, and the first one is why oil fell out of bed. Alex, the guns went quiet. They did — at least for now. After nearly two weeks of nightly US strikes on Iran, the campaign paused. Iran's health ministry described Saturday as, quote, a peaceful night — the first with no US strikes — and by Sunday the pause held for a second day. Iran, in turn, held its retaliatory fire. And running underneath the ceasefire in the air is a diplomatic track over the water. The Strait of Hormuz. Oman is mediating. Iranian and Omani technical teams spent the weekend on how to let Iran's vessels transit the strait with fewer restrictions — the mechanics of reopening the chokepoint that's been the beating heart of this oil premium. That's what the market seized on. Brent fell as much as 8% to trade near 89, WTI down toward 83 and a half. But you're being careful with the word "ceasefire," and I want listeners to hear why. Because it isn't one. There's no signed deal, no confirmed reopening date, no tanker traffic figure yet. Iran's foreign ministry went out of its way to say it has no direct negotiations with Washington — only with Oman. And the US naval posture around Hormuz is technically still in place. So this is a de-escalation built on a strike pause and a mediator, not on a fundamental return of supply. Meaning the premium can snap right back. That's exactly the asymmetry. The move down is real, but it's a diplomacy headline, and diplomacy headlines are reversible in a single overnight session. So the right way to hold this is: the oil tail risk has gone from live to dormant, not from live to dead. It hands the Fed room this week — but it's borrowed room, not banked room. File that distinction. Story two is a physical disaster with a macro shadow — the wildfires tearing through southwestern Europe. This is staggering. France has carried out its largest peacetime evacuation since the Second World War — roughly 220,000 people cleared out of the Gironde region around Bordeaux. Combine it with Spain and you're over 320,000 displaced. France has now lost about 115,000 hectares to fire so far this year, at least one person is dead, and the smoke plume is visible from space. And there was a strikingly visible second-order hit. The final stage of the Tour de France, on Sunday, was shortened so security could be pulled off the route and sent to the fire lines. When a country reroutes its biggest sporting event to fight wildfires, that's the climate-risk premium showing up in real time. For markets it's a slow burn — literally — but it feeds the same European story we keep circling: heat, energy stress, and an insurance bill that keeps climbing. Two fires, one in the oil market cooling off and one in the Gironde that won't. Let's bring it to the tape. Market Overview Let's set the board. Friday's close, the last completed session, and it was a split tape — which is the tell for the whole week. The S&P 500 finished essentially flat at 7,411.98, up just 0.05%. But underneath that calm surface, the Dow rose 0.46% to 51,947, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.64% to 24,975.82. And the Russell 2000 slipped 0.35% to 2,930. So the average did nothing, but the rotation did everything. That's the key read. Value and cyclicals up, mega-cap tech down. This was not a broad risk-off — it was a targeted de-rating of the AI leadership even on a day the oil scare was already fading. Tesla fell about 3% for its third straight down day, leaving it off roughly 19% on the week and about 26% for July after Thursday's earnings plunge. The Nasdaq-100 booked its first back-to-back weekly loss since March. And the bond market started to exhale. It did — the first relief in a week. The 10-year yield eased to 4.69%, down from 4.71%, the 2-year down to 4.33% from 4.37%, the 30-year at 5.16%. That's the oil bid coming out of the curve. Remember, last week yields were climbing on the war premium feeding inflation expectations. Take crude down 8% over a weekend and that pressure reverses — which is precisely why this Fed meeting just got more interesting, not less. And this morning the relief globalized. Everything green. The Nikkei rose 0.5% to 64,931, the KOSPI up 1% to 6,755, the Hang Seng up 1% to 25,207, Shanghai up 1.2% to 3,858. Europe's STOXX 600 is up about 1%, the FTSE up a quarter percent to 10,766. Gold is firm at 4,103, up 0.8%. The yen sits at 163.6, the yuan at 6.75, the euro at 1.139. It's a clean oil-relief bounce — the mirror image of last week's oil-and-rates risk-off. So walk into the setup, because the calendar is where the tension lives. This is the collision. The Fed decides Wednesday afternoon. The market has hold at roughly 63 to 65%, with a live 25-basis-point hike still priced near 35 to 38% — those hike odds tripled over the past week purely on the oil spike. And now the spike has half-unwound before they even sit down. So the question flips: does Chair Warsh's committee lean on the cooler-oil relief and hold comfortably, or does it stay hawkish on an inflation rate still near 3.7%? And the earnings stack right on top of it. In the same 72 hours: Microsoft and Meta report Wednesday evening, Apple and Amazon Thursday. Four of the biggest capex guides in the world, landing the same day the Fed reads out. There is no room to take these one at a time — the tape has to price a monetary decision and the AI-spending verdict essentially simultaneously. That's why a flat Friday is deceiving. This is the loaded week. Macro relief, micro reckoning. Let's talk US business. U.S. Business Two marquee US prints tee up tomorrow, Tuesday, and together they're a clean read on the thing the market's obsessing over — capex that actually converts to cash. Start with Boeing. The turnaround everyone keeps waiting on. And it just cleared a real hurdle. Effective July 20th, the FAA restored Boeing's authority to issue final airworthiness certificates for all newly built 737 MAX and 787 jets — a bottleneck the regulator had held since the door-plug crisis. That directly speeds deliveries, and deliveries are cash. For the quarter, Wall Street sees the loss narrowing to about 34 cents a share on roughly 24 billion in revenue, with commercial deliveries up 14% year over year to 171 jets — 129 of them 737s. So the story is the free-cash-flow inflection. Exactly. 737 production has stabilized around 42 a month and Boeing is preparing to push toward 47. The tell tomorrow isn't the headline loss — it's the delivery rate and the cash conversion. And notice the irony against our whole throughline: while the market punishes hyperscalers for capex outrunning cash, here's an industrial whose entire bull case is capex finally turning into cash. Same verb, opposite direction. The one caveat: the 787 line is still gated by engine supply and premium-seat certification, so some deliveries slip into the back half. The second print is the consumer's turn — Visa. Visa reports fiscal Q3 tomorrow too, and it's the broad read the affluent-only Amex number couldn't give us Friday. Consensus is 3.22 a share, up about 8% year over year, on roughly 11.4 billion in revenue. The number I'd watch is total payments volume, seen near 3.9 trillion dollars, up about 8.8%, with cross-border the swing factor. Why cross-border specifically? Because it's the high-margin, travel-and-tourism pulse of the global consumer — and it's the first place you'd see a crack if the year's rate and oil stress were actually biting spending. Visa has beaten on earnings four quarters running. If payments volume holds near 3.9 trillion, it tells you the consumer that powered the soft landing is still transacting — which is the ground truth under a market busy pricing a slowdown into rate-cut bets. Boeing on cash conversion, Visa on the consumer — two Tuesday tells on whether the real economy is as wobbly as the AI multiple. Capex that converts, and a consumer that spends. Let's go international. International Business & Politics Two from overseas, and the first is a genuine upside surprise out of Europe. The eurozone's July flash PMI came in hot. The composite jumped to 51.9 — a 5-month high — from 50.0, well above the 50.3 the Street expected. And the internals are better than the headline: the manufacturing output index hit 53.0, a 52-month high, with services at 51.6. That's the first real expansion in activity in four months, consistent with GDP growth around 0.3% for the quarter. So the calm central bank looks vindicated. It reinforces the ECB's whole posture. They held last week and called themselves, in Nagel's phrase, in a good position — and now the data backs it. But hold the second-order read we keep coming back to: Europe is growing without an AI-capex engine. It's a real-economy, manufacturing-led expansion. Which is exactly why European equities keep getting the value multiple, not the growth multiple — earnings without the AI story. Good economy, cheaper stocks, on purpose. Story two is the other central bank in the frame — the Bank of Japan, Friday. And there's a new wrinkle. The BOJ meets Friday and is still expected to hold at 1%, which is already a 31-year high after June's hike. But officials are now said to be open to hiking faster than the market assumed, because the yen at 163.6 is itself an inflation source. Governor Ueda is expected to sound hawkish, and markets have started pricing a meaningful chance of an October move. And the oil drop cuts across that. It does — that's the fresh cross-current. Part of the case for the BOJ to hurry was imported energy inflation. Knock 8% off crude and you soften that argument at the margin, even as the weak yen keeps pushing the other way. So Friday's BOJ read lands right after Wednesday's Fed, and both are being pulled by the same two variables — oil down, currencies weak. Washington, remember, is openly pressing Tokyo to keep tightening. Two central banks, back to back, both boxed by the same forces, just from opposite sides. One oil price, every monetary policy. Speaking of which — China. China China gave us a fresh data point this morning that quietly captures the whole two-speed story. June industrial profits rose 15.1% year over year — which sounds strong until you see the trend: that's a slowdown for the second straight month, down from 21.1% in May. For the first half, profits are up 18.7%. So the profit engine is decelerating even as the number stays positive. And the reason it's decelerating is the reason it matters today. A big chunk of this year's profit rebound wasn't underlying demand — it was a base effect from higher energy and producer prices, plus a genuine boom in AI-related chips and equipment. Now take energy prices back down, and that flattering tailwind fades. The reflation that padded the numbers is thinning out. Which is the debt-deflation trap in one data series. It really is. This is an economy that needs price increases to power profits and pay down debt, and it keeps not getting durable ones. The AI and export-equipment strength is real — that's the fast lane. But the broad industrial economy underneath is running on base effects that are rolling off. So Beijing gets a headline that looks like a 15% profit expansion, while the momentum quietly bleeds lower. Two speeds, and the slow one is the whole economy. A recovery that flatters on the way in and fades on the way through. Let's talk power. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities This is where the micro reckoning gets physical, and the single best data point this week came out of PG&E's quarter — because it tells you the shape of AI demand is changing, not just the size. Give me the number. PG&E's data-center interconnection pipeline hit 12.7 gigawatts, up from 5.1 gigawatts just one quarter ago. That's a two-and-a-half-times jump in a single quarter. But CEO Patti Poppe said the thing that actually matters: they're focusing, quote, not on size, but on quality — and most of the new applications are now 100 megawatts or smaller. Only about 1.8 gigawatts of that pipeline is expected online by 2030. So the pipeline exploded, but the individual loads shrank. That's the tell, and it's a regime change. The single-campus, gigawatt training whale is being joined — maybe displaced — by a swarm of smaller, latency-sited inference nodes. Inference wants to sit close to users, so you get many sub-100-megawatt requests scattered across the map instead of one giant one. And that reshapes everything downstream: interconnection study queues, and crucially, it lets a utility cherry-pick creditworthy loads instead of betting its whole rate base on a single hyperscaler off-taker. Smaller, more numerous, more diversifiable. You've also got a genuinely new kind of constraint surfacing this week — not megawatts, but the behavior of the megawatts. This is my favorite item of the week. Crusoe and ON.energy are deploying 5 gigawatts of medium-voltage — call it an AI uninterruptible power system — across hyperscale campuses, commissioning through 2026 into 2027. It's an inline power-electronics layer that decouples the facility from the grid and rides through voltage faults without disconnecting. But the real job is taming load volatility. Explain the volatility problem, because I don't think people picture it. A large AI training cluster doesn't draw steady power. When the GPUs synchronize on a training step, the load can swing from high to low and back hundreds, even thousands of times a day. To a utility, a gigawatt of training doesn't look like a gigawatt of steady factory load — it looks like a gigawatt that's constantly slamming up and down, which is genuinely destabilizing to the local grid. So this buffering layer is becoming a gating requirement to interconnect at all. And the investable read? It opens a whole new behind-the-meter equipment category, and it means grid planners will start pricing ride-through capability — not just raw capacity. You don't just have to prove you can supply the electrons; you have to prove your load won't wreck the neighborhood. That's a new bar, and a new margin pool. Third item, and it ties straight to Wednesday and Thursday: SemiAnalysis reports that Nvidia's next platform, Vera Rubin, delivers roughly 5.4 times the performance per megawatt of the current generation on inference workloads. 5.4 times per megawatt — if it holds. Big if — that number is off CoreWeave engineering samples, SemiAnalysis says it hasn't independently verified it, and audited figures come in Q3. But take it seriously as a direction. A five-fold jump in tokens-per-megawatt is the first real efficiency valve on the electrons wall. A fixed substation feed suddenly buys you five times the inference output next cycle. And that cuts two ways — it could blunt near-term megawatt demand, or, by Jevons paradox, it could pull even more compute onto the same interconnection because compute just got cheaper to power. And that's the lens for the capex prints. Precisely. When Microsoft and Meta guide Wednesday and Amazon guides Thursday, the question isn't just how many billions. It's whether their capex plans assume this efficiency step is coming — in which case the raw-megawatt panic is overdone — or whether they're still provisioning power as if every token needs today's wattage. That single assumption sits under every gigawatt in every one of these pipelines. Philippines To the Philippines, and for once the weather desk leads with good news — the storm has cleared out. It has. Typhoon Kiyapo — international name Noul — has exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility. As of PAGASA's latest bulletin it was about 745 kilometers west-northwest of Itbayat in Batanes, still a strong system with 140 kilometer-per-hour sustained winds and gusts to 195, but moving away to the northwest. And critically, all wind signals are down — no areas under storm warning this morning. But you're not calling the all-clear. Not quite, because the monsoon doesn't leave with the typhoon. Kiyapo is still enhancing the habagat — the southwest monsoon — so PAGASA has moderate-to-heavy rain over Pangasinan and Zambales, and scattered rain and thunderstorms across Metro Manila and the rest of Luzon, with the usual flash-flood and landslide watch. So the acute landfall threat is gone, but the chronic rain tax on Luzon stays — and that's the piece that keeps hitting food prices and daily disruption. And the macro tape is where the throughline finally hands the Philippines a break. For the first time in weeks, yes — with a caveat. The peso closed Friday at a fresh record low, around 61.85 to the dollar, and the stock market, the PSEi, fell about 2% on the week to 6,283. So the pressure was still building into the weekend. But then crude fell 8%. For an economy that imports something like 98% of its oil, that overnight drop in Brent is the single most powerful variable in the entire macro picture, and it just flipped favorable. So the peso's chief tormentor eased. The peso's tormentor has been the oil import bill — every dollar on the barrel widened the trade gap and pushed the currency down. Knock 8% off crude and you relieve exactly that channel. Now, analysts are still warning of a possible test of 62, because a strike pause isn't a peace deal and the oil relief could reverse. But for today, the BSP gets to breathe. It hasn't had to hike into weakness, its reserves buffer is intact, and the external shock that was doing the damage just softened on its own. And all of this is the backdrop to the day's big set-piece. The politics. President Marcos delivers his fifth State of the Nation address this afternoon in Manila, and he's framing it around austerity — no red carpet, no pageantry, resources redirected to the Middle East crisis response. The economic asks are expansive, though: 23 free-trade agreements to lift exports, around 100 job fairs, a food-security push with farm-insurance payouts and land titles for farmers by 2027, and a headline tax-relief pitch to raise the minimum taxable income to 350,000 pesos. And there's an energy angle that's right up our alley. There is — he's expected to call to strip the electricity system-loss charge and the VAT off power bills, and to amend the country's power-industry law, EPIRA, immediately. That's a direct cost-of-living lever aimed at the same electricity affordability fight we track everywhere else. Layer on an anti-graft message — his line is, quote, I am not president of my family — and hundreds of millions of pesos clawed back from flood-control corruption. But the ceiling on all of it is the debt: national debt is now around 18.6 trillion pesos, roughly 165,000 pesos for every Filipino. Expansive promises, austerity staging, a debt wall behind it — and, for once, a tailwind from cheaper oil. Vocab Of The Day Vocab of the day. Two Mandarin, then two Tagalog, each tied to a story we ran — and we do this in-language. Alex, kick us off in Mandarin. 今天第一个词是"回落"。(Today's first word is huíluò, to fall back, to retreat.) 油价从100美元回落到89美元左右。(Oil prices fell back from 100 dollars to around 89.) 注意,"回落"不是普通的"下跌"。(Note — huíluò isn't the ordinary word for a drop, xiàdiē.) 它特指从高点回到较低的水平。(It specifically means falling back from a high point to a lower level.) 对,这是关键的近义词对比。(Right, that's the key near-synonym contrast.) "下跌"只是往下走,而"回落"带有"回到原来水平"的意思。(Xiàdiē just means going down, but huíluò carries the sense of returning to a previous level.) 这是财经书面语。(It's formal, financial-desk register.) 所以我们说股价回落、油价回落、通胀回落。(So we say stock prices, oil prices, inflation all huíluò — fall back.) 搭配很自然。(The collocation is very natural.) 第二个词是连词:"与此同时"。(The second word is a connective — yǔcǐ tóngshí, meanwhile, at the same time.) 油价回落;与此同时,人工智能股票继续下跌。(Oil prices fell back; meanwhile, AI stocks kept falling.) 这正是今天的主线。(That's exactly today's throughline.) 一个压力消退,与此同时,另一个压力还在。(One pressure recedes; meanwhile, the other one persists.) 很好。"与此同时"比口语的"同时"更正式、更书面。(Good — yǔcǐ tóngshí is more formal and written than the colloquial tóngshí.) 在新闻报道里,连接两件同时发生的事,用"与此同时"最地道。(In news reporting, to link two things happening at once, yǔcǐ tóngshí is the most idiomatic choice.) 记住:它常常放在句子开头,引出第二件事。(Remember — it usually sits at the start of a sentence, introducing the second event.) 现在换成菲律宾语。(Now let's switch to Tagalog.) Ang unang salita ay "kaluwagan." (The first word is kaluwagan — easing, relief, breathing room.) Ang pagbaba ng presyo ng langis ay nagbigay ng kaluwagan sa piso. (The fall in oil prices gave the peso some relief.) Tama. At mahalaga ang pagkakaiba sa "ginhawa." (Right, and the difference from ginhawa is important.) Ang "ginhawa" ay pakiramdam ng kaginhawahan; ang "kaluwagan" ay puwang o luwag pagkatapos ng higpit. (Ginhawa is a feeling of comfort; kaluwagan is space or slack after a tightness.) Kaya sa ekonomiya, ang mababang langis ay nagdudulot ng kaluwagan sa badyet ng pamilya. (So in the economy, cheaper oil brings relief to the family budget.) Kolokasyon: magbigay ng kaluwagan, or may kaluwagan. (Collocation — to give relief, or to have some breathing room.) Ang pangalawang salita ay "katipiran" — austerity o pagtitipid. (The second word is katipiran — austerity or thrift.) Ang tema ng SONA ni Marcos ay katipiran. (The theme of Marcos's State of the Nation address is austerity.) Mas pormal ito kaysa sa "tipid" lang. (This is more formal than just tipid.) Ang "tipid" ay pang-araw-araw; ang "katipiran" ay isang patakaran o prinsipyo — para sa gobyerno o buong bansa. (Tipid is everyday; katipiran is a policy or principle — for a government or a whole nation.) Kaya may katipiran sa gitna ng 18.6 trilyong utang. (So there's austerity in the middle of 18.6 trillion in debt.) Apat na salita: 回落, 与此同时, kaluwagan, katipiran. Arts & Culture Arts and culture. Alex, let's start where the eye goes — with two faces, five centuries apart. Two portrait stories, and the first is a quiet coup for a tiny Sicilian museum. In Cefalù, the Museo Mandralisca has taken its most famous possession — Antonello da Messina's "Portrait of an Unknown Man," painted around 1465 — and placed it face to face with a second Antonello portrait, on loan from the Palazzo Madama in Turin. Two of the sharpest psychological studies in all of Quattrocento painting, in one small room. And Antonello's the painter who bridged two worlds. That's why it matters. Antonello fused Flemish oil technique — that jewel-like precision, the way light sits on skin — with Italian monumentality and structure. His "Unknown Man" has this faint, knowing half-smile that people have argued about for 150 years. Seeing two of these heads in dialogue lets you read the artist's mind: how he builds a living, skeptical human being out of oil and light. For a regional museum to stage that is a real critical event, not a listings entry. Story two keeps us on the human face but jumps to the 20th century. The National Portrait Gallery in London has "Marilyn Monroe: A Portrait," marking the centenary of her birth, on through early September. Warhol, Richard Avedon, Cecil Beaton, and — the one to notice — Pauline Boty, the British Pop artist. The show's argument is that Monroe wasn't just the most photographed woman of her age; she was a co-author of her own image, deliberately building the persona rather than passively wearing it. So it's about image-making, not nostalgia. Exactly — it's a show about authorship and control, which is a far more interesting subject than celebrity. Put it beside the Antonello and you get a lovely rhyme: two exhibitions, 500 years apart, both about how a face gets constructed into a picture. And on the page, the calendar peg is tomorrow: the Booker Prize 2026 longlist drops Tuesday at 2 PM London time. It's chaired by the classicist Mary Beard, with a genuinely eclectic panel — the musician Jarvis Cocker and the poet Patricia Lockwood among them. A classicist steering the year's biggest literary-fiction prize should make for unusual, argumentative picks. And a note for the music lovers. One from the summer festivals: the BBC Proms staged a Prog Rock Prom this season — Carl Palmer of Emerson, Lake and Palmer, and Guy Garvey of Elbow, backed by the BBC Concert Orchestra. It sounds like a novelty, but the curatorial argument is serious: progressive rock always aspired to the scale and structure of orchestral music, so scoring it for a full orchestra in the Albert Hall treats it as repertoire, not nostalgia. A face built in oil, a face built in photographs, and prog rock built for an orchestra — a week about how things get made into art. Nicely tied. One good thing to close. One Good Thing One good thing, and it's a genuine advance in men's health. Imperial College London reported the results of a 10-year trial following about 3,500 men with prostate cancer — and it found that focal therapy, which targets only the tumor rather than treating the whole prostate, is as effective as full surgery or radiotherapy at controlling the cancer. As effective — but easier on the patient? That's the breakthrough. Treating the whole gland is what causes the two side effects men dread most: incontinence and erectile dysfunction. By treating only the diseased tissue, focal therapy roughly halved both. Same cancer control, about half the life-altering harm — and now with a decade of data behind it, which is what turns a promising idea into a standard of care. So it's not a trade-off anymore — you don't have to choose between beating it and living well after. That's the whole point. For years the deal was: we can treat this, but it may cost you your continence or your sex life. A 10-year study of 3,500 men says, increasingly, that's a false choice. For the hundreds of thousands of men diagnosed every year, that's a very good thing to wake up to. A good place to end. That's The Morning Commute for Monday, July 27th. The war premium receded, the AI reckoning rolled on, and the whole week now funnels into 72 hours of Fed and mega-cap earnings. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Whatever this Monday holds, take good care of yourself, and we'll be right back here with you tomorrow. 回落 to fall back, retreat, ease off (of a price/level from a high) Brent crude falling back ~8% from ~$100 toward $89 on the Iran strike pause 与此同时 meanwhile; at the same time (formal connective linking two simultaneous developments) the throughline — war premium receding while the AI-capex de-rating continues at the same time kaluwagan easing, relief, breathing room; slack or leeway after a period of tightness cheaper oil easing the pressure on the peso and the family budget (98%-oil-import economy) katipiran austerity; thrift or economizing as a policy or principle Marcos's fifth SONA framed around austerity against ₱18.6T national debt

docs.title: Friday, July 24, 2026
docs.text: Friday, July 24, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. It's Friday, July 24th. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Here's the thread this morning: two verdicts, one week, and everything is now a countdown to the collision. Unpack that. The AI-capex de-rating that started with Alphabet and Tesla has broken into a full global risk-off. Yesterday was the S&P's worst day in a month, down 1.2%, the Nasdaq off 2.2%. And overnight it went around the world — Tokyo down 2.7%, SoftBank alone off 7.4%. The market has stopped paying for the build, and now it's actively charging for it. That's verdict one — Wall Street's verdict, and it's about cash. Capex is outrunning free cash flow, and the tape is finally putting a price on that gap. Right. Verdict two is the grid's verdict, and it's about electrons — the same capex slamming into turbines, transformers, and transmission. And sitting underneath both is a war premium that stopped being a threat and became kinetic on land: Iran hit a second Gulf power-and-water plant in two days, and Brent traded through 100 dollars for the first time this cycle. Oil up, gold down, yields steepening — an inflation impulse, not a fear bid. And all of it funnels into one 72-hour window next week: the Fed meets Tuesday and Wednesday, in the exact same stretch that Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and Amazon all report. Two verdicts, one week — Wall Street on cash, the grid on electrons, the Fed on oil. Let's get into it, starting overseas. Headlines Two world stories to open, and the first one is why crude broke 100. Alex, the war moved onto land. It did. The escalation everyone feared has jumped from shipping to fixed infrastructure. Kuwait says Iranian strikes hit a second power-and-desalination plant in two days — a fire, several generating units knocked offline. And Bahrain's military says it intercepted projectiles fired from Iran overnight. So this is no longer just tankers in the strait. It's the Gulf's water and power. That's the pivot. Up to now the war premium lived at sea — Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, hulls on fire. Now Iran is targeting the thing the Gulf states cannot lose: desalination. Much of the Gulf drinks water that comes from those plants. Hitting them turns an oil story into a survival story, and it widens the set of targets that can gap crude at any hour. And the market read that instantly — Brent up 7% to settle around 100.65, its first print through 100 this cycle, WTI up better than 6% toward 92. Which is exactly why this trades as a supply shock and not a fear bid. A fear bid pulls money into Treasuries and yields fall. This did the opposite — oil up, yields up — because it's an inflation impulse landing straight on a Fed that meets in five days. And the desalination angle changes the escalation math in a way I want to make sure people catch. It does, because it removes an off-ramp. As long as the war lived on tankers, there was always a de-escalation path — reroute the ships, escort the convoys, price in a freight premium and move on. Water plants are fixed, and they're existential. You can't reroute a country's drinking water. So striking them raises the stakes for the Gulf states to respond, which is precisely the kind of feedback loop that keeps a war premium bid rather than fading. Meaning the market can't confidently sell the rip anymore. Right — every attempt to fade the oil spike now has to price the tail that the next target is another plant, not another hull. That asymmetry is why crude held 100 into the close instead of giving it back. Story two is the currency side of the same pressure — Japan, where the yen just hit a 40-year low and Washington is leaning on Tokyo in public. The yen sank to about 163.8 to the dollar, the weakest since 1986. What's new is the US posture: the Treasury is now openly pressing the Bank of Japan to keep hiking. Finance Minister Katayama says Tokyo and Washington are in, quote, 24-hour contact, and that Japan is, quote, ready to act decisively. So the US actually wants Japan to tighten — a mirror image of the usual currency fight. And notice the second-order risk they're both worried about, which is the carry trade. When the yen is this cheap and BOJ rates are this low, global investors borrow yen for nothing and buy higher-yielding assets everywhere else. A disorderly snap-back in the yen forces all of those positions to unwind at once — that's what triggered the August 2024 global equity air-pocket. With the AI complex already wobbling, nobody wants a yen unwind stacked on top. It's a striking reversal. Normally Washington complains a trading partner is too weak on purpose. Here it's urging the BOJ to normalize faster to arrest the yen slide, because a collapsing yen exports deflation and stokes carry-trade risk. It all points at the BOJ's July 31 decision — and note that lands the day after the Fed. Two central banks, back to back, both boxed by the same oil-and-dollar squeeze. File that BOJ date. Let's bring it home to the tape. Market Overview Let's set the board. Thursday's close, the last completed session, and it was an ugly one. The S&P 500 finished at 7,408.30, down 1.2% — 90 points, the steepest single day in a month. The Nasdaq Composite at 25,137.69, down 2.2%, the worst of the majors on the AI de-rate. The Dow at 51,711.65, down 1%. And the Russell 2000 actually held up best in relative terms, down just 0.7% to 2,940.16. So for once small caps weren't the worst — the pain was concentrated in mega-cap tech. Which tells you the character of the day. This wasn't a growth scare pulling everything down. It was a positioning unwind in the AI leadership, led by Tesla, which cratered 14.5% to 319.69 after its print. STMicro fell almost 19% on chips. That's the de-rating spreading name to name. And the bond market didn't offer any cover. No — it bear-steepened. The 2-year rose 6 basis points to 4.37%, the 10-year up 4 to 4.71%, the 30-year at 5.17%. The 10-year is up 11 basis points on the week, grinding higher right into the July 28th-29th FOMC. That is the oil bid feeding straight into the curve. Gold? Gold fell about 2.5% to roughly 4,050 dollars — again, the reflation tell. Oil up, gold down, real yields up. If this were fear, gold would be flying. And the VIX popped 12% to 18.70, its biggest one-day jump in weeks, though notably still below 20 — so stress, not panic. And this morning it globalized. Overnight the selloff went around the world. The Nikkei fell 2.7% to 64,611, SoftBank down 7.4% as the poster child for the AI-capex trade. Hang Seng and Shanghai both off about 1.4%, the ASX down 0.8%. Brent gave back a little in Asia, off 0.8% toward 99.87. US futures are mixed, trying to steady after the oil-driven Thursday. SoftBank down 7.4% is worth pausing on — that's a leveraged proxy for the entire trade. It's the cleanest single ticker for AI-capex sentiment. SoftBank is levered to its chip and data-center bets, so when the market decides it's overpaying for the build, SoftBank moves like the trade's beta with the amplifier on. A 7% down day there is the market saying the de-rating isn't a one-name Tesla story — it's the whole thesis being marked. And the setup into next week makes it heavier, because the calendar is brutal. It's the collision I mentioned. In a single 72-hour window you get the FOMC decision Wednesday afternoon, then Microsoft and Meta that same evening, then Apple and Amazon Thursday. So the market has to digest the Fed's read on the oil shock and the four biggest capex guides in tech essentially simultaneously. There's no room to take them one at a time. So we walk into a Friday with the whole AI complex on the back foot, oil hovering at 100, and a Fed that now has every reason to stay hawkish. Let's talk US business. U.S. Business Two prints this morning, and the first is a clean read on the American consumer. American Express delivered a record quarter — revenue 17.9 billion dollars, up 9% year over year, earnings of 4.08 a share, net income 2.9 billion. And the board raised the dividend 15% to 95 cents a quarter. A 15% dividend hike is not what you do if you're seeing cracks in the cardholder. Exactly the tell. Amex skews affluent, and billed business was strong — the high-end consumer is still spending. Put that next to a market pricing recession risk into rate-cut bets and you get the tension of this tape: the real economy keeps printing fine while the multiple on the AI trade gets marked down. The consumer isn't the problem; the capex math is. The second print is a telecom double-header, and it's the opposite mood. It is. Charter reported before the bell — Street looking for about 10.17 a share on 13.52 billion in revenue, which would be down almost 2% year over year. The number that matters isn't EPS, it's broadband net adds — or rather net losses. Charter has missed on broadband subscribers four straight quarters, squeezed from two sides: fiber overbuilders taking share and fixed-wireless — the cable operators call it "the phone companies' 5G home internet" — poaching the low end. And Verizon on the other side of that same fight. Verizon printed around 1.27 in adjusted earnings on roughly 35.3 billion in revenue, but the story is the restructuring — it's cutting 13,000 jobs and closing 274 stores, all while carrying a dividend yielding about 6.5% and digesting the Frontier fiber integration. So you've got cable and telecom both spending heavily to defend turf in a no-growth broadband market. It's the un-glamorous mirror of the AI capex story: capex with no revenue acceleration behind it. Capex everywhere, growth nowhere. Let's go international. International Business & Politics Two from overseas. Start with the German auto complex, because Volkswagen just cut its outlook. Volkswagen's Q2 was a miss and a guide-down. Operating profit came in at 3.5 billion euros, roughly 10% lower year over year and well short of the 4.3 billion consensus. More important, VW withdrew its upbeat full-year outlook — it now sees 2026 revenue down as much as 3%, having previously guided to 3% growth. That's a real reversal. And the driver is where you'd expect. China. VW's China deliveries fell about 37%. This is the China-EV squeeze showing up in the P&L of the West's biggest carmaker — domestic Chinese brands, BYD and the rest, are taking the home market VW built its franchise on. The stock fell 3% and dragged the whole European auto sector with it. It's China-shock, autos edition, and it's not a forecast anymore — it's in the quarter. Story two, the ECB held. The European Central Bank left all key rates unchanged Wednesday — the deposit rate at 2.25%, the main refi at 2.40%, marginal lending at 2.65%. It stays meeting-by-meeting with no pre-commitment. Bundesbank's Nagel said the ECB is, quote, in a good position, that the next real look is September, and — tellingly — he flagged Middle East energy costs as the live risk. The euro sat around 1.138. So even the ECB, which has been the calm one, is now watching the oil channel. Everyone is. That's the through-line of the whole show — the crude spike is the variable that boxes in every central bank at once. The Fed can't cut into it, the BOJ is being pushed to hike into it, and now the ECB is naming it as the thing that could stop the easing. One barrel, five monetary policies. China And China is the clearest case of a central bank easing with the brakes half on. The People's Bank just announced its biggest liquidity injection in five months — about 2.1 trillion yuan of overnight reverse repos staggered across the month-end, plus a 500 billion yuan one-year policy loan, for a net add of around 100 billion. That's a lot of plumbing. Why now? Because Q2 GDP cooled to 4.3%, the weakest in about three and a half years, and the month-end is always a liquidity crunch. But here's the tell: the PBOC is easing the quantity of money while holding the loan prime rate flat. It's flooding liquidity but refusing to cut the actual policy rate. And that refusal is the oil story again. It is. China imports enormous volumes of crude, so a run through 100-dollar Brent narrows the room to cut rates without stoking import inflation and pressuring the yuan, which sat around 6.774. So Beijing does the thing it can — pump liquidity — and withholds the thing it can't, a rate cut. It's a debt-deflation economy that needs lower rates and an oil shock that won't let it have them. Two-speed, and boxed. And there's a signal in preferring quantity over price that's easy to miss. There is. Injecting liquidity through reverse repos is temporary and reversible — it eases the month-end crunch without committing to a lower rate structure. Cutting the loan prime rate is a durable signal that lowers financing costs across the whole economy and, critically, widens the rate gap with the US, which pushes capital out and the yuan down. So the PBOC is threading it: relieve the plumbing, protect the currency. It's the policy posture of a central bank that has decided the exchange rate is the constraint that binds first. One barrel, five policies, and China's the tightest box of all. Let's talk power. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities This is where verdict two lives — the grid's verdict. And the single best data point this week came out of GE Vernova's quarter, because it quietly tells you the "turbines are sold out to 2030" story is only half true. Give me the number. The gas turbine backlog jumped from 100 to 116 gigawatts quarter over quarter. Sounds like the wall got taller. But look at the composition: only 53 gigawatts of that is firm equipment orders. 63 gigawatts — the majority — is slot-reservation agreements. Placeholders. So more than half the "sold out" backlog is options, not steel. Correct. And a slot reservation is cheap and cancelable — developers are hoarding turbine slots the exact same way they hoard interconnection-queue positions. The number that actually matters is the conversion rate: this quarter GE Vernova converted 10 gigawatts of prior reservations into firm orders, and shipped 3. That conversion pace — reservations turning into committed capacity — is the real tell, not the headline backlog. And the second-order read? The turbine constraint is softer than the 116 number implies. Reservation-holders who can't reach a final investment decision eventually free those slots for developers who can. So watch cancellation and conversion disclosures the way you'd watch queue-withdrawal rates. Revenue was 11.1 billion, up 22%, and they raised the full-year guide — the business is real. But the scarcity is being overstated by a queue of optionality. You've also got a genuinely new policy lever this week — on the transmission side. This is the one to file. At a Senate energy hearing Tuesday, FERC Chair Swett said the commission is standing up a grid-enhancing-technology task force — GETs. That's dynamic line ratings, advanced power-flow controllers, and high-performance conductors — reconductoring existing lines with carbon-fiber-core wire that carries roughly twice the power on the same poles and the same right-of-way. Why does that matter against everything else we track? Because every constraint we usually talk about — the interconnection queue, cost allocation, 160-week transformer lead times — is on the generation or interconnection side. GETs attack the deliverability wall from the corridor side. You squeeze more megawatts through right-of-way you already own, without a new transformer or a new line. It's the one lever that can add effective transfer capacity on a 12-to-24-month clock instead of a 5-to-7-year one. And if FERC attaches a return incentive to it? Then reconductoring becomes a rate-based growth line for the transmission owners — a distinct investable theme from the data-center cost-allocation fight. Watch for return-on-equity adders. And the third piece ties the turbines and the policy together: the behind-the-meter gas boom just added an oil-major counterparty. Chevron's Project Kilby, near Pecos, Texas — 2.67 gigawatts, 7 to 9 billion dollars of capex, final investment decision targeted for year-end, first power 2028, a 20-year deal with Microsoft, and the majority of generation coming from large GE Vernova turbines. A supermajor becoming a power developer. That's the new margin pool. Chevron monetizes Permian gas as firm electrons, off the interconnection queue entirely, off the hyperscaler's balance sheet. And notice the ownership split emerging: in Wisconsin, We Energies wants to own the gas plants outright and socialize the cost across ratepayers. In Texas, Chevron owns and sells, keeping it off ratepayers. Same megawatts, opposite ratepayer incidence. That split — who owns the on-site plant — is going to be the whole political fight. And all of this is being ordered against a demand curve we find out more about next week. Right — the hyperscaler capex prints land next Tuesday through Thursday. Meta's guiding to 125 to 145 billion this year, AWS to around 200 billion, Alphabet already printed 195 to 205 with negative free cash flow. That's the demand those 116 gigawatts of reservations and every Kilby-type campus are being built against. The question into next week is whether any of them trims the guide — because that would be the first crack in the reservation-to-firm pipeline. Philippines To the Philippines, and the weather desk leads — the storm intensified overnight. It did. Tropical Storm Kiyapo — international name Noul — strengthened from a depression into a tropical storm. As of PAGASA's 11 AM bulletin it was about 135 kilometers east of Aparri, Cagayan, packing 75 kilometer-per-hour winds, gusts to 90, central pressure 996 hectopascals, moving west at 30. Signal Number 2 is up over Batanes, northern mainland Cagayan including the Babuyan Islands, and northern Ilocos Norte. Track? It passes very close to northeastern Cagayan through the afternoon, with landfall over the Babuyan Islands expected Friday evening. And here's the part to watch: PAGASA sees it strengthening to a severe tropical storm after Babuyan and possibly rapidly intensifying into a typhoon over the West Philippine Sea before it heads for southern China. Meanwhile the southwest monsoon — the habagat — stays enhanced, so much of Luzon gets rain regardless of the storm's exact center. And the macro tape is where the throughline comes home. Hard. The peso sank to a fresh all-time intraday low of 61.845 to the dollar this morning, breaking yesterday's 61.75 record. And the driver is exactly the crude spike we opened with — Brent back above 100 for the first time since May. The Philippines imports something like 98% of its oil, so every dollar on the barrel widens the import bill and pushes the peso down. How is the BSP playing it? Unchanged posture. Governor Remolona is sticking to "smooth the volatility, small amounts, orderly markets" — limited dollar-selling, no policy shift, no hike. The buffer is the reserves: gross international reserves sat at 104.8 billion dollars at end-June, up slightly on the month. Fitch's BMI sees a 61-to-63 range near term and warns plainly that renewed energy-price gains will keep weighing on the peso through the import bill. Why not just hike to defend the currency? That's the textbook move. Because the domestic economy can't take it. Philippine growth is already running below target, and a rate hike aimed purely at the peso would tighten into weakness caused by an external oil shock — importing someone else's war into your own mortgage rates. So the BSP is choosing the lesser evil: let the peso find a level, lean on reserves to keep the descent orderly, and hope the oil spike proves temporary. It's the same box as the PBOC, just with a thinner buffer and a currency already at a record low. And there's a second hit landing the same morning. A new tariff wall. The US Trade Representative finalized a 12.5% tariff on Philippine goods, up from the 10% in place since February, citing Manila's failure to enforce a forced-labor import ban. The Philippines is among 41 economies hit at that 12.5% rate. Trade Secretary Roque says Manila will keep engaging and has stood up an inter-agency panel to prove its policy. So you have oil widening the import bill from one side and a tariff widening the trade gap from the other, both hitting the same peso on the same day. Which sets up Monday. It does. President Marcos delivers his fifth State of the Nation address Monday, July 27th — kept deliberately "simple" under an austerity frame tied to the Middle East crisis. Business groups want execution on jobs and food security over politics, and the backdrop is a national debt that hit 18.55 trillion pesos at end-May. A boxed central bank, a record-low currency, a fresh tariff, and an austerity speech — all downstream of one barrel of oil. Vocab Of The Day Vocab of the day. Two Mandarin, then two Tagalog, each tied to a story we ran — and we do this in-language. Alex, kick us off in Mandarin. 今天第一个词是"后果"。(Today's first word is "consequence.") 后果 指不好的结果 — 严重的、需要承担的那种。(Hòuguǒ means an outcome, specifically a bad one — serious, something you have to bear.) 我们可以说,资本开支超过现金流会带来严重的后果。(We can say: capital spending outrunning cash flow brings serious consequences.) 对。注意搭配:"承担后果" — 就是 to bear the consequences。(Right. Note the collocation: chéngdān hòuguǒ, to bear the consequences.) 还有一个近义词的对比很重要:后果 是负面的,而"结果"是中性的。(And an important near-synonym contrast: hòuguǒ is negative, while jiéguǒ, "result," is neutral.) 所以谈判有"结果",但错误的政策有"后果"。(So negotiations have a jiéguǒ, a result, but a wrong policy has hòuguǒ, consequences.) 这是书面语,对吧?(This is formal, written register, right?) 是,书面和新闻语体。(Yes — formal and newsroom register.) 第二个词是连词:"否则"。(The second word is a connective: fǒuzé, "otherwise.") 开发商必须做出投资决定,否则就会失去涡轮机的名额。(Developers must reach an investment decision, otherwise they lose the turbine slot.) 央行不能忽视油价冲击,否则通胀会失控。(The central bank can't ignore the oil shock, otherwise inflation gets out of control.) 否则 和"不然"有什么区别?(How is fǒuzé different from bùrán?) 意思一样,但"否则"更正式、更书面,"不然"更口语。(Same meaning, but fǒuzé is more formal and written; bùrán is more colloquial.) 在财经报道里用"否则"最合适。(In financial reporting, fǒuzé fits best.) 很好。现在换成菲律宾语。(Good. Now let's switch to Tagalog.) Ang unang salita ay "lubog." (The first word is "lubog," submerged or sunk.) Lumubog ang piso sa bagong record na mababa. (The peso sank to a new record low.) Tama. At ang magandang bahagi ay ang matalinghagang gamit. (Right. And the nice part is the figurative use.) Puwede kang lubog sa tubig, pero puwede ka ring lubog sa utang. (You can be submerged in water, but you can also be drowning in debt.) Kaya sa 18.55 trilyong piso na utang, puwedeng sabihin: lubog sa utang ang bansa. (So with 18.55 trillion pesos of debt, you could say: the nation is drowning in debt.) Ang kolokasyon na "lubog sa utang" ay napaka-natural. (The collocation "lubog sa utang" is very natural.) Ang pangalawang salita ay "pananggalang" — shield o depensa. (The second word is "pananggalang" — a shield or buffer.) Ang dolyar na reserba ng BSP ay pananggalang laban sa pagbagsak ng piso. (The BSP's dollar reserves are a buffer against the peso's fall.) Mas pormal ito kaysa sa "depensa," na hiram sa Espanyol. (This is more formal than "depensa," which is borrowed from Spanish.) Ang "pananggalang" ay mula sa "sanggalang" — proteksiyon. (Pananggalang comes from sanggalang — protection.) At ang kolokasyon: pananggalang laban sa — a shield against. (And the collocation: pananggalang laban sa, a shield against.) Kaya: ang 104.8 bilyong dolyar na reserba ay pananggalang ng piso. (So: the 104.8 billion dollars in reserves are the peso's buffer.) Apat na salita: 后果, 否则, lubog, pananggalang. Arts & Culture Arts and culture. Alex, there's a real market story hiding in the oldest, least-hyped corner of the auction world. There is, and it's a genuine bright spot against all the K-shaped gloom. Christie's and Sotheby's took a combined 76.7 million pounds — about 101.6 million dollars — across their Old Master and 19th-century evening sales in London's Classics week at the start of the month. That's up roughly 9.4% year over year. But you said the total isn't the story. The buyer base is. Sotheby's says about 20% of the bidders at its Old Masters evening were new to the house, and nearly a quarter of the lots went to collectors new to the field entirely. There's new money walking into the market's most traditional category — a rediscovered youthful Rembrandt, a Botticelli Madonna and Child, early Netherlandish works by Memling and van Orley, and a bronze Laocoön that drew fierce bidding. Fresh entrants are quietly re-rating the oldest paint on the wall. Story two stays British and goes to Constable. For the Constable 250 anniversary, The Hay Wain — the 1821 picture that basically is the English countryside in the popular imagination — is traveling for the very first time to the Suffolk it depicts. It's at Christchurch Mansion in Ipswich through October 4th, reunited with Constable's own preparatory sketches and loans from the Tate, the V&A, the Royal Academy. And there's a lovely irony the critics have seized on. The picture synonymous with painting the English countryside from life was actually finished in a London studio. The Guardian's Jonathan Jones reads the show as, in his words, a masterpiece for the climate-crisis age — a vision of a landscape we're now anxious about losing. It's a reminder that the most familiar image in British art was, in part, a studio construction. And on the page? Maggie O'Farrell is back with her tenth novel, "Land" — her first fiction since the Hamnet phenomenon. It's Ireland, 1865, in the shadow of the Famine, following an Ordnance Survey mapmaker and his young son charting a remote coastal peninsula. Reviews are admiring but split — Kirkus calls it evocative and impassioned, Publishers Weekly devastating yet tender, while some critics think the back half loses the thread. And the calendar peg for next week: the Booker Prize 2026 longlist drops Tuesday, judged by a panel chaired by the classicist Mary Beard. A mapmaker charting land we're about to lose, and a Hay Wain for the climate age — the arts are circling the same anxiety this week. Nicely rhymed. One Good Thing One good thing to close, and it comes from the North Atlantic. The 2026 right whale calving season just closed with 23 mother-and-calf pairs — the first season above 20 in fifteen years. For a species that's how endangered? That's what makes it matter — there are only about 380 North Atlantic right whales left on Earth. So 23 calves is a real number against that base. And the encouraging detail underneath it: 13 of the mothers were returning females calving on roughly a four-year interval, which is close to the healthy norm, after years of stretched seven-to-ten-year gaps that signaled a stressed, underfed population. So it's not just more calves — it's the population getting its rhythm back. Exactly. The calving interval is the vital sign, and this year it moved the right way. One good season doesn't save a species that fragile, but after a long run of grim counts, the whales gave the scientists something to be glad about. A good place to end. That's The Morning Commute for Friday, July 24th. Two verdicts, one week — Wall Street on cash, the grid on electrons, the Fed on oil — and 23 new whales to leaven it. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Take good care of yourself this weekend, and we'll see you Monday. 后果 consequence(s) — the (usually bad) outcome you have to answer for AI capex outrunning free cash flow / market de-rating 否则 otherwise; if not (formal connective introducing the negative alternative) turbine slot-reservations converting to firm orders / FERC energy policy lubog submerged, sunk; (figuratively) drowning under something peso sinking to a record-low 61.845 / national debt pananggalang a shield, buffer, or defense against something BSP's $104.8B gross international reserves as the peso's buffer

docs.text: Thursday, July 23, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. It's Thursday, July 23rd. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Here's the thread this morning: the market has stopped paying for the build. Meaning? Meaning Alphabet and Tesla both reported after the bell last night, and both beat on the top line — and both got punished anyway, because free cash flow went negative. The spending is now outrunning the cash, and the tape is finally charging for that. And the twist is that the same spending — the AI capex — is running straight into a physical wall. Power, water, transformers. Two verdicts landing at once. Exactly. Wall Street's verdict is about cash. The grid's verdict is about electrons. And sitting underneath both of them is a war premium that turned kinetic overnight — the Houthis actually set two Saudi tankers on fire, Brent is bid toward 98 dollars, and that's pushing yields up into next week's Fed meeting. So the oil-and-rates vise and the AI-cash reckoning are the same story today. Let's get into it, starting overseas. Headlines Two world stories to open, and both of them are why crude is up almost 5% this morning. Alex, the Red Sea first. This is the escalation everyone was worried about. Overnight, Houthi forces struck two Saudi oil tankers — the Encelia and the Layla — with missiles and drones. Both caught fire. UK Maritime Trade Operations confirmed a strike roughly 70 nautical miles southwest of Al Shuqaiq, with crews fighting the blaze. So this is no longer a blockade on paper. Earlier this week the Houthis declared Bab el-Mandeb closed. Now they're hitting hulls. That's the key distinction. This is the first actual vessel strike since the blockade declaration. The Houthis say roughly 10 ships have turned back; the Institute for the Study of War counts at least 7 rerouting around to the Suez approaches or holding off. Give people the scale of what Bab el-Mandeb actually is. Bab el-Mandeb carries about 5% of seaborne oil. The reason the market cares so much is the stacking: Hormuz is still effectively shut, and now you've got a second chokepoint under fire. Put a closed Hormuz together with a contested Bab el-Mandeb and you're threatening something like a quarter of global oil and gas flow. And that's why this reads as a supply shock, not a fear bid. It lifts real yields instead of crushing them. Right. A fear bid sends money into Treasuries and pulls yields down. This is doing the opposite — oil up, yields up, because it's an inflation impulse. It keeps the Fed's hold-versus-hike box firmly shut. Story two is the other end of that war premium — Iran and the strait itself, where the rhetoric got very specific. President Trump laid out what you might call a "bridge-for-a-ship" doctrine. He warned that every time Iran targets a vessel in Hormuz, the US will destroy one bridge or one power plant inside Iran. Tit-for-tat, infrastructure for shipping. And Tehran's answer? Iran said the strait will "never return to pre-war conditions" and threatened regional energy infrastructure in kind. US forces carried out their 12th consecutive night of strikes on Iranian targets. So this is a fully articulated escalation ladder now, and it's tied directly to shipping. Which is exactly what removes the off-ramp. When the trigger is a passing tanker, any single ship can re-light the whole thing. That's why the strait trades as a live tail risk that can gap oil at any hour. One diplomatic thread worth watching: Secretary of State Rubio publicly credited China — of all countries — for backing freedom of navigation through Hormuz. China takes a huge share of Gulf crude, so its incentive to keep the strait open is real. Interesting that Washington is leaning on Beijing as a stabilizer here. File that one away. Let's bring it home to the tape. Market Overview Let's set the board. Wednesday's close, the last completed session: the S&P 500 finished at 7,498.96, down 0.14%. The Nasdaq Composite at 25,690.90, down 0.57% — the laggard again on chips. The Dow essentially flat at 52,218.58, down 6 points. And the Russell 2000 was the worst of the majors, down 0.92% to 2,959.94. So small caps at the bottom, Nasdaq soft, Dow flat. That's a rates-and-positioning day, not a growth scare. Precisely. Look at the bond market: the 2-year rose 5 basis points to 4.31%, the 10-year up 4 to 4.67%, the 30-year at 5.15%. Yields grinding higher right into the July 28th-29th FOMC. That's the oil bid feeding straight into the curve. And gold? Gold pulled back to about 4,097 dollars from a 4,152 close — consistent with a real-yields-up day rather than a pure panic. The yen stayed weak past 163. But honestly, Wednesday's tape was just the warm-up act. The real verdict came after the bell. The Magnificent-7 earnings jury. Alphabet first — and this one is the template for the whole day. Alphabet beat almost everywhere. Revenue 119.8 billion dollars, up 24%. Google Cloud 24.8 billion, up 82% — and the cloud backlog ballooned to 514 billion dollars, from roughly 106 billion a year ago. Search 63.3 billion, up 17%. Operating income 40.8 billion, up 30%. That is a monster quarter. So why did the stock fall 5% after hours? Two numbers. Adjusted earnings came in at 2.85 dollars a share, just under the 2.89 the Street wanted — a rare bottom-line miss. But the real trigger was capital spending. Q2 capex hit 44.9 billion dollars, roughly double year-on-year, and that pushed free cash flow to negative 5.9 billion, versus positive 10.4 billion a year ago. So the company is generating enormous revenue and burning cash at the same time. And it guided the spend higher. Alphabet raised full-year capex to 195 to 205 billion dollars, up from 180 to 190, and said 2027 will rise "significantly." That's the third capex guide-up in three quarters. The market's message is blunt: a beat on fundamentals is not enough when the spend curve keeps bending up and cash flow goes negative. And Tesla told the exact same story in a different accent. Almost eerily so. Tesla's revenue was actually a beat — 28.24 billion dollars, up 26%, its first quarter over 100 billion on a trailing-twelve-month basis. Deliveries were a record second quarter: 480,126 vehicles, up 25%, about 74,000 above consensus. So the top line and the units were fine. Where's the damage? Everywhere below the top line. Non-GAAP earnings were 33 cents a share against expectations closer to 48 to 53 cents — a big miss. Operating margin collapsed to 1.4%, from 4.1%. Operating income fell 57% to 398 million dollars. And here's the punchline that rhymes with Alphabet: capex jumped 142% to 5.79 billion dollars, and free cash flow was negative 1.09 billion — Tesla's first cash burn since early 2024. Regulatory credits? Down 67%, to just 146 million. So the cushion is gone too. The stock closed at 374 and drifted to around 371 after hours. The read across both names is identical: the AI-and-robotaxi story stock is now spending like a hyperscaler while the actual margins evaporate. Negative free cash flow is the new verdict. And there's a third shoe still to drop tonight — Intel. Right, and let's be careful here: Intel has not reported yet. It prints tonight, Thursday, after the close. So we have no numbers. The Street is looking for about 14.4 billion in revenue and 21 to 22 cents a share. The things that matter for our purposes: external foundry revenue — it was only 174 million last quarter — plus 18A yields, and whether any large cloud customer commits to 18A. The stock ran up hard into the number, so the bar is high. So we frame Intel as tonight's catalyst, not last night's. The next shoe, not a result. Exactly. Don't report numbers that don't exist yet. U.S. Business Two US business stories, and the first is a regulatory knot rather than a financing one. Paramount, Skydance, and Warner Bros. Discovery. This is the roughly 110-billion-dollar media combination, and it's now caught in a genuinely unusual split. On Wednesday the European Commission granted conditional approval — Paramount agreed to drop its Universal film-distribution joint venture in Europe to get it through. So Brussels is a green light. But at home it's tangled. Very. The Department of Justice already approved the deal. But a 12-state coalition, led by California Attorney General Bonta, is suing to block it on Clayton Act antitrust grounds — and a federal judge issued a 14-day temporary restraining order on Monday freezing the whole thing. So you have state attorneys general fighting a merger that the federal DOJ has already blessed. That's the story — not whether they can pay for it. That's exactly it. The gating item here is regulatory risk from an unusual direction — a state-versus-federal antitrust split over one of the largest media deals ever attempted. If you own either stock, the courtroom calendar matters more than the synergy math right now. Story two is a cleaner, number-first deal — Repligen buying BioLife Solutions. Announced Wednesday. Repligen is acquiring BioLife for roughly 1.5 billion dollars in cash and stock. BioLife holders get 11.25 dollars in cash plus 0.1442 of a Repligen share — that works out to about 31 dollars a share, a 24% premium to the 90-day average price. Enterprise value around 1.5 billion, closing expected in the fourth quarter. And the signal in that? Bioprocessing and cell-therapy tools consolidation is alive and well. Even with the tape fretting about AI spend, bolt-on M&A in life-sciences tools keeps happening — Repligen is buying into the cold-chain and biopreservation layer that every cell-therapy pipeline depends on. Before we leave the US, give people the breadth check — the non-AI economy. It held up nicely on Wednesday. General Motors beat and raised — 3.57 dollars a share against 3.13 expected — and popped almost 5%. ServiceNow beat and raised, subscription revenue up 23% in constant currency, its AI annual contract value crossed 1 billion dollars, and the stock jumped almost 5% after hours. AT&T beat on subscribers — 65 cents against 59, with more than a million net adds — up about 5%. 3M rose 7%. Any cracks? One worth flagging: Synchrony Financial missed on revenue and fell about 2%. That's a card lender, so it's a small tell on the consumer-credit side. But the through-line is that the old economy — autos, industrials, enterprise software, telecom — is compounding just fine. The crack is specifically in negative-free-cash-flow AI names, which is why value and cash-return stories are being bid as the AI-capex names get sold. International Business & Politics Across the Atlantic, two European prints this morning that tell the same margin story in different sectors. Nestlé first. Nestlé reported first half numbers. And here's the shape: the volumes are finally coming back. Organic growth was 3.6%, with the second quarter at 3.7%, and — importantly — real internal growth, the actual volume number, turned positive at 1.5%. For a company that spent two years pushing price and losing volume, that's a genuine recovery. But the profit line? That's the catch. First-half net profit fell 31.4%, to 3.5 billion Swiss francs from 5.1 billion. So growth returned, and margins paid for it — restructuring and input costs biting while pricing power fades. Management raised the full-year organic guide to 3 to 4%, and unveiled a waters and premium-beverages joint venture with Platinum Equity that's expected to raise around 3 billion euros. So the CEO is signaling a leaner portfolio while eating the cost of the volume rebuild. And BNP Paribas is the mirror image of the US bank tape. Completely. BNP's second-quarter net income rose about a third to 4.35 billion euros — that's 4.97 billion dollars — beating the 4.21 billion consensus. The driver was record equity-trading revenue plus a retail-banking rebound. Group revenue up 12% to 14.1 billion euros, and they lifted the interim dividend 24% to 3.23 euros a share. So the volatility-driven trading windfall we saw at the US banks is global. That's the takeaway. It isn't a Wall Street quirk. When markets are choppy and volumes are huge, the big universal banks on both sides of the Atlantic print records off the same market structure. The war premium and the AI-capex churn are, ironically, very good for the people making the markets. China One China item, and it's the two-speed economy showing up in the government's own books. China released first-half fiscal data. Fiscal revenue rose 4.7% year-on-year to 12.1 trillion yuan, with tax revenue up 5.3% to 9.79 trillion — and the pace is actually accelerating, up from 4% in the first five months. On the surface, that's fine. So where's the two-speed part? On the spending side. Fiscal expenditure rose only 1.5%, to 14.33 trillion yuan. So revenue is growing more than three times as fast as spending. That is de facto passive tightening — the government is collecting faster than it's spending, at exactly the moment it keeps promising a fiscal push to hit around 5% growth. Li Qiang has been out there pledging stimulus. But it's not in the outlay data yet. It isn't. And the constraint is partly the oil story we opened with — imported energy inflation narrows the PBOC's room to ease. They held the loan prime rate for a 14th straight month, at 3.00 and 3.50%, and set the yuan fixing weaker, at 6.7933 to the dollar. So Beijing is walking the currency lower and talking up stimulus, while the actual spending stays cautious. The rhetoric and the ledger don't match — and for a debt-deflation economy, that gap is the whole ballgame. The tell is always the spending, not the speeches. Let's go to the segment where the AI story stops being abstract — the power. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities And this is where the two verdicts I mentioned up top actually connect. Because the same Alphabet capex number that spooked equity investors is a demand signal for the grid — 514 billion dollars of cloud backlog is contracted compute that has to find a substation. Start with that Alphabet capex through the energy lens, because there was a line in the call that matters for your world. There was. Alphabet — a company with one of the best-funded fleets on Earth — said it will expand third-party capacity, meaning neocloud rental, "as a bridge." Read that carefully: even Alphabet cannot self-build electrons and shells fast enough, so it's renting. Every one of these capex guide-ups widens what these reports keep calling a 100-gigawatt-plus generation deficit. And Microsoft did the same thing in Europe this week — literally became a tenant. On Tuesday. Microsoft struck a multi-billion-dollar deal to rent AI compute from Mistral, the French model company, which is targeting 200 megawatts by 2027 and 1 gigawatt by 2030 on 4 billion euros of European data-center investment. So the buy-versus-rent line is blurring at the gigawatt scale. And note the siting problem: 1 gigawatt of new load landing on French and Nordic grids that are already tighter than PJM or ERCOT. Let's get concrete on projects, because you always say the megawatts are where the truth is. What caught your eye? Two, and they're a study in contrast. First, in Arizona: Salt River Project is taking a 1.7-gigawatt "Marigold Energy Center" to its board in September. The mix is the story — 600 megawatts of solar, up to 675 megawatts of gas, and 400 megawatts of battery storage, plus four miles of 230-kV line and a new substation, about 45 miles south of Phoenix. So solar for the energy, a big gas block for firm capacity, storage to shape it. And it's a public-power utility. That's what makes it interesting. A public-power utility building an integrated firm-power package on its own balance sheet, right in the Phoenix load pocket. It skips both the merchant interconnection queue and the risk of the turbine makers being sold out. Watch whether that gas block is what actually clears the board — the gas is the firm capacity everyone's fighting over. And the second project is the one with the ratepayer fight baked in. Wisconsin. We Energies is seeking to acquire two Invenergy gas plants — Red Oak Ridge at 1,186 megawatts and Foundry Ridge at 324 — so 1,510 megawatts combined, for 2.26 billion dollars. And they've said out loud what it's for: a Microsoft campus, and a Vantage project leased to OpenAI and Oracle. So the data centers are named. And the reason this is a fight? Wisconsin has no integrated resource plan. That sounds procedural, but it's the whole game. Without an IRP, plant-construction approval and the utility's "public need" acquisition review are separate steps. By the time the utility has to prove the need, the gas plant is already permitted to be built. It's a template for how gas-for-data-centers gets rate-based with the cost-and-alternatives test effectively neutered. The cost-allocation battle is moving upstream, into siting and approval sequencing. And who ends up paying is exactly the fight at FERC right now. It is. Consumer advocates from Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, Ohio, and Pennsylvania are pressing FERC for a rehearing of its late-June show-cause order in PJM. Their argument is sharp: they call it "arbitrary and capricious" for FERC to declare a duty to prevent cost-shifting while leaving the actual cost shifts in the PJM tariff intact. They want data centers forced to pay the full cost of their network upgrades. And if they win that "data center pays 100%" standard? It reprices every interconnection cost model in PJM overnight — and it pushes even more load toward behind-the-meter generation, where you can escape the network-upgrade allocation entirely. So the FERC fight and the behind-the-meter gas boom are two ends of the same lever. There was also a striking data point on the raw scale of the demand — and on water. A Kansas Health Institute report put US data centers at 183 terawatt-hours in 2024 — already more than 4% of national electricity — and projected that to grow 133% to 426 terawatt-hours by 2030. But the underpriced constraint is water: direct data-center water use was 17 billion gallons in 2023 and could double to quadruple by 2028. Because cooling. Because cooling, and because 20% of US data centers already sit in water-stressed basins — the same arid load pockets, Phoenix, West Texas, that are chasing the cheap solar. So deliverability isn't only an electron problem; water permitting is becoming a parallel gate. And that report's power mix — 56% fossil, 22% renewables, 21% nuclear — is exactly the counterfactual keeping a coal revival politically alive. Which is the last energy item — Washington reaching for coal. On Monday, the Department of Energy's coal advisory council formally recommended loan guarantees, grants, and federal power-purchase agreements to keep existing coal online and even build new plants, on reliability and load-growth grounds. That sits on top of about 850 million dollars DOE already put toward two new coal plants — 2.85 gigawatts combined, in Alaska and West Virginia — plus 425 million to preserve 14 gigawatts of existing coal. Federal PPAs for coal. That's the sovereign balance sheet stepping in. That's the whole idea — using the government's balance sheet to keep dispatchable megawatts that the markets are retiring. For a developer, it changes the merit-order math: coal that couldn't clear on economics may get kept as a capacity backstop. It softens the turbine bottleneck at the margin, but it adds carbon and stranded-asset risk to any grid your data center plugs into. The through-line for the whole segment: the constraint isn't capital anymore — it's a firm electron, at a substation, on a date, with water to cool it. Philippines To the Philippines, and the weather lead has escalated overnight. Alex, Kiyapo. Yes — what we flagged earlier this week as a low-pressure area is now Tropical Depression Kiyapo. As of the late-morning PAGASA bulletin, it was about 830 kilometers east of Northern Luzon, with maximum sustained winds of 45 kilometers per hour, gusts to 55, central pressure 1002 hectopascals, and it's accelerating — moving northwest at 25 kilometers per hour. And signals are up. Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal Number 1 is hoisted over parts of Northern Luzon — expanded across roughly 11 to 14 areas through the day. PAGASA sees a possible landfall tomorrow, Friday, over extreme Northern Luzon. The highest expected signal is Number 2, but Number 3 is possible if it strengthens to a severe tropical storm crossing the Batanes-Babuyan area. They're flagging 50 to 100 millimeters of rain for Cagayan into Friday. And it's dragging the monsoon in behind it. That's the second-order effect. Kiyapo is enhancing the habagat — the southwest monsoon — which means strong-to-gale-force gusts over much of Mindanao, plus Siquijor, Bohol, and Southern Leyte, with flood and landslide risk in the north. And in the Philippines, weather is a monetary variable, because food is such a heavy weight in the inflation basket. Which takes us straight to the peso. And the peso is at the wall. It matched its all-time record low, 61.75 to the dollar, in the latest session — from 61.745 the day before and 61.686 on Monday. The driver is the oil bid we opened the show with; Brent pushing toward the mid-90s and up revives the imported-inflation fear directly, because the Philippines imports about 98% of its oil. And here's the genuinely new development — the BSP didn't just talk this time. Correct. This is the escalation. The Bangko Sentral intervened — it sold dollars in the onshore market, after Wednesday's close, to defend the line. That's a step beyond the verbal jawboning and the warnings on FX derivatives we discussed before. It's actual reserves being spent to hold 61.75. The Philippines joins India in defending an oil-hit currency with intervention. What are forecasters saying about the floor? The near-term calls have crept lower. Reyes Tacandong sees 61.60 to 61.90; BMI, Fitch's shop, sees 61 to 63 in the coming months, citing the US-Iran escalation, dollar firmness, and the seasonal import-demand peak. Analysts are now openly pricing a break past 63. And all of this lands on a central bank that's already boxed. Completely boxed. There's a piece out this morning framed as "twin inflation shocks and growth woes test the BSP's credibility." Growth has slowed three straight quarters to a post-pandemic low of 2.8% in the first quarter, and the government just cut its 2026 GDP target to 3.5 to 4.5%. So oil and the currency argue for hikes; sub-target growth argues for cuts. That's the vise. And there's a fiscal-cushion angle too. The BSP now expects cash remittances to grow just 2.7% this year, to 36.6 billion dollars — slower than last year's 3.3%. Remittances are about a tenth of GDP, the classic shock-absorber, and it's thinning right as the oil-import bill widens the trade gap. All of this is the backdrop for President Marcos's fifth State of the Nation address on Monday — Metro Manila goes on full alert from 5 p.m. Friday, with protest groups mobilizing. A record-low peso, mid-90s oil, and sticky inflation is a hostile stage to walk onto. Vocab Of The Day Vocab of the day. Two Mandarin, then two Tagalog — and today every word is tied to a story we just told.
