Alex, take us into Mandarin. 今天的两个中文词都跟"钱花光了"这个主题有关。(Today's two Chinese words both connect to the theme of "the money running out.") 第一个词是"从而"。(The first word is "cóng ér.") 从而是一个很正式的连接词,对吗?(是——它是书面语。) (Is "cóng ér" a very formal connective? — Yes, it's written-language register.) 没错。我们可以说:资本支出激增,从而自由现金流转为负。(Exactly. We can say: capital spending surged, thereby free cash flow turned negative.) 谷歌和特斯拉就是这样。(Google and Tesla are exactly like this.) 我想确认一下用法。从而、因此、于是——它们有什么区别?(I want to confirm the usage. "Cóng ér," "yīn cǐ," "yú shì" — what's the difference?) 好问题。因此比较普通,就是"所以"。(Good question. "Yīn cǐ" is more ordinary — it just means "therefore.") 于是强调时间上的先后。(Yú shì" emphasizes temporal sequence.) 但是从而不一样:它表示前一句"使得"后一句发生,主语要一致。(But "cóng ér" is different: it means the first clause brings about the second, and the subject must be the same.) 所以从而更强调"结果是有目的的"。(So "cóng ér" stresses that the result is purposeful.) 对。在分析报告里,从而用得非常多。(Right. In analyst reports, "cóng ér" is used very often.) 第二个词是"势必"——意思是"一定会",但是更正式、更有逻辑。(The second word is "shì bì" — it means "will definitely," but more formal and more logical.) 造个句子吧。(Make a sentence.) 油价持续上涨,势必推高通胀预期。(If oil keeps rising, it is bound to push up inflation expectations.) 这就是今天的主线。(That's exactly today's main thread.) 势必和"一定"有什么不一样?(How is "shì bì" different from "yí dìng"?) 一定是口语,什么都能用。(Yí dìng" is colloquial — you can use it for anything.) 势必是书面语,而且它表示一种"从前提推出来的必然"。(Shì bì" is written-language, and it expresses an inevitability derived from a premise.) 它常常跟"推高"、"导致"、"影响"这样的词搭配。(It often pairs with verbs like "push up," "lead to," "affect.") 懂了。势必——逻辑上的必然。(Got it. "Shì bì" — a logical inevitability.) 现在换到菲律宾语。(Now let's switch to Tagalog.) Sa Tagalog, ang unang salita ay "ubos." (In Tagalog, the first word is "ubos.") Ang ibig sabihin: wala nang natira — lahat nagamit na. (It means: nothing left — everything's been used up.) Kaya perpekto ito para sa negatibong free cash flow. (So it's perfect for negative free cash flow.) Halimbawa? (An example?) Naubos ang cash ng kumpanya kahit tumaas ang benta. (The company's cash got used up even though sales rose.) O kaya: inubos ng BSP ang ilang dolyar para depensahan ang piso. (Or: the BSP spent down some dollars to defend the peso.) Ano ang pagkakaiba ng "ubos" sa "kulang" o "salat"? (What's the difference between "ubos," "kulang," and "salat"?) Magandang tanong. Ang "kulang" ay hindi sapat — mayroon pa, pero hindi tama ang dami. (Good question. "Kulang" is insufficient — there's still some, but not enough.) Ang "salat" ay kakaunti, mahirap. (Salat" is scarce, meagre.) Pero ang "ubos" — wala na talaga, tuyot na ang balon. (But "ubos" — there's genuinely nothing, the well is dry.) Kaya ang "ubos" ay may pakiramdam ng katapusan. (So "ubos" carries a sense of finality.) Tama. Hindi ka makakakuha ng wala. (Right. You can't draw from nothing.) Ang pangalawang salita ay "hadlang" — ibig sabihin, isang bagay na humaharang. (The second word is "hadlang" — meaning something that blocks the way.) Parang ang pader ng kuryente at tubig sa data center? (Like the wall of power and water for the data center?) Eksakto. Ang kakulangan ng kuryente at tubig ang pinakamalaking hadlang sa pagbuo ng data center. (Exactly. The lack of power and water is the biggest barrier to building the data center.) O ang utos ng korte na naging hadlang sa deal ng Paramount. (Or the court order that became a barrier to the Paramount deal.) At paano ito naiiba sa "sagabal" o "balakid"? (And how is it different from "sagabal" or "balakid"?) Ang "sagabal" ay abala lang — nakakaistorbo pero naikakansa mo. (Sagabal" is just a nuisance — annoying but you can step around it.) Ang "balakid" ay parang hurdle na nalalagpasan mo. (Balakid" is like a hurdle you get over.) Pero ang "hadlang" ay tunay na humaharang — pader na pumipigil sa iyo. (But "hadlang" genuinely blocks — a wall that stops you.) 从而, 势必, ubos, hadlang. Apat na salita, isang kuwento. (Four words, one story.) Napakaganda. Sa susunod na segment naman. (Beautiful. On to the next segment.) Arts & Culture Arts and culture, and we're leading with photography this morning. Alex, the Morgan. The lead is a show at the Morgan Library in New York called "Hujar: Contact" — Peter Hujar, the great chronicler of downtown, queer 1970s and 80s New York. What makes this one unusual is that it's built from more than 110 contact sheets and 20 enlargements — the darkroom work-prints, the ones never meant to hang on a wall. Which sounds, on paper, like archive-milking. A show of contact sheets? That was exactly the critic's skepticism going in — Hyperallergic's reviewer admits she expected a scraping-the-vaults exercise. And then recants. Because the sheets reveal Hujar's famous portraits as, in her phrase, "excerpts of a conversation, rather than memories snatched from the ether." You watch him work toward the image. The contact sheet is the sketchbook of a photographer who almost never showed his hand. So the throwaway becomes the revelation. What's the market backdrop this morning — because the auction houses just closed their books on the first half. They did, and the verdict is a very 2026 word: K-shaped. ArtTactic's half-year report has Christie's, Sotheby's, and Phillips taking a combined 6.8 billion dollars including fees, up 70% year-on-year — the best first half since 2022. But look under it: Christie's did 3.4 billion, Sotheby's 2.8, and Phillips trails badly at about 505 million. So the recovery is real, but it's stacked at the very top. Stacked at the top and propped by death and estates. Nearly a third of the total came from single-owner estate sales — the S.I. Newhouse collection over 630 million, the Joe Lewis collection 406 million, a UK record. So it's a rebound built on trophy consignments while the market's middle still gasps for air. A masterpiece market, not a healthy one. To opera — Glyndebourne, and a Strauss that apparently sounds better than it looks. A lovely line from the critic on this one. It's Richard Strauss's "Ariadne auf Naxos" at the Glyndebourne Festival, Robin Ticciati conducting the London Philharmonic in Laurent Pelly's staging. Rachel Willis-Sørensen sings Ariadne, Samantha Hankey the Composer. Four stars from BroadwayWorld, whose reviewer said it's "not always a visual feast for the eyes" but "a mouthwatering banquet for the ears" — and singled out Alina Wunderlin's Zerbinetta as "worth the ticket price alone." And a classical recording pick to go with it. Gramophone's Recording of the Month is the complete Martinů symphonies — the Bamberg Symphony under Jakub Hrůša, on Deutsche Grammophon. It's the first complete Martinů symphony cycle DG has ever issued, and Gramophone says Hrůša makes a "wonderfully powerful case," the textures "stunningly vivid." Timely, because Hrůša is one of the most-watched conductors of his generation right now. And close us on a book. Claire Vaye Watkins is back — the author of "Battleborn" and "Gold Fame Citrus" — with a novel called "Yellow Pine," out this week from Riverhead. It's a Mojave-homestead story of eco-activism and a troubled love. Publishers Weekly starred it, and Joy Williams — no soft touch — calls it "a fresh classic of desert writing, a lament and hymn to the great Mojave." If you liked the parched, luminous California of her earlier work, this is that voice, matured. A banquet for the ears and a hymn to the desert. Good morning to that. One more. One Good Thing One good thing, and it's a genuine wonder-of-the-world story. Scientists have formally described a brand-new species of monkey deep in the Congo Basin. A whole new monkey. In 2026. A whole new monkey. It's called the likweli — scientific name Colobus congoensis — a small, black, long-tailed monkey with striking orange-cream patches on its face and white markings under its tail. It lives in lowland rainforest between the Lomami and Lilo rivers in the Democratic Republic of Congo. How rare is it to describe a new primate? This is only the fifth new African monkey species described in 75 years — and it's the first primate ever named for the DRC itself. The team, led by John Hart, Junior Amboko, and Kate Detwiler, logged 114 field observations before publishing in the journal PLOS One in mid-July. It's a discovery, not a rediscovery. I love that the map still has blank spaces on it. That in one of the most-studied disciplines on Earth, in a forest people have walked through for millennia, there was a monkey nobody had named. That's exactly the feeling. It's a reminder that the natural world is still, quietly, larger than our catalog of it — and that patient people in the field, watching and counting, are still adding to the sum of what we know. A good note to carry into the day. The likweli. Named at last. That's The Morning Commute for Thursday, July 23rd. Take care of each other. And we'll see you tomorrow. 从而 thus; thereby; consequently (formal connective linking a cause to its resulting effect) Alphabet/Tesla capex surge turning free cash flow negative 势必 be bound to; will inevitably (expresses logical inevitability) Brent toward $98 → inflation and yields up into the Fed ubos used up; depleted; completely spent, with nothing left Negative free cash flow / the BSP spending dollar reserves hadlang a barrier; an obstacle that actively blocks progress or passage The power-and-water wall blocking the AI build / the court order blocking the Paramount–WBD deal

docs.title: Wednesday, July 22, 2026
docs.text: Wednesday, July 22, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. It's Wednesday, July 22. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Here's the thread we're pulling this morning: the war premium just went geographic. For weeks the oil story was about one chokepoint getting deeper — Hormuz, throttled tighter and tighter. As of this week it stopped deepening and started widening. Widening is the word. Overnight the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia at Bab el-Mandeb, and two Saudi supertankers physically turned around in the Red Sea rather than run it. So now there are two straits under pressure at the same time, and Brent is up almost 4% this morning, back through 94 dollars. And that one fact — a wider premium, not just a higher one — is what's boxing in every central bank at once. The Fed meets a week from today with the 10-year at 4.63% and a live hold-versus-hike debate. China's central bank just sat on its hands for the 14th straight month. And the Philippine peso is pinned at a record low. Same fuse, three continents. And running underneath all of it, the AI build that will not quit — except this week it finally meets two walls. The first is its earnings jury: the mega-cap verdicts land in the next few days. The second is physical — the grid can't get transformers fast enough, and the fight over who pays for the wires is heading to a courtroom. So two engines this morning: a widening oil-and-rates vise, and an AI machine roaring straight into its earnings jury and its hardware ceiling. Let's get into it. Two world stories first. Headlines Start with the story that's moving the oil tape — because for once it's a new chokepoint, not the old one. Bab el-Mandeb. Right. On Monday the Houthis declared a formal naval blockade of Saudi Arabia at the Bab el-Mandeb strait — the southern gate of the Red Sea. And this wasn't rhetoric. Two Saudi VLCCs — the Xin Long Yang, carrying around 2 million barrels bound for China, and the Rodos, hauling crude to India — both U-turned mid-voyage and rerouted toward Suez rather than transit the strait. And that's the escalation that matters, because think about where Saudi barrels were already going. With Hormuz effectively shut, the Red Sea was Saudi Arabia's alternative ocean outlet to the west. Contest Bab el-Mandeb too, and you've closed the side door right after the front door. So it's not a deeper premium at one strait anymore — it's a second strait. What does that do to the physical math? It doesn't just raise the price, it lengthens the journey. Forcing those Asia-bound cargoes the long way around adds something like 5 to 10% to global tonne-miles. That's a freight-rate shock stacked on top of a crude shock. The war premium has jumped from the barrel into the boat. And that's the piece that's genuinely new. For two weeks this was an Iran-and-Hormuz story. Now the risk is spread across the whole Red Sea complex, which is exactly why Brent went through 94 this morning even with diplomacy supposedly in the air. And you can't wave it away with a ceasefire headline, because there are now multiple hands on the tap. Which is the perfect segue to the second story — Ukraine, and a command shakeup that's about to test the other front. This one's remarkable. On Monday, President Zelensky sacked his Commander-in-Chief, Oleksandr Syrsky, and replaced him with the Joint Forces chief Mykhailo Drapatyi — who's 43. And this comes right after Zelensky fired his reformist defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, who's 35, a move that triggered nationwide protests earlier in the week. So this is a doctrine clash boiling over into an actual command purge. Syrsky was the face of the older, Soviet-style centralized approach. Drapatyi and Fedorov are the drone-modernizer camp. Zelensky just fired one of them and promoted the other, and the country's in the streets over it. And the timing is brutal, because the next round of Istanbul talks is Thursday, July 23 — tomorrow. You're walking into a negotiation with your own command structure mid-reshuffle and protesters outside. It dents his leverage at exactly the wrong moment. And tie it back to our throughline: Ukraine has spent the last two weeks hitting Russia's shadow-fleet tankers — the ships that move sanctioned barrels. A weaker, distracted Kyiv is a variable in the oil premium too. Two wars, two fronts, and both of them keep a bid under crude no matter what the diplomats say. A month ago a ceasefire would have drained the premium cleanly. Now there's no single switch to flip. Which is the whole reason the tape traded the way it did. Let's do the markets. Market Overview So here's Tuesday's close, and the shape of it tells you the AI panic has, for now, gone quiet. Give me the board. The S&P 500 finished at 7,509.20, up 19.25 points, so up 0.26%. The Nasdaq Composite basically matched it — 25,837.21, up 64.66, up 0.25%. The Dow was the leader, up 307.85 points to 52,224.64, up 0.59%. And the Russell 2000 led everything, up 1.29% to 2,987.40. And that's the tell, isn't it? Small-caps and the Dow out front, mega-cap tech merely along for the ride. That is the opposite of a semis panic. Exactly the opposite. Ten days ago the Nasdaq was bleeding and the Dow held up. Tuesday you had the Russell leading by more than a full percent — that's a breadth-broadening, risk-on-underneath tape, not a flight to the generals. But under the surface the mega-caps were split, and it's earnings-driven. It is. On the green side: AMD up 3.50% to 544.43, and the chip names generally firm — TSM up 1.40%. And Intel — this is a story on its own — up 2.19% to 105.45, reclaiming a hundred-dollar handle. On the red side, the ones reporting this week traded heavy: Alphabet down 1.19% to 347.15, Meta the worst of the majors, down 1.59% to 643.81. Nvidia was a rounding error, down 0.12%. So the market's de-risking the names on the earnings calendar and buying almost everything else. What's driving Intel back over 100? Two things landed for Intel. It named Fortinet as its first cybersecurity foundry customer — a real external name on the foundry order book — plus an expanded Google Cloud AI collaboration. For a company whose whole bull case is "can the foundry win outside customers," a marquee logo matters. The catch is the foundry is still running an operating loss around 2.4 billion dollars a quarter, and Intel reports Thursday, so that's the number that gets marked. Now the rates picture, because that's the macro spine this week. Yields backed up across the curve. The 2-year at 4.26%, up from 4.21. The 10-year at 4.63%, up 3 basis points. The 30-year at 5.13%. That is a market leaning less dovish into next week's Fed — pricing a real chance the FOMC stays put or even debates a hike, not a cut. And commodities are the reason why. This morning Brent is up 3.89%, pushing through 94.55 a barrel on the Bab el-Mandeb news. Gold is firm near 4,122, up about 1.1%, silver at 59.67. The dollar's strong — dollar-yen at 163, the yen near a one-year low — and Bitcoin slipped a touch to around 66,000. So it's the classic reflation posture: hard assets bid, yields up, the safe-haven dollar firm, all of it pointing at the same oil fuse. Higher oil, higher yields, a firmer dollar — and every central bank staring at the same problem. Speaking of which, let's do U.S. business, because tonight is the jury. U.S. Business The headline U.S.-business story this week is the mega-cap earnings jury — and I want to be careful here, because the verdicts are landing over the next few days, not already in. Which means we talk about the bars, not the results. Precisely. We are not going to invent numbers that haven't printed. What we can do is set the test, because it's a genuine referendum on whether AI revenue is finally validating AI capex. Start with Tesla. Tesla's already given us the volume line — a record 480,126 deliveries, up about 25% year on year. So the top-line's known-ish. The consensus wants roughly 27.6 billion dollars of revenue, GAAP earnings around 36 cents a share, non-GAAP nearer 55. And the swing factor isn't deliveries, it's auto gross margin — because Tesla is spending heavily on the robotaxi and Optimus programs, and the market wants to know whether the core car business still funds the moonshots. The stock jumped 3.7% into the print, to about 383, but remember it's still down roughly 17% on the year. So it's a "prove it" setup, not a victory lap. Then Alphabet, which is really the one that matters for our throughline. It is, because Alphabet is where AI capex meets AI revenue in the same report. Consensus is looking for earnings around 2.87 a share on revenue near 116.5 billion, with Google Cloud growth seen close to 60%. Hold that number against the capex line: Alphabet has guided to something like 180 to 190 billion dollars of capex this year. So the question is whether 60% cloud growth is enough to justify a 185-billion-dollar spend. That's the entire debate in one sentence. And here's the tell I'd watch even more than tonight's print — the 2027 capex language. If Alphabet says it will "significantly increase" spending again next year, that is a bigger signal for the power grid and the data-center build than any single quarter's earnings. The capex guide is the demand curve for electricity. We'll have the actuals for you as they land. Second U.S. story — Trump and a tariff cliff on generic drugs. This one's a slow-fuse policy story. On Monday, Trump said imported generic drugs stay tariff-free until August 2028 — then face a 100% tariff for one year, and 200% after that. Generics are the workhorse of the U.S. system — the bulk of prescriptions filled — and they're overwhelmingly made in India. So this is a reshoring cliff aimed straight at the Indian pharma supply chain. And the structure is clever, politically. It's back-end-loaded — nothing bites until 2028 — so it's near-term price-neutral, no immediate hit to consumers. But it's a very loud signal to reprice the entire generic supply chain now, and it's a fresh input into the tariff-driven-inflation debate the Fed is already wrestling with. A cost-push threat with a three-year fuse. Another slow-burn inflation input, right when the fast-burn one — oil — is flaring. Let's go overseas. International Business & Politics Two international stories, and the first is a quality-of-earnings tale from Swiss private banking — Julius Baer. Big headline number. First-half net profit up 128% year on year to 673 million Swiss francs — call it 828 million dollars — and record assets under management of 547 billion francs, up 5%. On paper, a blowout. And yet the shares dipped. Why? Because management warned that its revamped risk-and-compliance framework — the cleanup after its credit-loss troubles — will keep weighing on results into 2027. So the profit surge is partly the base effect of a bad prior year, and the forward message is "we're still repairing the balance sheet." So it's a European wealth-management tell: repair over growth. That's the read. The whole Swiss private-bank cohort is prioritizing balance-sheet hygiene and de-risking over chasing new assets. When the highest-quality client franchises are playing defense, that tells you something about how late in the cycle these institutions think we are. Second international story — France, and another cabinet exit. Environment Minister Monique Barbut resigned this morning, right after parliament gave final adoption to the Duplomb law. That law reinstates, via a waiver, a banned neonicotinoid pesticide — acetamiprid — plus another compound, for crops like hazelnuts, sugar beet, apples and cherries. And she didn't go quietly. She said the government "prevented any debate" on stripping the measure out. Which makes it a green-versus-farm rupture inside Macron's own bloc — the agricultural lobby winning over the environmental wing, and a minister walking rather than own it. And layer it onto the backdrop: France already has a fragile governance-and-fiscal picture. Every cabinet exit is another incremental drip of political risk into French government bonds — the OATs — at a moment when the market is watching that spread closely. So a wealth manager playing defense and a government shedding ministers. Now to China, where the central bank is doing the most consequential thing a central bank can do — nothing. China China's story this week is a non-move that speaks volumes. The People's Bank of China left its benchmark loan prime rates unchanged — the 1-year at 3.00%, the 5-year at 3.50%. That's the 14th straight month on hold. And the context makes the hold striking, because the growth data is deteriorating. Right. This came just five days after second-quarter GDP printed at 4.3% year on year — the weakest since the fourth quarter of 2022, and a sharp step down from the first quarter's 5.0%. So growth is cooling meaningfully, and Beijing is still refusing to cut. Which on its face is strange. Weak growth is the textbook case for easing. So why sit still? This is where our oil throughline reaches all the way to Beijing. The same Hormuz-and-Red-Sea premium that's lifting global crude is imported inflation for China — a huge net oil importer. Cutting rates into a rising oil-price shock risks fanning exactly the price pressure the PBOC doesn't want. So the oil premium is narrowing China's room to ease at the precise moment its economy needs easing. And that's the debt-deflation trap in one move. It's the trap exactly. Nominal demand and prices are sagging — that's the deflationary side — but real interest rates stay too high because the central bank won't or can't cut. And who does that crush? The over-leveraged players: the local-government financing vehicles and the property developers, who need lower real rates to survive. The anti-involution capacity-cut campaign was supposed to fix the deflation. It hasn't. And now an external oil shock is tying the PBOC's hands on the one tool that would help. A central bank boxed by a strait 6,000 miles away. That's the throughline in its purest form. Let's take that idea into the segment where it lives — energy. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities So we've spent a lot of this show on the AI build as an electricity-demand story. This week the story moved — twice — and both moves are about who actually pays, and what actually breaks. Let's take the "who pays" one first, because it's heading to a ruling on August 1. This is Virginia. Dominion. Virginia's State Corporation Commission is deciding Dominion's Rider T-1 case — roughly 1.5 billion dollars of transmission cost recovery. But the money isn't the headline. The methodology is. The commission is deciding how to allocate the cost of transmission network upgrades to large loads — meaning data centers. And there was a line from the commission's own counsel that basically frames the whole fight. The SCC counsel, Andrew Major, called it "a glaring cross-class subsidization occurring to the benefit of new large-load customers." In plain terms: right now, ordinary ratepayers are helping fund the wires that exist to serve hyperscaler data centers. And the governor's office — through testimony filed July 9 by Josephus Allmond — is pushing a strict causation standard: data centers should pay for any line that "would otherwise not be built but for" them. The "but-for" test. That's a strong principle if it sticks. It's a very strong principle, and it sits on top of something already approved — a new large-load customer class, the GS-5, that carries an 85% transmission demand charge phasing in next year. So Virginia is stacking a high fixed demand charge and a but-for causation test on the same customers. Now give me the second-order read, because this is the part that travels. Here's why it matters far beyond Virginia. Dominion serves the densest concentration of data centers on earth — Loudoun County, "Data Center Alley." So whatever causation standard the SCC lands on August 1 becomes the copy-paste template for every other utility commission facing the same load. And the knock-on effect: if you raise the all-in delivered cost of grid power for a Loudoun hyperscaler, you make building your own generation behind the meter look better and better. This ruling is quietly an argument for more off-grid gas and on-site power. So the transmission fight actually accelerates the behind-the-meter build. That's the irony. Now the second move — what actually breaks. This is the one I think is underpriced. For a year the bottleneck story was turbines — the gas-turbine OEMs sold out to the end of the decade. That constraint just migrated downstream, to the boring iron: transformers and circuit breakers. Give me the lead times, because the numbers here are almost comic. They're staggering. Generator step-up transformers — the big units that connect a power plant to the grid — lead times pushed past 160 weeks in the first quarter of this year. That's more than three years. It was 143 weeks back in 2024. High-voltage circuit breakers are now 125 weeks, versus 77 weeks in 2023. And equipment prices are set to climb another 4 to 10% over the next year. More than three years to get a transformer. And the market for this gear? The U.S. data-center electrical-equipment market is projected to go from about 20 billion dollars this year to 65 billion by 2030. More than triple. And because you can't buy time, utilities are now asking customers to pre-pay for long-lead gear, and they're refurbishing decades-old transformers as stopgaps. Both of those have consequences. Walk me through the second-order read. Two things. First, the financing model is quietly shifting. When a utility asks a developer to pre-pay for a transformer, it's pushing the procurement risk and the multi-year lead-time risk onto the developer's balance sheet. That changes the economics of a project before a single server is racked. Second — and this is the one that should worry people — refurbishing old transformers as a bridge means you're running aging iron at exactly the interconnection points feeding the biggest new loads. That quietly degrades N-minus-1 redundancy — the grid's ability to lose one component and keep running — right where the grid is under the most stress. So the constraint isn't the sexy stuff, the GPUs or even the turbines. It's a three-year queue for a steel box full of copper. That's the whole game now. Power is the ceiling on AI, and inside power, the ceiling is the switchgear. You can sign all the PPAs you want — if you can't get a transformer until 2029, your data center is a very expensive parking lot. A perfect place to leave it. Let's go to the Philippines. Philippines Philippines this morning, and there's a fresh weather system forming — so a new name is about to enter the rotation. Give me the bulletin. As of 7 a.m. Wednesday, PAGASA says a low-pressure area entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility, spotted roughly 940 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon. It's got a high chance of strengthening into a tropical depression — and once it does, it gets the local name Kiyapo. That would make it the country's 11th tropical cyclone of 2026, and the fourth just this month. Fourth of July — and I mean the month, not the holiday. What's the forecast track and intensity? PAGASA's Benison Estareja says it could reach tropical-storm strength. There are no wind signals up yet, because it's still a low-pressure area, not a named system. But the track has it moving toward Northern Luzon by Friday into Saturday — the 24th and 25th — so the back half of the week is the watch window for Northern and Central Luzon. And it's not arriving into calm, either. No — the southwest monsoon, the habagat, is already active alongside it. You've got scattered rains and thunderstorms over Mindanao, Palawan, the Western and Central Visayas and Negros, while the low-pressure area's trough soaks Bicol and the Eastern Visayas — moderate-to-heavy rain with real flash-flood and landslide risk. So this is a fresh system building in, replacing the one that just moved off. Now the macro, and this is where the throughline comes home to roost — the peso. The peso weakened to match its record low on Wednesday — around 61.75 to the dollar. The 21 close was 61.745. And the driver is exactly the story we opened with: higher oil. The same war premium lifting Brent and pushing up U.S. yields is imported inflation for a big net oil importer like the Philippines, and it pins the currency at its weakest level ever. And yet — there was a genuinely surprising data point out of the central bank this morning that cuts the other way. There was. The balance of payments for June swung to a 3.4-billion-dollar surplus. That's a 21-month high — the largest since September 2024 — against just 131 million in May, and 226 million a year ago. On the surface, a huge positive. So why doesn't that rescue the peso? Because of what's inside it. This wasn't an export boom. The surplus came from remittances, government foreign borrowing, services and foreign direct investment — the financing side of the ledger — offsetting a goods-trade deficit and foreign portfolio outflows. It's a financing-account surplus, not export strength. So it pads the reserves, but it does nothing to relieve the oil-driven pressure on the currency. And the first-half tally is actually well below last year's. The BSP is still holding its policy rate at 4.75%. A reserves cushion that doesn't fix the underlying squeeze. Anything on the diplomatic front? Yes — Secretary of State Rubio paid a courtesy call on President Marcos on Wednesday, on the sidelines of the ASEAN ministerial meetings. Trade was front and center, with the U.S. pitching a "Pax Silica" framing as helpful to the Philippine economy. And in the background, tension flared again at Ayungin — Second Thomas Shoal — with Manila condemning a clash and Beijing summoning the Philippine envoy. So the South China Sea is back in the frame, right as the peso and the oil bill are already squeezing. Oil, trade, and the currency, all knotted together. Which is a perfect bridge into today's vocab, because both of our themes are about to become sentences. Vocab Of The Day 今天我们学四个词 — 先两个中文，再两个他加禄语。(Today we'll learn four words — first two in Chinese, then two in Tagalog.) 每个都跟今天的新闻有关。(Each one is tied to today's news.) 好，第一个词是什么？(Good — what's the first word?) 第一个是 "随着"。(The first is "suí zhe" — "as" or "along with.") 我给你造个句子：随着油价上涨，比索跌到了历史新低。(Let me make a sentence: As oil prices rise, the peso has fallen to a record low.) 我懂了。所以 "随着" 表示两件事一起发生，一个跟着另一个变化。(I see — so "suí zhe" expresses two things happening together, one changing along with the other.) 对。它是书面语，新闻里特别常见。(Right. It's formal, written register — very common in the news.) 比如：随着战争溢价扩散，各国央行都被套住了。(For example: As the war premium spreads, central banks everywhere are boxed in.) 那 "随着" 和 "跟着" 有什么区别？我常常搞混。(What's the difference between "suí zhe" and "gēn zhe"? I always mix them up.) 好问题。"跟着" 是具体地跟在后面 — 比如跟着一个人走。(Good question. "Gēn zhe" is physically following behind — like following a person as you walk.) "随着" 更抽象，表示 "随着…的变化"，通常接一个大趋势。(But "suí zhe" is more abstract — "along with the change of something" — it usually attaches to a big trend.) 明白。搭配是 "随着…的" 加名词，对吧？像 "随着时间的推移"。(Got it — the collocation is "suí zhe … de" plus a noun, right? Like "as time goes by.") 完全正确。第二个词更抽象一点："导致"。(Exactly right. The second word is a bit more abstract: "dǎo zhì" — "to lead to" or "to result in.") 意思是 "造成一个结果"？(It means "to cause a result"?) 对，但是要注意 — "导致" 通常接不好的结果。(Yes, but note — "dǎo zhì" usually leads to a bad result.) 比如：油价冲击导致了输入型通胀。(For example: The oil shock has led to imported inflation.) 再比如：这可能导致央行更难降息。(Or: This could make it harder for the central bank to cut rates.) 那 "导致"、"造成"、"使得" 呢？它们差别在哪里？(What about "dǎo zhì," "zào chéng," and "shǐ dé"? Where's the difference?) 很好的对比。"导致" 和 "造成" 都是负面的，但 "造成" 更具体 — 造成损失，造成破坏。(Great contrast. "Dǎo zhì" and "zào chéng" are both negative, but "zào chéng" is more concrete — to cause a loss, to cause damage.) "使得" 是中性的，只是 "让某事发生"。(But "shǐ dé" is neutral — it just means "to cause something to happen.") 所以在财经新闻里，"导致" 是最书面、最抽象的那个。(So in financial news, "dǎo zhì" is the most formal, most abstract of the three.) 说得对。好，现在换他加禄语。(Well put. Okay — now let's switch to Tagalog.) Lumipat tayo sa Tagalog. (Let's move to Tagalog.) Sige. Ano ang unang salita? (Go ahead. What's the first word?) Ang unang salita ay "humina" — ibig sabihin, to weaken. (The first word is "humina" — meaning, to weaken.) Halimbawa: Humina ang piso hanggang umabot muli sa pinakamababang halaga nito. (For example: The peso weakened until it reached its lowest value again.) Kaya perpekto ito para sa balita ngayon — ang piso sa record low. (So this is perfect for today's news — the peso at a record low.) Pero paano ito naiiba sa "bumagsak"? (But how is it different from "bumagsak"?) Magandang tanong. "Humina" ay unti-unti — dahan-dahang panghihina. (Good question. "Humina" is gradual — a slow weakening.) Pero "bumagsak" ay biglaan at malakas — parang isang pagbagsak. (But "bumagsak" is sudden and strong — like a crash.) At "lumubog" ay mas matindi pa — parang lumulubog na barko. (And "lumubog" is even more severe — like a sinking ship.) Kaya para sa piso, "humina" ang tama — hindi ito bumagsak, unti-unti itong humina. (So for the peso, "humina" is the right one — it didn't crash, it weakened gradually.) Tama. Ang pangalawang salita ay "kalakalan" — trade o commerce. (Correct. The second word is "kalakalan" — trade or commerce.) Halimbawa: Ang kalakalang panlabas ang sentro ng usapan nina Rubio at Marcos. (For example: Foreign trade is the center of the Rubio–Marcos talks.) At iba ba ito sa "negosyo"? (And is it different from "negosyo"?) Oo — malaki ang pagkakaiba. "Negosyo" ay isang partikular na kompanya o hanapbuhay. (Yes — a big difference. "Negosyo" is a specific company or livelihood.) Pero "kalakalan" ay ang buong sistema ng pagbili at pagbebenta — ang macro. (But "kalakalan" is the whole system of buying and selling — the macro.) Kaya "kalakalang panlabas" — foreign trade — ang gagamitin mo para sa balance of payments at sa freight sa Bab el-Mandeb. (So "kalakalang panlabas" — foreign trade — is what you'd use for the balance of payments and the freight at Bab el-Mandeb.) Eksakto. Apat na salita: 随着, 导致, humina, kalakalan. (Exactly. Four words: suí zhe, dǎo zhì, humina, kalakalan.) Ang buong kuwento ng araw sa apat na salita. (The whole story of the day in four words.) From a strait to a currency to a trade balance — that's the show in four words. Let's do arts and culture. Arts & Culture Arts this morning, and we lead with a story that's really about power and provenance — the Met's antiquities reckoning just got deeper. This is the Manhattan DA again. It is. DA Alvin Bragg announced the repatriation of 59 trafficked antiquities — going back to Italy, Iraq and Indonesia. 48 of them to Italy alone, valued north of 300,000 dollars. And here's the part that stings for the institution: 45 of those objects were seized from the Metropolitan Museum of Art itself. 45 pieces pulled out of the Met in a single action. What's the showpiece? A terracotta krater attributed to the Troilus Painter — that's roughly 480 to 470 BCE. And the biography of the object is the whole scandal in miniature: illegally exported by the dealer Fritz Burki, restored by Sandro Cimicchi, laundered through Christie's in London, and then acquired by the Met. The same names keep recurring across these cases — Hecht, Rosen, Burki — the pipeline the DA's Antiquities Trafficking Unit has been unspooling for a decade. And the critical angle — because this isn't just a crime-blotter item. The angle is that the Met's own provenance research team, the one it stood up in 2023, is now finding objects faster than the museum can defend them. The tally of loot the Met has surrendered since 2017 has crossed 95 million dollars. And that reframes the whole idea of the encyclopedic museum — the "we collect the world" model — as an unpaid debt that's finally coming due. It's the accounting catching up with the acquisition. Second art story, and it's a quieter one about where the market physically sits — David Zwirner. Right. Zwirner has closed its townhouse gallery at 34 East 69th Street — the Upper East Side space it opened in 2017 — and is consolidating New York around its newly completed, Selldorf-redesigned Chelsea campus on West 19th, plus the Tribeca space at 52 Walker. On its own, one gallery closing a townhouse. But you're reading it as a signal. It's a small closure with a large meaning. The Upper East Side townhouse model was about proximity — being steps from old-money collectors. Zwirner is betting that matters less now than a consolidated Chelsea-and-Tribeca footprint plus the global network — London, Paris, LA, Hong Kong. It's the center of gravity of the blue-chip trade shifting off the old map. When a mega-dealer votes with its real estate, that's worth noticing. And close on literature. A good one for the second-novel watchers. Julie Buntin's Famous Men just landed from Riverhead — nine years after her beloved debut Marlena, back in 2017. It drew strong reviews in early and mid-July — the Boston Globe, and a spot among LitHub's best-reviewed of the week. Nine years is a long time to sit under the weight of a debut. What's it about? It's a bildungsroman, narrated by a young woman named Will Miles leaving Greening, Michigan, chasing two things at once — an unknown father and literary success. Critics are calling it audacious, with a kind of thriller pulse, and reading it as a MeToo-era anatomy of male power and abused ambition, rendered in what one review called "exquisite prose." The verdict on the second-book question — can she clear the bar of Marlena — is, for the critics at least, yes. A debt coming due, a market shifting its ground, and a writer clearing the second-novel bar. Let's end where we always do — one good thing. One Good Thing One good thing this morning, and it is genuinely, wonderfully out of this world. Go on. On July 14, NASA's Perseverance rover crossed a milestone in Jezero Crater on Mars — 26.2 cumulative miles of driving. A full marathon. On another planet. A marathon on Mars. And it's not just trundling for the sake of the odometer, is it? That's the lovely part — it clocked the distance while it was doing real science, still collecting and caching rock samples along the way. So it's not a stunt lap. It's an endurance record set almost as a byproduct of patient, careful work — inch by inch, sol by sol, across an alien crater floor, for years. There's something quietly moving about that. A little machine, tens of millions of miles from anyone who built it, just... keeping going. One careful step at a time until it's run a marathon nobody on Earth could run there. A marathon of patience, really. And on a morning full of straits and premiums and central banks all tangled together, it's a nice reminder that some of the best work is just persistence — showing up, moving forward a little, and not stopping. On that note — thank you for spending your morning with us. This has been The Morning Commute for Wednesday, July 22. Take care of each other out there, and we'll see you tomorrow. 随着 as; along with; in step with (a trend or change) The war premium widening → peso and yields moving with oil 导致 to lead to; to result in (usually a negative outcome) Oil shock → imported inflation boxing the PBOC / Fed humina to weaken; to grow faint or feeble (gradually) The peso matching its record low on higher oil kalakalan trade; commerce (as a system) PH balance of payments, Rubio–Marcos trade talks, Bab el-Mandeb freight

docs.title: Tuesday, July 21, 2026
docs.text: Tuesday, July 21, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. It's Tuesday, July 21. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Here's the thread we're pulling this morning: think of today as referendum day. For a week the story has been an AI-stock panic — a chip rout that spread from one name to the whole complex and across to Asia. And then, quietly, on Monday, it stopped. It didn't just stop, it reversed. Semis were the green on the board yesterday, and this morning the futures are pointing higher — Nasdaq-100 up more than 1%. The thing that was breaking is, for now, un-breaking. And the timing is almost too neat, because after the close tonight the first Magnificent-7 verdicts land — Tesla, Alphabet, and Intel all report. The very names at the center of the wobble finally get to answer with numbers instead of sentiment. So the panic pauses right as the jury gets seated. But — and this is the whole point — the pressure didn't vanish. It moved. It migrated. Out of equities and into the oil-and-rates vise. Brent is toggling around 90 dollars on whether a 10-day Iran ceasefire actually holds, the 10-year yield has climbed to 4.60%, and the Fed meets a week from today with a live hold-versus-hike debate. So the mic passes from sentiment to fundamentals. Let's get into it. Two world stories first. Headlines Start with the one bleeding into everything else — Hormuz. And for the first time in weeks, the oil tape actually went two ways. That's the tell. Brent poked above 91 dollars intraday Monday, and then faded back toward 88, because there are suddenly signs of renewed US-Iran diplomatic contact — Qatari mediation, and reporting of a proposed 10-day ceasefire. Which is a genuine shift in what the market is pricing. For two weeks crude has only traded escalation. Monday was the first session where it traded de-escalation odds — the war premium moving in the tails, not just spot. And yet the physical picture is still ugly. A products tanker, the Kavomaleas, halted and anchored empty near Musandam after Iran's navy targeted vessels. That's 9 ships attacked since July 6. War-risk insurance is running roughly 8 times pre-crisis. And the strait is effectively closed — you had something like 10 transits on July 12 against a normal 88. So even as the diplomatic headline pulls the price down, the plumbing says the risk is very much still on. So the trade now is a coin held mid-air. If the 10-day ceasefire is real, you get a fast unwind of the premium. If it collapses again — and it has collapsed before — you're straight back above 90 with a closed strait. Right. Which is exactly why the second story matters, because there's now a second front pointed at the oil complex — and it's Ukraine. This was the deadliest set of strikes inside Russia in more than two years. Over July 19 and 20, Ukraine destroyed 7 Russian "shadow fleet" vessels — the tankers Moscow uses to dodge the oil sanctions — plus power substations in Crimea. That's on top of 13 substations and 4 vessels the day before. And Russia answered in kind — roughly 40 Iskander-M and Zircon missiles on Kyiv, and a drone strike that started a major fire in Sumy. So this is a real escalation, not a probe. But the piece that ties back to our throughline is the target selection. Ukraine is now systematically hitting the sanctions-evasion export fleet — the ships that actually move Russian barrels. So you've got two separate wars both squeezing the same barrel — Iran throttling the strait, Ukraine going after Russia's ability to sell around sanctions. The oil premium isn't a one-country story anymore. It's structural. And that's the fuse under everything the Fed does next week. And it changes how you read a ceasefire, doesn't it? Even if Iran and the US settle, the Ukraine-Russia front keeps a bid under crude. That's the subtle point. A month ago, "ceasefire" would have meant the premium drains out cleanly. Now there are two hands on the tap, and only one of them is at the negotiating table. So the floor under oil is higher than the headlines suggest — which is precisely the Fed's problem. Which is the perfect handoff to the tape. Let's do the markets. Market Overview So here's Monday's close, and the headline is: mild risk-off, but not the risk-off you'd expect from the week we just had. Give me the board. S&P 500 finished at 7,443.28, down 14.41 points, off 0.19%. The Nasdaq Composite was basically flat — 25,508.07, down just 12 points, a rounding error. The Dow was the laggard, down 307 points to 51,839.26, off 0.59%. And the Russell 2000 was the worst of the four, down 0.67% to 2,942.43. And that shape is the whole story. Because if this were still the AI panic, the Nasdaq is the one bleeding and the Dow holds up. This is the opposite. Exactly the opposite. Semis actually led green. Broadcom up 1.98%, Intel up 2.13%, Micron up 1.94%, AMD up 1.58%, Taiwan Semi up 1%, Nvidia flat but green. The chip rout didn't just pause — it bounced. So what pulled the tape down, if not chips? Single names and old-economy weight. Apple was down 2.14%, and because it's a price-weighted drag it took a chunk out of the Dow single-handed. Oracle was down 4%. Dell down 3.69%. That's what a Dow-and-small-cap down day looks like — it's not a growth-stock unwind. And the bond market is where the actual pressure showed up. Yields up across the curve. The 2-year at 4.21%, up 3 basis points. The 10-year at 4.60%, up 5 — it was 4.55 on Friday. The 30-year at 5.11%. That is the vise tightening, and it's oil-driven, not growth-driven. And the tell that it's oil and not fear — gold went up with yields. Gold at 4,068.90, up 1.32%. When gold and yields rise together, that's a reflation and war-premium signal, not a flight to safety. A fear bid buys bonds. This sold them. Currencies? Dollar-yen at 162.70, the yen still pinned near record-weak — the carry trade lives. Euro at 1.1420. And crude we covered — Brent 90.34 at the settle, up 1.26%. And then the overnight flips the mood again. It does. This morning US futures are higher — Nasdaq-100 up about 1.3%, S&P up half a percent, Dow up a bit. Chips reviving again, and Brent easing toward 89.80 on that ceasefire push. So the machine keeps toggling. One data point worth flagging — Germany. Yes. German ZEW economic sentiment blew out — 26.3 against an expected 18, up from 10.5. The EU-wide read was 23.4. That's a real optimism surprise out of Europe, and it lands right as European earnings are coming in strong. Roughly 87% of the S&P names that have reported this season have beaten on EPS. So put the two halves together — a rebounding chip complex, a beat-rate near 87%, and a European confidence spike — and the "global risk-off" narrative starts to look overdone. It does. What actually happened this week is a positioning unwind dressed up as a fundamental scare. The bodies were crowded into the same momentum names, and when they de-grossed, it looked like the sky was falling. Underneath, the earnings kept printing. That's the gap tonight's numbers get to close. Which brings us to the main event tonight. U.S. Business After the close tonight, the earnings jury gets seated. Tesla, Alphabet, and Intel all report Q2 — the first Magnificent-7 prints of the season. And this is the referendum. For a week the AI trade has been sold on sentiment and a Gemini-delay scare. Tonight the actual numbers arrive. The consensus bars: Alphabet is seen at 2.90 dollars of EPS, up 25.5%, on 116.9 billion dollars of revenue, up 21.3%. Tesla at 54 cents, up 35%, on 26.4 billion in revenue. And 73 companies report today all told. The Alphabet number is the one I'd watch, because the whole "AI leaders get punished for any deceleration" theme lives or dies on the cloud growth rate and the capex guide. Right — it's not the headline beat, it's the second derivative. Does cloud reaccelerate, and does the capex number go up again? If it does, the buildout story we talk about every day gets a fresh receipt. If the guide wobbles, the de-rating has more room. And Tesla is almost a different company to think about — margins, the energy-storage business, and whatever they say about autonomy. Fair caveat for everyone listening: all of this lands after the bell, so at this hour it's the setup, not the result. But the setup is the market's entire focus today. Second US story, and it's a cleaner read on the real economy — Charles Schwab. Schwab reports today, and the preview is a machine running hot. Consensus around 1.55 dollars of EPS against 1.14 a year ago — up roughly 37% — on about 6.9 billion in revenue, up 18%. The asset-gathering piece is the tell for me. It's remarkable — record total client assets of 13.14 trillion dollars, up 27% year on year, and a best-ever May for net new assets at 49.9 billion. That's the retail-brokerage read on the "resilient consumer plus higher-for-longer rates" world — they earn more on cash, and the client money keeps coming in. And underneath the AI drama, the boring earnings breadth held up too. It did. GM beat and raised its full-year profit guide — stock up a couple percent. 3M beat and popped around 7%. This is the point we keep making: there's a whole non-AI economy compounding quietly, and it's what makes an AI de-rating survivable rather than systemic. And that's the frame for tonight, really. If Tesla and Alphabet disappoint, the question isn't whether the market can absorb it — the breadth says it can. The question is whether the multiple can. Exactly right. The earnings have been fine. What's fragile is the price you're paying for the growth. A miss doesn't break the economy; it re-rates the premium. And that's a much more contained problem than the tape has been acting like all week. Let's take that breadth international. International Business & Politics Two from overseas, and the first is the European version of that same "earnings without an AI story" trade — Novartis. They reported this morning, and it was a beat. Core operating income of 5.94 billion dollars against roughly 5.31 billion expected, and they reaffirmed full-year guidance — low-single-digit sales growth. The momentum is coming off the launch portfolio: Kisqali, Kesimpta, Scemblix, Pluvicto — plus pipeline progress, including a del-zota FDA submission. This is exactly the trans-Atlantic split we've flagged. European large-caps are printing genuinely strong earnings, but because there's no AI narrative attached, the market pays them a value multiple, not a growth multiple. Right — a Swiss pharma beating on drug launches while it manages a patent cliff is a beautiful business. It just doesn't get the same re-rating a US hyperscaler gets for the same growth. That gap is the opportunity, or the trap, depending on your view. Second international story is Brussels flexing — and it's aimed at China. The European Commission hit AliExpress — the Alibaba-owned marketplace — with a record 550-million-euro fine under the Digital Services Act. That's for failing to curb illegal, counterfeit, and unsafe goods on the platform. And the size is the message. 550 million euros dwarfs the 200 million Temu fine and the 120 million X fine. It does. AliExpress has an action plan due October 20, and it's calling the fine "disproportionate." But the read-through is bigger than one company — Brussels is turning the DSA into a genuine cost center for Chinese cross-border commerce. It's trade friction with a price tag, wearing a consumer-protection jacket. Which sets up the one China story nicely. China The policy-response shoe finally dropped in Beijing. After second-quarter growth slipped below the official target range, the State Council held an executive meeting chaired by Premier Li Qiang. And they blinked toward stimulus. They pledged to hit the roughly 5% full-year growth goal and — the phrase from the Xinhua readout — to "maximize efficient use of fiscal funds." Markets read that as accelerated infrastructure and investment spending in the second half. This is the follow-on to the GDP undershoot we covered, not a recap of it. The number was the diagnosis; this is the treatment. And it's the same bind China's been in all year. They can lean on fiscal spending to hit the number, but the underlying problem is overcapacity and weak domestic demand — which keeps them export-reliant, which is exactly what's drawing fines like the AliExpress one and tariffs elsewhere. It's a two-speed economy trying to spend its way to the target. And the deflation angle is the global piece — a China exporting overcapacity is a China exporting disinflation, which normally is a gift to the Fed. Except right now the Fed's problem is oil, not goods. So the usual China deflation anchor is getting overwhelmed by the war premium. That's the world in one sentence today. Let's go to the desk that lives one layer under all of this — energy. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities And we're sourcing this one from the practitioner newsletters this morning — the CTVC and Utility Dive editions — so let's go deep. What's the lead? The lead is a groundbreaking that tells you where hyperscaler power procurement is actually heading. Cypress Creek broke ground July 14 on the Steel River Energy Center in Mississippi County, Arkansas. Scale it for me. Phases 1 and 2 are 1.6 gigawatts DC of solar plus 1.9 gigawatt-hours of battery storage. The full three-phase build is 2.5 gigawatts DC and 2.9 gigawatt-hours by 2029. And here's the tell — Google has a power-purchase agreement with Cypress Creek covering phases 1 and 2. It's Google's largest solar-plus-storage offtake globally. And there's a second package alongside it. There is — a separate Entergy Arkansas deal, Cypress Solar, 600 megawatts of PV and 350 megawatt-hours of storage near Pine Bluff, and that one underpins a 4-billion-dollar Google data center build. So what's the second-order read? Because on the surface this just looks like a big renewables deal. The read is that hyperscalers are now anchoring merchant-scale solar-plus-storage directly — bypassing the utility's integrated resource plan entirely — and siting it on cheap industrial land in a steel county. This isn't ESG box-ticking. Solar is being bought as a firming input for a data center. And watch the storage ratio — 2.9 gigawatt-hours is sized to shift power across hours, not just shave a peak. Which connects to the cost story, because gas isn't the cheap answer people assume anymore. This is the Lazard 2026 number and it's striking. Unsubsidized, utility-scale solar is at 40 dollars a megawatt-hour, onshore wind at 37, against a combined-cycle gas floor of 51. Everything is rising on capex and rates — but new-build gas is now at a 15-year-high levelized cost. And yet everyone's ordering gas anyway. That's the paradox. Announced gas capacity is surging on demand-forecast revisions and long equipment lead times — even as gas is the most expensive it's been in 15 years to build. So developers are paying up for dispatchability and speed, not economics. The clean read: solar-plus-storage is the near-term megawatt, and gas is the firm tail you pay a premium for. Give me the policy piece, because FERC moved again. FERC's July open meeting — and this is distinct from the large-load show-cause we covered. This time FERC ordered NERC to file initial reliability standards for large computational loads — data centers and crypto — plus load-registry criteria, by year-end. So this is reliability, not cost allocation. Exactly the distinction. Everything to date has been about who pays. This is about how these loads have to behave on the grid — registration, ride-through, the ability to stay online or shed cleanly during a disturbance. It's a whole new compliance surface for data-center developers. FERC also told CAISO and SPP to file a joint seams-coordination report by September 30, which points at West-wide interregional transfer as a relief valve for load growth. And there's a cautionary tale in here too — the New York cable. The Champlain Hudson Power Express. 1,250 megawatts, 6 billion dollars, a 339-mile high-voltage DC line. It energized July 1 and then went dark repeatedly on a terrestrial cable fault — likely offline for most of July, during a heat wave. Governor Hochul called it "unacceptable." And the lesson for the data-center world is the redundancy one. It's the N-minus-1 lesson. New York bet roughly 1.25 gigawatts of firm import on a single new HVDC tie with no redundancy, and one fault took it all out. Every data-center campus leaning on one big interconnection should read that as a warning — and it reinforces the behind-the-meter, on-site generation case we keep coming back to. If your whole load hangs on one wire, you don't have firm power. You have a single point of failure. And it ties the whole segment together, actually. The Google-Arkansas deal, the gas paradox, the FERC reliability rule — they're all circling the same anxiety. They are. The anxiety is deliverability. Everyone can name a gigawatt of nameplate capacity somewhere; the scarce thing is a firm electron at a specific substation on a specific date. That's why Google is co-locating solar-plus-storage on-site, why developers pay a 15-year-high price for gas turbines they can actually get, and why FERC suddenly cares whether these loads can ride through a disturbance. So the buildout isn't constrained by capital anymore. It's constrained by delivery. Capital is the easy part. The binding constraints are turbines, transformers, interconnection slots, and now regulatory ride-through. And the CHPE outage is the whole thesis in one cable — you can spend 6 billion dollars and still not have firm power if there's no redundancy behind it. Well said. Let's go to Manila. Philippines Weather first, and the good news is there's no named storm — but there's a system worth watching. What's PAGASA saying? No active typhoon, no signals up. The habagat — the southwest monsoon — is bringing isolated rains and thunderstorms across Metro Manila, Ilocos, the Cordillera, MIMAROPA, Western Visayas, and the Zambales-Bataan-Cavite-Batangas corridor. But the new wrinkle: cloud clusters east of Visayas and Mindanao consolidated into a low-pressure area as of 8pm Monday, with a medium chance of becoming a tropical depression within 24 hours. So the last system, Inday-Bavi, is gone, and this is the next one forming. Right — fresh system, still unnamed, still just an LPA. Watching it, not sounding an alarm. And the peso is the macro story, because it's flirting with the record again. It closed at 61.745 to the dollar on Monday — Friday it was 61.686. And the all-time low is 61.75. So it's within a fraction of a centavo of the record. What's driving it? RCBC's Michael Ricafort ties it straight to the oil story — dollar strength as crude sits near one-month highs for a second straight session, Hormuz traffic near-stalled, and that proposed 10-day ceasefire keeping everyone guessing. This is our throughline landing in a specific currency: the Philippines imports almost all its oil, so a war premium is an imported inflation tax and a peso problem at the same time. And the central bank did something interesting — a verbal move. This is the new angle. The BSP warned banks against using FX derivatives to profit off the peso's volatility, and Malacañang reaffirmed the BSP as the lead FX-stabilizing institution. So without touching the policy rate, the BSP is trying to curb the speculative feedback loop — jawboning the banks to keep the currency slide orderly. Which is a very different tool than a hike. It is — and it tells you they'd rather not spend reserves or hike into an oil shock if a firm word can slow the momentum. It's defense by other means. And there's the politics too — the SONA is coming. Marcos delivers his fifth State of the Nation Address on July 27. The police are finalizing security — deploying 20,229 personnel, plus military and coast guard reinforcements, around the Batasang Pambansa. At least four groups have applied for rally permits in Quezon City. And the Palace is framing this one as "simple but dignified" — no celebrity directors, no A-list performers for what's his penultimate SONA. A more austere tone for a president heading into the back half of his term. And a telling one — you go austere on the pageantry when the household budget is the story. Which it is. Between a near-record peso, an imported oil bill, and core inflation that's been hardening, the SONA lands into a cost-of-living moment. So "simple but dignified" is as much fiscal signal as it is stagecraft. Alright — that's the news. Time to switch languages. Vocab Of The Day 今天我们学四个词，两个中文，两个他加禄语，都跟今天的新闻有关系。(Today we learn four words — two Mandarin, two Tagalog, all tied to today's news.) 第一个词：究竟。(The first word: jiūjìng.) 究竟。我们今天一直在问一个问题：市场究竟在担心什么？是芯片，还是石油和利率？(Jiūjìng. We've been asking one question all day: what exactly is the market worried about — chips, or oil and rates?) 对，"究竟" 就是用来加强这个问题的语气 —— 到底、真正是什么。它是一个书面语，比较正式。(Right — jiūjìng intensifies the question: what is it really, after all. It's written-language, fairly formal.) 那它跟 "到底" 有什么区别？(So how is it different from dàodǐ?) 意思差不多，但是 "到底" 更口语，"究竟" 更书面。你在财经评论里常看到 "究竟"，在聊天里常用 "到底"。(The meaning is close, but dàodǐ is more spoken and jiūjìng more written. You see jiūjìng in financial commentary, dàodǐ in casual chat.) 明白。所以我可以说：投资者究竟该不该相信这次反弹？(Got it. So I can say: should investors really trust this rebound, after all?) 完美 —— 而且你刚才用了第二个词：反弹。(Perfect — and you just used the second word: fǎntán.) 反弹！这个词今天太合适了。星期一芯片股大幅反弹，绿了一整天。(Fǎntán! So fitting today. Monday chip stocks rebounded sharply, green all day.) 对。"反弹" 是从低点弹回来，通常很快、很猛。金融里常说 "技术性反弹" 或者 "报复性反弹"。(Right. Fǎntán is bouncing back off a low — usually fast and sharp. In finance you say "technical rebound" or "revenge rebound.") 那 "反弹" 和 "回升" 呢？(And fǎntán versus huíshēng?) 好问题。"回升" 是慢慢地、稳稳地涨回去；"反弹" 是突然地弹一下。所以市场情绪是 "反弹"，经济数据是 "回升"。(Good question. Huíshēng is a slow, steady climb back; fǎntán is a sudden bounce. So sentiment "rebounds," economic data "recovers.") 所以今天的标题应该是：芯片股反弹，但投资者究竟会不会追？(So today's headline is: chips rebound, but will investors really chase it?) 说得好。现在换他加禄语。第一个词：bumawi。(Well put. Now to Tagalog. The first word: bumawi.) Bumawi. Ang ibig sabihin, mabawi ang natalo o nawala — tulad ng merkado na bumawi ng lugi noong Lunes. (Bumawi means to recoup what was lost — like the market recouping its losses on Monday.) Tama. Ang ugat ay "bawi." Kapag sinabi mong "bumawi ng lugi," ibig sabihin binalik mo ang perang nawala. (Right. The root is bawi. When you say bumawi ng lugi, you mean you won back the money you lost.) Ano ang pagkakaiba ng "bumawi" at "bumangon"? (What's the difference between bumawi and bumangon?) Magandang tanong. Ang "bumangon" ay tumayong muli pagkatapos madapa — mas malawak, mas pisikal. Ang "bumawi" ay partikular: binabawi mo ang isang bagay na nawala sa iyo. (Good question. Bumangon is to get back on your feet after falling — broader, more physical. Bumawi is specific: you're winning back something that was taken from you.) Kaya sa merkado: bumawi ang mga semiconductor, pero hindi pa bumabangon nang lubusan ang buong sektor. (So in the market: the semiconductors recouped, but the whole sector hasn't fully gotten back on its feet yet.) Eksakto. At ang huling salita: pigilin. (Exactly. And the last word: pigilin.) Pigilin. Ang ugat ay "pigil" — ibig sabihin, hadlangan ang isang bagay na kumikilos na. (Pigilin — the root is pigil, meaning to hold back something already in motion.) Tulad ng BSP na sinusubukang pigilin ang pagbagsak ng piso — binabalaan ang mga bangko laban sa FX derivatives. (Like the BSP trying to curb the peso's slide — warning the banks against FX derivatives.) Ano ang pagkakaiba ng "pigilin" at "hadlangan"? (What's the difference between pigilin and hadlangan?) Ang "hadlangan" ay harangan nang tuluyan — parang pader. Ang "pigilin" ay pabagalin o supilin ang isang puwersang gumagalaw na — hindi mo tuluyang mapapatigil, pero mapapabagal mo. (Hadlangan is to block outright — like a wall. Pigilin is to slow or restrain a force already moving — you may not stop it fully, but you can slow it.) Kaya hindi mahahadlangan ng BSP ang oil shock, pero puwede nilang pigilin ang bilis ng paghina ng piso. (So the BSP can't block the oil shock, but they can curb how fast the peso weakens.) Perpekto. 四个词：究竟、反弹、bumawi、pigilin。(Perfect. Four words: jiūjìng, fǎntán, bumawi, pigilin.) Arts & Culture From currency defense to something much older and stranger. Arts and culture — and Alex, you've got a genuinely wild one to lead with. I do. In London, the Royal Academy opens "Richard Dadd: Beyond Bedlam" on July 25, running through October 25. And Dadd is one of the most extraordinary figures in Victorian art. Give people the story, because it's almost unbelievable. Dadd, born 1817, was a rising talent — and then, in the grip of a psychotic breakdown, he killed his father. He spent the rest of his life, until 1886, painting inside the asylums at Bethlem and Broadmoor. And what he produced there is astonishing — needle-sharp fairy paintings, obsessive in detail. The masterpiece is "The Fairy Feller's Master-Stroke," which he worked on from 1855 to 1864. And this is the first major reckoning with him in a long time. It's the most comprehensive show since the 1974 Tate survey — over 100 works, guest-curated by Nicholas Tromans, who wrote the definitive study. And the curatorial argument is the interesting part: it deliberately pushes past the "mad genius" cliché to make the case for the sheer technical virtuosity and narrative density of the work. The illness is context, not the whole story. From an asylum in Victorian England to a very loud summer in opera. Bayreuth's having a big year. An enormous one — it's the festival's 150th anniversary, opening July 24 and 25. Two headline events. First, Bayreuth's first-ever staging of Wagner's early opera "Rienzi" — which is a real curiosity, because it's traditionally not performed on that stage. And second, a brand-new "Ring" cycle billed as "RING 10010110," using AI-generated projections as, in their words, a generative visual force reflecting 150 years of interpretation. An AI "Ring." That will divide people. It will absolutely divide the Wagnerians. And down in Salzburg — which opened on the 17th under the theme "Panorama of Love" — there's a new "Carmen" premiering July 26 that's a genuine high-wire act. Asmik Grigorian sings the title role for the first time, Teodor Currentzis conducts, and it's staged and choreographed by Gabriela Carrizo of the Belgian dance-theatre troupe Peeping Tom, with Jonathan Tetelman as Don José. Grigorian doing Carmen for the first time, with a dance-theatre director — that's the kind of pairing that's either a triumph or a scandal. And no in-between. Both of those are previews — they open this week, so no reviews yet. Worth circling on the calendar. And on the page — Colson Whitehead closes out a trilogy. He does. "Cool Machine," out this month from Doubleday, is the third and final Ray Carney novel — the Harlem trilogy. It carries the furniture-salesman-and-fence Carney into Reaganomics-era New York, across 1981, 1983, and 1986. Publishers Weekly called it "the greatest New York novel in years." And this is a two-time Pulitzer winner landing the plane on a trilogy. Which is the hard thing to do well, and the early word is he sticks it. And one to hold for next week — the Booker Prize 2026 longlist drops on July 28, with a judging panel chaired by Mary Beard, alongside Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus. That'll be a conversation. Quick one to close the segment? Daniel Mason's "A Vermont Novel," out this month — his first since "North Woods" in 2023, which a lot of people loved. Early notices call it witty and gorgeous. A good stack. And speaking of things growing back — let's end on the good thing. One Good Thing Here's the one to leave you with — and it's a genuinely clever answer to one of the ugliest problems in materials science. Scientists have built a "living plastic" that self-destructs on command, and breaks down completely in six days — without leaving any microplastics behind. The microplastics part is the whole game, isn't it? Because normally when plastic "degrades," it just shatters into smaller and smaller pieces. That's exactly the trap this gets around. A team at the Shenzhen Institute of Synthetic Biology — published in ACS Applied Polymer Materials — engineered two cooperating strains of the bacterium Bacillus subtilis and baked them, in dormant spore form, right into the plastic film itself. So the microbes live inside the material. Dormant, until you trigger them. Add a warm nutrient broth — around 50 degrees Celsius — and the spores wake up and produce two complementary enzymes. One acts like a random chopper, slicing the long polymer chains into shorter pieces. The other is a patient nibbler, chewing those pieces from the ends all the way down to the base building blocks. And because the two work together, there's no intermediate microplastic stage. Right — that's the elegance of it. The material goes all the way back to monomers, not to a cloud of tiny fragments. They used polycaprolactone, which is common in 3D printing and some surgical sutures. Six days, fully gone, on command. A plastic that cleans up after itself. That's the kind of small, concrete win that actually compounds. It's engineering biology doing what it does best — building the solution into the problem. A lovely place to end. A good note to end on. That's The Morning Commute for Tuesday, July 21. Tonight the earnings jury comes back — Tesla, Alphabet, Intel — and we'll have the verdict tomorrow. Until then, take it easy, and we'll see you in the morning. 究竟 actually; after all; exactly (what) — an emphatic adverb that presses a question to its core referendum day — pressing the real question of what the market is actually worried about, chips or oil and rates 反弹 to rebound; to bounce back (of a price, index, or sentiment) off a low the week-long chip rout reversing — semis leading green on Monday bumawi to recoup; to win back or make up for something lost (root: bawi) the market recouping losses — chip stocks bouncing back off the week's rout pigilin to curb; to restrain or hold back a force already in motion (root: pigil) the BSP moving to curb peso volatility and rein in FX-derivative speculation

docs.title: Monday, July 20, 2026
docs.text: Monday, July 20, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Monday, July twentieth. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. Here's the throughline for the week's open: the AI-stock wobble stopped being about one name and became about the whole complex. Friday was the third straight down day, and this time it broadened — the Dow, which had been the hiding place all week, fell too, and the selling spread clear across the Pacific into a China-tech rout. The trigger moved on, from a single model delay to a structural cost scare, with a Netflix growth crack on top. And underneath it, the same vise keeps tightening — oil bid on fresh Iran risk, yields stuck high, gold near 4,000 dollars, a live hold-versus-hike Fed just eight days out. Yet the physical build behind the whole trade only accelerates. Fundamentals roaring, prices flinching. Let's get into it. Headlines Headlines. Two from the world desk before we hit the tape, and the first is a genuine landmark out of Sudan. An army-aligned court has sentenced the Rapid Support Forces chief, Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo — the man everyone knows as Hemedti — to death, in absentia, for genocide and crimes against humanity in Darfur. Roughly a dozen to fifteen senior RSF figures were sentenced alongside him, including his own brothers, tied to the 2023 atrocities in el-Geneina and the killing of the West Darfur governor. And Britain layered fresh sanctions on top, targeting RSF commanders and the gold-and-finance networks bankrolling the war. A death sentence for a warlord who is nowhere near a courtroom. What does a verdict with no arrest power actually change? On the ground, not much tomorrow — there's no one to serve the warrant. But it hardens the split. It formally brands one side of this civil war a genocidal enterprise, which slams the door on the negotiated settlement diplomats keep reaching for, and it puts a legal target on the money. And the market-adjacent read is the gold. Sudan's war is financed through smuggled gold moving out through the Gulf, so tighter scrutiny of those chains keeps a risk premium on the whole Red Sea and Sahel corridor — the same corridor a lot of the world's shipping and a chunk of its informal gold trade run through. So a symbolic verdict with a very real financial tail. Second world story — and it's a fight inside the European Union itself. It is. Denmark, which took over the rotating EU Council presidency on the first of July, is formally pushing to trigger Article 7 — the so-called nuclear option — to strip Hungary of its voting rights in the bloc. The Danish minister Marie Bjerre is leading it, and the grievance is Viktor Orban's serial vetoes on Ukraine's accession, plus what Brussels calls core-values breaches on rule of law. Article 7 is the thing everyone always threatens and never does. Is this actually different? Procedurally it's still uphill — you need near-unanimity for the harshest step, and France and Germany haven't fully signed on, so an actual suspension isn't happening next week. But the fact that the presidency is driving it out in the open is the signal. This is really a proxy war over Ukraine. Orban has been the single point of failure blocking accession talks and tranches of aid, and if the bloc ever found a way to route around Budapest's veto, it re-rates everything Ukraine-exposed — the reconstruction names, the aid timeline, and the political-risk premium sitting on the euro. Watch it as a slow burn, not a same-day move. To the tape. Market Overview Friday's close, and it was ugly and — the important word — broad. The S&P 500 fell 1.01%, off 76 points to 7,457.69. The Nasdaq took the brunt again, down 1.4%, off 362 points to 25,520.24. But the tell was the Dow: down 0.77%, more than 400 points, to 52,146.42. On Thursday the Dow had barely moved while the Nasdaq bled — a clean growth-only story. Friday, the hiding place stopped hiding. So this is the part that matters. Two days ago it was a chips-and-growth problem. Friday it was a market problem. Exactly — the selling spread. That's the whole character change. When it's just the crowded AI names, you can call it a positioning unwind. When the Dow gives back 400 points on the same day, the de-grossing has widened into something closer to a broad risk-off. And the proximate trigger evolved with it. Thursday it was Alphabet and a model delay. Friday it was structural: TSMC guided capital spending higher than the street wanted, which spooked everyone about the cost curve of the whole AI build, and — the sharper one — a Chinese lab, Moonshot, dropped a model they're calling Kimi K3, billed as the largest openly downloadable open-weight model yet. And an open-weight model that good is a dagger at the "more compute forever" thesis. That's precisely why the semis took it hardest. If a free, downloadable model closes the gap on the frontier, the market starts asking whether the trillion-dollar compute build is as defensible as the multiples assume. AMD was down 5% intraday, Intel off 4%, Nvidia down 3% before trimming to close off 2.2% at 202.81. The whole megacap block went with it — Meta down 2.8%, Tesla off 2.6%, Alphabet down 2.2%. The philadelphia semiconductor index is now off 13% in a month. And the single-name gut-punch was Netflix. It was — down 7.3% Friday to a fifty-two-week low, and it traded down as much as 12% at the worst. The print itself was fine: earnings 80 cents, revenue 12.56 billion, up 13%. What did the damage was the guide — third-quarter revenue guided to 12.86 billion, a hair light of the 13 billion the street wanted — plus a decision to stop reporting engagement data twice a year and only disclose it annually. So they dimmed the lights on their own metrics in the exact week the market has zero tolerance for it. Zero tolerance is right. In this tape, any growth name that decelerates and then reduces disclosure gets taken to the woodshed. It's the same reflex that hit Alphabet — the market is repricing every richly-valued growth story at the first hint the trajectory is flattening. Netflix is now on track for its worst year since 2022. And underneath the equity drama, the rates and commodity picture is the part that should still unsettle people. This is the crux, and it hasn't changed — it's gotten more acute. The 10-year sits at 4.55%, the 2-year at 4.18%, the 30-year at 5.06%. Yields are not coming down to rescue equities, and the reason is oil. West Texas crude jumped 4.5% on Friday to about 82 and a half dollars, Brent up near 88, on fresh US-Iran violence and the same Hormuz shipping risk we keep circling. So the bond market is looking straight through Wednesday's cool June inflation print — 3.5% headline, 2.6% core — to a forward oil chart that just turned higher again. And gold, with a live war and a shaky stock market, is doing what? Sitting around 4,030 dollars and going nowhere — which is itself the message. When gold can't catch a bid with equities falling and missiles flying, it's telling you high real yields and a firm dollar are the dominant force, not fear. The dollar's strong, the yen is pinned at a shockingly weak 162.4 to the dollar, near its cycle low. Rates are running this market. So what does all of that do to the Fed, eight days out? It boxes them further in. The July meeting is the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth, no new dot plot attached. And the debate is not hold-versus-cut anymore — it's hold-versus-hike. Markets have a hold as the overwhelming base case, but the only alternative anyone is pricing is a hike, roughly a one-in-five tail, because core is stuck at 2.6% and the oil bid threatens to reverse this month's energy relief. A cut is simply not in the conversation. Constructive on earnings, cautious on rates, and every model still runs through the price of a barrel. US business. U.S. Business US business — two earnings from Friday, and both cut to a theme we've been tracking. Start with the banks. Fifth Third. Second-quarter net income 763 million dollars, GAAP earnings 83 cents — that actually missed the street's 84 by a penny — but adjusted earnings were 1.02.
