The number that matters is net interest income: up 48% year on year to 2.22 billion. Because this was the first full quarter with Comerica folded in — the 10.9 billion-dollar acquisition that closed earlier this year and made Fifth Third the ninth-largest bank in the country. So the marquee regional-bank merger of the cycle is finally showing up in the financials. And that's the story — the deal thesis was always scale and a bigger interest-margin engine, and you can see the engine in that 48% NII jump. The penny miss on the headline is the flip side: integration costs and one-time charges still weigh while you're bolting two banks together. But this is the number regional-bank investors wanted — proof the consolidation wave is translating into earnings power, not just press releases. In a year when the mid-cap banks needed a reason to re-rate, a working merger is it. Second name — and it was the rare clean beat on a filthy day. Travelers, and it was a blowout. Core income of 10.04 a share against a street around 5.33 — call it an 88% beat. Net income 2.2 billion, revenue 12.15 billion. And the number the whole insurance complex watches, the combined ratio, came in at 83.6% — anything under 100 is an underwriting profit, and the low 80s is exceptional. What drove a beat that size — is it real, or is it one-off? A bit of both, honestly. Catastrophe losses ran about half what they did a year ago — a quieter quarter for storms — and they booked a 578 million-dollar favorable reserve release, which means prior years' claims came in cheaper than they'd set aside. That's not repeatable every quarter. But the underlying underwriting margin is genuinely strong, and here's why it fits the day: on a tape punishing every growth name that so much as blinks, a boring property-casualty insurer printed a huge beat and was one of the only large caps green on Friday, next to Exxon and Apple. Money leaving the crowded AI trade has to land somewhere, and Friday it went to the compounder that beat. Two financials, both telling you where the safety is right now. International. International Business & Politics Two from abroad, and the first keeps building one of the year's cleanest secular trades. Saab — the Swedish defense group — beat on the second quarter Friday, and the headline is the backlog: a record order book, powered by a Polish submarine order that added something like 47 billion Swedish kronor, roughly 7 billion dollars, of new bookings in the quarter alone. The chief executive used the results to lecture Europe about overhauling how it buys weapons. So the European rearmament story isn't slowing — it's compounding. It's compounding, and that's the point to hold. We've flagged the continental defense build as a structural, multi-year capex cycle, and a record backlog at Saab is the hard evidence — order books that stretch years out, not a single good quarter. It's why the defense primes — Saab, Rheinmetall, BAE Systems — keep re-rating even on days the broad market is falling apart. When the tape sells off but the backlog names hold, that's the market telling you which themes it believes are real. Second one — Airbus, and it's really a China-and-geopolitics story wearing an aviation jacket. Nicely put. Airbus landed a fresh round of orders from Chinese state carriers on Friday — Air China taking 15 A350-900 widebodies, Shenzhen Airlines 40 of the A320neo family. And the subtext is everything: China is steering its aircraft demand to Europe while Boeing is mired in its own troubles. So Beijing is using plane orders as a diplomatic instrument. Exactly — aircraft orders are one of the most visible geopolitical bargaining chips there is, because each one is billions of dollars and thousands of jobs, and Beijing knows precisely which capitals feel it. Tilting that demand toward Toulouse and away from an American manufacturer is a message wrapped in a purchase order. For Airbus it's a real win — it extends their dominance in the single most important growth market in aviation, and it deepens their backlog at exactly the moment Boeing can least afford to lose ground. China to close the block. China And China is where Friday's selloff went to get worse. While Wall Street was falling, the Chinese tech complex was in a genuine rout: the Shanghai Composite down 3.1%, the STAR 50 — Shanghai's answer to the Nasdaq — off a brutal 7.1%, and Hong Kong's tech index down more than 4%. This wasn't a spillover from New York. It was its own bubble getting a leg cut out. And the backdrop is almost surreal, because Beijing was simultaneously throwing itself a party for AI. That's the contradiction of the whole thing. All this happened around the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, where Xi Jinping gave a speech pushing global AI cooperation, and China and 28 other nations signed on to a new Shanghai-based body — they're calling it the World AI Cooperation Organization, an explicit bid to write the world's AI-governance rules from Shanghai rather than Washington. And under that official optimism, the froth was extreme: Zhipu's latest GLM model, a startup called MiniMax teasing a 2.7-trillion-parameter monster, and Moonshot's Kimi K3 — the same open-weight model that helped knock the American semis down. So the same model that spooked Nvidia spooked its own home market harder. Which is the sharp read. The Chinese AI names had run on pure euphoria — governance leadership, model-size bragging rights, national-champion status — and when the market started to ask whether any of it makes money, the de-rating was violent, far worse than the US version. And it lands right on top of the two-speed economy we keep describing: a technology sector priced for a revolution sitting on top of a real economy with soft consumption and stubborn deflationary pressure. Beijing wants to lead the world on AI rules while its own AI stocks just told you what happens when narrative meets valuation. That's the block. To the desk this whole show keeps circling back to. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities Segment two — the energy desk. And Alex, here's the thing that makes today's data so striking: while the AI stocks were being cut apart, the physical evidence that the build is accelerating got more concrete, not less. Start with the capacity auction. Start with PJM, because the number is almost poetic in how broken it is. PJM — the biggest grid operator in America, serving 65 million people — ran its 2028-2029 capacity auction, and the results landed Monday the fourteenth. It cleared roughly 138,000 megawatts, and it cleared at 325 dollars per megawatt-day — which is the legislated price cap. The absolute ceiling. Third auction in a row pinned to its own cap. And clearing at the cap sounds bullish for generators, but you're telling me it's actually a broken signal. It's a broken signal, and that's the whole insight. Look underneath: the auction cleared about 6.8 gigawatts below the reliability requirement — it literally could not buy enough capacity to meet the target — and it drew only about 500 megawatts of genuinely new supply. FERC's new chair, Laura Swett, said that out loud on the sixteenth. So the market is screaming scarcity at maximum price, and the response is 500 megawatts of new build. A functioning market clears higher and summons supply. This one has hit its ceiling and summoned almost nothing. So the price mechanism has stopped doing its job. It's stopped doing its job, and that's the story of the whole sector right now. When the capacity market can't call forth new plants even at its legal maximum, scarcity stops being a price-discovery problem and becomes a governance problem — which is exactly why the action is moving to Washington. And that brings us to the single most important thing happening today, literally today, that almost nobody outside this desk is watching. Which is? Today, July twentieth, is the deadline for all six of the country's grid operators — PJM, MISO, SPP, California, New England, and New York — to file generation-adequacy reports with FERC, under show-cause orders FERC issued back on June eighteenth. This is the federal government stepping in to standardize the rules for how these enormous data-center loads connect to the grid, and how co-located power — a data center bolting its own gas plant on behind the meter — gets treated across every market at once. So instead of every state and every utility improvising, Washington is trying to write one rulebook. One rulebook, and the stakes are the cost-shift. FERC named five reform priorities, and the big one is protecting ordinary ratepayers from subsidizing the grid upgrades these hyperscalers trigger — plus a formal study process for generators sitting "electrically proximate" to a large load. Get this right and the behind-the-meter gas deals get a clean, repeatable tariff path. Get it wrong and every one of them stays bespoke and litigated for years. The outcome quietly decides how fast the whole build can actually plug in. And put the scale of the demand next to the scale of the supply, because that gap is the investable fact. Bank of America did exactly that mid-month, and the numbers are stark. Data centers alone add about 125 gigawatts of US electricity load between now and 2030. Total power demand growing at a 4.1% compound rate — which sounds small until you remember US power demand was essentially flat for two decades. And here's the gap: BofA models more than 230 gigawatts of capacity demand against roughly 93 gigawatts of supply. Call it a 100-gigawatt shortfall by 2030. A hundred gigawatts short. That's not a rounding error, that's a hundred large power plants that don't exist. And the binding constraint is not money — it's turbines. Large gas turbines are sold out through 2030. You cannot buy a slot. So developers are pivoting to on-site gas engines — reciprocating engines, the kind that can be delivered in quarters not years — while utilities quietly extend the life of coal plants, bolt on batteries, and race to build transmission. When the constraint is a manufacturing queue and not capital, the whole game becomes who has secured their megawatts, physically, on paper, today. And you can see that in how the deals are now being structured. You can, and it's the sharpest change in the market. Look at the joint venture that launched on the fifteenth — Coravel, a fifty-fifty between the Spanish builder ACS and BlackRock's infrastructure arm. Their very first act was to sign a hyperscaler lease — about 140 megawatts of critical IT load at a Dallas-Fort Worth campus, with rights to another 100 on top, and a pipeline of 1.7 gigawatts behind it. And the model is the point: they wrap the power, the building, and the operations into a single contract. Power, shell, and operations sold as one product. That's a direct threat to the plain-vanilla data-center landlord. It's an existential threat to the standalone developer who can only offer the building and says "go find your own electricity." When power is the scarce input, whoever controls the megawatts controls the deal — and the capital pooling into this, BlackRock-scale capital, is betting the integrated model wins. The land is no longer the asset. The deliverable megawatt is the asset. And that scarcity is exactly what turns this into the cost-of-living fight we keep flagging. It is, and the concentration is the trigger. Digital Realty just locked up 1,440 acres near Kansas City — but the gating piece wasn't the land, it was a signed energy agreement with the local utility for 600 megawatts by early 2028, scaling to 2 gigawatts. And in one rural Missouri county, Montgomery County, Amazon and Google announced separate campuses — 10 billion dollars from one, 15 from the other. 25 billion dollars of hyperscale capex dropped into a single county's utility footprint. And that whole cost lands on one small utility and its existing customers. That's the powder keg. When you concentrate that much new load on one utility, the grid upgrades to serve it get spread across everybody's bill — and that's precisely the ratebase fight that started in Virginia and Pennsylvania and is now going nationwide. It's why FERC's rulebook today matters so much: the entire question is whether grandmother's power bill subsidizes a hyperscaler, or the hyperscaler pays for the capacity it causes. The stocks wobbled on Friday. The build did not. Bring it home to the Philippines. Philippines Segment three — the Philippines, where that same oil bid we keep tracking lands as a very direct squeeze. Weather first, and the good news is it's quiet. Quiet for once. As of Sunday and into today, PAGASA has no tropical cyclone in the country, no low-pressure area worth naming, and no wind signals up anywhere. What's active is just the habagat — the southwest monsoon — bringing isolated afternoon downpours to the western side of the country. Over the weekend the rain focused on the far north of Luzon: Ilocos, Zambales, Batanes, the Babuyan Islands, Apayao, Abra — the usual flash-flood and landslide watch during the heavy cells, but nothing widespread or prolonged. Metro Manila hit about 33 and a half degrees today. A rare calm week on the weather map. So the story is the macro, and the macro is a squeeze. It is, and it starts with the central bank. The BSP is holding its policy rate at 4.75% after hiking a quarter-point in June — its second straight hike. And it turned more hawkish, not less: it raised its own 2026 inflation forecast to 6.4%, and pegged 2027 at 4.5% — both above the 2-to-4% target band. Governor Remolona called June's move "pre-emptive" and pointedly did not rule out more. The street — MUFG, Nomura, Citi — is penciling in another 50 basis points of hikes ahead. A central bank hiking into a slowdown. That only happens when it's defending something. It's defending the currency and fighting imported inflation — and you can see why in the prints. Headline inflation did cool to 6.4% in June from 6.8%, which sounds like relief. But look under it: core inflation actually rose, to 4.4% from 4.1%. The cooling was all transport and food — the volatile stuff — while the underlying, stickier pressure got worse. That's the worst kind of inflation mix for a central banker: the headline improves, the core hardens. And the peso is the pressure gauge. The peso is sitting at 61.67 to the dollar — a hair off the record low around 61.75 it touched earlier in the week, and down more than 4% on the year. And the mechanism is brutally simple and ties straight to our throughline: the Philippines imports almost all of its oil, so every dollar that Hormuz and the Iran risk adds to crude widens the import bill, pressures the peso, and feeds the very inflation the BSP is fighting. You can see it in the trade numbers — the May trade deficit blew out to 5.5 billion dollars, more than half again wider than a year ago, with fuel imports alone at 1.75 billion in the month. So it's the global oil story with a national price tag attached. That's exactly it — a fuel-importing economy absorbing an oil shock with a currency near a record low and a central bank forced to keep tightening into it. The BSP is leaning on reserves to smooth the peso rather than spend all its rate ammunition at once. It's a holding action: defend the currency, keep policy tight, and hope the crude bid fades before patience does. And there's a big political week landing on top of it — President Marcos delivers his fifth State of the Nation Address next Monday, the twenty-seventh, and the cost of living is going to be the whole subtext, because families feel this oil-and-peso squeeze at the pump and in the market basket every single day. Structurally intact, cyclically squeezed. Onward — and this next one is my favorite. Vocab Of The Day Segment four — vocab of the day. Two Mandarin, two Tagalog, all tied to today's stories, and we do this one in-language. Alex, start us in Mandarin. 第一个词是"然而",意思是"但是、可是",不过它更正式、更书面。造个句子:AI 的建设还在加速,然而相关股票却连跌三天。(The first word is "rán'ér," meaning "however, yet" — but it's more formal, more written. A sentence: the AI buildout keeps accelerating, however the related stocks have fallen three days straight.) 所以"然而"跟"但是"意思一样,只是语气不同?(So "rán'ér" means the same as "dànshì," just a different register?) 对,意思几乎一样,但"然而"用在书面语、财经评论里,"但是"更口语。(Right, nearly the same meaning, but "rán'ér" belongs to written language and financial commentary, while "dànshì" is more colloquial.) 它常常引出一个跟前面相反的、让你意外的结果。(It often introduces a result that contradicts what came before, one that surprises you.) 基本面很强,然而市场并不买账。(The fundamentals are strong; however, the market isn't buying it.) 我懂了——用"然而"听起来更像财经社论。第二个词呢?(I see — using "rán'ér" sounds more like a financial editorial. And the second word?) 第二个词是"蔓延",本义是像火或藤蔓一样扩散,现在多用来形容负面情绪或危机的扩散。(The second word is "mànyán" — literally to spread like fire or a creeping vine, now mostly used for the spread of negative sentiment or a crisis.) 星期五,恐慌从科技股蔓延到整个市场,甚至蔓延到亚洲。(On Friday, the panic spread from tech stocks to the whole market, and even spread across to Asia.) "蔓延"和"扩大"有什么不同?(What's the difference between "mànyán" and "kuòdà," to expand?) 好问题。"扩大"是主动地、有意地把范围做大,比如扩大投资;"蔓延"是失控地、自己往外爬,通常是坏事。(Good question. "Kuòdà" is to enlarge a scope deliberately, on purpose — like expanding investment; "mànyán" is uncontrolled, creeping outward on its own, and usually it's something bad.) 所以我们说恐慌蔓延、危机蔓延、抛售蔓延——绝不会说"恐慌扩大"那么自然。(So we say panic spreads, crisis spreads, the selloff spreads — you'd never say "panic expands" as naturally.) 这是书面语,新闻里到处都是。(It's written register, and it's everywhere in the news.) 太贴切了,正好是今天的行情。现在换菲律宾语。(Perfectly apt — that's exactly today's market. Now let's switch to Tagalog.) Ang unang salita ay "lumaganap" — ang kumalat nang malawakan, parang apoy o balita na kumakalat sa lahat ng dako. (The first word is "lumaganap" — to spread widely, like a fire or news spreading everywhere.) Noong Biyernes, mabilis na lumaganap ang benta mula sa Wall Street hanggang sa Asya. (On Friday, the selloff spread fast from Wall Street all the way to Asia.) Ano ang pagkakaiba ng "lumaganap" sa "kumalat"? (What's the difference between "lumaganap" and "kumalat"?) Magkalapit sila, pero ang "kumalat" ay pang-araw-araw — kumalat ang tsismis, kumalat ang sakit. Ang "lumaganap" ay mas malawak, mas pormal ang dating — paglaganap ng teknolohiya, paglaganap ng krisis. (They're close, but "kumalat" is everyday — a rumor spreads, a disease spreads. "Lumaganap" is broader and sounds more formal — the spread of technology, the spread of a crisis.) Ito ang katumbas ng Mandarin na 蔓延 na kasama natin kanina. (It's the counterpart of the Mandarin "mànyán" we just had.) Magandang tulay 'yan. At ang huling salita? (Nice bridge. And the last word?) "Tiisin" — mula sa "tiis," ang matiyagang pagbata sa hirap o sakit nang hindi sumusuko. Tinitiis ng ekonomiya ng Pilipinas ang pagsipa ng langis at ang paghina ng piso. (The word is "tiisin," from "tiis" — to bear hardship or pain patiently without giving up. The Philippine economy is enduring the surge in oil and the weakening of the peso.) Iba ba ito sa "batahin"? (Is this different from "batahin," to carry a load?) Oo. Ang "batahin" ay pagbubuhat ng bigat; ang "tiisin" ay pagtitiis — may tapang at pasensya, kahit masakit, nagpapatuloy ka pa rin. (Yes. "Batahin" is to lift a weight; "tiisin" is to endure — there's courage and patience in it, and even when it hurts, you keep going.) Isang salita na puno ng damdaming Pilipino: ang matiisin. (One word full of Filipino feeling — the quality of being long-suffering, "matiisin.") Language living inside the news. Two Mandarin, two Tagalog — a formal "however," a crisis that spreads, a selloff spreading wide, and an economy enduring. That's today's show in four words. Couldn't have scripted the throughline better. Arts & Culture Segment five — arts and culture. And we lead with the galleries today, not the box office. Alex, there's a major reappraisal opening in London. A big one, at Tate Modern — a career survey of Ana Mendieta, the Cuban-American artist, her first major UK show in over a decade. More than 120 works: the famous Silueta series, where she pressed the silhouette of her own body into earth, sand, and fire and photographed the trace; newly remastered films; and rarely seen early paintings and late sculptures. It runs into January. Mendieta is a name a lot of people know for the tragedy of how she died, more than for the work itself. And that's exactly what this show sets out to correct. For years her death — the fall from a New York window in 1985, and the acquittal of her husband, the sculptor Carl Andre — has overshadowed the art. What Tate is doing is restoring the films and the objects behind those iconic photographs, and arguing that she was central, not marginal, to how we now think about the body, gender, and land in art. It's a reframing of the canon, not just a retrospective — putting a woman who worked with earth and absence back at the center of the story. And there's a quieter rediscovery on at the National Gallery too. There is, and it's a lovely counterpoint — Waldmüller: Landscapes. Ferdinand Georg Waldmüller was an Austrian Biedermeier painter, early 1800s, and this is the first-ever UK exhibition devoted to him, done with the Belvedere in Vienna. The argument the show makes is that he was painting hard, clear, sunstruck Alpine light out of doors decades before the French Impressionists got the credit for it. A realist ahead of his moment, finally getting his English-language hearing. From canvas to the concert hall — the summer festivals are in full swing. They are, and the standout was the First Night of the BBC Proms on Friday, at the Royal Albert Hall. Dalia Stasevska conducted the BBC Symphony in an all-American program for the United States' 250th year — Copland's Fanfare rolling into Gershwin's An American in Paris. But the moment everyone wrote about was the young pianist Yunchan Lim playing Ravel's Piano Concerto in G. The critics used words like "startling assurance" — the way he balanced the percussive bite of the outer movements against the aching lyricism of that slow middle movement. Lim is the one who won the Van Cliburn a few years back at eighteen, isn't he — the phenomenon. The very same, and this is him proving the phenomenon has real depth. And there's a wall of opera behind it if you want it — Salzburg opened the same night with a new Carmen, Asmik Grigorian in the title role under Teodor Currentzis, and Bayreuth's 150th-anniversary season opens later this week. A rich few days for anyone who follows the voice. And one for the readers to close: Sigrid Nunez — the National Book Award winner behind The Friend — has just published her first-ever story collection, called It Will Come Back to You. Thirteen stories gathered across her whole career. And the reviews on that? Warm — critics are saying her trademark wit and quiet empathy are actually sharper in miniature than at novel length, plot turns so gentle they barely register as turns, and never a slide into sentiment. And the timing's neat, because the book world is holding its breath for next Tuesday, the twenty-eighth, when the 2026 Booker Prize longlist drops — a panel chaired, wonderfully, by the classicist Mary Beard. So a good week to have a novelist's short stories on the nightstand while the big list gets argued over. One good thing to finish. One Good Thing And to close — one good thing, and it's a slow-motion miracle hiding in plain sight. It's the forests of New England. A scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, Bill Moomaw, has been pointing at a fact most people who live there never notice: Massachusetts, which was roughly 90% cleared of its forest by the mid-1800s — stripped for farms and timber — is now back to about 60% forest cover. New England as a whole was logged down by around 80%, and it has quietly regrown. Moomaw calls it, flatly, "the greatest forest recovery in the history of the world." And nobody planted it — this is the land just taking itself back. That's the wonderful part. When the farms moved west and the fields were abandoned, the forest simply walked back in on its own, tree by tree, over a century and a half — no grand restoration program, no ribbon-cutting. And now those regrown woods are pulling carbon out of the air, holding soil, cooling towns, and sheltering wildlife that had nowhere to go. It's a reminder that nature's default setting, given half a chance and a little time, is to heal. A century and a half of quiet regrowth. A good one to start the week on. That's your Morning Commute for Monday. Whatever this week has in store — — take it steady, look after each other, and we'll be right back here tomorrow. Have a good one. 然而 however; yet; nevertheless (formal contrastive connective) the gap between a roaring AI buildout and a third straight down day in AI stocks 蔓延 to spread; to creep outward (like fire or a vine) — now mostly of negative sentiment or a crisis Friday's selloff spreading from tech to the whole market and across to Asia lumaganap to spread widely; to proliferate (of news, fire, a crisis) the selloff spreading from Wall Street across to Asian markets tiisin to endure; to bear hardship or pain patiently without giving up (root: tiis) the Philippine economy absorbing the oil shock and a near-record-low peso

docs.title: Friday, July 17, 2026
docs.text: Friday, July 17, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Friday, July seventeenth. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. The throughline today: the AI trade just took its second straight down day, and the tell is who's getting punished — the growth names slipping on their guides. Alphabet led it lower on a model delay. Meanwhile the same oil bid that's keeping the Fed boxed in is showing up as real costs everywhere else: a 6-billion-dollar fuel hit one airline just swallowed, a data-center line item landing on ordinary power bills, and a rare-earth chokehold with a trillion-dollar price tag on it. Let's get into it. Headlines Headlines. World desk first — the Middle East, still setting the tempo for everything downstream. The war's into its second week with no ceasefire in sight, and the market-relevant fact is the chokepoint. Iran's keeping the pressure on shipping through Hormuz, tanker traffic is running thin, insurers are repricing war-risk cover, and crude is holding its bid — Brent up around the mid-80s, near one-month highs, with the market still carrying a tail toward 90 if a tanker or a terminal actually goes. And that's the whole macro pivot we've been living in — the war premium that bled out in June is back in the curve. It is, and the point today is the second-order damage, not the headline count. And it isn't just crude — watch the refined products, because that's where households and airlines actually feel it. Diesel and jet-fuel cracks widen when refiners fear feedstock disruption, so the pump price and the airfare can move even before the barrel does. Higher crude flows into corporate fuel bills, into freight and shipping rates, into the Philippine import tab, into a Fed that can't declare victory on inflation. We'll hit all three today. The oil chart is still the single most important input on the board, and it's being set in a strait most listeners will never see. And the risk asymmetry from here? Skewed to the upside on price. The spot move has mostly happened; what's cheap is the optionality on a genuine supply disruption. So you don't chase crude here — you own the tail. And every desk is watching the same thing: does OPEC-plus lean in with spare barrels to cap it, or defend price and let it run. That single decision sets the inflation path for the back half of the year. Second world story, and it's a leadership shock in Kyiv. Zelensky cleaned house. He dismissed his defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, and parliament moved to approve a new wartime government — hundreds turned out to protest in Kyiv. The reporting ties it to a doctrine clash with the army chief, Oleksandr Syrsky: Fedorov was the asymmetric-warfare bet, the drones and the cyber, and Syrsky wants the resources going to holding territory. So it's a strategy fight dressed as a personnel move, at a terrible moment to be re-litigating strategy. Exactly — re-arguing doctrine mid-war. The market read is narrow but real: it matters for how durable Western resolve looks into the autumn, and for the European defense-capex theme that's been one of the year's cleaner secular trades. Instability atop Kyiv's command is not what the re-armament complex wants to see priced. Onto markets. Market Overview Thursday's close, and it was a second straight down day led by the AI complex. The S&P 500 off 51 basis points to 7,533.77, the Nasdaq down a heavier 1.5% to 25,881.95, and the Dow far more resilient — off just 20 basis points, down 105.67 points, to 52,552.97. So a growth-and-chips problem, not a market problem. The Dow barely moved. Right. Under the hood the breadth wasn't nearly as ugly as the Nasdaq headline — it was concentrated in the biggest, most crowded AI names. And the proximate trigger was Alphabet, down more than 4% after Bloomberg reported it's behind schedule delivering Gemini 3.5 Pro, its flagship model. A model delay knocks four percent off a company that size? When it's priced for AI leadership, yes. The whole terminal-value story for these names rests on staying at the frontier, so any slip in the roadmap reprices the multiple at the margin — and it pulled the semis and the memory names down with it, SanDisk and Western Digital among the hardest hit. That's the week in one trade: no forgiveness for any crack in the AI-growth story. And the rates picture is the part that should still surprise people. This is the crux. June CPI landed Tuesday at 3.5% headline, below the 3.8% consensus, month-over-month minus four-tenths — the biggest drop since April 2020, almost entirely energy. Core 2.6%, flat. On paper, a green light to cut. And yet the 10-year sits around 4.57%, the 2-year near 4.17% — yields ticked up, not down. Which is the counterintuitive bit. Cooler inflation, higher yields. Because the bond market is looking straight through a backward-looking, energy-driven print to a forward crude chart that just turned higher. The disinflation in that number is the very oil that's already reversing. So the July meeting — the FOMC's the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth — isn't hold-versus-cut anymore. It's hold-versus-hike. Wednesday's PPI, minus three-tenths on the month, tells the same story: soft realized inflation, hard forward risk. And the positioning underneath the tape? Because two down days in the crowded names smells like more than fundamentals. It is. What you're watching is a de-grossing in the most consensus book on the street. Everybody owns the same handful of AI winners, so when one cracks, the risk managers trim the whole basket at once — that's why a single-name model delay becomes a sector-wide 1.5% down day. It's mechanical, not a change of thesis. The equal-weight index held up far better than the cap-weight, which is the classic signature of a positioning unwind rather than a growth scare. So a crowded-trade wobble, not a top. That's the base case — a crowded trade shaking out weak hands, not the end of the theme. But it's fragile precisely because it's so concentrated. When the top seven names are this much of the index, the market's health and a handful of AI roadmaps are the same sentence. And the cross-asset tells? The interesting one is gold — around 4,000 dollars and drifting lower even with a live war, because a firmer dollar and higher real yields are outmuscling the haven bid. The dollar index up near 100 and a half. When gold can't rally on a Middle-East escalation, that tells you rates are the dominant force right now, not fear. And the backdrop under all of it? Earnings, and they're the cushion. FactSet has Q2 S&P growth tracking north of 23%, revised up from about 19% at quarter start — an unusually large upward revision mid-season. So the E in the multiple is compounding even as the macro gets noisier. So what actually breaks the standoff — the cool inflation or the hot oil? Oil, in the near term. If crude keeps climbing into the meeting, the July inflation print reverses this month's energy relief and the hold-to-hike debate tips hawkish for real. If the barrel fades, the disinflation trend reasserts and the cut comes back onto the table for the autumn. It genuinely is that binary, which is why the whole desk is watching the Strait of Hormuz instead of the dot plot. Net it out: constructive on earnings, cautious on rates, and every model runs through the price of a barrel. US business — and it's a tale of two guides. U.S. Business US business. Two earnings that dropped after yesterday's close, and both cut straight to today's throughline. Start with the airline. United Airlines. Adjusted earnings of 1 dollar 99 a share, revenue 17.7 billion, up 16%, premium revenue up 16%, cargo up 23%, a pre-tax margin near 6%. And here's the line that matters: they raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to 9-to-11 dollars — while absorbing nearly 6 billion dollars of extra fuel cost this year. The fuel bill alone was up 2.3 billion in the quarter, 84%, worth more than a dollar a share. So this is the oil story with a P&L attached. A company eating the crude spike in real time and still guiding up. That's exactly why it's the tell. The demand side — premium cabins, corporate travel, international, cargo — is strong enough to eat an 84% jump in jet fuel and still raise the number. It tells you the consumer at the top end is intact, and it tells you where the oil shock actually lands first: on margins, quietly, not on demand. If crude keeps climbing, that 6-billion becomes the headline instead of the footnote, and the guide gets a lot harder to defend. Second name — UnitedHealth, and it was a monster. A blowout. Adjusted earnings of 6 dollars 38 against about 4.90 expected, revenue 112 billion, and the number the whole managed-care complex watches — the medical loss ratio — improved to 86.7%. They raised full-year adjusted EPS to 19.50-to-20 dollars, and the stock jumped around 7%. After the year that sector's had, a clean beat on the loss ratio is a real signal. It's the signal. The bear case on managed care all year was that medical costs were running away from them — utilization normalizing higher, seniors using more care. A loss ratio back under 87% with raised guidance says they've got their arms around it again. And notice the rotation it captures: in a tape punishing every growth name that decelerates, here's a defensive healthcare giant re-rating higher on execution. Money leaving the crowded AI trade has to go somewhere, and yesterday it went into the boring compounder that beat. And the read-through for the rest of the group? That's why it's a market event, not just a company event — UnitedHealth is the bellwether, so a loss-ratio beat de-risks the read into the rest of the managed-care names reporting over the next two weeks. If the biggest, most complex book in the industry got costs under control, the smaller players probably did too. It's the kind of print that quietly resets an entire sector's multiple. Two guides, two directions — the whole market in a pair of earnings. International next. International Business & Politics Two across the Atlantic. First, pharma M&A: Novartis is buying the UK biotech Myricx Bio for up to 1.5 billion dollars — 1.1 billion upfront, up to 400 million in milestones. It's a next-generation antibody-drug-conjugate platform, a novel payload chemistry, with lead oncology assets aimed at B7-H3 and HER2. Closing expected in the second half. Another big-pharma bolt-on into the ADC race. And that's the pattern to hold. Antibody-drug conjugates are the hottest modality in oncology — a targeted warhead that delivers chemo straight to the tumor — and with the patent cliffs looming late-decade, the majors are buying the next platform rather than waiting to invent it. Small, targeted, science-led deals. When organic growth is scarce, the balance sheets go shopping, and biotech is where they shop. Second, a genuine political milestone in Britain — Labour has its new leader. Andy Burnham is set to be elected Labour leader today, and to replace Starmer as prime minister on Monday. We flagged this as a slow-burn gilt story when Starmer stepped down; now it's real. Burnham runs to Starmer's left, so the market question is fiscal — does he reopen the spending envelope Rachel Reeves spent two years defending? And the gilt market's answer so far? No gap move yet — this isn't a Truss-style event, there's no fiscal statement attached to the handover. But this is exactly the kind of thing that sits under the long end for months. If the market starts to sniff a looser fiscal stance under a Burnham government, it re-rates the 30-year first, and it shows up in sterling. Watch the gilt curve into his first budget, whenever that lands. A change of prime minister on Monday is a slow-burn risk, not a same-day one. China to close the block. China The fresh China story isn't a data print — it's leverage. The IEA's new Global Critical Minerals Outlook, out yesterday, warns that if China fully implements its expanded rare-earth export controls, it could put roughly 6.5 trillion dollars of downstream Western production at risk — autos, high-tech, defense, and clean energy. 6.5 trillion. Put that number in context, because it's enormous. It's the estimated value of all the manufacturing that depends on those inputs — the magnets and motors inside an EV, a wind turbine, a fighter jet, a data-center cooling system. Beijing broadened the controls last October and then delayed full implementation by a year, and that delay is the tell: it's a loaded weapon sitting on the table through the trade talks. And the exposure isn't evenly shared — the US and Europe would absorb nearly half the hit. So it's the mirror image of the AI-power story we keep telling. Instead of being short electrons, the West is short the minerals. That's the sharp read, and it's why this is more than a headline. The entire re-industrialization push — reshoring, defense rebuild, the energy transition — runs on a supply chain China dominates end to end, from the mine to the refined magnet. This report is just the IEA putting a number on the chokehold. It reframes every reshoring announcement: you can permit the factory, pour the concrete, and still not have the neodymium to run it. Strategic dependency with a price tag attached. And we've seen the dress rehearsal for how China uses this. We have — the gallium and germanium curbs a couple of years back were the proof of concept, targeted controls that sent Western buyers scrambling and prices spiking. Rare earths are that same playbook at a hundred times the scale, because there's no quick substitute and no Western refining capacity that can spin up in under a decade. The investable read is that anything tied to ex-China supply — a Western magnet maker, a rare-earth miner, a recycler — carries a strategic premium now that has nothing to do with this quarter's earnings and everything to do with who controls the inputs. That's the block. Changing gears to the desk this whole show keeps circling. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities Segment two — the energy desk. And Alex, the fresh angle today isn't the queue or the auction we keep tracking. It's the bill. It's the bill, and it just went from theory to a number on a statement. PPL in Pennsylvania raised residential rates 4.9% on July first — about 7 dollars and 42 cents a month on a thousand-kilowatt-hour bill — and, crucially, it created a new large-load "data-center" rate class. That's the first Pennsylvania utility to try to wall off data-center costs from ordinary ratepayers. Which is the fight we said would turn political the moment it hit people's wallets. And now it has. For contrast, take Virginia — the data-center capital of the world — where a resident's January bill hit 281 dollars, roughly three times normal. So you've got two models crystallizing in real time. Model one, the Virginia path: the grid upgrades for hyperscaler load get socialized into everyone's bill. Model two, the new Pennsylvania path: you create a separate rate class and make the data centers pay for the capacity they cause. Every state regulator in the country is about to have to choose between those two, and it's a genuinely hard political question. And Washington is leaning in. The White House is convening a second, expanded ratepayer-protection summit, and Michigan's governor rolled out a data-center energy and water plan this week. This is the moment the AI buildout stops being a pure capex story and becomes a cost-of-living story. Power is turning into the political variable that gasoline prices always were — and in an election-conscious environment, no one wants to be the governor who let grandma's bill triple to subsidize a hyperscaler. Meanwhile the physical build doesn't wait for the regulators. What's new on the supply side? The equipment tells the real timeline better than any forecast. GE Vernova's gas-turbine backlog is now up to 100 gigawatts, from 83 in the first quarter, and they're targeting north of 110 by year-end. And last week Baker Hughes and Kodiak signed a behind-the-meter turbine deal — 1 gigawatt by 2030, scalable to 1.8 — purpose-built to power data centers on-site. Behind-the-meter because the grid queue is too slow. That's the whole logic. When you can't wait years for an interconnection, you build your own generation on the fence line and skip the grid entirely. It's faster, but it's also a quiet disintermediation of the utility — the biggest new loads in the country generating their own power and barely touching the public system. And those turbine order books, sold out into the back half of the decade, are the clearest proof anywhere that this buildout is real, whatever the stocks did this week. There's a nasty feedback loop hiding in that, though. There is, and it's the one regulators are starting to fear. If the largest, most creditworthy loads self-supply and leave the grid, the fixed cost of the whole system — the poles, the wires, the peaker plants — gets spread across a smaller base of ordinary ratepayers. That's the utility death-spiral in miniature: the hyperscalers get cheap, fast, dedicated power, and the household left on the public system pays more to hold up infrastructure the data center no longer leans on. Which is exactly why that Pennsylvania rate class matters so much — it's an early attempt to keep the big loads paying their share. Which connects right back to the trade. It does — that's the gap the whole market is wrestling with. The IEA has global data-center electricity demand doubling by 2030, and the AI slice tripling. The physical evidence — turbines, transformers, nuclear PPAs, on-site gas — says the build is accelerating. And yet the equities can sell off 4% on a model delay. Fundamentals roaring, sentiment wobbling. Chips get the headlines; electrons and turbines are the binding constraint. And the through-line to inflation. It's direct, and it's the uncomfortable part. Power bills going up, fuel bills going up, critical minerals at strategic risk — the AI build and the oil shock are pushing on the exact same cost structure the Fed is trying to bring to heel. That's why the disinflation in Tuesday's CPI feels so fragile. The cheap-energy tailwind of the spring has become a headwind. Bring it home to the Philippines. Philippines Segment three — the Philippines, and this is where the oil bill bites hardest. Weather first. Quieter skies than last week — no typhoon on the landmass right now. PAGASA is tracking a low-pressure area well east of Mindanao with a high chance of becoming a tropical depression, but it's not expected to hit land for two to three days. The active story is the habagat, the southwest monsoon, soaking the far north of Luzon today with flash-flood and landslide warnings across Ilocos and the Cordilleras. Now the macro, and the new data point landed yesterday. It did — remittances, and they printed soft. Cash remittances up just 2% in May, to 2.71 billion dollars, the slowest monthly pace in years, even though the first-half total is still a record 14.11 billion. That 2% is the number to sit with. Because remittances are the shock absorber. Exactly — they're roughly a tenth of GDP, the most reliable dollar inflow the country has, and the thing that keeps household consumption steady when the peso wobbles. So watching that growth rate flatten toward 2% tells you the cushion is thinning at precisely the wrong moment — because the shock on the other side is getting bigger. The shock being the oil bill. Right. The Philippines imports something like 98% of its oil, so every dollar Hormuz adds to crude widens the import tab, pressures a peso already pinned near its record low around 61.7 to the dollar, and feeds the inflation the central bank is already fighting at a 4.75% policy rate. The June relief we all cheered a month ago is precisely what's reversing on them now. So the shock absorber is thinning right as the shock gets heavier — that's the bind in one sentence. And the central bank's room to maneuver? Narrow, and getting narrower. They're already at 4.75% after two straight hikes, and the peso near a record low means every cut risks importing more inflation through a weaker currency. So the BSP is leaning on reserves to smooth the peso rather than spend its rate ammunition — you can see the intervention capping the currency just under 61.7. It's a holding action: defend the peso, keep policy tight, and pray the oil bid fades before the reserves or the political patience runs out. Structurally intact, cyclically squeezed. That's the honest summary. The long-term story is still there — a young workforce, and the two great dollar earners, remittances and the outsourcing sector. But cyclically it's an economy absorbing an external oil shock with a weakening currency and a thinning buffer, hostage to a crude chart being set an ocean away. A little local color to close: the president declared eight local holidays across July — this week the Araw ng Mauban in Quezon, and later the Kinabayo Festival in Dapitan. Life goes on around the macro, as it always does. Onward — and this next one is my favorite. Vocab Of The Day Segment four — vocab of the day. Two Mandarin, two Tagalog, all tied to today's stories, and we do this one in-language. Alex, start us in Mandarin. 第一个词是"尽管",意思是"虽然、即使如此"。造个句子:尽管芯片股昨天大跌,AI 的建设还在加速。(The first word is "jǐnguǎn," "although / even so." A sentence: although chip stocks plunged yesterday, the AI buildout keeps accelerating.) 尽管……还是……——所以它常常跟"还是"或"仍然"搭配?(So "jǐnguǎn… háishì…" — it often pairs with "háishì" or "réngrán," "still"?) 对,这是固定搭配,语气比较书面、比较强。(Right, that's the fixed pairing, and the tone is more formal and emphatic.) 跟"虽然"比,"尽管"更强调"不管阻力多大,结果照样发生"。(Compared with "suīrán," "although," "jǐnguǎn" stresses that no matter the obstacle, the outcome happens anyway.) 尽管市场恐慌,基本面还是很强。(Despite the market panic, the fundamentals are still strong.) 我懂了——"尽管"带一点"顶着压力"的意思。第二个词呢?(I get it — "jǐnguǎn" carries a sense of pushing against pressure. And the second word?) 第二个词是"加剧",意思是"变得更严重"。(The second word is "jiājù," to intensify or aggravate — for something to get more severe.) 中东局势加剧,通胀压力也随之加剧。(As the Middle East situation intensifies, inflationary pressure intensifies right along with it.) "加剧"和"增加"有什么区别?(What's the difference between "jiājù" and "zēngjiā"?) "增加"只是数量变多,是中性的;"加剧"是负面的、紧张的东西变得更强烈。(Zēngjiā is just a neutral increase in quantity; jiājù is when something tense or negative grows more intense.) 这是书面语,财经新闻里到处都是:紧张局势加剧,通胀压力加剧,矛盾加剧。(It's formal, written register — all over financial news: tensions intensify, inflation pressure intensifies, contradictions sharpen.) 太好了。现在换菲律宾语。(Excellent. Now let's switch to Tagalog.) Ang unang salita ay "igting" — ang tindi o tensyon ng isang sitwasyong hila nang hila. (The first word is "igting" — the intensity or tension of a situation stretched tighter and tighter.) Lalong tumindi ang igting sa Gitnang Silangan ngayong linggo. (The tension in the Middle East intensified further this week.) Ano ang pagkakaiba ng "igting" sa "init"? (What's the difference between "igting" and "init," heat?) Ang "init" ay galit o tensyong pulitikal na pansamantala; ang "igting" ay ang paghigpit ng sitwasyon, parang lubid na binabatak. (Init is anger or passing political heat; igting is the tightening of a situation, like a rope pulled taut.) Kaya bagay na bagay sa merkado at sa digmaan: igting ng benta, igting ng labanan. (So it fits markets and war alike: the intensity of a selloff, the intensity of the fighting.) Ito ang katumbas ng Mandarin na 加剧. (It's the counterpart of the Mandarin jiājù.) Magandang tulay 'yan. At ang huling salita? (Nice bridge. And the last word?) "Pasanin" — ang bigat na dinadala mo sa balikat mo. Mabigat na pasanin ng bawat OFW ang kanyang pamilya, lalo na ngayong mahina ang piso. (The burden you carry on your shoulders. Each overseas worker carries the heavy burden of family, especially now with a weak peso.) Iba ito sa "dalahin," tama? (This is different from "dalahin," right?) Tama. Ang "dalahin" ay simpleng bagay na binubuhat; ang "pasanin" ay mabigat, madalas hindi pisikal — responsibilidad, hirap. (Correct. "Dalahin" is a simple object you carry; a "pasanin" is heavy, often not physical — responsibility, hardship.) At may kaugnay: ang "pasan-pasan," ibig sabihin, buong-buong dinadala mo. (And there's a relative — "pasan-pasan," meaning you shoulder the whole of it.) Isang salita, buong ekonomiya ng pamilya. (One word, and it holds a whole family economy.) Language living inside the news. Two Mandarin, two Tagalog — a holding-firm-despite, an intensifying, a tension pulled taut, and a burden carried. That's today's show in four words. Couldn't have scripted the throughline better. Art / Pop Segment five — art and pop, quick. New Music Friday is stacked, and the headline drop is Rick Ross — his new album "Set In Stone" is out today, alongside Steve Lacy, a new DJ Khaled record, Lil Baby, and, of all pairings, Nickelback. A heavy hip-hop-led slate to close the week. And the box office finally has a real bright spot. A big one. "Toy Story 5" just crossed 808.6 million dollars worldwide — 381 million domestic, 427 million overseas — after only three weekends. That makes it the number-three Hollywood release of 2026, behind "Super Mario Galaxy" at just over a billion and "Michael" at 991 million, and it's on a clear pace to clear a billion of its own. So legacy animation delivering while the live-action experiments keep stumbling. That's the read — Pixar's core franchise printing money in an otherwise soft box-office year. When audiences are choosy, the trusted brand with the real emotional hook still opens wallets, and a fifth Toy Story could easily have been a cash-in but it's playing like an event. A billion-dollar animated hit is exactly the anchor the studios needed this summer. Good cue for the meme. Trending Meme Segment six — the trending meme, and we just report it. This one runs on the World Cup. With the 2026 tournament into the knockout rounds, fans have decided that each winning nation gets temporary "custody" of Hatsune Miku — the virtual Vocaloid pop star — and after every match, artists post fresh illustrations of her dressed in the victor's kit and colors. So it's a fan-art relay tied to the bracket. Exactly — they're calling it the World Cup custody battle. Win your match, and the internet's most famous digital character is "yours" until you lose, complete with a wave of new artwork in your team's strip. It's wholesome, purely online, and endlessly renewable, because the bracket itself generates the content — a new custody handover every time a favorite goes through or a giant gets knocked out. Reporting it, not performing it. Last segment. One Good Thing And to close — one good thing. A genuinely hopeful one out of medicine. A blood test called PinPoint hit 99% accuracy detecting or ruling out gynaecological cancers — evaluated on 16,481 patients across 170 GP practices in Yorkshire, in the UK. And NHS trusts are now rolling it out so that women at low risk can skip the invasive endometrial biopsies they'd otherwise face just to be cleared. So it's not only accuracy — it's spared procedures and faster answers for a lot of frightened people. That's exactly it — a single blood draw standing in for an invasive work-up, at 99%. It speeds diagnosis for the women who do have cancer, and it spares thousands of others the ordeal and the anxious waiting just to find out they don't. It's the kind of quiet, unglamorous progress that never makes the front page but quietly changes a great many lives. A 99% worth ending the week on. That's your Morning Commute for Friday. Whatever this Friday holds for you — — take it a little easy, stay cool out there, and we'll be right back here on Monday. Have a good one. 尽管 although; even though; despite (the outcome happens anyway) the AI buildout accelerating despite the chip-stock rout 加剧 to intensify; to aggravate; to sharpen (something tense or negative) escalating Middle East conflict feeding the inflation and oil bid igting intensity; mounting tension; the tautness of a situation stretched tight the escalating Middle East conflict and the two-day market selloff pasanin a burden one shoulders; a load of responsibility or hardship carried the weakening peso, the oil-import bill, and softening OFW remittances

docs.title: Thursday, July 16, 2026
docs.text: Thursday, July 16, 2026 Cold Open Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Thursday, July sixteenth. I'm Sam. And I'm Alex. The throughline today is a market priced for perfection — TSMC just printed a record quarter and raised its capex, and chip stocks are cratering anyway, because the bar was set impossibly high. The gap between what AI is actually doing and what its stocks are pricing is the whole trade. Let's get into it. Headlines Headlines. World desk first. The Gulf. The Iran story escalated again, but the vector changed. This isn't a tanker headline — it's a US ultimatum. Trump said Tuesday that if negotiations don't resume, the US targets Iranian infrastructure next week. Tehran answered by calling any strike on its infrastructure a red line and promising retaliation. So we've gone from a shipping-lane risk to a state-on-state strike calendar. That's a different kind of tail — it's got a date attached now. Which is why the oil bid won't leave. Brent settled 84.95, WTI around 79.60, forecast desks drawing lines toward 90. And the second-order tell is the real one: India just raised windfall taxes on diesel and jet-fuel exports because cracks are blowing out, and US refiners are looking at a quarter where profits could triple. When the refiners are the trade, the barrel isn't the story — the spread is. Exactly. And that's the part markets underprice — a Hormuz scare shows up in the crack spread and the retail pump price before it shows up in the CPI. Kalshi's got an 88% chance the national gas average tops $4 by month-end. That's the political transmission of an oil shock, in real time. And a strike-next-week clock isn't something the curve can price cleanly. It can't, so it doesn't try — it keeps a premium in the front and fat tails in the options. It's the same inflationary fuse we've been tracking, still lit under a market that spent yesterday celebrating disinflation. Hold that contradiction; it runs through the whole show. Second world story — Brazil. Trade. The US is putting a 25% tariff on most Brazilian goods, framed as a Section 301 unfair-trade action. And notably it replaces the tariffs the Supreme Court struck down — so this is the administration rebuilding the wall on firmer legal ground. On top of it, a separate forced-labor probe could stack another 12.5 points. 25, potentially 37.5. That's not a warning shot, that's a rupture between the two biggest economies in the Americas. What breaks first? Coffee and orange juice on the soft-commodity side — coffee futures already sold off on demand-destruction math — then the retaliation question. Lula called it a lamentable milestone, which is diplomatic for "we will respond." And it's not isolated: there's a Russia-sanctions bill moving through Congress that hands the White House new tariff powers against India, Japan, and parts of the EU. The tariff machine is moving from goods-deficit logic to political-leverage logic. And that's a harder thing for markets to hedge, because it's discretionary and it's fast. Right — you can model a trade deficit; you can't model a grievance. That's the new risk premium in cross-border supply chains, and it's why you're seeing front-running everywhere. The Port of Los Angeles just set a June cargo record — retailers and data-center builders rushing goods in ahead of both the tariffs and higher fuel costs. Good bridge to the tape. Market overview. Market Overview Wednesday's close: S&P up 38 basis points to 7,572, Nasdaq up 62 to 26,269, Dow up 0.29% to 52,659. Records within reach. The engine was a cooler June PPI landing on top of the cooler June CPI — two disinflation prints in a row, so the rates fear drained out. And you can see it in the curve. 10-year down 3 to 4.55%, 2-year down 5 to 4.13%. That's a small bull-steepening — the front end rallying harder as the hike scare eases. Gold gave back to 4,051, off about 0.4%, which fits: less inflation panic, less debasement bid. But here's the part that matters — the leadership was inside-out. Money rotated out of semiconductors and into megacap tech. Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon led; the chips lagged. The momentum trade had its biggest single unwind since 2001. Since 2001. That's a positioning earthquake, not a fundamentals story. It's entirely positioning, and it set up the whiplash. Because overnight, while New York slept, the chip complex came apart in Asia. Kospi down 6.4%. SK Hynix off 11. Samsung down 8. Korea Exchange briefly halted trading. Micron's down 2 pre-market here, and US futures are pointing lower on what the tape's calling a fresh AI wobble. So the setup is almost comic. The best data point of the week is about to hit the wires — and the stocks that should love it are getting hit. Priced-for-perfection in one sentence. And it's landed the market squarely in the bubble debate. Cramer said out loud he wants cold, hard proof AI is paying off for the customers, not just the infrastructure sellers. Apollo's Torsten Slok is running around saying the 60/40 portfolio is dead because AI is now too big to avoid. And there's a liquidity worry underneath it — the buildout only works if investors keep financing it. So the bull case and the bear case are the same fact. AI is enormous — which is either why you can't lose or why you can't diversify away the risk. That's the whole tension. The bulls call it the new exceptionalism — the AI capex cycle as the dominant force behind global growth, shrugging off every geopolitical shock. The bears point at a consumer that's softening underneath the megacap tape — the Fed's own beige book flagged warning signs, with a World Cup tourism bump papering over weakness elsewhere. And into all of that, Warsh spent two days in front of Congress. He did, and he mostly held serve. He said the AI build-out's price effects are "not necessarily inflationary" — which is his cover to look through it. He got into it with Elizabeth Warren, who floated corruption accusations; he defended Fed independence, said he meets often with the administration but wouldn't say whether he's spoken directly with Trump since taking the chair. Net: a chair signaling patience while both parties tell him prices are still rising too fast. So the reaction function is "look through oil, look through AI power, wait for the data." That's a lot of looking-through with a strike calendar on the wires. It is — and that's the risk. He's reduced forward guidance, so the market's flying on backward-looking prints, which is exactly when a supply shock catches everyone offside. The June CPI is a photograph of a month when oil dipped; the oil's already reversed. The market's trading the photo while the movie's moved on. And there's a competitive-dynamics footnote to the AI trade worth flagging — Mira Murati's shop shipped its first model. Thinking Machines, yes — an open-weight model aimed at loosening the frontier labs' grip, and notably positioned as a Western alternative to the open Chinese models. So even inside the bull case, the moat is getting contested from below — smaller, customizable models chipping at the giants. That's a margin story the megacap multiples don't fully reflect. US business. Start with the referee. U.S. Business TSMC. Second-quarter net income was 706.6 billion Taiwan dollars — call it $22 billion US — up 77% year on year, a record, and it blew past the roughly $625 billion estimate. Fifth straight record quarter. And they didn't just beat; they raised the full-year revenue outlook and lifted capex, with management calling AI demand "extremely robust." So the single most important supply-chain node in the entire AI trade just told you demand is accelerating and put its capex where its mouth is. And the stock fell. The stock fell. On profit-taking, on "expectations are now exceptionally high" — a fund-manager phrase doing a lot of work. They also bumped US investment by another $100 billion to $265 billion, 4 new 2-nanometer fabs in Arizona. Cleanest possible print, and the reaction is the throughline: when a name is priced for perfection, a blowout isn't a catalyst, it's an exit. Which is the same argument the memory crater is making — Hynix and Samsung didn't get worse overnight, the price just got ahead of the story. And it validates the capex, which is the thing the bears keep saying is speculative. That's the underrated read. TSMC raising capex is contracted demand, not a hope. When the foundry commits to four more fabs, that's Nvidia and Apple orders it can see. The de-rating is happening in the stocks, not in the order book — and that divergence is the entire market right now. Second US story — away from AI entirely. The real economy. And it's printing fine. The bank season was a record windfall — trading desks, prime brokerage, investment-banking fees all humming; the prime-brokerage engine in particular had a record quarter, and the banks flagged a resilient consumer with rising loan balances and clean credit. Now the handoff: J-and-J beat, 2.90 against 2.84, on 25.3 billion in revenue. United Airlines crushed it — 2.46 against a 1.89 estimate. And UnitedHealth reports this morning, where the whole story is the medical-cost trend. So the breadth is real even if the headline index is a megacap puppet show. Banks, healthcare, airlines — that's the non-AI economy compounding. That's the underappreciated story of the season: you don't need the AI names to work for earnings to grow. Which, ironically, is what makes the AI de-rating survivable — the E is broadening out from under the narrow tape. If the megacaps wobble and financials, industrials, and healthcare pick up the slack, the index has a floor even on an ugly chip day. And UnitedHealth this morning is the one to watch on the health side — the medical-cost ratio's been the whole managed-care story for a year. It is. If the cost trend keeps running hot, that's the tell that the healthcare consumer is finally catching up on deferred care — which is a real-economy signal, not a company one. And back on the banks: the read-through everyone's underplaying is the deal pipeline. Raymond James just got upgraded ahead of its print on capital-markets strength, and the message from the whole cohort is that M&A and IPO fees are re-accelerating after two dead years. That's the other side of the volatility — the same choppy tape that makes trading desks rich also fills the banking backlog. So volatility is a revenue line, not just a risk. Two international. International Business & Politics The Bank of Korea hiked — 25 basis points, its first hike since 2023. And read why: to counter inflation fueled by the US-Iran conflict. So Korea joins the ECB, the BOJ, and the Philippine central bank all tightening into the oil shock, while the Fed sits on its hands debating. That's the global picture nobody's framing cleanly. The Fed is the outlier dove, and everyone else is fighting imported inflation. For a chip-heavy economy like Korea, hiking on the same morning the Kospi's down more than 6% is a genuinely brutal bind. It's the same bind we keep circling — defend the currency, fight the fuel-price pass-through, and pay for it by tightening into an equity air-pocket. The synchronized-tightening trade is back on, and it keeps a floor under global yields even when US disinflation prints cool. That floor is why the US ten-year can't rally as far as the data alone would justify. Second story — Europe. Europe Inc is heading into its strongest earnings season in more than three years — genuinely good numbers coming. But the investor worry is structural: Europe doesn't have the AI growth engines to keep pace with the US, so even a strong season reads as "good, but not compounding." And the regulatory backdrop tightened — Brussels accepted Musk's X remediation plan under the Digital Services Act, after last year's €120 million fine. So Europe's problem isn't the quarter, it's the multiple. Earnings without an AI story get a value multiple, not a growth one. That's the whole trans-Atlantic valuation gap in a sentence. Strong cash flows, cheap stocks, no terminal-value dream. It's why the flows keep coming to US megacap even on days the chips break. And one geopolitical footnote with a commodities tail: a worsening Ebola outbreak in Congo is disrupting the US-backed critical-minerals talks — the ones meant to loosen China's grip on copper and cobalt. So the one lever the West has on China's mineral dominance just got harder to pull. China to close the block. China The China story ties directly into the memory crater. CXMT — China's DRAM champion — is running an $8.6 billion Shanghai IPO, and analysts are already calling it China Shock 3.0. Same playbook they ran in steel and EVs: scale hard at the low end, take share on price, then move up the stack at Samsung, Hynix, and Micron. Even the underwriting tells the story — 6 Chinese banks splitting $41 million in fees, reviving a domestic IPO machine that had gone quiet. So the same week the Korean memory names crater on valuation, the Chinese memory challenger raises a war chest. That's not a coincidence, that's the incumbents' whole bear case wearing a party hat. And it's not standalone. Xi outlines an AI-diplomacy vision at a Shanghai forum Friday, and Huawei is showcasing its most advanced AI computing cluster yet — Beijing's answer to being cut off from the US stack. A coordinated push: domestic memory, domestic compute, a domestic governance framework, all pointed at self-sufficiency. The investable read being that the AI trade is bifurcating into two stacks — and the incumbents' terminal value gets a China discount whether or not CXMT's yields are actually there yet. Exactly. The market prices the threat years before the wafers are competitive — same as it did with BYD, which is now taking on European supercars on their own turf, not just on price. That anticipation is the risk premium, and it just got repriced onto the memory names overnight. Though the decoupling cuts both ways — China's got its own talent bottleneck. It does, and it's a good check on the panic. Chinese drugmakers with global ambitions are struggling to recruit the internationally experienced staff they need to commercialize overseas — the same soft-power, human-capital gap that shows up in frontier AI. So it's self-sufficiency with an asterisk: they can build the fab, they can't yet import the org chart. That's the block. Onto the power desk. Energy / Data Centers / Utilities Segment two — energy, data centers, utilities. And Alex, the frame today isn't the chips, it's whether we can plug them in. That's the whole segment. Here's the twist the TSMC number exposes: silicon is no longer the binding constraint — electrons and siting are. And the US just built a new wall. New York's governor barred certain large-scale data centers for up to a year — an outright moratorium. Trump blasted it publicly and demanded a reversal, immediately. So we've moved past the interconnection queue as the constraint. Now it's political — a flat-out ban. When siting becomes a ballot-box fight, the queue stops being the ceiling; the permit does. And the physical grid is straining in real time to make the point. PJM — the largest US grid operator — issued a run of warnings Wednesday as heat spiked demand and transmission-line congestion drove wholesale spot prices up. That's the system telling you the margin is gone — not in a 2027 model, today, on a hot afternoon. And that congestion point is underrated. It's not just "not enough generation" — it's that the electrons can't physically move from where they're made to where the load is. Right, the wires are the bottleneck as much as the megawatts. You can have spare generation in one zone and a shortfall 200 miles away and no way to shuttle it — because the transformer and high-voltage line lead times run years, and the OEM backlog on large power transformers and gas turbines stretches toward the end of the decade. That's why the build keeps going behind-the-meter: hyperscalers signing dedicated on-site generation to skip the queue entirely. Which sets up the contrast that actually decides the AI race. Lay it out. Here's the strategic read. The US can now build the chips — TSMC's four new Arizona fabs prove it. What the US struggles to do is power and site them: the queue, the transformer backlog, and now moratoria. China has the opposite problem set — it's power-abundant. It's been adding generation at a pace the US structurally can't match, so its constraint isn't the electron, it's the leading-edge wafer. And Huawei's new cluster is Beijing saying "we're closing the wafer gap too." So the two superpowers are constrained on opposite ends of the same stack. The US is compute-rich and power-poor; China is power-rich and compute-catching-up. Whoever closes their gap first sets the pace. And that reframes every US energy trade. If the binding constraint is electrons and permits, value accrues to whoever controls firm power and interconnection rights — regulated utilities with rate base, IPPs with merchant upside into rising spot prices, gas-turbine OEMs with multi-year backlogs, and the behind-the-meter self-supply deals that route around the queue. And the commodity underneath all of it is copper. Copper's up 12.5% on the year, shadowing the hyperscaler stocks almost tick for tick — you can't build a substation, a transformer, or a campus without tonnes of it. And US industrial construction is up 18%, led specifically by suppliers of data-center equipment. Even the warehouse builders are back, stocking the gear for the buildout. The physical economy is repricing around this whether or not the chip stocks have a good week. So the tell isn't Nvidia's multiple — it's the copper price and the permit queue. And there's a water angle folded into the siting fight too. There is — evaporative cooling means millions of gallons a day per large campus, and it collides with exactly the hot, cheap-land geographies where the interconnect is easiest. So a campus needs three things at once: firm power, high-voltage lines, and water — and the map where all three overlap is small and shrinking. That's why you're seeing the nuclear-restart deals and the small-modular-reactor pre-orders, even though none of that delivers this decade — it's the only firm, water-light, carbon-light power on the board. So the near-term answer is still gas, and the long-term bet is nuclear, and neither closes the gap in the window that matters. That's the honest read. Gas bridges it, nuclear eventually backstops it, and in between you keep retiring coal online longer than anyone planned. The buildout is real; it's the timeline that's fictional. And that gap is exactly where the merchant power price lives — which is the trade. That's the whole segment. The bottleneck moved from the fab to the feeder line, and the second-order political fuse is still the ratepayer — the moment households see grid upgrades for hyperscaler load in their bills, moratoria like New York's stop being outliers. Philippines Segment three — the Philippines. Weather first, then the macro. The typhoon story eased. Inday — international name Bavi — weakened and pulled out of the Philippine area of responsibility. But it left the tap open: the enhanced southwest monsoon, the habagat, is dumping heavy rain and flooding across Northern Luzon and Metro Manila. So the acute threat's gone; the chronic one — waterlogged fields and disrupted logistics feeding the food-inflation print — is still running. And that lands straight on a central bank that's already boxed in. Where's the peso and where's the BSP? Peso's near 61.70, back toward its record low. And the important thing is why — it's not a policy failure, it's oil. The Hormuz premium widens the import bill and hits every energy-importing emerging-market currency at once; the peso's just the cleanest expression of it in the region. The BSP is already at 4.75% after June's second straight hike, and MUFG is now penciling a peak of 5.25% by year-end — another 50 basis points of tightening. So they're hiking into a currency problem that's really an oil problem, and today's oil headline is a US strike calendar. That's a brutal external position to manage. It's importing your monetary policy from someone else's war. And it compounds regionally — India's fuel-export tax hike tightens the diesel Manila buys, so the pass-through squeeze is coming from the supply side too, not just the currency. The BSP has essentially no room; every rate decision is hostage to the barrel. Any relief valve at all? The structural ones cushion it. Remittances — roughly a tenth of GDP — hold up household spending, and a weak peso actually flatters the converted value when the dollars come home. The BPO sector is the dollar earner that keeps the external accounts from tipping over. But those are shock-absorbers, not a fix — and the AI overhang we spent the whole show on is a genuine medium-term risk to the lower rungs of the outsourcing stack. So the same AI story that's roaring in the market is a slow-burn threat to a chunk of Philippine growth. That's the uncomfortable link. The thing lifting Nasdaq megacaps is the thing that could hollow out entry-level BPO seats in a few years. For now, growth's still holding up and the consumer's resilient — but the BSP's path only goes one way until the Hormuz premium comes out of crude. And the domestic politics of that squeeze — the wage side is heating up. It is. There's a minimum-wage push running alongside the inflation print, and that's the loop the BSP fears most — imported energy inflation feeding into wage demands feeding into services prices. Once it's in wages, it's sticky in a way an oil spike isn't. That's the difference between a headline the bank can look through and a core problem it has to lean against. And the flooding this week doesn't help — when the habagat waterlogs the food-supply chain, the food weight in the CPI basket does the rest. So weather is genuinely a monetary variable there. In the Philippines it's one of the biggest — the food share of the basket is large enough that a bad monsoon can move the whole print. Meteorology and monetary policy in the same sentence, which is not something you can say about many economies. Onward. Vocab. Vocab Of The Day Segment four — vocab of the day. Two Mandarin, then two Tagalog, each tied to today's show. Mandarin first — and we're doing this in Mandarin. 第一个词是"却"。 (Our first word is "què.") 今天的整个故事就是一个"却"字： 台积电业绩创纪录，股价却大跌。 (Today's whole story is the single word "què": TSMC's results hit a record, yet the stock plunged.) "却"—— 所以它表示转折，对不对？ ("Què" — so it marks a turn, a contrast, right?) 基本面很强，股价却下跌。 (The fundamentals are strong, yet the share price falls.) 对。 (Right.) 注意用法： "却"放在动词前面，不能放在句子开头。 (Note the usage: "què" goes right before the verb, never at the head of the sentence.) 我们说"股价却下跌"， 不说"却股价下跌"。 (We say "the share price yet falls," not "yet the share price falls.") 那"却"和"但是"有什么区别？ (Then what's the difference between "què" and "dànshì"?) "但是"放在句子开头，语气比较普通、比较直接。 ("Dànshì" sits at the front of the clause, plainer and more direct in tone.) "却"更书面、更委婉，藏在句子中间，转折的味道更细。 ("Què" is more written, more understated — tucked mid-sentence, its contrast is subtler.) 财经报道最爱用"却"。 (Financial reporting loves "què.") 懂了。 (Got it.) 再给我一个例子？ (Give me one more example?) 好。 (Sure.) 市场预期降息，美联储却按兵不动。 (The market expected a rate cut, yet the Fed held still.) 你看，前后一转，用"却"最自然。 (See — that pivot from expectation to reality, "què" carries it most naturally.) 完美。 (Perfect.) 第二个词？ (The second word?) 第二个词就在里面—— "预期"。 (The second word was just in there — "yù qī," expectations.) 台积电的利润超出预期。 (TSMC's profit exceeded expectations.) 但是市场对它的预期太高了。 (But the market's expectations of it were too high.) "超出预期"—— 我常听到。 ("Exceed expectations" — I hear that one a lot.) 还有"符合预期"、"低于预期"。 (Also "in line with expectations," "below expectations.") 正是。 (Exactly.) 这是标准的财经搭配。 (These are the standard finance collocations.) 注意"预期"和"希望"不一样： (Note "yù qī" is not "xī wàng":) "希望"是感情上的愿望， "预期"是理性的判断。 ("Xī wàng," hope, is an emotional wish; "yù qī" is a rational forecast.) 分析师有"预期"，不是"希望"。 (An analyst has "expectations," not "hopes.") 所以今天的市场就是—— 业绩超出预期，股价却下跌。 (So today's market is exactly this — earnings beat expectations, yet the stock falls.) 两个词一起用上了。 (Both words in one line.) 完美。 (Perfect.) 现在换成他加禄语。 (Now let's switch to Tagalog.) 第一个词： kakapusan. Ang unang salita ay "kakapusan" — ibig sabihin, kakulangan sa suplay. (The first word is "kakapusan" — it means a shortage of supply.) Sa Estados Unidos, may kakapusan sa kuryente para sa mga data center. (In the United States, there's a power shortage for the data centers.) "Kakapusan sa kuryente" — power shortage. Ano ang pagkakaiba nito sa "kakulangan"? (What's the difference between this and "kakulangan"?) Magandang tanong. (Good question.) Ang "kakulangan" ay mas malawak — pwedeng depekto, pagkukulang, o kawalan. ("Kakulangan" is broader — a defect, a failing, a lack.) Ang "kakapusan" ay tiyak: kulang ka sa isang mapagkukunan — tubig, kuryente, o pera. ("Kakapusan" is specific: you're short of a resource — water, power, or money.) Kaya sinasabi natin, kakapusan sa langis. (So we say, a shortage of oil.) At dahil sa langis, may kakapusan din ng dolyar ang Pilipinas. (And because of oil, the Philippines is also short of dollars.) Angkop na angkop sa balita ngayon. (It fits today's news perfectly.) Tama. (Right.) Ikalawang salita: "agam-agam." (Second word: "agam-agam.") Ibig sabihin, hindi mapakaling pag-aalinlangan — isang bahagyang takot sa kung ano ang mangyayari. (It means a restless misgiving — a slight dread about what's to come.) May agam-agam ang mga mamumuhunan tungkol sa AI. (Investors have misgivings about AI.) "Agam-agam" — parang "alinlangan"? (Like "alinlangan," hesitation?) Malapit, pero magkaiba.
